31. “Sabbamaññitasamugghātasappāyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, paṭipadaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamā ca sā, bhikkhave, sabbamaññitasamugghātasappāyā paṭipadā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhuṃ na maññati, cakkhusmiṃ na maññati, cakkhuto na maññati, cakkhuṃ meti na maññati. Rūpe na maññati…pe… cakkhuviññāṇaṃ na maññati, cakkhusamphassaṃ na maññati, yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi na maññati, tasmimpi na maññati, tatopi na maññati, taṃ meti na maññati. Yañhi, bhikkhave, maññati, yasmiṃ maññati, yato maññati, yaṃ meti maññati, tato taṃ hoti aññathā. Aññathābhāvī bhavasatto loko bhavamevābhinandati…pe… jivhaṃ na maññati, jivhāya na maññati, jivhāto na maññati, jivhā meti na maññati. Rase na maññati…pe… jivhāviññāṇaṃ na maññati, jivhāsamphassaṃ na maññati. Yampidaṃ jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ [P 4.0024] sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ [T 4.0029] vā tampi na maññati, tasmimpi na maññati, tatopi na maññati, taṃ meti na maññati. Yañhi, bhikkhave, maññati, yasmiṃ maññati, yato maññati, yaṃ meti maññati, tato taṃ hoti aññathā. Aññathābhāvī bhavasatto loko bhavamevābhinandati…pe… manaṃ na maññati, manasmiṃ na maññati, manato na maññati, mano meti na maññati. Dhamme na maññati…pe… manoviññāṇaṃ na maññati, manosamphassaṃ na maññati. Yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā [V 2.0022] uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi na maññati, tasmimpi na maññati, tatopi na maññati, taṃ meti na maññati. Yañhi, bhikkhave, maññati, yasmiṃ maññati, yato maññati, yaṃ meti maññati, tato taṃ hoti aññathā. Aññathābhāvī bhavasatto loko bhavamevābhinandati. Yāvatā, bhikkhave, khandhadhātuāyatanaṃ tampi na maññati, tasmimpi na maññati, tatopi na maññati, taṃ meti na maññati. So evaṃ amaññamāno na ca kiñci loke upādiyati. Anupādiyaṃ na paritassati. Aparitassaṃ paccattaññeva parinibbāyati. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti[M 2.0255]. Ayaṃ kho sā, bhikkhave, sabbamaññitasamugghātasappāyā paṭipadā”ti. Navamaṃ.

31. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the practice conducive to the uprooting of all conceiving. Listen to it. And what, bhikkhus, is that practice conducive to the uprooting of all conceiving? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu does not conceive the eye, does not conceive in the eye, does not conceive from the eye, does not conceive ‘the eye is mine.’ He does not conceive forms… he does not conceive eye-consciousness, he does not conceive eye-contact, and whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he does not conceive that, does not conceive in that, does not conceive from that, does not conceive ‘that is mine.’ For, bhikkhus, whatever one conceives, in whatever one conceives, from whatever one conceives, whatever one conceives as ‘mine’—from that it becomes otherwise. The world, which is subject to becoming otherwise and attached to existence, delights only in existence.… He does not conceive the tongue, he does not conceive in the tongue, he does not conceive from the tongue, he does not conceive ‘the tongue is mine.’ He does not conceive tastes… he does not conceive tongue-consciousness, he does not conceive tongue-contact. And whatever feeling arises with tongue-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he does not conceive that, does not conceive in that, does not conceive from that, he does not conceive ‘that is mine.’ For, bhikkhus, whatever one conceives, in whatever one conceives, from whatever one conceives, whatever one conceives as ‘mine’—from that it becomes otherwise. The world, which is subject to becoming otherwise and attached to existence, delights only in existence.… He does not conceive the mind, he does not conceive in the mind, he does not conceive from the mind, he does not conceive ‘the mind is mine.’ He does not conceive mental objects… he does not conceive mind-consciousness, he does not conceive mind-contact. And whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he does not conceive that, does not conceive in that, does not conceive from that, he does not conceive ‘that is mine.’ For, bhikkhus, whatever one conceives, in whatever one conceives, from whatever one conceives, whatever one conceives as ‘mine’—from that it becomes otherwise. The world, which is subject to becoming otherwise and attached to existence, delights only in existence. As far, bhikkhus, as the aggregates, elements, and sense bases extend, he does not conceive that, does not conceive in that, does not conceive from that, he does not conceive ‘that is mine.’ Not conceiving thus, he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not agitated. Being unagitated, he personally attains Parinibbāna. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ This, bhikkhus, is that practice conducive to the uprooting of all conceiving.”

10. Dutiyasamugghātasappāyasuttaṃ

10. The Second Discourse Conducive to Uprooting

32. “Sabbamaññitasamugghātasappāyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, paṭipadaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamā ca sā, bhikkhave, sabbamaññitasamugghātasappāyā [T 4.0030] paṭipadā?

32. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the practice conducive to the uprooting of all conceiving. Listen to it. And what, bhikkhus, is that practice conducive to the uprooting of all conceiving?

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, cakkhuṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“What do you think, bhikkhus, is the eye permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ, bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ[P 4.0025], bhante”.

“Suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti?

“But is it proper to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ bhante”.

“Indeed not, venerable sir.”

“Rūpā…pe… cakkhuviññāṇaṃ… cakkhusamphasso nicco vā anicco vā”ti?

“Are forms… eye-consciousness… eye-contact permanent or impermanent?”

“Anicco, bhante”…pe….

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”…

“Yampidaṃ [V 2.0023] cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“And whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—is that also permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ, bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“Suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti?

“But is it proper to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”…pe….

“Indeed not, venerable sir.”…

“Jivhā niccā vā aniccā vā”ti?

“Is the tongue permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccā bhante”…pe….

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”…

“Rasā… jivhāviññāṇaṃ… jivhāsamphasso…pe… yampidaṃ jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“Are tastes… tongue-consciousness… tongue-contact… and whatever feeling arises with tongue-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—is that also permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ, bhante”…pe… dhammā… manoviññāṇaṃ… manosamphasso nicco vā anicco vāti?

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”… “Are mental objects… mind-consciousness… mind-contact permanent or impermanent?”

“Anicco, bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“And whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—is that also permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ, bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ bhante”.

“Suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ [V 2.0024] panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ [T 4.0031] nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti?

“But is it proper to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Indeed not, venerable sir.”

“Evaṃ [P 4.0026] passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati, rūpesupi nibbindati, cakkhuviññāṇepi nibbindati, cakkhusamphassepi nibbindati. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tasmimpi nibbindati…pe… jivhāyapi nibbindati, rasesupi…pe… yampidaṃ jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tasmimpi nibbindati. Manasmimpi nibbindati, dhammesupi nibbindati, manoviññāṇepi nibbindati, manosamphassepi nibbindati. Yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti[M 2.0256]. Ayaṃ kho sā, bhikkhave, sabbamaññitasamugghātasappāyā paṭipadā”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, and disenchanted with eye-contact. Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he becomes disenchanted with that too. … He becomes disenchanted with the tongue, disenchanted with tastes… Whatever feeling arises dependent on tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he becomes disenchanted with that too. He becomes disenchanted with the mind, disenchanted with mental objects, disenchanted with mind-consciousness, and disenchanted with mind-contact. Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he becomes disenchanted with that too. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’ This, monks, is the practice suitable for the uprooting of all conceiving.” The Tenth.

Sabbavaggo tatiyo.

The Third Chapter on the All.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of this is:

Sabbañca dvepi pahānā, parijānāpare duve;

Ādittaṃ addhabhūtañca, sāruppā dve ca sappāyā;

Vaggo tena pavuccatīti.

The All, and two on Abandoning; two further on Full Understanding; The Burning, and Addhabhūta; one on Suitability, and two on Conduciveness; therefore it is called a chapter.

4. Jātidhammavaggo

4. 4. The Chapter on the Nature of Birth

1-10. Jātidhammādisuttadasakaṃ

1-10. The Ten Suttas on the Nature of Birth, etc.

33. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 4.0032][V 2.0025]. Tatra kho…pe… “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, jātidhammaṃ. Kiñca, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ jātidhammaṃ? Cakkhu, [P 4.0027] bhikkhave, jātidhammaṃ. Rūpā… cakkhuviññāṇaṃ… cakkhusamphasso jātidhammo. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi jātidhammaṃ…pe… jivhā… rasā… jivhāviññāṇaṃ… jivhāsamphasso… yampidaṃ jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi jātidhammaṃ. Kāyo…pe... mano jātidhammo, dhammā jātidhammā, manoviññāṇaṃ jātidhammaṃ, manosamphasso jātidhammo. Yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi jātidhammaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati, rūpesupi… cakkhuviññāṇepi… cakkhusamphassepi…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

33. At Sāvatthī. There… “Monks, the all is subject to birth. And what, monks, is the all that is subject to birth? The eye, monks, is subject to birth. Forms… eye-consciousness… eye-contact is subject to birth. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is subject to birth. … The tongue… tastes… tongue-consciousness… tongue-contact… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is subject to birth. The body… The mind is subject to birth, mental objects are subject to birth, mind-consciousness is subject to birth, mind-contact is subject to birth. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is subject to birth. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, with forms, with eye-consciousness, with eye-contact… and understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’” The First.

34. “Sabbaṃ[V 2.0026], bhikkhave, jarādhammaṃ…pe… saṃkhittaṃ. Dutiyaṃ.

34. “Monks, the all is subject to aging… (in brief). The Second.

35. “Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, byādhidhammaṃ…pe…. Tatiyaṃ.

35. “Monks, the all is subject to sickness… (in brief). The Third.

36. “Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, maraṇadhammaṃ…pe…. Catutthaṃ.

36. “Monks, the all is subject to death… (in brief). The Fourth.

37. “Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, sokadhammaṃ…pe…. Pañcamaṃ.

37. “Monks, the all is subject to sorrow… (in brief). The Fifth.

38. “Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, saṃkilesikadhammaṃ…pe…. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

38. “Monks, the all is subject to defilement… (in brief). The Sixth.

39. “Sabbaṃ[T 4.0033][M 2.0257][P 4.0028], bhikkhave, khayadhammaṃ…pe…. Sattamaṃ.

39. “Monks, the all is subject to destruction… (in brief). The Seventh.

40. “Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, vayadhammaṃ…pe…. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

40. “Monks, the all is subject to passing away… (in brief). The Eighth.

41. “Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, samudayadhammaṃ…pe…. Navamaṃ.

41. “Monks, the all is subject to arising… (in brief). The Ninth.

42. “Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, nirodhadhammaṃ…pe…. Dasamaṃ.

42. “Monks, the all is subject to cessation… (in brief). The Tenth.

Jātidhammavaggo catuttho.

The Fourth Chapter on the Nature of Birth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of this is:

Jātijarābyādhimaraṇaṃ, soko ca saṃkilesikaṃ;

Khayavayasamudayaṃ, nirodhadhammena te dasāti.

Birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and defilement; destruction, passing away, arising, and with the nature of cessation, these are the ten.

5. Sabbaaniccavaggo

5. 5. The Chapter on the All as Impermanent

1-9. Aniccādisuttanavakaṃ

1-9. The Nine Suttas on Impermanence, etc.

43. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 4.0034][V 2.0027]. Tatra kho…pe… “sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ. Kiñca, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ aniccaṃ? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, rūpā aniccā, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ, cakkhusamphasso anicco. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccaṃ…pe… jivhā aniccā, rasā aniccā, jivhāviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ, jivhāsamphasso anicco. Yampidaṃ jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccaṃ. Kāyo anicco…pe… mano anicco, dhammā aniccā, manoviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ, manosamphasso anicco. Yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati, rūpesupi nibbindati, cakkhuviññāṇepi nibbindati, cakkhusamphassepi nibbindati. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tasmimpi nibbindati…pe… manasmimpi nibbindati, dhammesupi nibbindati, manoviññāṇepi nibbindati, manosamphassepi nibbindati, yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti [M 2.0258] ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

43. At Sāvatthī. There... “Monks, the all is impermanent. And what, monks, is the all that is impermanent? The eye, monks, is impermanent. Forms are impermanent. Eye-consciousness is impermanent. Eye-contact is impermanent. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent. ... The tongue is impermanent. Tastes are impermanent. Tongue-consciousness is impermanent. Tongue-contact is impermanent. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent. The body is impermanent... The mind is impermanent. Mental objects are impermanent. Mind-consciousness is impermanent. Mind-contact is impermanent. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent. Seeing thus, monks, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, disenchanted with eye-contact. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he becomes disenchanted with that too. ... He becomes disenchanted with the mind, disenchanted with mental objects, disenchanted with mind-consciousness, disenchanted with mind-contact. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—he becomes disenchanted with that too. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When he is liberated, the knowledge arises, ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’” The First.

44. “Sabbaṃ[V 2.0028], bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ…pe…. Dutiyaṃ.

44. “Monks, the all is suffering… (in brief). The Second.

45. “Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, anattā…pe…. Tatiyaṃ.

45. “Monks, the all is not-self… (in brief). The Third.

46. “Sabbaṃ[P 4.0029], bhikkhave, abhiññeyyaṃ…pe…[V 2.0029]. Catutthaṃ.

46. “Monks, the all is to be directly known… (in brief). The Fourth.

47. “Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, pariññeyyaṃ…pe…. Pañcamaṃ.

47. “Monks, the all is to be fully comprehended… (in brief). The Fifth.

48. “Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, pahātabbaṃ…pe…. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

48. “Bhikkhus, the all is to be abandoned…” The sixth.

49. “Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, sacchikātabbaṃ…pe…[V 2.0030]. Sattamaṃ.

49. “Bhikkhus, the all is to be realized…” The seventh.

50. “Sabbaṃ, bhikkhave, abhiññāpariññeyyaṃ…pe…. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

50. “Bhikkhus, the all is to be fully comprehended with direct knowledge…” The eighth.

51. “Sabbaṃ[T 4.0035], bhikkhave, upaddutaṃ…pe…. Navamaṃ.

51. “Bhikkhus, the all is afflicted…” The ninth.

10. Upassaṭṭhasuttaṃ

10. The Sutta on Being Beset

52. “Sabbaṃ[V 2.0031], bhikkhave, upassaṭṭhaṃ upasaṭṭhaṃ (ka.). Kiñca, bhikkhave, sabbaṃ upassaṭṭhaṃ? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, upassaṭṭhaṃ, rūpā upassaṭṭhā, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ upassaṭṭhaṃ, cakkhusamphasso upassaṭṭho. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi upassaṭṭhaṃ…pe… jivhā upassaṭṭhā, rasā upassaṭṭhā, jivhāviññāṇaṃ upassaṭṭhaṃ, jivhāsamphasso upassaṭṭho. Yampidaṃ jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi upassaṭṭhaṃ. Kāyo upassaṭṭho… mano upassaṭṭho, dhammā upassaṭṭhā, manoviññāṇaṃ upassaṭṭhaṃ, manosamphasso upassaṭṭho. Yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ [P 4.0030] vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi upassaṭṭhaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati, rūpesupi nibbindati, cakkhuviññāṇepi nibbindati, cakkhusamphassepi nibbindati. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tasmimpi nibbindati…pe… manasmimpi nibbindati, dhammesupi nibbindati, manoviññāṇepi nibbindati, manosamphassepi nibbindati. Yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti[M 2.0259]. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

52. “Bhikkhus, the all is beset. And what, bhikkhus, is the all that is beset? The eye, bhikkhus, is beset; forms are beset; eye-consciousness is beset; eye-contact is beset. Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is beset… The tongue is beset; flavors are beset; tongue-consciousness is beset; tongue-contact is beset. Whatever feeling arises dependent on tongue-contact—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is beset. The body is beset… The mind is beset; mental objects are beset; mind-consciousness is beset; mind-contact is beset. Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is beset. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, a learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, and disenchanted with eye-contact. Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—with that too he becomes disenchanted… He becomes disenchanted with the mind, disenchanted with mental objects, disenchanted with mind-consciousness, and disenchanted with mind-contact. Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—with that too he becomes disenchanted. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, there is the knowledge: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’” The Tenth.

Sabbaaniccavaggo pañcamo.

The Fifth Chapter on the All and Impermanence.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse for this chapter:

Aniccaṃ [V 2.0032] dukkhaṃ anattā, abhiññeyyaṃ pariññeyyaṃ;

Pahātabbaṃ sacchikātabbaṃ, abhiññeyyapariññeyyaṃ abhiññeyyaṃ pariññeyyaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ.), abhiññātaṃ pariññeyyaṃ (pī. ka.);

Upaddutaṃ upassaṭṭhaṃ, vaggo tena pavuccatīti.

“Impermanent, Suffering, and Not-self; To Be Directly Known, and To Be Fully Understood; To Be Abandoned, and To Be Realized; To Be Directly Known and Fully Understood; Afflicted, and Beset. By these, it is called a chapter.”

Saḷāyatanavagge paṭhamapaṇṇāsako samatto.

The first fifty discourses in the Book of the Six Sense Bases is completed.

Tassa vagguddānaṃ –

The summary verse for its chapters:

Aniccavaggaṃ [T 4.0036] yamakaṃ, sabbaṃ vaggaṃ jātidhammaṃ;

Aniccavaggena paññāsaṃ, pañcamo tena pavuccatīti.

“The Chapter on Impermanence, the Chapter of Pairs, the Chapter on the All, the Chapter on the Nature of Birth; with the Chapter on Impermanence, there are fifty. Therefore, it is called the fifth.”

6. Avijjāvaggo

6. The Chapter on Ignorance

1. Avijjāpahānasuttaṃ

1. The Sutta on the Abandonment of Ignorance

53. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 4.0037]. Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ [P 4.0031] nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “kathaṃ nu kho, bhante, jānato kathaṃ passato avijjā pahīyati, vijjā uppajjatī”ti?

53. At Sāvatthī. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, for one who knows in what way, for one who sees in what way, is ignorance abandoned and knowledge arises?”

“Cakkhuṃ kho, bhikkhu, aniccato jānato passato avijjā pahīyati, vijjā uppajjati. Rūpe aniccato jānato passato avijjā pahīyati, vijjā uppajjati. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ… cakkhusamphassaṃ… yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccato jānato passato avijjā pahīyati, vijjā uppajjati. Sotaṃ… ghānaṃ… jivhaṃ… kāyaṃ… manaṃ aniccato jānato passato avijjā pahīyati, vijjā uppajjati. Dhamme [M 2.0260]… manoviññāṇaṃ… manosamphassaṃ… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā [V 2.0033] uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccato jānato passato avijjā pahīyati, vijjā uppajjati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, jānato evaṃ passato avijjā pahīyati, vijjā uppajjatī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“Bhikkhu, for one who knows and sees the eye as impermanent, ignorance is abandoned and knowledge arises. For one who knows and sees forms as impermanent, ignorance is abandoned and knowledge arises. For one who knows and sees eye-consciousness… eye-contact… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as impermanent, for him, too, ignorance is abandoned and knowledge arises. For one who knows and sees the ear… the nose… the tongue… the body… the mind as impermanent, ignorance is abandoned and knowledge arises. For one who knows and sees mental objects… mind-consciousness… mind-contact… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as impermanent, for him, too, ignorance is abandoned and knowledge arises. In this way, bhikkhu, for one who knows thus and sees thus, ignorance is abandoned and knowledge arises.” The first.

2. Saṃyojanapahānasuttaṃ

2. The Sutta on the Abandonment of Fetters

54. “Kathaṃ nu kho, bhante, jānato, kathaṃ passato, saṃyojanā pahīyantī”ti? “Cakkhuṃ kho, bhikkhu, aniccato jānato passato saṃyojanā pahīyanti. Rūpe… [T 4.0038] cakkhuviññāṇaṃ… cakkhusamphassaṃ… yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccato jānato passato saṃyojanā pahīyanti. Sotaṃ… ghānaṃ… jivhaṃ… kāyaṃ… manaṃ… dhamme… manoviññāṇaṃ… manosamphassaṃ… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccato jānato passato saṃyojanā pahīyanti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, jānato evaṃ passato saṃyojanā pahīyantī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

54. “Venerable Sir, for one who knows in what way, for one who sees in what way, are the fetters abandoned?” “Bhikkhu, for one who knows and sees the eye as impermanent, the fetters are abandoned. For one who knows and sees forms… eye-consciousness… eye-contact… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as impermanent, for him, too, the fetters are abandoned. For one who knows and sees the ear… the nose… the tongue… the body… the mind… mental objects… mind-consciousness… mind-contact… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—as impermanent, for him, too, the fetters are abandoned. In this way, bhikkhu, for one who knows thus and sees thus, the fetters are abandoned.” The second.

3. Saṃyojanasamugghātasuttaṃ

3. The Sutta on the Eradication of Fetters

55. “Kathaṃ nu kho, bhante, jānato, kathaṃ passato saṃyojanā samugghātaṃ gacchantī”ti? “Cakkhuṃ kho, bhikkhu, anattato jānato passato saṃyojanā [P 4.0032] samugghātaṃ gacchanti. Rūpe anattato… cakkhuviññāṇaṃ… cakkhusamphassaṃ… yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi anattato jānato passato saṃyojanā samugghātaṃ gacchanti. Sotaṃ… ghānaṃ… jivhaṃ… kāyaṃ… manaṃ… dhamme… manoviññāṇaṃ… manosamphassaṃ… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi anattato jānato passato saṃyojanā samugghātaṃ gacchanti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, jānato evaṃ passato saṃyojanā samugghātaṃ gacchantī”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

55. “Venerable sir, for one who knows how, and sees how, are the fetters eradicated?” “Bhikkhu, for one who knows and sees the eye as not-self, the fetters are eradicated. For one who knows and sees forms as not-self… eye-consciousness… eye-contact… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—be it pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—for one who knows and sees that too as not-self, the fetters are eradicated. For one who knows and sees the ear… the nose… the tongue… the body… the mind… mental objects… mind-consciousness… mind-contact… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—be it pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—for one who knows and sees that too as not-self, the fetters are eradicated. It is in this way, bhikkhu, for one who knows thus and sees thus, that the fetters are eradicated.”

4. Āsavapahānasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on the Abandoning of Taints

56. “Kathaṃ [V 2.0034] nu kho, bhante, jānato, kathaṃ passato āsavā pahīyantī”ti…pe…. Catutthaṃ.

56. “Venerable sir, for one who knows how, and sees how, are the taints abandoned?”…

5. Āsavasamugghātasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on the Eradication of Taints

57. “Kathaṃ [M 2.0261] nu kho, bhante, jānato, kathaṃ passato āsavā samugghātaṃ gacchantī”ti…pe…[V 2.0035]. Pañcamaṃ.

57. “Venerable sir, for one who knows how, and sees how, are the taints eradicated?”…

6. Anusayapahānasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on the Abandoning of Underlying Tendencies

58. “Kathaṃ nu kho…pe… [T 4.0039] anusayā pahīyantī”ti…pe…. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

58. “Venerable sir, for one who knows how… are the underlying tendencies abandoned?”…

7. Anusayasamugghātasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on the Eradication of Underlying Tendencies

59. “Kathaṃ nu kho…pe… anusayā samugghātaṃ gacchantī”ti? “Cakkhuṃ kho, bhikkhu, anattato jānato passato anusayā samugghātaṃ gacchanti…pe… sotaṃ… ghānaṃ… jivhaṃ… kāyaṃ… manaṃ… dhamme… manoviññāṇaṃ… manosamphassaṃ… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi anattato jānato passato anusayā samugghātaṃ gacchanti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, jānato evaṃ passato anusayā samugghātaṃ gacchantī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

59. “Venerable sir, for one who knows how… are the underlying tendencies eradicated?” “Bhikkhu, for one who knows and sees the eye as not-self, the underlying tendencies are eradicated… the ear… the nose… the tongue… the body… the mind… mental objects… mind-consciousness… mind-contact… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—be it pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—for one who knows and sees that too as not-self, the underlying tendencies are eradicated. It is in this way, bhikkhu, for one who knows thus and sees thus, that the underlying tendencies are eradicated.”

8. Sabbupādānapariññāsuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on the Full Understanding of All Clinging

60. “Sabbupādānapariññāya [V 2.0036] vo, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sabbupādānapariññāya dhammo? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā. Evaṃ passaṃ[P 4.0033], bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati, rūpesupi nibbindati, cakkhuviññāṇepi nibbindati, cakkhusamphassepi nibbindati, vedanāyapi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimokkhā vimokkhaṃ (ka.), vimokkha (syā. kaṃ.) ‘pariññātaṃ me upādāna’nti pajānāti. Sotañca paṭicca sadde ca uppajjati… ghānañca paṭicca gandhe ca… jivhañca paṭicca rase ca… kāyañca paṭicca phoṭṭhabbe ca… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako manasmimpi nibbindati[T 4.0040], dhammesupi nibbindati, manoviññāṇepi nibbindati, manosamphassepi nibbindati, vedanāyapi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimokkhā ‘pariññātaṃ me upādāna’nti [M 2.0262] pajānāti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, sabbupādānapariññāya dhammo”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

60. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma for the full understanding of all clinging. Listen to it. And what, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma for the full understanding of all clinging? Conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, an instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, disenchanted with eye-contact, and disenchanted with feeling. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. Upon liberation, he knows: ‘My clinging has been fully understood.’ Conditioned by the ear and sounds… conditioned by the nose and odors… conditioned by the tongue and tastes… conditioned by the body and tangibles… conditioned by the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, an instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the mind, disenchanted with mental objects, disenchanted with mind-consciousness, disenchanted with mind-contact, and disenchanted with feeling. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. Upon liberation, he knows: ‘My clinging has been fully understood.’ This, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma for the full understanding of all clinging.”

9. Paṭhamasabbupādānapariyādānasuttaṃ

9. The First Discourse on the Complete Exhaustion of All Clinging

61. “Sabbupādānapariyādānāya vo, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sabbupādānapariyādānāya dhammo? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati, rūpesupi nibbindati, cakkhuviññāṇepi nibbindati, cakkhusamphassepi nibbindati, vedanāyapi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimokkhā ‘pariyādinnaṃ sabbatthapi evameva dissati dantaja-nakāreneva me upādāna’nti pajānāti…pe… [V 2.0037] jivhañca paṭicca rase ca uppajjati jivhāviññāṇaṃ…pe… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako manasmimpi nibbindati, dhammesupi nibbindati, manoviññāṇepi nibbindati [P 4.0034] manosamphassepi nibbindati, vedanāyapi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimokkhā ‘pariyādinnaṃ me upādāna’nti pajānāti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, sabbupādānapariyādānāya dhammo”ti. Navamaṃ.

61. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma for the complete exhaustion of all clinging. Listen to it. And what, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma for the complete exhaustion of all clinging? Conditioned by the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, an instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, disenchanted with eye-contact, and disenchanted with feeling. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. Upon liberation, he knows: ‘My clinging has been completely exhausted.’… Conditioned by the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises… Conditioned by the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, an instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the mind, disenchanted with mental objects, disenchanted with mind-consciousness, disenchanted with mind-contact, and disenchanted with feeling. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate; through dispassion, he is liberated. Upon liberation, he knows: ‘My clinging has been completely exhausted.’ This, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma for the complete exhaustion of all clinging.”

10. Dutiyasabbupādānapariyādānasuttaṃ

10. The Second Discourse on the Complete Exhaustion of All Clinging

62. “Sabbupādānapariyādānāya vo, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha[T 4.0041]. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sabbupādānapariyādānāya dhammo”?

62. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the Dhamma for the complete exhaustion of all clinging. Listen to it. And what, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma for the complete exhaustion of all clinging?”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, cakkhu niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“What do you think, bhikkhus, is the eye permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ, bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“Suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti?

“But is it fitting to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Rūpā…pe… cakkhuviññāṇaṃ niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“Forms… eye-consciousness—is it permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ, bhante”…pe….

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”…

“Cakkhusamphasso [V 2.0038] nicco vā anicco vā”ti?

“Is eye-contact permanent or impermanent?”

“Anicco, bhante”…pe….

“Impermanent, venerable sir.” …

“Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“And whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—is that also permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ, bhante”…pe….

“Impermanent, venerable sir.” …

“Sotaṃ… ghānaṃ… jivhā… kāyo… mano… dhammā… manoviññāṇaṃ… manosamphasso… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā, tampi niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“The ear … the nose … the tongue … the body … the mind … mental phenomena … mind-consciousness … mind-contact … and whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—is that also permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ[M 2.0263], bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“Suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti?

“But is it fitting to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“No, venerable sir.”

“Evaṃ [P 4.0035] passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati, rūpesupi nibbindati, cakkhuviññāṇepi nibbindati, cakkhusamphassepi nibbindati. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tasmimpi nibbindati…pe… jivhāyapi nibbindati, rasesupi nibbindati, jivhāviññāṇepi [T 4.0042] nibbindati, jivhāsamphassepi nibbindati, yampidaṃ jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati…pe… manasmimpi nibbindati, dhammesupi nibbindati, manoviññāṇepi nibbindati, manosamphassepi nibbindati. Yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimuttasmiṃ [V 2.0039] vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, sabbupādānapariyādānāya dhammo”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“Seeing thus, monks, a well-instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, disenchanted with eye-contact, and also with whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant… He becomes disenchanted with the tongue, disenchanted with flavors, disenchanted with tongue-consciousness, disenchanted with tongue-contact, and also with whatever feeling arises with tongue-contact as condition… He becomes disenchanted with the mind, disenchanted with mental phenomena, disenchanted with mind-consciousness, disenchanted with mind-contact, and also with whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When he is liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’ This, monks, is the Dhamma for the complete exhaustion of all clinging.” The tenth.

Avijjāvaggo chaṭṭho.

The Chapter on Ignorance, the Sixth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Avijjā saṃyojanā dve, āsavena duve vuttā;

Anusayā apare dve, pariññā dve pariyādinnaṃ;

Vaggo tena pavuccatīti.

Ignorance and Fetters are two; two are stated on Taints; two others on Latent Tendencies; two on Full Comprehension, and Exhaustion. By these, the chapter is proclaimed.

7. Migajālavaggo

7. The Chapter on Migajāla

1. Paṭhamamigajālasuttaṃ

1. The First Discourse on Migajāla

63. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 4.0043]. Atha kho āyasmā migajālo yena bhagavā…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā migajālo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “‘ekavihārī, ekavihārī’ti, bhante, vuccati. Kittāvatā [P 4.0036] nu kho, bhante, ekavihārī hoti, kittāvatā ca pana sadutiyavihārī hotī”ti?

63. At Sāvatthī. Then the Venerable Migajāla approached the Blessed One… and sat down to one side. Having sat down to one side, the Venerable Migajāla said to the Blessed One: “‘One who dwells alone, one who dwells alone,’ it is said, venerable sir. To what extent, venerable sir, is one a solitary dweller, and to what extent is one a dweller with a companion?”

“Santi kho, migajāla, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya [M 2.0264] tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ abhinandato abhivadato ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato uppajjati nandī nandi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). Nandiyā sati sārāgo hoti; sārāge sati saṃyogo hoti. Nandisaṃyojanasaṃyutto kho, migajāla, bhikkhu sadutiyavihārīti vuccati. Santi…pe… santi kho, migajāla, jivhāviññeyyā rasā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ abhinandato abhivadato ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato uppajjati [V 2.0040] nandī. Nandiyā sati sārāgo hoti; sārāge sati saṃyogo hoti. Nandisaṃyojanasaṃyutto kho, migajāla, bhikkhu sadutiyavihārīti vuccati. Evaṃvihārī ca, migajāla, bhikkhu kiñcāpi araññavanapatthāni pantāni senāsanāni paṭisevati [T 4.0044] appasaddāni appanigghosāni vijanavātāni manussarāhasseyyakāni manussarāhaseyyakāni (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) paṭisallānasāruppāni; atha kho sadutiyavihārīti vuccati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Taṇhā hissa dutiyā, sāssa appahīnā. Tasmā sadutiyavihārī”ti vuccati.

“Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, agreeable, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains engrossed in them, delight arises in him. When there is delight, there is passion; when there is passion, there is yoking. A bhikkhu yoked by the fetter of delight, Migajāla, is called one who dwells with a companion. … There are, Migajāla, flavors cognizable by the tongue—desirable, agreeable, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains engrossed in them, delight arises in him. When there is delight, there is passion; when there is passion, there is yoking. A bhikkhu yoked by the fetter of delight, Migajāla, is called one who dwells with a companion. Even if such a bhikkhu, Migajāla, resorts to remote lodgings in the forest and woodland—with little sound and little noise, free from the bustle of people, suitable for privacy, and fit for solitary retreat—he is still called one who dwells with a companion. For what reason? Because craving is his companion, and it has not been abandoned by him. Therefore, he is called one who dwells with a companion.”

“Santi ca kho, migajāla, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ anabhinandato anabhivadato anajjhosāya tiṭṭhato nandī nirujjhati. Nandiyā asati sārāgo na hoti; sārāge asati saṃyogo [P 4.0037] na hoti. Nandisaṃyojanavisaṃyutto kho, migajāla, bhikkhu ekavihārīti vuccati…pe… santi ca kho, migajāla, jivhāviññeyyā rasā…pe… santi ca kho, migajāla, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ anabhinandato anabhivadato anajjhosāya tiṭṭhato nandī nirujjhati. Nandiyā asati sārāgo na hoti; sārāge asati saṃyogo na hoti. Nandisaṃyojanavippayutto kho, migajāla, bhikkhu ekavihārīti vuccati. Evaṃvihārī ca, migajāla, bhikkhu kiñcāpi gāmante viharati ākiṇṇo bhikkhūhi bhikkhunīhi upāsakehi upāsikāhi rājūhi rājamahāmattehi titthiyehi titthiyasāvakehi[T 4.0045]. Atha kho ekavihārīti vuccati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Taṇhā hissa dutiyā, sāssa pahīnā. Tasmā ekavihārīti vuccatī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“There are, Migajāla, forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, agreeable, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain engrossed in them, then for him who does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain engrossed in them, delight ceases. When delight is absent, there is no passion; when passion is absent, there is no yoking. A bhikkhu disjoined from the fetter of delight, Migajāla, is called a solitary dweller. … There are, Migajāla, flavors cognizable by the tongue… There are, Migajāla, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind—desirable, agreeable, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain engrossed in them, then for him who does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain engrossed in them, delight ceases. When delight is absent, there is no passion; when passion is absent, there is no yoking. A bhikkhu disjoined from the fetter of delight, Migajāla, is called a solitary dweller. Even if such a bhikkhu, Migajāla, dwells near a village, crowded with bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, male and female lay followers, kings, royal ministers, sectarians, and their disciples, he is still called a solitary dweller. For what reason? Because craving, his companion, has been abandoned by him. Therefore, he is called a solitary dweller.” The First.

2. Dutiyamigajālasuttaṃ

2. The Second Discourse on Migajāla.

64. Atha [M 2.0265] kho āyasmā migajālo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā migajālo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetu, yamahaṃ bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto vihareyya”nti.

64. Then the Venerable Migajāla approached the Blessed One... and so on... Seated to one side, the Venerable Migajāla said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.”

“Santi [V 2.0041] kho, migajāla, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ abhinandato abhivadato ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato uppajjati nandī. Nandisamudayā dukkhasamudayo, migajālāti vadāmi…pe… santi ca kho, migajāla, jivhāviññeyyā rasā…pe… santi ca kho, migajāla, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ abhinandato abhivadato ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato uppajjati nandī[P 4.0038]. Nandisamudayā dukkhasamudayo, migajālāti vadāmi.

“Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, delightful, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and arousing of passion. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains clinging to them, then for him who delights in them, welcomes them, and remains clinging to them, delight arises. From the arising of delight, there is the arising of suffering, I say, Migajāla... and so on... There are tastes cognizable by the tongue... and so on... There are mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, agreeable, delightful, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and arousing of passion. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains clinging to them, then for him who delights in them, welcomes them, and remains clinging to them, delight arises. From the arising of delight, there is the arising of suffering, I say, Migajāla.”

“Santi ca kho, migajāla, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ anabhinandato anabhivadato anajjhosāya [T 4.0046] tiṭṭhato nandī nirujjhati. Nandinirodhā dukkhanirodho, migajālāti vadāmi…pe… santi ca kho, migajāla, jivhāviññeyyā rasā iṭṭhā kantā…pe… santi ca kho, migajāla, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ anabhinandato anabhivadato anajjhosāya tiṭṭhato nandī nirujjhati. Nandinirodhā dukkhanirodho, migajālāti vadāmī”ti.

“And Migajāla, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, delightful, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and arousing of passion. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them, then for him who does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them, delight ceases. From the cessation of delight, there is the cessation of suffering, I say, Migajāla... and so on... There are tastes cognizable by the tongue that are desirable... and so on... And Migajāla, there are mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, agreeable, delightful, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and arousing of passion. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them, then for him who does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain clinging to them, delight ceases. From the cessation of delight, there is the cessation of suffering, I say.”

Atha kho āyasmā migajālo bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Atha kho āyasmā migajālo eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto viharato nacirasseva – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ – brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva [M 2.0266] dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsi. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti abbhaññāsi. Aññataro ca panāyasmā migajālo arahataṃ ahosīti. Dutiyaṃ.

Then the Venerable Migajāla, having delighted in and rejoiced at the Blessed One’s statement, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him clockwise, and departed. Then, while dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Migajāla, before long, realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life that unsurpassed consummation of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness, and having attained it, he dwelt therein. He understood: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’ And the Venerable Migajāla became one of the Arahants. The second.

3. Paṭhamasamiddhimārapañhāsuttaṃ

3. The First Discourse on Samiddhi’s Question about Māra

65. Ekaṃ [V 2.0042] samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Atha kho āyasmā samiddhi yena bhagavā…pe… bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “‘māro, māro’ti, bhante, vuccati. Kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, māro vā assa mārapaññatti vā”ti?

65. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrel Sanctuary. Then the Venerable Samiddhi approached the Blessed One… and so on… and said this to the Blessed One: “‘Māra, Māra,’ venerable sir, it is said. To what extent, venerable sir, is there Māra, or the designation ‘Māra’?”

“Yattha kho, samiddhi, atthi [T 4.0047] cakkhu, atthi rūpā, atthi cakkhuviññāṇaṃ[P 4.0039], atthi cakkhuviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā, atthi tattha māro vā mārapaññatti vā. Atthi sotaṃ, atthi saddā, atthi sotaviññāṇaṃ, atthi sotaviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā, atthi tattha māro vā mārapaññatti vā. Atthi ghānaṃ, atthi gandhā, atthi ghānaviññāṇaṃ, atthi ghānaviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā, atthi tattha māro vā mārapaññatti vā. Atthi jivhā, atthi rasā, atthi jivhāviññāṇaṃ, atthi jivhāviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā, atthi tattha māro vā mārapaññatti vā. Atthi kāyo, atthi phoṭṭhabbā, atthi kāyaviññāṇaṃ, atthi kāyaviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā, atthi tattha māro vā mārapaññatti vā. Atthi mano, atthi dhammā, atthi manoviññāṇaṃ, atthi manoviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā, atthi tattha māro vā mārapaññatti vā.

“Samiddhi, where there is the eye, there are forms, there is eye-consciousness, and there are phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness, there, there is Māra or the designation ‘Māra’. Where there is the ear, there are sounds, there is ear-consciousness, and there are phenomena cognizable by ear-consciousness, there, there is Māra or the designation ‘Māra’. Where there is the nose, there are odors, there is nose-consciousness, and there are phenomena cognizable by nose-consciousness, there, there is Māra or the designation ‘Māra’. Where there is the tongue, there are tastes, there is tongue-consciousness, and there are phenomena cognizable by tongue-consciousness, there, there is Māra or the designation ‘Māra’. Where there is the body, there are tangibles, there is body-consciousness, and there are phenomena cognizable by body-consciousness, there, there is Māra or the designation ‘Māra’. Where there is the mind, there are mental objects, there is mind-consciousness, and there are phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness, there, there is Māra or the designation ‘Māra’.”

“Yattha ca kho, samiddhi, natthi cakkhu, natthi rūpā, natthi cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, natthi cakkhuviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā, natthi tattha māro vā mārapaññatti vā. Natthi sotaṃ…pe… natthi ghānaṃ…pe… natthi jivhā, natthi rasā, natthi jivhāviññāṇaṃ, natthi jivhāviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā, natthi tattha māro vā mārapaññatti vā. Natthi kāyo…pe…. Natthi mano, natthi dhammā, natthi manoviññāṇaṃ, natthi manoviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā, natthi tattha māro vā mārapaññatti vā”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

“But where, Samiddhi, there is no eye, no forms, no eye-consciousness, and no phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness, there, there is no Māra or the designation ‘Māra’. Where there is no ear, no sounds, no ear-consciousness, and no phenomena cognizable by ear-consciousness, there, there is no Māra or the designation ‘Māra’. Where there is no nose, no odors, no nose-consciousness, and no phenomena cognizable by nose-consciousness, there, there is no Māra or the designation ‘Māra’. Where there is no tongue, no tastes, no tongue-consciousness, and no phenomena cognizable by tongue-consciousness, there, there is no Māra or the designation ‘Māra’. Where there is no body, no tangibles, no body-consciousness, and no phenomena cognizable by body-consciousness, there, there is no Māra or the designation ‘Māra’. Where there is no mind, no mental objects, no mind-consciousness, and no phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness, there, there is no Māra or the designation ‘Māra’.” Third.

4. Samiddhisattapañhāsuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on Samiddhi’s Question about a Being

66. “‘Satto[T 4.0048], satto’ti, bhante, vuccati. Kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, satto vā assa sattapaññatti vā”ti…pe…. Catutthaṃ.

66. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘a being, a being.’ To what extent, venerable sir, might there be a being or the designation ‘a being’?”… and so on… The Fourth.

5. Samiddhidukkhapañhāsuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Samiddhi’s Question about Suffering

67. “‘Dukkhaṃ[M 2.0267][V 2.0043], dukkha’nti, bhante, vuccati. Kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, dukkhaṃ vā assa dukkhapaññatti vā”ti…pe…. Pañcamaṃ.

67. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘suffering, suffering.’ To what extent, venerable sir, might there be suffering or the designation ‘suffering’?”… and so on… The Fifth.

6. Samiddhilokapañhāsuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Samiddhi’s Question about the World

68. “‘Loko, loko’ti, bhante, vuccati. Kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, loko vā assa lokapaññatti vā”ti? Yattha kho, samiddhi, atthi cakkhu, atthi rūpā, atthi cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, atthi cakkhuviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā, atthi tattha loko vā lokapaññatti vāti…pe… atthi jivhā…pe… atthi [P 4.0040] mano, atthi dhammā, atthi manoviññāṇaṃ, atthi manoviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā, atthi tattha loko vā lokapaññatti vā.

68. “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘the world, the world.’ To what extent, venerable sir, might there be a world or the designation ‘world’?” “Samiddhi, where there is the eye, there are forms, there is eye-consciousness, there are phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness—there, there is a world or the designation ‘world.’ … Where there is the tongue … Where there is the mind, there are mental objects, there is mind-consciousness, there are phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness—there, there is a world or the designation ‘world.’”

“Yattha ca kho, samiddhi, natthi cakkhu, natthi rūpā, natthi cakkhuviññāṇaṃ, natthi cakkhuviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā, natthi tattha loko vā lokapaññatti vā…pe… natthi jivhā…pe… natthi mano, natthi dhammā, natthi manoviññāṇaṃ, natthi manoviññāṇaviññātabbā dhammā, natthi tattha loko vā lokapaññatti vā”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“And Samiddhi, where there is no eye, no forms, no eye-consciousness, no phenomena cognizable by eye-consciousness—there, there is no world or the designation ‘world.’ … Where there is no tongue … Where there is no mind, no mental objects, no mind-consciousness, no phenomena cognizable by mind-consciousness—there, there is no world or the designation ‘world.’” The Sixth.

7. Upasenaāsīvisasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on Upasena and the Venomous Snake

69. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā ca sāriputto āyasmā ca upaseno rājagahe viharanti sītavane sappasoṇḍikapabbhāre. Tena kho pana samayena āyasmato upasenassa kāye āsīviso patito [T 4.0049] hoti. Atha kho āyasmā upaseno bhikkhū āmantesi – “etha me, āvuso, imaṃ kāyaṃ mañcakaṃ āropetvā bahiddhā nīharatha. Purāyaṃ kāyo idheva vikirati; seyyathāpi bhusamuṭṭhī”ti.

69. On one occasion, the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Upasena were dwelling at Rājagaha in the Cool Wood, in the Sappasoṇḍika ravine. Now at that time, a venomous snake had fallen on the Venerable Upasena’s body. Then the Venerable Upasena addressed the monks: “Come, friends, place this body of mine on a small couch and carry it outside before this body disintegrates right here like a handful of chaff.”

Evaṃ [V 2.0044] vutte, āyasmā sāriputto āyasmantaṃ upasenaṃ etadavoca – “na kho pana mayaṃ passāma āyasmato upasenassa kāyassa vā aññathattaṃ indriyānaṃ vā vipariṇāmaṃ. Atha ca panāyasmā upaseno evamāha – ‘etha me, āvuso, imaṃ kāyaṃ mañcakaṃ āropetvā bahiddhā nīharatha. Purāyaṃ kāyo idheva vikirati; seyyathāpi bhusamuṭṭhī’”ti. “Yassa nūna, āvuso sāriputta, evamassa – ‘ahaṃ cakkhūti vā mama cakkhūti vā…pe… ahaṃ jivhāti vā mama [M 2.0268] jivhāti vā… ahaṃ manoti vā mama manoti vā’. Tassa, āvuso sāriputta, siyā kāyassa vā aññathattaṃ indriyānaṃ vā vipariṇāmo. Mayhañca kho, āvuso sāriputta, na evaṃ hoti [P 4.0041] – ‘ahaṃ cakkhūti vā mama cakkhūti vā…pe… ahaṃ jivhāti vā mama jivhāti vā…pe… ahaṃ manoti vā mama manoti vā’. Tassa mayhañca kho, āvuso sāriputta, kiṃ kāyassa vā aññathattaṃ bhavissati, indriyānaṃ vā vipariṇāmo”ti!

When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Venerable Upasena: “We do not see any alteration in the Venerable Upasena’s body or any change in his faculties. And yet the Venerable Upasena says: ‘Come, friends, place this body of mine on a small couch and carry it outside before this body disintegrates right here like a handful of chaff.’” “Friend Sāriputta, for one for whom it might be thus: ‘I am the eye,’ or ‘The eye is mine’… or ‘I am the tongue,’ or ‘The tongue is mine’… or ‘I am the mind,’ or ‘The mind is mine’—for such a one, friend Sāriputta, there might be an alteration of the body or a change of the faculties. But for me, friend Sāriputta, it is not so: ‘I am the eye,’ or ‘The eye is mine’… or ‘I am the tongue,’ or ‘The tongue is mine’… or ‘I am the mind,’ or ‘The mind is mine.’ For me, friend Sāriputta, how could there be an alteration of the body or a change of the faculties?”

“Tathā hi panāyasmato upasenassa dīgharattaṃ ahaṅkāramamaṅkāramānānusayo susamūhato. Tasmā āyasmato upasenassa na evaṃ hoti – ‘ahaṃ cakkhūti vā mama cakkhūti vā…pe… ahaṃ jivhāti vā mama jivhāti vā…pe… ahaṃ manoti vā mama manoti vā’”ti. Atha [T 4.0050] kho te bhikkhū āyasmato upasenassa kāyaṃ mañcakaṃ āropetvā bahiddhā nīhariṃsu. Atha kho āyasmato upasenassa kāyo tattheva vikiri; seyyathāpi bhusamuṭṭhīti. Sattamaṃ.

Indeed, in the Venerable Upasena the underlying tendency to the conceit of ‘I-making’ and ‘mine-making’ had been well uprooted for a long time. Therefore, it was not so for the Venerable Upasena: ‘I am the eye,’ or ‘The eye is mine’… or ‘I am the tongue,’ or ‘The tongue is mine’… or ‘I am the mind,’ or ‘The mind is mine.’ Then those monks, having placed the Venerable Upasena’s body on a small couch, carried it outside. Then the Venerable Upasena’s body disintegrated right there, just like a handful of chaff. The Seventh.

8. Upavāṇasandiṭṭhikasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse to Upavāṇa on What is Directly Visible

70. Atha kho āyasmā upavāṇo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā upavāṇo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “‘sandiṭṭhiko dhammo, sandiṭṭhiko dhammo’ti, bhante, vuccati. Kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, sandiṭṭhiko dhammo hoti, akāliko ehipassiko opaneyyiko paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhī”ti?

70. Then the Venerable Upavāṇa approached the Blessed One…and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Upavāṇa said to the Blessed One: “‘The Dhamma is directly visible, the Dhamma is directly visible,’ it is said, venerable sir. To what extent, venerable sir, is the Dhamma directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading inward, to be personally realized by the wise?”

“Idha pana, upavāṇa, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā rūpappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti rūparāgappaṭisaṃvedī ca. Santañca ajjhattaṃ rūpesu rāgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ rūpesu rāgo’ti pajānāti. Yaṃ taṃ, upavāṇa, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā rūpappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti rūparāgappaṭisaṃvedī [V 2.0045] ca. Santañca ajjhattaṃ rūpesu rāgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ rūpesu rāgo’ti pajānāti. Evampi kho, upavāṇa, sandiṭṭhiko dhammo hoti akāliko ehipassiko opaneyyiko paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhī”ti…pe….

“Here, Upavāṇa, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, both experiences the form and experiences lust for the form. There being internal lust for forms, he knows distinctly: ‘There is internal lust for forms in me.’ When that bhikkhu, Upavāṇa, having seen a form with the eye, both experiences the form and experiences lust for the form, and there being internal lust for forms, he knows distinctly: ‘There is internal lust for forms in me’—in this way too, Upavāṇa, the Dhamma is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading inward, to be personally realized by the wise.”…

“Puna [P 4.0042] caparaṃ, upavāṇa, bhikkhu jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā rasappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti rasarāgappaṭisaṃvedī ca. Santañca ajjhattaṃ rasesu rāgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ rasesu rāgo’ti pajānāti. Yaṃ taṃ, upavāṇa, bhikkhu jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā rasappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti rasarāgappaṭisaṃvedī [T 4.0051] ca. Santañca ajjhattaṃ rasesu [M 2.0269] rāgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ rasesu rāgo’ti pajānāti. Evampi kho, upavāṇa, sandiṭṭhiko dhammo hoti akāliko ehipassiko opaneyyiko paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhī”ti…pe….

“Furthermore, Upavāṇa, a bhikkhu, having tasted a flavor with the tongue, both experiences the flavor and experiences lust for the flavor. There being internal lust for flavors, he knows distinctly: ‘There is internal lust for flavors in me.’ When that bhikkhu, Upavāṇa, having tasted a flavor with the tongue, both experiences the flavor and experiences lust for the flavor, and there being internal lust for flavors, he knows distinctly: ‘There is internal lust for flavors in me’—in this way too, Upavāṇa, the Dhamma is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading inward, to be personally realized by the wise.”…

“Puna caparaṃ, upavāṇa, bhikkhu manasā dhammaṃ viññāya dhammappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammarāgappaṭisaṃvedī ca. Santañca ajjhattaṃ dhammesu rāgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ dhammesu rāgo’ti pajānāti. Yaṃ taṃ, upavāṇa, bhikkhu manasā dhammaṃ viññāya dhammappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti dhammarāgappaṭisaṃvedī ca. Santañca ajjhattaṃ dhammesu rāgaṃ ‘atthi me ajjhattaṃ dhammesu rāgo’ti pajānāti. Evampi kho, upavāṇa, sandiṭṭhiko dhammo hoti…pe… paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhī”ti…pe….

“Furthermore, Upavāṇa, a bhikkhu, having known a mental object with the mind, both experiences the mental object and experiences lust for the mental object. There being internal lust for mental objects, he knows distinctly: ‘There is internal lust for mental objects in me.’ When that bhikkhu, Upavāṇa, having known a mental object with the mind, both experiences the mental object and experiences lust for the mental object, and there being internal lust for mental objects, he knows distinctly: ‘There is internal lust for mental objects in me’—in this way too, Upavāṇa, the Dhamma is directly visible… to be personally realized by the wise.”…

“Idha pana, upavāṇa, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā rūpappaṭisaṃvedī ca hoti, no ca rūparāgappaṭisaṃvedī. Asantañca ajjhattaṃ rūpesu rāgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ rūpesu rāgo’ti pajānāti. Yaṃ taṃ, upavāṇa, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā rūpappaṭisaṃvedīhi kho hoti, no ca rūparāgappaṭisaṃvedī. Asantañca ajjhattaṃ rūpesu rāgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ rūpesu rāgo’ti pajānāti. Evampi kho, upavāṇa, sandiṭṭhiko dhammo hoti, akāliko ehipassiko opaneyyiko paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhī”ti…pe….

“Here, Upavāṇa, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, is one who experiences the form, but not one who experiences lust for the form. There being no internal lust for forms, he knows distinctly: ‘There is no internal lust for forms in me.’ When that bhikkhu, Upavāṇa, having seen a form with the eye, experiences only the form and does not experience lust for the form, and, there being no internal lust for forms, he knows distinctly: ‘There is no internal lust for forms in me’—in this way too, Upavāṇa, the Dhamma is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading inward, to be personally realized by the wise.”…pe….

“Puna [T 4.0052] caparaṃ, upavāṇa, bhikkhu jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā rasappaṭisaṃvedīhi kho hoti, no ca rasarāgappaṭisaṃvedī. Asantañca ajjhattaṃ rasesu rāgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ rasesu rāgo’ti pajānāti…pe….

“Furthermore, Upavāṇa, a bhikkhu, having tasted a flavor with the tongue, experiences only the flavor, but does not experience lust for the flavor. There being no internal lust for flavors, he knows distinctly: ‘There is no internal lust for flavors in me.’…pe….

“Puna [V 2.0046][P 4.0043] caparaṃ, upavāṇa, bhikkhu manasā dhammaṃ viññāya dhammappaṭisaṃvedīhi kho hoti, no ca dhammarāgappaṭisaṃvedī. Asantañca ajjhattaṃ dhammesu rāgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ dhammesu rāgo’ti pajānāti. Yaṃ taṃ, upavāṇa, bhikkhu manasā dhammaṃ viññāya dhammappaṭisaṃvedīhi kho hoti, no ca dhammarāgappaṭisaṃvedī. Asantañca ajjhattaṃ dhammesu rāgaṃ ‘natthi me ajjhattaṃ dhammesu rāgo’ti pajānāti. Evampi kho, upavāṇa, sandiṭṭhiko dhammo hoti, akāliko ehipassiko opaneyyiko paccattaṃ veditabbo viññūhī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Furthermore, Upavāṇa, a bhikkhu, having known a mental object with the mind, experiences only the mental object, but does not experience lust for the mental object. There being no internal lust for mental objects, he knows distinctly: ‘There is no internal lust for mental objects in me.’ When that bhikkhu, Upavāṇa, having known a mental object with the mind, experiences only the mental object and does not experience lust for the mental object, and, there being no internal lust for mental objects, he knows distinctly: ‘There is no internal lust for mental objects in me’—in this way too, Upavāṇa, the Dhamma is directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, leading inward, to be personally realized by the wise.” The Eighth.

9. Paṭhamachaphassāyatanasuttaṃ

9. The First Discourse on the Six Bases for Contact

71. “Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, bhikkhu channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Avusitaṃ [M 2.0270] tena brahmacariyaṃ, ārakā so imasmā dhammavinayā”ti.

71. “Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu does not discern as it really is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact, by him the holy life has not been lived; he is far from this Dhamma and Discipline.”

Evaṃ vutte, aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “etthāhaṃ, bhante, anassasaṃ anassasiṃ (sī.), anassāsaṃ (syā. kaṃ.), anassāsiṃ (pī.). Ahañhi, bhante, channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāmī”ti.

When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, in this matter I am undone. For I, venerable sir, do not discern as it really is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, bhikkhu, cakkhuṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi[T 4.0053], eso me attā’ti samanupassasī”ti?

“What do you think, bhikkhu? Do you regard the eye as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Indeed not, venerable sir.”

“Sādhu, bhikkhu, ettha ca te, bhikkhu, cakkhu ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ bhavissati. Esevanto dukkhassa…pe… jivhaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassasī”ti?

“Good, bhikkhu. Here, bhikkhu, the eye will be well seen by you with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ This itself is the end of suffering…pe… Do you regard the tongue as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Indeed not, venerable sir.”

“Sādhu, bhikkhu, ettha ca te, bhikkhu, jivhā ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ bhavissati. Esevanto dukkhassa…pe… manaṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’ti samanupassasī”ti?

“Good, bhikkhu. Here, bhikkhu, the tongue will be well seen by you with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ This itself is the end of suffering…pe… Do you regard the mind as: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Indeed not, venerable sir.”

“Sādhu, bhikkhu, ettha ca te, bhikkhu, mano ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti [V 2.0047] evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ bhavissati. Esevanto dukkhassā”ti. Navamaṃ.

“Good, bhikkhu. Here, bhikkhu, the mind will be well seen by you with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ This itself is the end of suffering.” The Ninth.

10. Dutiyachaphassāyatanasuttaṃ

10. The Second Discourse on the Six Bases for Contact

72. “Yo [P 4.0044] hi koci, bhikkhave, bhikkhu channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Avusitaṃ tena brahmacariyaṃ, ārakā so imasmā dhammavinayā”ti.

72. “Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu does not discern as it really is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact, by him the holy life has not been lived; he is far from this Dhamma and Discipline.”

Evaṃ vutte, aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “etthāhaṃ, bhante, anassasaṃ panassasaṃ. Ahañhi, bhante, channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāmī”ti.

When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, in this matter I am undone, utterly undone. For I, venerable sir, do not discern as it really is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in the case of the six bases for contact.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, bhikkhu, cakkhuṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi[T 4.0054], na meso attā’ti samanupassasī”ti?

“What do you think, bhikkhu? Do you regard the eye as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’?”

“Evaṃ, bhante”.

“Even so, venerable sir.”

“Sādhu, bhikkhu, ettha ca te, bhikkhu, cakkhu ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ bhavissati. Evaṃ te etaṃ paṭhamaṃ phassāyatanaṃ pahīnaṃ bhavissati [M 2.0271] āyatiṃ apunabbhavāya…pe….

“Good, bhikkhu. Here, bhikkhu, the eye will be well seen by you with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Thus this first base for contact will be abandoned by you for the sake of no future re-becoming…pe….

“Jivhaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassasī”ti?

“Do you regard the tongue as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’?”

“Evaṃ, bhante”.

“Even so, venerable sir.”

“Sādhu[V 2.0048], bhikkhu, ettha ca te, bhikkhu, jivhā ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ bhavissati. Evaṃ te etaṃ catutthaṃ phassāyatanaṃ pahīnaṃ bhavissati āyatiṃ apunabbhavāya…pe….

“Good, bhikkhu. Here, bhikkhu, the tongue will be well seen by you with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Thus this fourth base for contact will be abandoned by you for the sake of no future re-becoming…pe….

“Manaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti samanupassasī”ti?

“Do you regard the mind as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self’?”

“Evaṃ, bhante”.

“Even so, venerable sir.”

“Sādhu, bhikkhu, ettha ca te, bhikkhu, mano ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ bhavissati. Evaṃ te etaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ phassāyatanaṃ pahīnaṃ bhavissati āyatiṃ apunabbhavāyā”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“Good, bhikkhu. Here, bhikkhu, the mind will be well seen by you with right wisdom as it really is: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ Thus this sixth base for contact will be abandoned by you for the sake of no future re-becoming.” The Tenth.

11. Tatiyachaphassāyatanasuttaṃ

11. The Third Discourse on the Six Bases for Contact

73. “Yo hi koci, bhikkhave, bhikkhu channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ [P 4.0045] samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Avusitaṃ tena brahmacariyaṃ, ārakā so imasmā dhammavinayā”ti.

73. “Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu does not know distinctly as it really is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to the six bases for contact, by him the holy life has not been lived; he is far from this Dhamma and Discipline.”

Evaṃ vutte, aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “etthāhaṃ, bhante, anassasaṃ panassasaṃ. Ahañhi, bhante, channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayañca [T 4.0055] atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāmī”ti.

When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, in this I am undone. Indeed, Venerable Sir, I do not know distinctly as it really is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to the six bases for contact.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, bhikkhu, cakkhu niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“What do you think of this, bhikkhu, is the eye permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ, bhante”.

“Impermanent, Venerable Sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“Suffering, Venerable Sir.”

“Yaṃ [V 2.0049] panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti?

“But is it fitting to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Indeed, it is not, Venerable Sir.”

“Sotaṃ… ghānaṃ… jivhā… kāyo… mano nicco vā anicco vā”ti?

“Is the ear… the nose… the tongue… the body… the mind permanent or impermanent?”

“Anicco, bhante”.

“Impermanent, Venerable Sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“Suffering, Venerable Sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti?

“But is it fitting to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Indeed, it is not, Venerable Sir.”

“Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhu, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati, sotasmimpi nibbindati, ghānasmimpi nibbindati, jivhāyapi nibbindati, kāyasmimpi nibbindati, manasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Ekādasamaṃ.

“Seeing thus, bhikkhu, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with the ear, disenchanted with the nose, disenchanted with the tongue, disenchanted with the body, and disenchanted with the mind. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When he is liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He knows distinctly: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’”

Migajālavaggo sattamo.

The Migajāla Chapter, the Seventh.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of this is:

Migajālena [M 2.0272] dve vuttā, cattāro ca samiddhinā;

Upaseno upavāṇo, chaphassāyatanikā tayoti.

Two were spoken by Migajāla, and four by Samiddhi; Upasena, Upavāṇa, and three on the six bases for contact.

8. Gilānavaggo

8. The Chapter on the Sick

1. Paṭhamagilānasuttaṃ

1. The First Discourse on the Sick

74. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[T 4.0056][V 2.0050][P 4.0046]. Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “amukasmiṃ, bhante, vihāre aññataro bhikkhu navo appaññāto ābādhiko dukkhito bāḷhagilāno. Sādhu, bhante, bhagavā yena so bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamatu anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti.

74. At Sāvatthī. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One… and sitting to one side, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, in such-and-such a monastery there is a certain bhikkhu who is new, unknown, sick, suffering, and gravely ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would approach that bhikkhu out of compassion.”

Atha kho bhagavā navavādañca sutvā gilānavādañca, “appaññāto bhikkhū”ti iti viditvā yena so bhikkhu tenupasaṅkami. Addasā kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ. Disvāna mañcake samadhosi samañcosi (sī.), samatesi (syā. kaṃ.), samañcopi (pī.). Atha kho bhagavā taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavoca – “alaṃ, bhikkhu, mā tvaṃ mañcake samadhosi. Santimāni āsanāni paññattāni, tatthāhaṃ nisīdissāmī”ti. Nisīdi bhagavā paññatte āsane.
