92. “Dvayaṃ [M 2.0291] vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha. Kiñca, bhikkhave, dvayaṃ? Cakkhuñceva rūpā ca, sotañceva saddā ca, ghānañceva gandhā ca, jivhā ceva rasā ca, kāyo ceva phoṭṭhabbā ca[T 4.0085], mano ceva dhammā ca – idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, dvayaṃ.

92. “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the pair. Listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, is the pair? The eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, the mind and mental objects—this, bhikkhus, is called the pair.”

“Yo, bhikkhave, evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ahametaṃ dvayaṃ paccakkhāya aññaṃ dvayaṃ paññapessāmī’ti, tassa vācāvatthukamevassa. Puṭṭho ca na sampāyeyya. Uttariñca vighātaṃ āpajjeyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yathā taṃ, bhikkhave, avisayasmi”nti. Navamaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, if anyone should say: ‘Having rejected this pair, I shall declare another pair,’ for him that would be a mere matter of speech. And when questioned, he would not be able to answer, and further, he would come to vexation. For what reason? Because, bhikkhus, it would be outside his domain.” The Ninth.

10. Dutiyadvayasuttaṃ

10. The Second Discourse on the Pair

93. “Dvayaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭicca viññāṇaṃ sambhoti. Kathañca, bhikkhave, dvayaṃ paṭicca viññāṇaṃ sambhoti? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Cakkhu aniccaṃ vipariṇāmi aññathābhāvi. Rūpā [P 4.0068] aniccā vipariṇāmino aññathābhāvino. Itthetaṃ dvayaṃ calañceva byathañca aniccaṃ vipariṇāmi aññathābhāvi. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ vipariṇāmi aññathābhāvi. Yopi hetu yopi paccayo cakkhuviññāṇassa uppādāya, sopi hetu sopi paccayo anicco vipariṇāmī aññathābhāvī. Aniccaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, paccayaṃ paṭicca uppannaṃ cakkhuviññāṇaṃ kuto niccaṃ bhavissati! Yā kho, bhikkhave, imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅgati sannipāto samavāyo, ayaṃ vuccati cakkhusamphasso. Cakkhusamphassopi anicco [V 2.0074] vipariṇāmī aññathābhāvī. Yopi hetu yopi paccayo cakkhusamphassassa uppādāya, sopi hetu sopi paccayo anicco vipariṇāmī aññathābhāvī. Aniccaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, paccayaṃ paṭicca uppanno cakkhusamphasso kuto nicco bhavissati! Phuṭṭho[T 4.0086], bhikkhave, vedeti, phuṭṭho ceteti, phuṭṭho sañjānāti. Itthetepi dhammā calā ceva byathā ca aniccā vipariṇāmino aññathābhāvino. Sotaṃ…pe….

93. “Bhikkhus, consciousness arises in dependence on a pair. And how, bhikkhus, does consciousness arise in dependence on a pair? In dependence on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The eye is impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Forms are impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Thus this pair is agitated and afflicted, impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Eye-consciousness is impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of eye-consciousness, that cause and that condition are also impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Bhikkhus, eye-consciousness having arisen in dependence on an impermanent condition, how could it be permanent? Bhikkhus, the meeting, concurrence, and convergence of these three phenomena is called eye-contact. Eye-contact is also impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of eye-contact, that cause and that condition are also impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Bhikkhus, eye-contact having arisen in dependence on an impermanent condition, how could it be permanent? Having been contacted, bhikkhus, one feels; having been contacted, one intends; having been contacted, one perceives. Thus these phenomena too are agitated and afflicted, impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. The ear…and so on….”

“Jivhañca paṭicca rase ca uppajjati jivhāviññāṇaṃ. Jivhā aniccā vipariṇāmī aññathābhāvī vipariṇāminī aññathābhāvinī (?). Rasā aniccā vipariṇāmino aññathābhāvino. Itthetaṃ dvayaṃ calañceva byathañca aniccaṃ vipariṇāmi aññathābhāvi. Jivhāviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ vipariṇāmi aññathābhāvi. Yopi hetu yopi paccayo jivhāviññāṇassa uppādāya[M 2.0292], sopi hetu sopi paccayo anicco vipariṇāmī aññathābhāvī. Aniccaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, paccayaṃ paṭicca uppannaṃ jivhāviññāṇaṃ, kuto niccaṃ bhavissati! Yā kho, bhikkhave, imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅgati sannipāto samavāyo, ayaṃ vuccati jivhāsamphasso. Jivhāsamphassopi anicco vipariṇāmī aññathābhāvī. Yopi hetu yopi paccayo jivhāsamphassassa uppādāya, sopi hetu sopi paccayo anicco vipariṇāmī aññathābhāvī. Aniccaṃ [P 4.0069] kho pana, bhikkhave, paccayaṃ paṭicca uppanno jivhāsamphasso, kuto nicco bhavissati! Phuṭṭho, bhikkhave, vedeti, phuṭṭho ceteti, phuṭṭho sañjānāti. Itthetepi dhammā calā ceva byathā ca aniccā vipariṇāmino aññathābhāvino. Kāyaṃ…pe….

“In dependence on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises. The tongue is impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Tastes are impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Thus this pair is agitated and afflicted, impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Tongue-consciousness is impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of tongue-consciousness, that cause and that condition are also impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Bhikkhus, tongue-consciousness having arisen in dependence on an impermanent condition, how could it be permanent? Bhikkhus, the meeting, concurrence, and convergence of these three phenomena is called tongue-contact. Tongue-contact is also impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of tongue-contact, that cause and that condition are also impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Bhikkhus, tongue-contact having arisen in dependence on an impermanent condition, how could it be permanent? Having been contacted, bhikkhus, one feels; having been contacted, one intends; having been contacted, one perceives. Thus these phenomena too are agitated and afflicted, impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. The body…and so on….”

“Manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Mano anicco vipariṇāmī aññathābhāvī. Dhammā aniccā vipariṇāmino aññathābhāvino. Itthetaṃ dvayaṃ calañceva [T 4.0087] byathañca aniccaṃ vipariṇāmi aññathābhāvi. Manoviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ vipariṇāmi aññathābhāvi. Yopi hetu yopi paccayo manoviññāṇassa uppādāya, sopi hetu sopi paccayo anicco vipariṇāmī aññathābhāvī. Aniccaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, paccayaṃ paṭicca uppannaṃ manoviññāṇaṃ, kuto niccaṃ bhavissati! Yā kho, bhikkhave, imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ dhammānaṃ saṅgati sannipāto samavāyo, ayaṃ vuccati manosamphasso. Manosamphassopi anicco vipariṇāmī aññathābhāvī. Yopi hetu yopi paccayo manosamphassassa uppādāya, sopi hetu sopi paccayo anicco vipariṇāmī aññathābhāvī. Aniccaṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, paccayaṃ paṭicca [V 2.0075] uppanno manosamphasso, kuto nicco bhavissati! Phuṭṭho, bhikkhave, vedeti, phuṭṭho ceteti, phuṭṭho sañjānāti. Itthetepi dhammā calā ceva byathā ca aniccā vipariṇāmino aññathābhāvino. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, dvayaṃ paṭicca viññāṇaṃ sambhotī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“In dependence on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The mind is impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Mental objects are impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Thus this pair is agitated and afflicted, impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Mind-consciousness is impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of mind-consciousness, that cause and that condition are also impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Bhikkhus, mind-consciousness having arisen in dependence on an impermanent condition, how could it be permanent? Bhikkhus, the meeting, concurrence, and convergence of these three phenomena is called mind-contact. Mind-contact is also impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of mind-contact, that cause and that condition are also impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. Bhikkhus, mind-contact having arisen in dependence on an impermanent condition, how could it be permanent? Having been contacted, bhikkhus, one feels; having been contacted, one intends; having been contacted, one perceives. Thus these phenomena too are agitated and afflicted, impermanent, subject to change, becoming otherwise. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that consciousness arises in dependence on a pair.” The Tenth.

Channavaggo navamo.

The Channa Chapter, the Ninth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary for this chapter:

Palokasuññā saṃkhittaṃ, channo puṇṇo ca bāhiyo;

Ejena ca duve vuttā, dvayehi apare duveti.

Paloka and Suñña, Saṃkhitta, Channa, Puṇṇa, and Bāhiya; two were taught regarding Agitation, and two others regarding the Pair.

10. Saḷavaggo

10. The Chapter on the Six

1. Adantaaguttasuttaṃ

1. The Untamed and Unguarded Discourse

94. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[M 2.0293]. “Chayime[T 4.0088][P 4.0070], bhikkhave, phassāyatanā adantā aguttā arakkhitā asaṃvutā dukkhādhivāhā honti. Katame cha? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, phassāyatanaṃ adantaṃ aguttaṃ arakkhitaṃ asaṃvutaṃ dukkhādhivāhaṃ hoti…pe… jivhā, bhikkhave, phassāyatanaṃ adantaṃ aguttaṃ arakkhitaṃ asaṃvutaṃ dukkhādhivāhaṃ hoti…pe… mano, bhikkhave, phassāyatanaṃ adantaṃ aguttaṃ arakkhitaṃ asaṃvutaṃ dukkhādhivāhaṃ hoti. Ime kho, bhikkhave, cha phassāyatanā adantā aguttā arakkhitā asaṃvutā dukkhādhivāhā honti”.

94. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, these six bases for contact, when untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained, bring suffering. Which six? The eye, bhikkhus, as a base for contact, when untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained, brings suffering… The tongue, bhikkhus, as a base for contact, when untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained, brings suffering… The mind, bhikkhus, as a base for contact, when untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained, brings suffering. These, bhikkhus, are the six bases for contact that, when untamed, unguarded, unprotected, and unrestrained, bring suffering.”

“Chayime, bhikkhave, phassāyatanā sudantā suguttā surakkhitā susaṃvutā sukhādhivāhā honti. Katame cha? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, phassāyatanaṃ sudantaṃ suguttaṃ surakkhitaṃ susaṃvutaṃ sukhādhivāhaṃ hoti…pe… jivhā, bhikkhave, phassāyatanaṃ sudantaṃ suguttaṃ surakkhitaṃ susaṃvutaṃ sukhādhivāhaṃ hoti…pe… mano, bhikkhave, phassāyatanaṃ sudantaṃ suguttaṃ surakkhitaṃ [V 2.0076] susaṃvutaṃ sukhādhivāhaṃ hoti. Ime kho, bhikkhave, cha phassāyatanā sudantā suguttā surakkhitā susaṃvutā sukhādhivāhā hontī”ti. Idamavoca bhagavā…pe… etadavoca satthā –

“Bhikkhus, these six bases for contact, when well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, and well-restrained, bring happiness. Which six? The eye, bhikkhus, as a base for contact, when well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, and well-restrained, brings happiness… The tongue, bhikkhus, as a base for contact, when well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, and well-restrained, brings happiness… The mind, bhikkhus, as a base for contact, when well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, and well-restrained, brings happiness. These, bhikkhus, are the six bases for contact that, when well-tamed, well-guarded, well-protected, and well-restrained, bring happiness.” The Blessed One said this… The Teacher said this:

“Saḷeva chaḷeva (ka.) phassāyatanāni bhikkhavo,

Asaṃvuto yattha dukkhaṃ nigacchati;

Tesañca ye saṃvaraṇaṃ avedisuṃ,

Saddhādutiyā viharantānavassutā.

“Bhikkhus, it is indeed in the six bases for contact that one who is unrestrained incurs suffering; but those who have understood the restraint of these, dwelling with faith as their companion, are without outflows.

“Disvāna rūpāni manoramāni,

Athopi disvāna amanoramāni;

Manorame [T 4.0089] rāgapathaṃ vinodaye,

Na cāppiyaṃ meti manaṃ padosaye.

“Having seen delightful forms, and also having seen undelightful forms, one should dispel the path of passion for the delightful, and not corrupt the mind with aversion, thinking, ‘This is unpleasing to me.’

“Saddañca [P 4.0071] sutvā dubhayaṃ piyāppiyaṃ,

Piyamhi sadde na samucchito siyā;

Athoppiye dosagataṃ vinodaye,

Na cāppiyaṃ meti manaṃ padosaye.

“Having heard a sound, both pleasant and unpleasant, one should not be elated by the pleasant sound; and upon the unpleasant, one should dispel aversion, and not corrupt the mind with aversion, thinking, ‘This is unpleasing to me.’

“Gandhañca [M 2.0294] ghatvā surabhiṃ manoramaṃ,

Athopi ghatvā asuciṃ akantiyaṃ;

Akantiyasmiṃ paṭighaṃ vinodaye,

Chandānunīto na ca kantiye siyā.

“Having smelled a fragrant and delightful scent, and also an impure and undesirable one, one should dispel aversion towards the undesirable, and not be led by desire towards the desirable.

“Rasañca bhotvāna asāditañca sāduṃ,

Athopi bhotvāna asādumekadā;

Sāduṃ rasaṃ nājjhosāya bhuñje,

Virodhamāsādusu nopadaṃsaye.

“Having partaken of a delicious flavor, and also, at times, an unpalatable one, one should not consume the delicious flavor with attachment, nor show hostility towards the unpalatable.

“Phassena [V 2.0077] phuṭṭho na sukhena majje majjhe (syā. kaṃ. pī.),

Dukkhena phuṭṭhopi na sampavedhe;

Phassadvayaṃ sukhadukkhe upekkhe,

Anānuruddho aviruddha kenaci.

“Touched by contact, one should not be intoxicated by pleasure; and when touched by pain, one should not be agitated. One should be equanimous toward both pleasure and pain, neither attached to nor opposed to anything.

“Papañcasaññā itarītarā narā,

Papañcayantā upayanti saññino;

Manomayaṃ gehasitañca sabbaṃ,

Panujja nekkhammasitaṃ irīyati.

“Ordinary people are beset by perceptions of proliferation; as perceivers, they proliferate and fall into its sway. Having dispelled all that is mind-made and home-based, one fares on grounded in renunciation.

“Evaṃ mano chassu yadā subhāvito,

Phuṭṭhassa cittaṃ na vikampate kvaci;

Te rāgadose abhibhuyya bhikkhavo,

Bhavattha bhavatha (sī. syā. kaṃ.) jātimaraṇassa pāragā”ti. paṭhamaṃ;

“When the mind is thus well-developed with regard to the six, the mind of one who is touched does not waver anywhere. Having overcome lust and hatred, bhikkhus, you shall become those who have gone beyond birth and death.” The First.

2. Mālukyaputtasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse to Mālukyaputta

95. Atha [P 4.0072] kho āyasmā mālukyaputto māluṅkyaputto (sī.) yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā mālukyaputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetu, yamahaṃ bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto [T 4.0090] ātāpī pahitatto vihareyya”nti.

95. Then the Venerable Mālukyaputta approached the Blessed One…and said to him: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, secluded, heedful, ardent, and resolute.”

“Ettha [M 2.0295] dāni, mālukyaputta, kiṃ dahare bhikkhū vakkhāma! Yatra hi nāma tvaṃ, bhikkhu, jiṇṇo vuddho mahallako addhagato vayoanuppatto saṃkhittena ovādaṃ yācasī”ti.

“Now, Mālukyaputta, what shall we say to the young bhikkhus? For you, a bhikkhu, are old, aged, burdened with years, having reached the final stage of life, yet you ask for brief instruction.”

“Kiñcāpāhaṃ, bhante, jiṇṇo vuddho mahallako addhagato vayoanuppatto. Desetu me, bhante[V 2.0078], bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ, desetu sugato saṃkhittena dhammaṃ, appeva nāmāhaṃ bhagavato bhāsitassa atthaṃ ājāneyyaṃ. Appeva nāmāhaṃ bhagavato bhāsitassa dāyādo assa”nti.

“Even though I am, venerable sir, old, aged, burdened with years, having reached the final stage of life, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief, let the Well-Gone One teach me the Dhamma in brief. Perhaps I might understand the meaning of the Blessed One’s words. Perhaps I might be an heir to the Blessed One’s teaching.”

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, mālukyaputta, ye te cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā adiṭṭhā adiṭṭhapubbā, na ca passasi, na ca te hoti passeyyanti? Atthi te tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṃ vā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“What do you think, Mālukyaputta? Regarding those forms cognizable by the eye that are unseen, have never been seen before, that you do not see, and for which the thought does not arise, ‘I should see them’—do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Ye te sotaviññeyyā saddā assutā assutapubbā, na ca suṇāsi, na ca te hoti suṇeyyanti? Atthi te tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṃ vā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Regarding those sounds cognizable by the ear that are unheard, have never been heard before, that you do not hear, and for which the thought does not arise, ‘I should hear them’—do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Ye te ghānaviññeyyā gandhā aghāyitā aghāyitapubbā, na ca ghāyasi, na ca te hoti ghāyeyyanti? Atthi te tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṃ vā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Regarding those odors cognizable by the nose that are unsmelled, have never been smelled before, that you do not smell, and for which the thought does not arise, ‘I should smell them’—do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Ye te jivhāviññeyyā rasā asāyitā asāyitapubbā, na ca sāyasi, na ca te hoti sāyeyyanti? Atthi te tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṃ vā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Regarding those flavors cognizable by the tongue that are untasted, have never been tasted before, that you do not taste, and for which the thought does not arise, ‘I should taste them’—do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Ye te kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā asamphuṭṭhā asamphuṭṭhapubbā, na ca phusasi, na ca te hoti phuseyyanti? Atthi te tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṃ vā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Regarding those tangibles cognizable by the body that are untouched, have never been touched before, that you do not touch, and for which the thought does not arise, ‘I should touch them’—do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Ye [P 4.0073] te manoviññeyyā dhammā [T 4.0091] aviññātā aviññātapubbā, na ca vijānāsi, na ca te hoti vijāneyyanti? Atthi te tattha chando vā rāgo vā pemaṃ vā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Regarding those mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are uncognized, have never been cognized before, that you do not cognize, and for which the thought does not arise, ‘I should cognize them’—do you have any desire, lust, or affection for them?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Ettha ca te, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhasutamutaviññātabbesu dhammesu diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ bhavissati, sute sutamattaṃ bhavissati, mute mutamattaṃ bhavissati, viññāte viññātamattaṃ bhavissati. Yato kho te, mālukyaputta, diṭṭhasutamutaviññātabbesu dhammesu diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ bhavissati, sute sutamattaṃ bhavissati[M 2.0296], mute mutamattaṃ bhavissati, viññāte viññātamattaṃ bhavissati; tato tvaṃ, mālukyaputta, na tena. Yato tvaṃ, mālukyaputta, na tena; tato tvaṃ, mālukyaputta[V 2.0079], na tattha. Yato tvaṃ, mālukyaputta, na tattha; tato tvaṃ, mālukyaputta, nevidha, na huraṃ, na ubhayamantarena. Esevanto dukkhassā”ti.

“In this regard, Mālukyaputta, with respect to things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized: in the seen there will be merely the seen; in the heard, merely the heard; in the sensed, merely the sensed; in the cognized, merely the cognized. When, Mālukyaputta, for you, with respect to things seen, heard, sensed, and cognized, in the seen there is merely the seen, in the heard merely the heard, in the sensed merely the sensed, and in the cognized merely the cognized, then, Mālukyaputta, you will not be ‘by that.’ When you are not ‘by that,’ then you will not be ‘in that.’ When you are not ‘in that,’ then, Mālukyaputta, you will be neither here, nor beyond, nor in between the two. This itself is the end of suffering.”

“Imassa khvāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ ājānāmi –

“Venerable sir, I understand the detailed meaning of what the Blessed One has stated in brief as follows:

“Rūpaṃ disvā sati muṭṭhā, piyaṃ nimittaṃ manasi karoto;

Sārattacitto vedeti, tañca ajjhosa ajjhosāya (sī.) tiṭṭhati.

“Having seen a form, mindfulness is lost for one who attends to a pleasing sign; with an impassioned mind one feels, and dwells clinging to it.

“Tassa vaḍḍhanti vedanā, anekā rūpasambhavā;

Abhijjhā ca vihesā ca, cittamassūpahaññati;

Evaṃ ācinato dukkhaṃ, ārā nibbānamuccati.

“For him, feelings increase, manifold, born of forms; covetousness and vexation assail his mind. Thus accumulating suffering, he is said to be far from Nibbāna.

“Saddaṃ sutvā sati muṭṭhā, piyaṃ nimittaṃ manasi karoto;

Sārattacitto vedeti, tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati.

“Having heard a sound, mindfulness is lost for one who attends to a pleasing sign; with an impassioned mind one feels, and dwells clinging to it.

“Tassa [T 4.0092] vaḍḍhanti vedanā, anekā saddasambhavā;

Abhijjhā ca vihesā ca, cittamassūpahaññati;

Evaṃ ācinato dukkhaṃ, ārā nibbānamuccati.

“For him, feelings increase, manifold, born of sounds; covetousness and vexation assail his mind. Thus accumulating suffering, he is said to be far from Nibbāna.

“Gandhaṃ [P 4.0074] ghatvā sati muṭṭhā, piyaṃ nimittaṃ manasi karoto;

Sārattacitto vedeti, tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati.

“Having smelled an odor, mindfulness is lost for one who attends to a pleasing sign; with an impassioned mind one feels, and dwells clinging to it.

“Tassa vaḍḍhanti vedanā, anekā gandhasambhavā;

Abhijjhā ca vihesā ca, cittamassūpahaññati;

Evaṃ ācinato dukkhaṃ, ārā nibbānamuccati.

“For him, feelings increase, manifold, born of odors; covetousness and vexation assail his mind. Thus accumulating suffering, he is said to be far from Nibbāna.

“Rasaṃ [V 2.0080] bhotvā sati muṭṭhā, piyaṃ nimittaṃ manasi karoto;

Sārattacitto vedeti, tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati.

“Having consumed a flavor, mindfulness is lost for one who attends to a pleasing sign; with an impassioned mind one feels, and dwells clinging to it.

“Tassa vaḍḍhanti vedanā, anekā rasasambhavā;

Abhijjhā ca vihesā ca, cittamassūpahaññati;

Evaṃ ācinato dukkhaṃ, ārā nibbānamuccati.

“For him, feelings increase, manifold, born of flavors; covetousness and vexation assail his mind. Thus accumulating suffering, he is said to be far from Nibbāna.

“Phassaṃ [M 2.0297] phussa sati muṭṭhā, piyaṃ nimittaṃ manasi karoto;

Sārattacitto vedeti, tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati.

“Having touched a tangible, mindfulness is lost for one who attends to a pleasing sign; with an impassioned mind one feels, and dwells clinging to it.

“Tassa vaḍḍhanti vedanā, anekā phassasambhavā;

Abhijjhā ca vihesā ca, cittamassūpahaññati;

Evaṃ ācinato dukkhaṃ, ārā nibbānamuccati.

“For him, feelings increase, manifold, born of tangibles; covetousness and vexation assail his mind. Thus accumulating suffering, he is said to be far from Nibbāna.

“Dhammaṃ ñatvā sati muṭṭhā, piyaṃ nimittaṃ manasi karoto;

Sārattacitto vedeti, tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati.

“Having known a mental phenomenon, mindfulness is lost for one who attends to a pleasing sign; with an impassioned mind one feels, and dwells clinging to it.

“Tassa vaḍḍhanti vedanā, anekā dhammasambhavā;

Abhijjhā ca vihesā ca, cittamassūpahaññati;

Evaṃ ācinato [T 4.0093] dukkhaṃ, ārā nibbānamuccati.

“For him, feelings increase, manifold, born of mental phenomena; covetousness and vexation assail his mind. Thus accumulating suffering, he is said to be far from Nibbāna.

“Na so rajjati rūpesu, rūpaṃ disvā paṭissato;

Virattacitto vedeti, tañca nājjhosa tiṭṭhati.

“He is not impassioned by forms; seeing a form, he is mindful. With a dispassionate mind, he feels, and does not dwell clinging to it.

“Yathāssa passato rūpaṃ, sevato cāpi vedanaṃ;

Khīyati nopacīyati, evaṃ so caratī sato;

Evaṃ apacinato dukkhaṃ, santike nibbānamuccati.

“As for him who sees a form and attends to the feeling, suffering is destroyed, it does not accumulate. Thus he, being mindful, conducts himself. For one who thus does not accumulate suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.

“Na so rajjati saddesu, saddaṃ sutvā paṭissato;

Virattacitto vedeti, tañca nājjhosa tiṭṭhati.

“He is not impassioned by sounds; having heard a sound, he is mindful. With a dispassionate mind, he feels, and does not dwell clinging to it.

“Yathāssa [V 2.0081] suṇato saddaṃ, sevato cāpi vedanaṃ;

Khīyati nopacīyati, evaṃ so caratī sato;

Evaṃ apacinato dukkhaṃ, santike nibbānamuccati.

“As for him who hears a sound and attends to the feeling, suffering is destroyed, it does not accumulate. Thus he, being mindful, conducts himself. For one who thus does not accumulate suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.

“Na [P 4.0075] so rajjati gandhesu, gandhaṃ ghatvā paṭissato;

Virattacitto vedeti, tañca nājjhosa tiṭṭhati.

“He is not impassioned by odors; having smelled an odor, he is mindful. With a dispassionate mind, he feels, and does not dwell clinging to it.

“Yathāssa ghāyato gandhaṃ, sevato cāpi vedanaṃ;

Khīyati nopacīyati, evaṃ so caratī sato;

Evaṃ apacinato dukkhaṃ, santike nibbānamuccati.

“As for him who smells an odor and attends to the feeling, suffering is destroyed, it does not accumulate. Thus he, being mindful, conducts himself. For one who thus does not accumulate suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.

“Na so rajjati rasesu, rasaṃ bhotvā paṭissato;

Virattacitto vedeti, tañca nājjhosa tiṭṭhati.

“He is not impassioned by flavors; having consumed a flavor, he is mindful. With a dispassionate mind, he feels, and does not dwell clinging to it.

“Yathāssa [M 2.0298] sāyato rasaṃ, sevato cāpi vedanaṃ;

Khīyati nopacīyati, evaṃ so caratī sato;

Evaṃ apacinato dukkhaṃ, santike nibbānamuccati.

“As for him who tastes a flavor and attends to the feeling, suffering is destroyed, it does not accumulate. Thus he, being mindful, conducts himself. For one who thus does not accumulate suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.”

“Na [T 4.0094] so rajjati phassesu, phassaṃ phussa paṭissato;

Virattacitto vedeti, tañca nājjhosa tiṭṭhati.

He is not impassioned by tangibles; having touched a tangible, he is mindful. With a dispassionate mind, he feels, and does not remain clinging to it.

“Yathāssa phusato phassaṃ, sevato cāpi vedanaṃ;

Khīyati nopacīyati, evaṃ so caratī sato;

Evaṃ apacinato dukkhaṃ, santike nibbānamuccati.

For one who touches a tangible and resorts to feeling, suffering is destroyed, it does not accumulate. Thus, being mindful, he conducts himself. For one who thus does not accumulate suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.

“Na [P 4.0076] so rajjati dhammesu, dhammaṃ ñatvā paṭissato;

Virattacitto vedeti, tañca nājjhosa tiṭṭhati.

He is not impassioned by mental phenomena; having known a mental phenomenon, he is mindful. With a dispassionate mind, he feels, and does not remain clinging to it.

“Yathāssa [V 2.0082] jānato dhammaṃ, sevato cāpi vedanaṃ;

Khīyati nopacīyati, evaṃ so caratī sato;

Evaṃ apacinato dukkhaṃ, santike nibbānamuccatī”ti.

For one who knows a mental phenomenon and resorts to feeling, suffering is destroyed, it does not accumulate. Thus, being mindful, he conducts himself. For one who thus does not accumulate suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.”

“Imassa khvāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa evaṃ vitthārena atthaṃ ājānāmī”ti. “Sādhu sādhu, mālukyaputta! Sādhu kho tvaṃ, mālukyaputta, mayā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa vitthārena atthaṃ ājānāsi –

“Venerable sir, I understand in detail the meaning of what the Blessed One has stated in brief in this way.” “Good, good, Mālukyaputta! It is good that you, Mālukyaputta, understand in detail the meaning of what I have stated in brief—

“Rūpaṃ disvā sati muṭṭhā, piyaṃ nimittaṃ manasi karoto;

Sārattacitto vedeti, tañca ajjhosa tiṭṭhati.

“Having seen a form, mindfulness is lost for one who attends to a pleasing sign. With an impassioned mind, he feels, and remains clinging to it.

“Tassa vaḍḍhanti vedanā, anekā rūpasambhavā;

Abhijjhā ca vihesā ca, cittamassūpahaññati;

Evaṃ ācinato dukkhaṃ, ārā nibbānamuccati.…pe….

For him, numerous feelings born of forms increase; covetousness and vexation assail his mind. For one who thus accumulates suffering, Nibbāna is said to be far. …and so on….

“Na so rajjati dhammesu, dhammaṃ ñatvā paṭissato;

Virattacitto vedeti, tañca nājjhosa tiṭṭhati.

He is not impassioned by mental phenomena; having known a mental phenomenon, he is mindful. With a dispassionate mind, he feels, and does not remain clinging to it.

“Yathāssa [T 4.0095] vijānato dhammaṃ, sevato cāpi vedanaṃ;

Khīyati nopacīyati, evaṃ so caratī sato;

Evaṃ apacinato dukkhaṃ, santike nibbānamuccatī”ti.

For one who knows a mental phenomenon and resorts to feeling, suffering is destroyed, it does not accumulate. Thus, being mindful, he conducts himself. For one who thus does not accumulate suffering, Nibbāna is said to be near.”

“Imassa kho, mālukyaputta, mayā saṃkhittena bhāsitassa evaṃ vitthārena attho daṭṭhabbo”ti.

“Mālukyaputta, the meaning of this which was stated in brief by me should be understood in detail in this way.”

Atha [M 2.0299] kho āyasmā mālukyaputto bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinanditvā anumoditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Atha kho āyasmā mālukyaputto eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto viharanto nacirasseva – yassatthāya kulaputtā sammadeva agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajanti tadanuttaraṃ brahmacariyapariyosānaṃ diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja vihāsi. “Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ [V 2.0083] karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā”ti abbhaññāsi. Aññataro ca panāyasmā mālukyaputto arahataṃ ahosīti. Dutiyaṃ.

Then the Venerable Mālukyaputta, having rejoiced in and approved of the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him, and departed. Then, dwelling alone, secluded, heedful, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Mālukyaputta, not long after, by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, entered and dwelled in that unsurpassed culmination of the holy life for which clansmen rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He knew directly: “Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.” And the Venerable Mālukyaputta became one of the Arahants. The Second.

3. Parihānadhammasuttaṃ

3. 3. The Discourse on the Quality of Decline

96. “Parihānadhammañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi aparihānadhammañca cha ca abhibhāyatanāni. Taṃ suṇātha. Kathañca, bhikkhave, parihānadhammo hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā sarasaṅkappā akusalā dhammā sarasaṅkappā (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) upari āsīvisavagge sattamasutte pana “ākusalā sarasaṅkappā” tveva sabbattha dissati saṃyojaniyā. Tañce bhikkhu adhivāseti nappajahati na vinodeti na byantīkaroti byantikaroti (pī.) byantiṃ karoti (ka.) na anabhāvaṃ gameti, veditabbametaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā – ‘parihāyāmi kusalehi [T 4.0096] dhammehi’. Parihānañhetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatāti…pe….

96. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the quality of decline, the quality of non-decline, and the six bases of mastery. Listen to that. And how, bhikkhus, is there the quality of decline? Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu sees a form with the eye, evil, unwholesome, discursive thoughts connected with the fetters arise. If that bhikkhu consents to them, does not abandon them, does not dispel them, does not make an end of them, and does not bring them to non-existence, it should be understood by that bhikkhu: ‘I am declining from wholesome qualities.’ For this has been called ‘decline’ by the Blessed One. …and so on….

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā uppajjanti…pe… puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno manasā dhammaṃ [P 4.0077] viññāya uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā sarasaṅkappā saṃyojaniyā. Tañce bhikkhu adhivāseti nappajahati na vinodeti na byantīkaroti na anabhāvaṃ gameti, veditabbametaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā – ‘parihāyāmi kusalehi dhammehi’. Parihānañhetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatāti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, parihānadhammo hoti.

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has tasted a flavor with the tongue… and so on… Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has known a mind-object with the mind, evil, unwholesome, discursive thoughts connected with the fetters arise. If that bhikkhu consents to them, does not abandon them, does not dispel them, does not make an end of them, and does not bring them to non-existence, it should be understood by that bhikkhu: ‘I am declining from wholesome qualities.’ For this has been called ‘decline’ by the Blessed One. Thus, bhikkhus, there is the quality of decline.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, aparihānadhammo hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā sarasaṅkappā saṃyojaniyā. Tañce bhikkhu nādhivāseti pajahati vinodeti byantīkaroti anabhāvaṃ gameti, veditabbametaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā – ‘na parihāyāmi kusalehi dhammehi’. Aparihānañhetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatāti…pe….

“And how, bhikkhus, is there the quality of non-decline? Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu sees a form with the eye, evil, unwholesome, discursive thoughts connected with the fetters arise. If that bhikkhu does not consent to them, but abandons them, dispels them, makes an end of them, and brings them to non-existence, it should be understood by that bhikkhu: ‘I am not declining from wholesome qualities.’ For this has been called ‘non-decline’ by the Blessed One. …and so on….

“Puna [M 2.0300] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā uppajjanti…pe… puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno manasā dhammaṃ viññāya uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā sarasaṅkappā saṃyojaniyā. Tañce bhikkhu nādhivāseti pajahati vinodeti byantīkaroti anabhāvaṃ gameti, veditabbametaṃ[V 2.0084], bhikkhave, bhikkhunā – ‘na parihāyāmi kusalehi dhammehi’. Aparihānañhetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatāti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, aparihānadhammo hoti.

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has tasted a flavor with the tongue… and so on… Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has known a mind-object with the mind, evil, unwholesome, discursive thoughts connected with the fetters arise. If that bhikkhu does not consent to them, but abandons them, dispels them, makes an end of them, and brings them to non-existence, it should be understood by that bhikkhu: ‘I am not declining from wholesome qualities.’ For this has been called ‘non-decline’ by the Blessed One. Thus, bhikkhus, there is the quality of non-decline.”

“Katamāni [T 4.0097] ca, bhikkhave, cha abhibhāyatanāni? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā nuppajjanti pāpakā akusalā sarasaṅkappā saṃyojaniyā. Veditabbametaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā – ‘abhibhūtametaṃ āyatanaṃ’. Abhibhāyatanañhetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatāti…pe… puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno manasā dhammaṃ viññāya nuppajjanti pāpakā akusalā dhammā sarasaṅkappā saṃyojaniyā. Veditabbametaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā – ‘abhibhūtametaṃ āyatanaṃ’. Abhibhāyatanañhetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatāti. Imāni vuccanti, bhikkhave, cha abhibhāyatanānī”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

“And what, bhikkhus, are the six bases of mastery? Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu sees a form with the eye, evil, unwholesome, discursive thoughts connected with the fetters do not arise. It should be understood by that bhikkhu: ‘This sense base has been mastered.’ For this has been called a ‘base of mastery’ by the Blessed One. …and so on… Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has known a mind-object with the mind, evil, unwholesome, discursive thoughts connected with the fetters do not arise. It should be understood by that bhikkhu: ‘This sense base has been mastered.’ For this has been called a ‘base of mastery’ by the Blessed One. These, bhikkhus, are called the six bases of mastery.” The Third.

4. Pamādavihārīsuttaṃ

4. 4. The Discourse on One Who Dwells Heedlessly

97. “Pamādavihāriñca [P 4.0078] vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi appamādavihāriñca. Taṃ suṇātha. Kathañca, bhikkhave, pamādavihārī hoti? Cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutassa, bhikkhave, viharato cittaṃ byāsiñcati byāsiccati (sī. syā. kaṃ.). Cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu tassa byāsittacittassa pāmojjaṃ na hoti. Pāmojje asati pīti na hoti. Pītiyā asati passaddhi na hoti. Passaddhiyā asati dukkhaṃ hoti. Dukkhino cittaṃ na samādhiyati. Asamāhite citte dhammā na pātubhavanti. Dhammānaṃ apātubhāvā pamādavihārī tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati…pe… jivhindriyaṃ asaṃvutassa, bhikkhave, viharato cittaṃ byāsiñcati jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu, tassa byāsittacittassa…pe… pamādavihārī tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati…pe… manindriyaṃ asaṃvutassa, bhikkhave, viharato cittaṃ byāsiñcati manoviññeyyesu dhammesu, tassa byāsittacittassa pāmojjaṃ na hoti. Pāmojje asati pīti na hoti[T 4.0098]. Pītiyā asati passaddhi na hoti. Passaddhiyā asati dukkhaṃ hoti. Dukkhino cittaṃ na samādhiyati. Asamāhite citte dhammā na pātubhavanti[M 2.0301]. Dhammānaṃ apātubhāvā pamādavihārī tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, pamādavihārī hoti.

97. “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you about one who dwells heedlessly and one who dwells heedfully. Listen to that. And how, bhikkhus, does one dwell heedlessly? For a bhikkhu who dwells with the eye faculty unrestrained, the mind is sullied by defilements regarding forms cognizable by the eye. For one whose mind is sullied, gladness is not present. When gladness is absent, rapture is not present. When rapture is absent, tranquility is not present. When tranquility is absent, there is suffering. For one who is suffering, the mind does not become concentrated. When the mind is not concentrated, wholesome states do not become manifest. Due to the non-manifestation of wholesome states, one is reckoned as dwelling heedlessly. … For a bhikkhu who dwells with the tongue faculty unrestrained, the mind is sullied by defilements regarding tastes cognizable by the tongue; for one whose mind is sullied… one is reckoned as dwelling heedlessly. … For a bhikkhu who dwells with the mind faculty unrestrained, the mind is sullied by defilements regarding mental objects cognizable by the mind. For one whose mind is sullied, gladness is not present. When gladness is absent, rapture is not present. When rapture is absent, tranquility is not present. When tranquility is absent, there is suffering. For one who is suffering, the mind does not become concentrated. When the mind is not concentrated, wholesome states do not become manifest. Due to the non-manifestation of wholesome states, one is reckoned as dwelling heedlessly. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one dwells heedlessly.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, appamādavihārī hoti? Cakkhundriyaṃ saṃvutassa, bhikkhave, viharato [V 2.0085] cittaṃ na byāsiñcati cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu, tassa abyāsittacittassa pāmojjaṃ jāyati. Pamuditassa pīti jāyati. Pītimanassa kāyo passambhati. Passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ viharati. Sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Samāhite citte dhammā [P 4.0079] pātubhavanti. Dhammānaṃ pātubhāvā appamādavihārī tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati…pe… jivhindriyaṃ saṃvutassa, bhikkhave, viharato cittaṃ na byāsiñcati…pe… appamādavihārī tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Manindriyaṃ saṃvutassa, bhikkhave, viharato cittaṃ na byāsiñcati, manoviññeyyesu dhammesu, tassa abyāsittacittassa pāmojjaṃ jāyati. Pamuditassa pīti jāyati. Pītimanassa kāyo passambhati. Passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ viharati. Sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Samāhite citte dhammā pātubhavanti. Dhammānaṃ pātubhāvā appamādavihārī tveva saṅkhaṃ gacchati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, appamādavihārī hotī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

“And how, bhikkhus, does one dwell heedfully? For a bhikkhu who dwells with the eye faculty restrained, the mind is not sullied by defilements regarding forms cognizable by the eye. For one whose mind is not sullied, gladness arises. For one who is gladdened, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body dwells happily. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. When the mind is concentrated, wholesome states become manifest. Due to the manifestation of wholesome states, one is reckoned as dwelling heedfully. … For a bhikkhu who dwells with the tongue faculty restrained, the mind is not sullied… one is reckoned as dwelling heedfully. For a bhikkhu who dwells with the mind faculty restrained, the mind is not sullied by defilements regarding mental objects cognizable by the mind; for one whose mind is not sullied, gladness arises. For one who is gladdened, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body dwells happily. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. When the mind is concentrated, wholesome states become manifest. Due to the manifestation of wholesome states, one is reckoned as dwelling heedfully. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that one dwells heedfully.” The fourth.

5. Saṃvarasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Restraint

98. “Saṃvarañca vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi, asaṃvarañca. Taṃ suṇātha. Kathañca, bhikkhave, asaṃvaro hoti? Santi, bhikkhave, cakkhuviññeyyā [T 4.0099] rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati, veditabbametaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā – ‘parihāyāmi kusalehi dhammehi’. Parihānañhetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatāti…pe… santi, bhikkhave, jivhāviññeyyā rasā…pe… santi, bhikkhave, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati, veditabbametaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā – ‘parihāyāmi kusalehi dhammehi’. Parihānañhetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatāti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, asaṃvaro hoti.

98. “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you restraint and non-restraint. Listen to that. And how, bhikkhus, is there non-restraint? There are, bhikkhus, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, it should be understood by that bhikkhu thus: ‘I am declining from wholesome states.’ For this has been spoken of by the Blessed One as decline. … There are, bhikkhus, tastes cognizable by the tongue… … There are, bhikkhus, mental objects cognizable by the mind that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, it should be understood by that bhikkhu thus: ‘I am declining from wholesome states.’ For this has been spoken of by the Blessed One as decline. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is non-restraint.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, saṃvaro hoti? Santi, bhikkhave, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati, veditabbametaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā – ‘na parihāyāmi kusalehi [P 4.0080] dhammehi’. Aparihānañhetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatāti [M 2.0302] …pe… santi, bhikkhave, jivhāviññeyyā rasā…pe… santi, bhikkhave, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā [V 2.0086] rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati, veditabbametaṃ bhikkhunā – ‘na parihāyāmi kusalehi dhammehi’. Aparihānañhetaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatāti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, saṃvaro hotī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

“And how, bhikkhus, is there restraint? There are, bhikkhus, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain attached to them, it should be understood by that bhikkhu thus: ‘I am not declining from wholesome states.’ For this has been spoken of by the Blessed One as non-decline. … There are, bhikkhus, tastes cognizable by the tongue… … There are, bhikkhus, mental objects cognizable by the mind that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain attached to them, it should be understood by that bhikkhu thus: ‘I am not declining from wholesome states.’ For this has been spoken of by the Blessed One as non-decline. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that there is restraint.” The fifth.

6. Samādhisuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Concentration

99. “Samādhiṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvetha. Samāhito, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Kiñca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti? ‘Cakkhu anicca’nti yathābhūtaṃ [T 4.0100] pajānāti; ‘rūpā aniccā’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; ‘cakkhuviññāṇaṃ anicca’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; ‘cakkhusamphasso anicco’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. ‘Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi anicca’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe… ‘mano anicca’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Dhammā… manoviññāṇaṃ… manosamphasso… ‘yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi anicca’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Samādhiṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvetha. Samāhito, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

99. “Bhikkhus, develop concentration. A concentrated bhikkhu, bhikkhus, understands as it really is. And what does he understand as it really is? He understands as it really is: ‘The eye is impermanent.’ He understands as it really is: ‘Forms are impermanent.’ He understands as it really is: ‘Eye-consciousness is impermanent.’ He understands as it really is: ‘Eye-contact is impermanent.’ He understands as it really is: ‘Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent.’ … He understands as it really is: ‘The mind is impermanent.’ He understands as it really is: ‘Mental phenomena are impermanent.’ He understands as it really is: ‘Mind-consciousness is impermanent.’ He understands as it really is: ‘Mind-contact is impermanent.’ He understands as it really is: ‘Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent.’ Bhikkhus, develop concentration. A concentrated bhikkhu, bhikkhus, understands as it really is.” The sixth.

7. Paṭisallānasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on Seclusion

100. “Paṭisallāne paṭisallānaṃ (sī. pī. ka.), paṭisallīnā (syā. kaṃ.), bhikkhave, yogamāpajjatha. Paṭisallīno, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Kiñca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti? ‘Cakkhu anicca’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; ‘rūpā aniccā’ti [P 4.0081] yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; ‘cakkhuviññāṇaṃ anicca’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; ‘cakkhusamphasso anicco’ti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. ‘Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi anicca’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe… ‘yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi anicca’nti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Paṭisallāne, bhikkhave, yogamāpajjatha. Paṭisallīno, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

100. “Bhikkhus, apply yourselves to the endeavor in seclusion. A secluded bhikkhu, bhikkhus, understands things as they really are. And what does he understand as they really are? He understands as it really is: ‘The eye is impermanent.’ He understands as it really is: ‘Forms are impermanent.’ He understands as it really is: ‘Eye-consciousness is impermanent.’ He understands as it really is: ‘Eye-contact is impermanent.’ He understands as it really is: ‘Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent.’ … He understands as it really is: ‘Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent.’ Bhikkhus, apply yourselves to the endeavor in seclusion. A secluded bhikkhu, bhikkhus, understands things as they really are.”

8. Paṭhamanatumhākaṃsuttaṃ

8. The First Discourse on What Is Not Yours

101. “Yaṃ [V 2.0087] yampi (pī. ka.), bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ, taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Kiñca, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ[M 2.0303]. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati[T 4.0101]. Rūpā na tumhākaṃ. Te pajahatha. Te vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissanti. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Cakkhusamphasso na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. So vo pahīno hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Sotaṃ na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Saddā na tumhākaṃ. Te pajahatha. Te vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissanti. Sotaviññāṇaṃ na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Sotasamphasso na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. So vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Yampidaṃ sotasamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Ghānaṃ na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Gandhā na tumhākaṃ. Te pajahatha. Te vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissanti. Ghānaviññāṇaṃ na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Ghānasamphasso na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. So vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Yampidaṃ ghānasamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati.

101. “Bhikkhus, abandon what is not yours. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. And what, bhikkhus, is not yours? The eye, bhikkhus, is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Forms are not yours. Abandon them. Those, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Eye-consciousness is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Eye-contact is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. The ear is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Sounds are not yours. Abandon them. Those, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Ear-consciousness is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Ear-contact is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Whatever feeling arises conditioned by ear-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. The nose is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Odors are not yours. Abandon them. Those, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Nose-consciousness is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Nose-contact is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Whatever feeling arises conditioned by nose-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness.

Jivhā na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Sā vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Rasā na tumhākaṃ. Te pajahatha. Te vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissanti. Jivhāviññāṇaṃ na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Jivhāsamphasso na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. So vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Yampidaṃ jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ [P 4.0082] sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati [V 2.0088] …pe….

The tongue is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Tastes are not yours. Abandon them. Those, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Tongue-consciousness is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Tongue-contact is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. …

Mano na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. So vo pahīno hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Dhammā na tumhākaṃ. Te pajahatha. Te vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissanti. Manoviññāṇaṃ na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Manosamphasso na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. So vo pahīno hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi na [T 4.0102] tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati.

The mind is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Mental objects are not yours. Abandon them. Those, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Mind-consciousness is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Mind-contact is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Whatever feeling—be it pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by mind-contact, that too is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yaṃ imasmiṃ jetavane tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṃ taṃ jano hareyya vā ḍaheyya vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā kareyya, api nu tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘amhe jano harati vā ḍahati vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karotī’”ti?

“Suppose, bhikkhus, people were to carry away, burn, or do with as they see fit the grass, wood, branches, and leaves in this Jeta's Grove, would it occur to you: ‘People are carrying us away, burning us, or doing with us as they see fit’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Taṃ kissa hetu”?

“For what reason?”

“Na hi no etaṃ, bhante, attā vā attaniyaṃ vā”ti.

“Because, venerable sir, that is neither our self nor what belongs to our self.”

“Evameva kho, bhikkhave, cakkhu na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Rūpā na tumhākaṃ… cakkhuviññāṇaṃ… cakkhusamphasso…pe… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“In the same way, bhikkhus, the eye is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Forms are not yours… eye-consciousness… eye-contact… Whatever feeling—be it pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by mind-contact, that too is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness.”

9. Dutiyanatumhākaṃsuttaṃ

9. The Second Discourse on What Is Not Yours

102. “Yaṃ[M 2.0304][V 2.0089], bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Kiñca, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Rūpā na tumhākaṃ. Te pajahatha. Te vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissanti. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Cakkhusamphasso na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. So vo pahīno hitāya sukhāya bhavissati…pe… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi na tumhākaṃ. Taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo [T 4.0103] pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Yampi, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ, taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti. Navamaṃ.

102. “Bhikkhus, whatever is not yours, abandon it. That, having been abandoned by you, will be for your welfare and happiness. And what, bhikkhus, is not yours? The eye, bhikkhus, is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned by you, will be for your welfare and happiness. Forms are not yours. Abandon them. Those, having been abandoned by you, will be for your welfare and happiness. Eye-consciousness is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned by you, will be for your welfare and happiness. Eye-contact is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned by you, will be for your welfare and happiness. … Whatever feeling—be it pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by mind-contact, that too is not yours. Abandon it. That, having been abandoned by you, will be for your welfare and happiness. Whatever, bhikkhus, is not yours, abandon it. That, having been abandoned by you, will be for your welfare and happiness.” The Ninth.

10. Udakasuttaṃ

10. The Udaka Sutta

103. “Udako [P 4.0083] uddako (sī. pī.) sudaṃ, bhikkhave, rāmaputto evaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati – ‘idaṃ jātu vedagū, idaṃ jātu sabbajī sabbaji (pī.), idaṃ jātu apalikhataṃ gaṇḍamūlaṃ palikhaṇi’nti. Taṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, udako rāmaputto avedagūyeva samāno ‘vedagūsmī’ti bhāsati, asabbajīyeva samāno ‘sabbajīsmī’ti bhāsati, apalikhataṃyeva gaṇḍamūlaṃ palikhataṃ me ‘gaṇḍamūla’nti bhāsati. Idha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sammā vadamāno vadeyya – ‘idaṃ jātu vedagū, idaṃ jātu sabbajī, idaṃ jātu apalikhataṃ gaṇḍamūlaṃ palikhaṇi’”nti.

103. “Bhikkhus, Udaka, the son of Rāma, would speak these words: ‘I am certainly a knower, I am certainly the all-conqueror, I have certainly dug up the undug root of the boil.’ But, bhikkhus, Udaka, the son of Rāma, being himself not a knower, says, ‘I am a knower’; being himself not an all-conqueror, says, ‘I am an all-conqueror’; the root of the boil being undug, he says, ‘The root of the boil has been dug up by me.’ Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu speaking rightly would say: ‘I am certainly a knower, I am certainly the all-conqueror, I have certainly dug up the undug root of the boil.’”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, vedagū hoti? Yato kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti; evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vedagū hoti.

“And how, bhikkhus, is one a knower? When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu truly understands the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to the six bases of contact, then, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is a knower.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbajī hoti? Yato kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā anupādāvimutto hoti; evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbajī hoti.

“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu an all-conqueror? When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having truly understood the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to the six bases of contact, is liberated without clinging, then, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is an all-conqueror.”

“Kathañca[V 2.0090], bhikkhave, bhikkhuno apalikhataṃ gaṇḍamūlaṃ palikhataṃ hoti? Gaṇḍoti kho, bhikkhave, imassetaṃ cātumahābhūtikassa kāyassa adhivacanaṃ [M 2.0305] mātāpettikasambhavassa odanakummāsūpacayassa aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammassa[T 4.0104]. Gaṇḍamūlanti kho, bhikkhave, taṇhāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Yato kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno taṇhā pahīnā hoti ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā [P 4.0084] anabhāvaṅkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā; evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno apalikhataṃ gaṇḍamūlaṃ palikhataṃ hoti.

“And how, bhikkhus, is it that for a bhikkhu the undug root of the boil is dug up? ‘Boil,’ bhikkhus, is a designation for this body composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, nourished on rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, to being rubbed and massaged, to breaking apart and dissolution. ‘Root of the boil,’ bhikkhus, is a designation for craving. When, bhikkhus, craving has been abandoned by a bhikkhu, its root cut off, made like a palm stump, obliterated, so that it is no longer subject to future arising; then, bhikkhus, for that bhikkhu the undug root of the boil is dug up.”

“Udako sudaṃ, bhikkhave, rāmaputto evaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati – ‘idaṃ jātu vedagū, idaṃ jātu sabbajī, idaṃ jātu apalikhataṃ gaṇḍamūlaṃ palikhaṇi’nti. Taṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, udako rāmaputto avedagūyeva samāno ‘vedagūsmī’ti bhāsati, asabbajīyeva samāno ‘sabbajīsmī’ti bhāsati; apalikhataṃyeva gaṇḍamūlaṃ ‘palikhataṃ me gaṇḍamūla’nti bhāsati. Idha kho taṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sammā vadamāno vadeyya – ‘idaṃ jātu vedagū, idaṃ jātu sabbajī, idaṃ jātu apalikhataṃ gaṇḍamūlaṃ palikhaṇi’”nti. Dasamaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, Udaka, the son of Rāma, would speak these words: ‘I am certainly a knower, I am certainly the all-conqueror, I have certainly dug up the undug root of the boil.’ But, bhikkhus, Udaka, the son of Rāma, being himself not a knower, says, ‘I am a knower’; being himself not an all-conqueror, says, ‘I am an all-conqueror’; the root of the boil being undug, he says, ‘The root of the boil has been dug up by me.’ Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu speaking rightly would say: ‘I am certainly a knower, I am certainly the all-conqueror, I have certainly dug up the undug root of the boil.’” The Tenth.

Saḷavaggo dasamo.

The Saḷa Chapter, the fifth, is finished.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of this is:

Dve saṃgayhā parihānaṃ, pamādavihārī ca saṃvaro;

Samādhi paṭisallānaṃ, dve natumhākena uddakoti.

Two Saṃgayha, Parihāna, Pamādavihārī, and Saṃvara; Samādhi, Paṭisallāna, two Na Tumhākaṃ, and Udaka.

Saḷāyatanavagge dutiyapaṇṇāsako samatto.

The second group of fifty in the Chapter on the Six Sense Bases is completed.

Tassa vagguddānaṃ –

The summary of the chapters is:

Avijjā migajālañca, gilānaṃ channaṃ catutthakaṃ;

Saḷavaggena paññāsaṃ, dutiyo paṇṇāsako ayanti.

Avijjā, Migajāla, Gilāna, and Channa as the fourth; with the Saḷa chapter, this makes fifty. This is the second group of fifty.

Paṭhamasatakaṃ.

The First Hundred.

11. Yogakkhemivaggo

11. The Chapter on Security from Bondage

1. Yogakkhemisuttaṃ

1. The Sutta on Security from Bondage

104. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0091]. “Yogakkhemipariyāyaṃ [T 4.0105][P 4.0085] vo, bhikkhave, dhammapariyāyaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, yogakkhemipariyāyo dhammapariyāyo? Santi, bhikkhave, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā [M 2.0306] piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Te tathāgatassa pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṅkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā. Tesañca pahānāya akkhāsi yogaṃ, tasmā tathāgato ‘yogakkhemī’ti vuccati…pe… santi, bhikkhave, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Te tathāgatassa pahīnā ucchinnamūlā tālāvatthukatā anabhāvaṅkatā āyatiṃ anuppādadhammā. Tesañca pahānāya akkhāsi yogaṃ, tasmā tathāgato ‘yogakkhemī’ti vuccati. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, yogakkhemipariyāyo dhammapariyāyo”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

104. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma exposition on security from the yogas. Listen to it. And what, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma exposition on security from the yogas? There are, bhikkhus, forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, agreeable, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, enticing. These have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future. And for their abandonment, he has taught the striving; therefore the Tathāgata is called ‘one who is secure from the yogas.’ … There are, bhikkhus, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind—desirable, agreeable, pleasing, endearing, connected with sensual desire, enticing. These have been abandoned by the Tathāgata, cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, brought to non-existence, and are of a nature not to arise again in the future. And for their abandonment, he has taught the striving; therefore the Tathāgata is called ‘one who is secure from the yogas.’ This, bhikkhus, is the Dhamma exposition on security from the yogas.” The First.

2. Upādāyasuttaṃ

2. The Sutta on Clinging

105. “Kismiṃ nu kho, bhikkhave, sati kiṃ upādāya uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkha”nti?

105. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, does internal pleasure and pain arise?”

“Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā…pe….

“Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One…”

“Cakkhusmiṃ kho, bhikkhave, sati cakkhuṃ upādāya uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ…pe… manasmiṃ sati manaṃ upādāya uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ. Taṃ [T 4.0106] kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, cakkhu niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“Monks, when the eye exists, by clinging to the eye, internal pleasure and pain arise. …When the mind exists, by clinging to the mind, internal pleasure and pain arise. What do you think, monks, is the eye permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ, bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“Suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya uppajjeyya ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkha”nti?

“But regarding that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, could internal pleasure and pain arise without clinging to it?”

“No hetaṃ bhante”…pe….

“Surely not, venerable sir.” …

“Jivhā [P 4.0086] niccā vā aniccā vā”ti?

“Is the tongue permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccā, bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“Suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ [V 2.0092] panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya uppajjeyya ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkha”nti?

“But regarding that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, could internal pleasure and pain arise without clinging to it?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”…pe….

“Surely not, venerable sir.” …

“Mano nicco vā anicco vā”ti?

“Is the mind permanent or impermanent?”

“Anicco, bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“But is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“Suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya uppajjeyya ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkha”nti?

“But regarding that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, could internal pleasure and pain arise without clinging to it?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Surely not, venerable sir.”

“Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati…pe… manasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

“Seeing thus, monks, an instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye…becomes disenchanted with the mind. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’”

3. Dukkhasamudayasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on the Arising of Suffering

106. “Dukkhassa[V 2.0093], bhikkhave, samudayañca atthaṅgamañca desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, dukkhassa samudayo? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ[M 2.0307]. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Ayaṃ dukkhassa samudayo…pe… [T 4.0107] jivhañca paṭicca rase ca uppajjati jivhāviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Ayaṃ dukkhassa samudayo…pe… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, dukkhassa samudayo.

106. “Monks, I shall teach the arising and the cessation of suffering. Listen to that. And what, monks, is the arising of suffering? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises. This is the arising of suffering. … Dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises. This is the arising of suffering. … Dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises. This, indeed, monks, is the arising of suffering.”

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, dukkhassa atthaṅgamo? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho; bhavanirodhā jātinirodho; jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā nirujjhanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti. Ayaṃ dukkhassa atthaṅgamo…pe… jivhañca paṭicca rase ca uppajjati jivhāviññāṇaṃ…pe… manañca [P 4.0087] paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho[T 4.0108]; bhavanirodhā jātinirodho; jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā nirujjhanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, dukkhassa atthaṅgamo”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

“And what, monks, is the cessation of suffering? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises. Through the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, there is the cessation of clinging; through the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence; through the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth; through the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This is the cessation of suffering. … Dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises… … Dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises. Through the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, there is the cessation of clinging; through the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence; through the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth; through the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This, indeed, monks, is the cessation of suffering.”

4. Lokasamudayasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on the Arising of the World

107. “Lokassa, bhikkhave, samudayañca atthaṅgamañca desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, lokassa samudayo? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā; taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ; upādānapaccayā bhavo; bhavapaccayā jāti; jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā sambhavanti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, lokassa samudayo [V 2.0094] …pe… jivhañca paṭicca rase ca uppajjati jivhāviññāṇaṃ…pe… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā; taṇhāpaccayā upādānaṃ; upādānapaccayā bhavo[M 2.0308]; bhavapaccayā jāti; jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā sambhavanti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, lokassa samudayo.

107. “Monks, I shall teach the arising and the cessation of the world. Listen to that. And what, monks, is the arising of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises; conditioned by craving, clinging arises; conditioned by clinging, existence arises; conditioned by existence, birth arises; conditioned by birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. This, indeed, monks, is the arising of the world. … Dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises… … Dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The coming together of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises; conditioned by craving, clinging arises; conditioned by clinging, existence arises; conditioned by existence, birth arises; conditioned by birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. This, indeed, monks, is the arising of the world.”

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, lokassa atthaṅgamo? Cakkhuñca paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā bhavanirodho[T 4.0109]; bhavanirodhā jātinirodho; jātinirodhā jarāmaraṇaṃ sokaparidevadukkhadomanassupāyāsā nirujjhanti. Evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, lokassa atthaṅgamo…pe… jivhañca paṭicca rase ca uppajjati…pe… manañca paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ saṅgati phasso. Phassapaccayā vedanā; vedanāpaccayā taṇhā. Tassāyeva taṇhāya asesavirāganirodhā upādānanirodho; upādānanirodhā…pe… evametassa kevalassa dukkhakkhandhassa nirodho hoti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, lokassa atthaṅgamo”ti. Catutthaṃ.

“And what, Bhikkhus, is the cessation of the world? Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises. Through the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, clinging ceases; through the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; through the cessation of existence, birth ceases; through the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This, indeed, Bhikkhus, is the cessation of the world. … Dependent on the tongue and tastes… … Dependent on the mind and mental objects, mind-consciousness arises. The meeting of the three is contact. Conditioned by contact, feeling arises; conditioned by feeling, craving arises. Through the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, clinging ceases; through the cessation of clinging… Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. This, indeed, Bhikkhus, is the cessation of the world.” Fourth.

5. Seyyohamasmisuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on 'I Am Superior'

108. “Kismiṃ [P 4.0088] nu kho, bhikkhave, sati kiṃ upādāya kiṃ abhinivissa seyyohamasmīti vā hoti, sadisohamasmīti vā hoti, hīnohamasmīti vā hotī”ti?

108. “Bhikkhus, when what exists, by clinging to what, by adhering to what, does conceit arise as: ‘I am superior,’ or ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior’?”

“Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā.

“Venerable sir, for us, the teachings have the Blessed One as their root.”

“Cakkhusmiṃ kho, bhikkhave, sati cakkhuṃ upādāya cakkhuṃ abhinivissa seyyohamasmīti vā hoti, sadisohamasmīti vā hoti, hīnohamasmīti vā hoti…pe… jivhāya sati…pe… manasmiṃ sati manaṃ upādāya manaṃ abhinivissa seyyohamasmīti vā hoti, sadisohamasmīti vā hoti, hīnohamasmīti vā hoti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, cakkhu niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“Bhikkhus, when the eye exists, by clinging to the eye, by adhering to the eye, conceit arises as: ‘I am superior,’ or ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior.’ … When the tongue exists… when the mind exists, by clinging to the mind, by adhering to the mind, conceit arises as: ‘I am superior,’ or ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior.’ What do you think, Bhikkhus, is the eye permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ[V 2.0095], bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“Suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya seyyohamasmīti vā assa, sadisohamasmīti vā assa, hīnohamasmīti [T 4.0110] vā assā”ti?

“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—without clinging to it, would conceit arise as: ‘I am superior,’ or ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”…pe… jivhā… kāyo nicco vā anicco vā”ti?

“Certainly not, venerable sir. … Is the tongue… is the body permanent or impermanent?”

“Anicco, bhante”…pe….

“Impermanent, venerable sir.” …

“Mano nicco vā anicco vā”ti?

“Is the mind permanent or impermanent?”

“Anicco, bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā [M 2.0309] taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“But that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“Suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, api nu taṃ anupādāya seyyohamasmīti vā assa, sadisohamasmīti vā assa, hīnohamasmīti vā assā”ti?

“But that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—without clinging to it, would conceit arise as: ‘I am superior,’ or ‘I am equal,’ or ‘I am inferior’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati…pe… manasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

“Seeing thus, Bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye… and becomes disenchanted with the mind. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When he is liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’” Fifth.

6. Saṃyojaniyasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Things Conducive to Fetters

109. “Saṃyojaniye [V 2.0096][P 4.0089] ca, bhikkhave, dhamme desessāmi saṃyojanañca. Taṃ suṇātha. Katame ca, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyā dhammā, katamañca saṃyojanaṃ? Cakkhuṃ, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyo dhammo. Yo tattha chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ…pe… jivhā saṃyojaniyo dhammo…pe… mano saṃyojaniyo dhammo. Yo tattha chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, saṃyojaniyā dhammā, idaṃ saṃyojana”nti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

109. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the things conducive to fetters and the fetter itself. Listen to that. And what, Bhikkhus, are the things conducive to fetters, and what is the fetter? The eye, Bhikkhus, is a thing conducive to fetters. Whatever desire and lust there is in relation to it, that is the fetter there. … The tongue… The mind is a thing conducive to fetters. Whatever desire and lust there is in relation to it, that is the fetter there. These, Bhikkhus, are called the things conducive to fetters, and this is the fetter.” Sixth.

7. Upādāniyasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on the Bases for Clinging

110. “Upādāniye ca, bhikkhave, dhamme desessāmi upādānañca. Taṃ suṇātha. Katame ca, bhikkhave, upādāniyā dhammā, katamañca upādānaṃ[T 4.0111]? Cakkhuṃ, bhikkhave, upādāniyo dhammo. Yo tattha chandarāgo, taṃ tattha upādānaṃ…pe… jivhā upādāniyo dhammo…pe… mano upādāniyo dhammo. Yo tattha chandarāgo, taṃ tattha upādānaṃ. Ime vuccanti, bhikkhave, upādāniyā dhammā, idaṃ upādāna”nti. Sattamaṃ.
