A bhikkhu with clinging, householder, does not attain final extinguishment. … There are, householder, tastes cognizable by the tongue… There are, householder, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind—desirable, agreeable, pleasing, of a lovable nature, connected with sensual desire, and enticing. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains adhering to them, his consciousness becomes dependent on them, with that as its object of clinging. A bhikkhu with clinging, householder, does not attain final extinguishment. This, householder, is the cause, this is the condition, whereby some beings here do not attain final extinguishment in this very life.”

“Santi [T 4.0138] ca kho, gahapati, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā, iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā [V 2.0117] rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ anabhinandato anabhivadato anajjhosāya tiṭṭhato na tannissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ hoti, na tadupādānaṃ. Anupādāno, gahapati, bhikkhu parinibbāyati…pe… santi kho, gahapati, jivhāviññeyyā rasā…pe… santi kho, gahapati, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati, tassa taṃ anabhinandato anabhivadato anajjhosāya tiṭṭhato. Na tannissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ hoti, na tadupādānaṃ. Anupādāno[M 2.0328], gahapati, bhikkhu parinibbāyati. Ayaṃ kho, gahapati, hetu ayaṃ paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva dhamme parinibbāyantī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“Furthermore, householder, there are forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, agreeable, pleasing, of a lovable nature, connected with sensual desire, and enticing. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain adhering to them, his consciousness does not become dependent on them, nor does it cling to them. A bhikkhu without clinging, householder, attains final extinguishment. … There are, householder, tastes cognizable by the tongue… There are, householder, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind—desirable, agreeable, pleasing, of a lovable nature, connected with sensual desire, and enticing. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain adhering to them, his consciousness does not become dependent on them, nor does it cling to them. A bhikkhu without clinging, householder, attains final extinguishment. This, householder, is the cause, this is the condition, whereby some beings here attain final extinguishment in this very life.” The First.

2. Vajjīsuttaṃ

2. 2. The Vajjī Sutta

125. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vajjīsu viharati hatthigāme. Atha kho uggo gahapati hatthigāmako yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho uggo gahapati hatthigāmako bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ko nu kho, bhante, hetu ko paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva dhamme no parinibbāyanti? Ko pana, bhante hetu ko paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva dhamme parinibbāyantī”ti? (Yathā purimasuttantaṃ, evaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ). Ayaṃ [P 4.0110] kho, gahapati, hetu ayaṃ paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva [T 4.0139] dhamme parinibbāyantīti. Dutiyaṃ.

125. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Vajjians at Hatthigāma. Then the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma approached the Blessed One; having approached, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the householder Ugga of Hatthigāma said this to the Blessed One: “What now, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition, whereby some beings here do not attain final extinguishment in this very life? And what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition, whereby some beings here do attain final extinguishment in this very life?” (This is to be elaborated as in the previous discourse.) “This, householder, is the cause, this is the condition, whereby some beings here do attain final extinguishment in this very life.” The Second.

3. Nāḷandasuttaṃ

3. 3. The Nāḷanda Sutta

126. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā nāḷandāyaṃ viharati pāvārikambavane. Atha kho, upāli gahapati, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho, upāli gahapati, bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ko nu kho, bhante, hetu, ko paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva dhamme no parinibbāyanti? Ko pana, bhante, hetu, ko paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva dhamme parinibbāyantī”ti? (Yathā purimasuttantaṃ, evaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ). Ayaṃ kho, gahapati, hetu ayaṃ paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva dhamme parinibbāyantīti. Tatiyaṃ.

126. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nāḷandā in Pāvārika’s mango grove. Then the householder Upāli approached the Blessed One… and said to him: “What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition, whereby some beings here do not attain final extinguishment in this very life? And what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition, whereby some beings here do attain final extinguishment in this very life?” (This is to be elaborated as in the previous discourse.) “This, householder, is the cause, this is the condition, whereby some beings here do attain final extinguishment in this very life.” The Third.

4. Bhāradvājasuttaṃ

4. 4. The Bhāradvāja Sutta

127. Ekaṃ [V 2.0118] samayaṃ āyasmā piṇḍolabhāradvājo kosambiyaṃ viharati ghositārāme. Atha kho rājā udeno yenāyasmā piṇḍolabhāradvājo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā piṇḍolabhāradvājena saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho rājā udeno āyasmantaṃ piṇḍolabhāradvājaṃ etadavoca – “ko nu kho, bho bhāradvāja, hetu [M 2.0329] ko paccayo yenime daharā bhikkhū susū susu (sī. ka.) kāḷakesā bhadrena yobbanena samannāgatā paṭhamena vayasā anikīḷitāvino kāmesu yāvajīvaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ caranti, addhānañca āpādentī”ti? “Vuttaṃ kho etaṃ, mahārāja, tena [T 4.0140] bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena – ‘etha tumhe, bhikkhave, mātumattīsu mātucittaṃ upaṭṭhapetha, bhaginimattīsu [P 4.0111] bhaginicittaṃ upaṭṭhapetha, dhītumattīsu dhītucittaṃ upaṭṭhapethā’ti. Ayaṃ kho, mahārāja, hetu, ayaṃ paccayo yenime daharā bhikkhū susū kāḷakesā bhadrena yobbanena samannāgatā paṭhamena vayasā anikīḷitāvino kāmesu yāvajīvaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ caranti, addhānañca āpādentī”ti.

127. On one occasion the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja was dwelling at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. Then King Udena approached the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja. After exchanging pleasant and memorable greetings, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, King Udena said to the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja: “What, venerable Bhāradvāja, is the cause, what is the condition, whereby these young monks—youthful, with black hair, endowed with fine youth, in the first stage of life—who have not indulged in sensual pleasures, lead the perfectly complete and pure holy life for their whole life and sustain it for a long time?” “Great king, this has been said by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One: ‘Come, monks, towards those of a mother's age, establish the mind of a mother; towards those of a sister's age, establish the mind of a sister; towards those of a daughter's age, establish the mind of a daughter.’ This, great king, is the cause, this is the condition, whereby these young monks—youthful, with black hair, endowed with fine youth, in the first stage of life—who have not indulged in sensual pleasures, lead the perfectly complete and pure holy life for their whole life and sustain it for a long time.”

“Lolaṃ loḷaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) kho, bho bhāradvāja, cittaṃ. Appekadā mātumattīsupi lobhadhammā uppajjanti, bhaginimattīsupi lobhadhammā uppajjanti, dhītumattīsupi lobhadhammā uppajjanti. Atthi nu kho, bho bhāradvāja, añño ca hetu, añño ca paccayo yenime daharā bhikkhū susū kāḷakesā…pe… addhānañca āpādentī”ti?

“The mind is fickle, venerable Bhāradvāja. Sometimes states of greed arise even toward those of a mother's age, states of greed arise toward those of a sister's age, and states of greed arise toward those of a daughter's age. Is there, venerable Bhāradvāja, another cause, another condition, whereby these young monks—youthful, with black hair…—sustain it for a long time?”

“Vuttaṃ kho etaṃ, mahārāja, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena – ‘etha tumhe, bhikkhave, imameva kāyaṃ uddhaṃ pādatalā adho kesamatthakā tacapariyantaṃ pūraṃ nānappakārassa asucino paccavekkhatha – atthi imasmiṃ kāye kesā lomā nakhā dantā taco maṃsaṃ nhāru nahāru (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) aṭṭhi aṭṭhimiñjaṃ aṭṭhimiñjā (sī.) vakkaṃ hadayaṃ yakanaṃ kilomakaṃ pihakaṃ papphāsaṃ antaṃ antaguṇaṃ udariyaṃ karīsaṃ pittaṃ semhaṃ pubbo lohitaṃ sedo medo assu vasā kheḷo siṅghāṇikā lasikā mutta’nti. Ayampi kho, mahārāja, hetu, ayaṃ paccayo yenime daharā bhikkhū susū kāḷakesā…pe… [T 4.0141] addhānañca āpādentī”ti. “Ye te, bho bhāradvāja, bhikkhū bhāvitakāyā bhāvitasīlā bhāvitacittā bhāvitapaññā, tesaṃ taṃ sukaraṃ hoti. Ye ca kho te[V 2.0119], bho bhāradvāja, bhikkhū abhāvitakāyā abhāvitasīlā abhāvitacittā abhāvitapaññā, tesaṃ taṃ dukkaraṃ hoti. Appekadā, bho bhāradvāja, asubhato manasi [M 2.0330] karissāmīti manasi karissāmāti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) subhatova subhato vā (sī.), subhato ca (syā. kaṃ.) āgacchati. Atthi nu kho, bho bhāradvāja[P 4.0112], añño ca kho hetu añño ca paccayo yenime daharā bhikkhū susū kāḷakesā…pe… addhānañca āpādentī”ti?

“Great king, this was spoken by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One: ‘Come, monks, contemplate this very body from the soles of the feet up and from the tips of the hair down, bounded by skin and full of various kinds of impurity: In this body there are head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, pleura, spleen, lungs, intestines, mesentery, stomach contents, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, saliva, mucus, synovial fluid, and urine.’ This too, great king, is a cause, this is a condition, whereby these young monks—youthful, with black hair…—continue for a long time.” “For those monks, venerable Bhāradvāja, who have developed bodies, developed virtue, developed minds, and developed wisdom, that is easy to do. But for those monks, venerable Bhāradvāja, who have undeveloped bodies, undeveloped virtue, undeveloped minds, and undeveloped wisdom, that is difficult to do. Sometimes, venerable Bhāradvāja, one thinks, ‘I will attend to it as unattractive,’ but it comes to be regarded as attractive. Is there, venerable Bhāradvāja, another cause, another condition, whereby these young monks—youthful, with black hair…—continue for a long time?”

“Vuttaṃ kho etaṃ, mahārāja, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena – ‘etha tumhe, bhikkhave, indriyesu guttadvārā viharatha. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā mā nimittaggāhino ahuvattha, mānubyañjanaggāhino. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjatha. Rakkhatha cakkhundriyaṃ; cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatha. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya mā nimittaggāhino ahuvattha, mānubyañjanaggāhino. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ manindriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjatha[T 4.0142]. Rakkhatha manindriyaṃ; manindriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjathā’ti. Ayampi kho, mahārāja, hetu ayaṃ paccayo yenime daharā bhikkhū susū kāḷakesā bhadrena yobbanena samannāgatā paṭhamena vayasā anikīḷitāvino kāmesu yāvajīvaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ caranti, addhānañca āpādentī”ti.

“Great king, this was said by the Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One: ‘Come, monks, dwell guarding the doors of your sense faculties. On seeing a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs or its minor features. For if you dwell with the eye faculty unrestrained, covetousness and displeasure, evil, unwholesome states, might assail you. Practice for its restraint. Guard the eye faculty; undertake restraint of the eye faculty. On hearing a sound with the ear… on smelling an odor with the nose… on tasting a flavor with the tongue… on touching a tangible with the body… on cognizing a mental object with the mind, do not grasp at its signs or its minor features. For if you dwell with the mind faculty unrestrained, covetousness and displeasure, evil, unwholesome states, might assail you. Practice for its restraint. Guard the mind faculty; undertake restraint of the mind faculty.’ This also, great king, is the cause, this is the condition why these young monks—youthful, with black hair, endowed with auspicious youth, in the first stage of life, who have not sported in sensual pleasures, lead the perfectly complete and pure holy life for as long as life lasts and continue for a long time.”

“Acchariyaṃ, bho bhāradvāja; abbhutaṃ, bho bhāradvāja! Yāva subhāsitaṃ cidaṃ yāva subhāsitamidaṃ (sī.), bho bhāradvāja, tena bhagavatā jānatā passatā arahatā sammāsambuddhena. Esova kho, bho bhāradvāja, hetu, esa paccayo yenime daharā bhikkhū susū kāḷakesā bhadrena yobbanena samannāgatā paṭhamena vayasā anikīḷitāvino kāmesu yāvajīvaṃ paripuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ caranti, addhānañca āpādentīti. Ahampi kho, bho ahampi bho (sī. pī.) bhāradvāja, yasmiṃ samaye arakkhiteneva kāyena, arakkhitāya vācāya, arakkhitena cittena, anupaṭṭhitāya satiyā, asaṃvutehi indriyehi antepuraṃ pavisāmi, ativiya maṃ tasmiṃ samaye lobhadhammā parisahanti. Yasmiñca khvāhaṃ, bho bhāradvāja, samaye rakkhiteneva kāyena, rakkhitāya vācāya, rakkhitena cittena, upaṭṭhitāya satiyā[P 4.0113], saṃvutehi indriyehi antepuraṃ pavisāmi, na maṃ tathā [M 2.0331] tasmiṃ samaye lobhadhammā parisahanti. Abhikkantaṃ, bho bhāradvāja; abhikkantaṃ, bho bhāradvāja! Seyyathāpi[V 2.0120], bho bhāradvāja, nikkujjitaṃ nikujjitaṃ (pī.) vā ukkujjeyya[T 4.0143], paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantīti; evamevaṃ bhotā bhāradvājena anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ, bho bhāradvāja, taṃ bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, dhammañca, bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ bhāradvājo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti. Catutthaṃ.

“Wonderful, venerable Bhāradvāja; astonishing, venerable Bhāradvāja! How well-spoken this is, venerable Bhāradvāja, by that Blessed One, who knows and sees, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. This indeed, venerable Bhāradvāja, is the cause, this is the condition why these young monks—youthful, with black hair, endowed with auspicious youth, in the first stage of life, who have not sported in sensual pleasures—lead the perfectly complete and pure holy life for as long as life lasts and continue for a long time. I too, venerable Bhāradvāja, at a time when I enter the inner palace with an unguarded body, unguarded speech, unguarded mind, with unestablished mindfulness, and with unrestrained sense faculties, at that time states of greed greatly overwhelm me. But when, venerable Bhāradvāja, I enter the inner palace with a guarded body, guarded speech, guarded mind, with established mindfulness, and with restrained sense faculties, at that time states of greed do not overwhelm me so. Excellent, venerable Bhāradvāja; excellent, venerable Bhāradvāja! Just as, venerable Bhāradvāja, one might set upright what has been overturned, reveal what has been hidden, show the path to one who is lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes may see forms; even so, the Dhamma has been made clear by you, venerable Bhāradvāja, in many ways. I go for refuge, venerable Bhāradvāja, to that Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of monks. May the venerable Bhāradvāja remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.” The fourth.

5. Soṇasuttaṃ

5. The Soṇa Sutta

128. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Atha kho soṇo gahapatiputto yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho soṇo gahapatiputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ko nu kho, bhante, hetu, ko paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva dhamme no parinibbāyanti? Ko pana, bhante, hetu, ko paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva dhamme parinibbāyantī”ti? (Yathā purimasuttantaṃ, evaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ). Ayaṃ kho, soṇa, hetu, ayaṃ paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva dhamme parinibbāyantīti. Pañcamaṃ.

128. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, at the Squirrels' Feeding Place. Then the householder's son, Soṇa, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the householder's son, Soṇa, said to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition, whereby some beings in this world do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? And what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the condition, whereby some beings in this world do attain final Nibbāna in this very life?” (This should be elaborated as in the previous sutta.) “This, Soṇa, is the cause, this is the condition whereby some beings in this world attain final Nibbāna in this very life.” The fifth.

6. Ghositasuttaṃ

6. The Ghosita Sutta

129. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā ānando kosambiyaṃ viharati ghositārāme. Atha kho ghosito gahapati yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho ghosito gahapati āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “‘dhātunānattaṃ, dhātunānatta’nti[P 4.0114], bhante ānanda, vuccati. Kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, dhātunānattaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā”ti? “Saṃvijjati kho, gahapati, cakkhudhātu, rūpā ca manāpā, cakkhuviññāṇañca [T 4.0144] sukhavedaniyaṃ. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhā vedanā. Saṃvijjati kho, gahapati, cakkhudhātu, rūpā ca amanāpā, cakkhuviññāṇañca dukkhavedaniyaṃ. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati dukkhā vedanā. Saṃvijjati kho, gahapati, cakkhudhātu, rūpā ca manāpā upekkhāvedaniyā, cakkhuviññāṇañca adukkhamasukhavedaniyaṃ. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati adukkhamasukhā [M 2.0332] vedanā…pe… saṃvijjati kho, gahapati, jivhādhātu, rasā ca manāpā, jivhāviññāṇañca sukhavedaniyaṃ. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati [V 2.0121] sukhā vedanā. Saṃvijjati kho, gahapati, jivhādhātu, rasā ca amanāpā, jivhāviññāṇañca dukkhavedaniyaṃ. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati dukkhā vedanā. Saṃvijjati kho, gahapati, jivhādhātu, rasā ca upekkhāvedaniyā, jivhāviññāṇañca adukkhamasukhavedaniyaṃ. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati adukkhamasukhā vedanā…pe… saṃvijjati kho, gahapati, manodhātu, dhammā ca manāpā, manoviññāṇañca sukhavedaniyaṃ. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhā vedanā. Saṃvijjati kho, gahapati, manodhātu, dhammā ca amanāpā, manoviññāṇañca dukkhavedaniyaṃ. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati dukkhā vedanā. Saṃvijjati kho, gahapati, manodhātu, dhammā ca upekkhāvedaniyā, manoviññāṇañca adukkhamasukhavedaniyaṃ. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Ettāvatā kho, gahapati, dhātunānattaṃ vuttaṃ bhagavatā”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

129. On one occasion, the Venerable Ānanda was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Park. Then the householder Ghosita approached the Venerable Ānanda… Seated to one side, the householder Ghosita said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Venerable Ānanda, it is said, ‘diversity of elements, diversity of elements.’ To what extent, venerable sir, has the diversity of elements been spoken of by the Blessed One?” “Householder, there is indeed the eye element, agreeable forms, and eye-consciousness. Dependent on contact to be felt as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises. Householder, there is indeed the eye element, disagreeable forms, and eye-consciousness. Dependent on contact to be felt as painful, a painful feeling arises. Householder, there is indeed the eye element, forms that are a basis for equanimity, and eye-consciousness. Dependent on contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. … Householder, there is indeed the tongue element, agreeable tastes, and tongue-consciousness. Dependent on contact to be felt as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises. Householder, there is indeed the tongue element, disagreeable tastes, and tongue-consciousness. Dependent on contact to be felt as painful, a painful feeling arises. Householder, there is indeed the tongue element, tastes that are a basis for equanimity, and tongue-consciousness. Dependent on contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. … Householder, there is indeed the mind element, agreeable mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness. Dependent on contact to be felt as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises. Householder, there is indeed the mind element, disagreeable mental phenomena, and mind-consciousness. Dependent on contact to be felt as painful, a painful feeling arises. Householder, there is indeed the mind element, mental phenomena that are a basis for equanimity, and mind-consciousness. Dependent on contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. To this extent, householder, the diversity of elements has been spoken of by the Blessed One.”

7. Hāliddikānisuttaṃ

7. The Discourse with Hāliddikāni

130. Ekaṃ [T 4.0145][P 4.0115] samayaṃ āyasmā mahākaccāno avantīsu viharati kuraraghare kulaghare (syā. ka.) papāte pavatte (sī. pī.), sampavatte (syā. kaṃ. ka.) ettheva aṭṭhamapiṭṭhepi pabbate. Atha kho hāliddikāni hāliddakāni (sī. syā. kaṃ.) gahapati yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho hāliddikāni gahapati āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etadavoca – “vuttamidaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā – ‘dhātunānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati phassanānattaṃ; phassanānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati vedanānānatta’nti. Kathaṃ nu kho, bhante, dhātunānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati phassanānattaṃ; phassanānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati vedanānānatta”nti? “Idha, gahapati, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā ‘manāpaṃ ittheta’nti pajānāti cakkhuviññāṇaṃ sukhavedaniyañca sukhavedaniyaṃ, sukhavedaniyaṃ (sī. pī.), sukhavedaniyañca, sukhavedaniyaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) evaṃ “dukkhavedaniyañca adukkhamasukhavedaniyañcā”ti padesupi. aṭṭhakathāṭīkā oloketabbā. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhā vedanā. Cakkhunā kho paneva panevaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) rūpaṃ disvā ‘amanāpaṃ ittheta’nti pajānāti cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dukkhavedaniyañca. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati dukkhā vedanā. Cakkhunā kho paneva rūpaṃ disvā ‘upekkhāṭṭhāniyaṃ [M 2.0333] upekkhāvedaniyaṃ (ka.) ittheta’nti pajānāti cakkhuviññāṇaṃ adukkhamasukhavedaniyañca. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati adukkhamasukhā vedanā.

130. On one occasion, the Venerable Mahākaccāna was staying in the Avanti country, at Kuraraghara on Mount Papāta. Then the householder Hāliddikāni approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna… Having sat down to one side, the householder Hāliddikāni said to the Venerable Mahākaccāna: "Venerable sir, this was said by the Blessed One: 'Dependent on the diversity of elements, diversity of contact arises; dependent on the diversity of contact, diversity of feeling arises.' How then, venerable sir, does diversity of contact arise dependent on the diversity of elements; and how does diversity of feeling arise dependent on the diversity of contact?" "Here, householder, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, cognizes it as agreeable. Dependent on eye-consciousness and contact productive of pleasant feeling, a pleasant feeling arises. Furthermore, having seen a form with the eye, he cognizes it as disagreeable. Dependent on eye-consciousness and contact productive of painful feeling, a painful feeling arises. Furthermore, having seen a form with the eye, he cognizes it as a basis for equanimity. Dependent on eye-consciousness and contact productive of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.

“Puna caparaṃ, gahapati, bhikkhu sotena saddaṃ sutvā…pe… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā…pe… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā…pe… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya ‘manāpaṃ ittheta’nti pajānāti manoviññāṇaṃ sukhavedaniyañca[P 4.0116]. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhā vedanā. Manasā kho paneva dhammaṃ viññāya [T 4.0146] ‘amanāpaṃ ittheta’nti pajānāti manoviññāṇaṃ [V 2.0122] dukkhavedaniyañca. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati dukkhā vedanā. Manasā kho paneva dhammaṃ viññāya ‘upekkhāṭṭhāniyaṃ ittheta’nti pajānāti manoviññāṇaṃ adukkhamasukhavedaniyañca. Phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Evaṃ kho, gahapati, dhātunānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati phassanānattaṃ; phassanānattaṃ paṭicca uppajjati vedanānānatta”nti. Sattamaṃ.

Furthermore, householder, a bhikkhu, having heard a sound with the ear… having smelled an odor with the nose… having tasted a flavor with the tongue… having felt a tangible object with the body… having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he cognizes it as agreeable. Dependent on mind-consciousness and contact productive of pleasant feeling, a pleasant feeling arises. Furthermore, having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he cognizes it as disagreeable. Dependent on mind-consciousness and contact productive of painful feeling, a painful feeling arises. Furthermore, having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he cognizes it as a basis for equanimity. Dependent on mind-consciousness and contact productive of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. Thus, householder, dependent on the diversity of elements, diversity of contact arises; dependent on the diversity of contact, diversity of feeling arises.”

8. Nakulapitusuttaṃ

8. The Discourse to Nakulapitā

131. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā bhaggesu viharati susumāragire bhesakaḷāvane migadāye. Atha kho nakulapitā gahapati yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho nakulapitā gahapati bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ko nu kho, bhante, hetu, ko paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva dhamme no parinibbāyanti? Ko pana, bhante, hetu, ko paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva dhamme parinibbāyantī”ti? “Santi kho, gahapati, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ abhinandato abhivadato ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato tannissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ hoti tadupādānaṃ. Saupādāno, gahapati, bhikkhu no parinibbāyati…pe… santi kho, gahapati, jivhāviññeyyā rasā…pe… santi kho, gahapati, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā[T 4.0147]. Tañce bhikkhu abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ abhinandato abhivadato ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato tannissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ hoti tadupādānaṃ. Saupādāno, gahapati, bhikkhu no parinibbāyati[M 2.0334]. Ayaṃ kho, gahapati, hetu ayaṃ paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva dhamme no parinibbāyanti”.

131. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Bhaggas at Susumāragira, in the deer park at Bhesakaḷā Grove. Then the householder Nakulapitā approached the Blessed One… Sitting to one side, the householder Nakulapitā said to the Blessed One: “What is the cause, venerable sir, what is the reason why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life? And what is the cause, venerable sir, what is the reason why some beings here do attain final Nibbāna in this very life?” “There are, householder, forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, agreeable, pleasing, of a dear form, connected with sensual desire, enticing. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, for him who delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, consciousness dependent on them arises, with that as its support. A bhikkhu with clinging, householder, does not attain final Nibbāna… There are, householder, tastes cognizable by the tongue… There are, householder, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind—desirable, agreeable, pleasing, of a dear form, connected with sensual desire, enticing. If a bhikkhu delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, for him who delights in them, welcomes them, and remains attached to them, consciousness dependent on them arises, with that as its support. A bhikkhu with clinging, householder, does not attain final Nibbāna. This, householder, is the cause, this is the reason why some beings here do not attain final Nibbāna in this very life.”

“Santi ca kho, gahapati, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhunābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ anabhinandato anabhivadato anajjhosāya tiṭṭhato na tannissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ hoti, na tadupādānaṃ. Anupādāno, gahapati, bhikkhu parinibbāyati…pe… santi kho, gahapati, jivhāviññeyyā rasā…pe… santi kho, gahapati, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Tassa taṃ nābhinandato nābhivadato anajjhosāya tiṭṭhato na tannissitaṃ viññāṇaṃ hoti na [V 2.0123] tadupādānaṃ. Anupādāno, gahapati, bhikkhu parinibbāyati. Ayaṃ kho, gahapati, hetu, ayaṃ paccayo yena midhekacce sattā diṭṭheva dhamme parinibbāyantī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“And there are, householder, forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, agreeable, pleasing, of a dear form, connected with sensual desire, enticing. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain attached to them, for him who does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain attached to them, consciousness dependent on them does not arise, nor does clinging to them arise. Without clinging, householder, a bhikkhu attains final Nibbāna… There are, householder, tastes cognizable by the tongue… There are, householder, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind—desirable, agreeable, pleasing, of a dear form, connected with sensual desire, enticing. If a bhikkhu does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain attached to them, for him who does not delight in them, does not welcome them, and does not remain attached to them, consciousness dependent on them does not arise, nor does clinging to them arise. Without clinging, householder, a bhikkhu attains final Nibbāna. This, householder, is the cause, this is the reason why some beings here attain final Nibbāna in this very life.”

9. Lohiccasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse with Lohicca

132. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā mahākaccāno avantīsu viharati makkarakate makkarakaṭe (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) araññakuṭikāyaṃ. Atha [P 4.0117] kho lohiccassa brāhmaṇassa sambahulā [T 4.0148] antevāsikā kaṭṭhahārakā māṇavakā yenāyasmato mahākaccānassa araññakuṭikā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā parito parito kuṭikāya anucaṅkamanti anuvicaranti uccāsaddā mahāsaddā kānici kānici seleyyakāni karonti selissakāni karontā (sī.) – “ime pana muṇḍakā samaṇakā ibbhā kaṇhā kiṇhā (sī. pī.) bandhupādāpaccā, imesaṃ bharatakānaṃ sakkatā garukatā mānitā pūjitā apacitā”ti. Atha kho āyasmā mahākaccāno vihārā nikkhamitvā te māṇavake etadavoca – “mā māṇavakā saddamakattha; dhammaṃ vo bhāsissāmī”ti. Evaṃ vutte, te māṇavakā tuṇhī ahesuṃ. Atha kho āyasmā mahākaccāno te māṇavake gāthāhi ajjhabhāsi –

132. On one occasion, Venerable Mahākaccāna was dwelling in the Avanti country, at Makkarakata in a forest hut. Then several young brahmin students, disciples of the brahmin Lohicca, who were gathering firewood, approached the forest hut of Venerable Mahākaccāna. Having approached, they walked and wandered around the hut, making loud and great noises, engaging in various boisterous games, saying: “These shaven-headed ascetics are merchants, of dark practices, born from the foot of our kinsman Brahma; yet these merchants are honored, respected, revered, venerated, and esteemed!” Then Venerable Mahākaccāna came out of his dwelling and said to those young students: “Do not make a noise, young men; I will teach you the Dhamma.” When this was said, those young students became silent. Then Venerable Mahākaccāna addressed those young students with these verses:

“Sīluttamā pubbatarā ahesuṃ,

Te brāhmaṇā ye purāṇaṃ saranti;

Guttāni dvārāni surakkhitāni,

Ahesuṃ tesaṃ abhibhuyya kodhaṃ.

“Those brahmins of old who remember the ancient way were supreme in virtue. Having subdued anger, their sense-doors were guarded and well-protected.

“Dhamme [M 2.0335] ca jhāne ca ratā ahesuṃ,

Te brāhmaṇā ye purāṇaṃ saranti;

Ime ca vokkamma japāmaseti,

Gottena mattā visamaṃ caranti.

“Those brahmins who remember the ancient way delighted in the Dhamma and in jhāna. But these, having abandoned that, think only ‘Let us chant,’ and intoxicated by lineage, they conduct themselves unrighteously.

“Kodhābhibhūtā puthuattadaṇḍā kodhābhibhūtāsuputhuttadaṇḍā (syā. kaṃ. ka.),

Virajjamānā sataṇhātaṇhesu;

Aguttadvārassa [V 2.0124] bhavanti moghā,

Supineva laddhaṃ purisassa vittaṃ.

“Overcome by anger, inflicting many punishments, acting corruptly towards those with and without craving; for one with unguarded sense-doors, all practices are in vain, like wealth obtained by a person in a dream.

“Anāsakā [P 4.0118] thaṇḍilasāyikā ca;

Pāto sinānañca tayo ca vedā.

“Fasting, sleeping on bare ground, morning bathing, and the three Vedas;

“Kharājinaṃ jaṭāpaṅko, mantā sīlabbataṃ tapo;

Kuhanā vaṅkadaṇḍā ca, udakācamanāni ca.

“Rough deerskins, matted hair and tooth-grime, mantras, vows and observances, asceticism, deceit, crooked staffs, and washing with water;

“Vaṇṇā [T 4.0149] ete brāhmaṇānaṃ, katā kiñcikkhabhāvanā;

Cittañca susamāhitaṃ, vippasannamanāvilaṃ;

Akhilaṃ sabbabhūtesu, so maggo brahmapattiyā”ti.

“These are the outward signs of brahmins, done for the increase of trivial gain. But a mind well-composed, clear and untroubled, without harshness towards all beings—that is the path to the attainment of Brahmā.”

Atha kho te māṇavakā kupitā anattamanā yena lohicco brāhmaṇo tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā lohiccaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ etadavocuṃ – “yagghe! Bhavaṃ jāneyya, samaṇo mahākaccāno brāhmaṇānaṃ mante mantaṃ (ka.) ekaṃsena apavadati, paṭikkosatī”ti? Evaṃ vutte, lohicco brāhmaṇo kupito ahosi anattamano. Atha kho lohiccassa brāhmaṇassa etadahosi – “na kho pana metaṃ patirūpaṃ yohaṃ aññadatthu māṇavakānaṃyeva sutvā samaṇaṃ mahākaccānaṃ akkoseyyaṃ akkoseyyaṃ virujjheyyaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) paribhāseyyaṃ. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā puccheyya”nti.

Then those young students, angry and displeased, approached the brahmin Lohicca. Having approached, they said to him: “Indeed, venerable sir, you should know that the ascetic Mahākaccāna utterly disparages and rejects the brahmins’ mantras!” When this was said, the brahmin Lohicca became angry and displeased. Then this occurred to the brahmin Lohicca: “It is not proper for me to insult or revile the ascetic Mahākaccāna merely on the word of these young students. What if I were to approach and question him myself?”

Atha kho lohicco brāhmaṇo tehi māṇavakehi saddhiṃ yenāyasmā mahākaccāno tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā [P 4.0119] āyasmatā mahākaccānena saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho lohicco brāhmaṇo [M 2.0336] āyasmantaṃ mahākaccānaṃ etadavoca – “āgamaṃsu nu khvidha, bho kaccāna, amhākaṃ sambahulā antevāsikā kaṭṭhahārakā māṇavakā”ti? “Āgamaṃsu khvidha te, brāhmaṇa, sambahulā antevāsikā kaṭṭhahārakā māṇavakā”ti. “Ahu pana bhoto kaccānassa tehi māṇavakehi saddhiṃ kocideva kathāsallāpo”ti? “Ahu kho me, brāhmaṇa, tehi māṇavakehi saddhiṃ kocideva kathāsallāpo”ti[T 4.0150]. “Yathā kathaṃ pana bhoto kaccānassa tehi māṇavakehi saddhiṃ ahosi [V 2.0125] kathāsallāpo”ti? “Evaṃ kho me, brāhmaṇa, tehi māṇavakehi saddhiṃ ahosi kathāsallāpo –

Then the brahmin Lohicca, together with those young men, approached the Venerable Mahākaccāna. Having approached, he exchanged polite greetings with the Venerable Mahākaccāna. Having exchanged courteous and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the brahmin Lohicca said to the Venerable Mahākaccāna: “Venerable Kaccāna, did our many resident pupils, the wood-gatherers, come here?” “Indeed, brahmin, your many resident pupils, the wood-gatherers, came here.” “And did the Venerable Kaccāna have any conversation with those young men?” “I did have some conversation with those young men, brahmin.” “And in what way was the conversation that the Venerable Kaccāna had with those young men?” “Brahmin, the conversation I had with those young men was in this way:

“Sīluttamā pubbatarā ahesuṃ,

Te brāhmaṇā ye purāṇaṃ saranti;…Pe…;

Akhilaṃ sabbabhūtesu,

So maggo brahmapattiyā”ti.

“The brahmins of former times were foremost in virtue, those who remember the ancient tradition... Gentleness towards all beings—that is the path to attaining the state of Brahmā.”

“Evaṃ kho me, brāhmaṇa, tehi māṇavakehi saddhiṃ ahosi kathāsallāpo”ti.

“Brahmin, this is the way the conversation I had with those young men went.”

“‘Aguttadvāro’ti aguttadvāro aguttadvāroti (ka.) bhavaṃ kaccāno āha. Kittāvatā nu kho, bho kaccāna, aguttadvāro hotī”ti? “Idha, brāhmaṇa, ekacco cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā piyarūpe rūpe adhimuccati, appiyarūpe rūpe byāpajjati, anupaṭṭhitakāyassati anupaṭṭhitāya satiyā (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) upari āsīvisavagge avassutasutte pana “anupaṭṭhitakāyassatī”tveva sabbattha dissati ca viharati, parittacetaso tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ [P 4.0120] yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya piyarūpe dhamme adhimuccati, appiyarūpe ca dhamme byāpajjati, anupaṭṭhitakāyassati ca viharati, parittacetaso tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Evaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, aguttadvāro hotī”ti. “Acchariyaṃ, bho kaccāna; abbhutaṃ, bho kaccāna! Yāvañcidaṃ bhotā [T 4.0151] kaccānena aguttadvārova samāno aguttadvāroti akkhāto.

“‘One with unguarded doors’—so says the Venerable Kaccāna. But in what way, Venerable Kaccāna, is one with unguarded doors?” “Here, brahmin, a certain person, having seen a form with the eye, is infatuated with an agreeable form and feels aversion toward a disagreeable form. He dwells with unestablished mindfulness and with a limited mind, and he does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states that have arisen cease without remainder. Having heard a sound with the ear… having smelled an odor with the nose… having tasted a flavor with the tongue… having felt a tangible object with the body… having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is infatuated with an agreeable mental object and feels aversion toward a disagreeable mental object. He dwells with unestablished mindfulness and with a limited mind, and he does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states that have arisen cease without remainder. In this way, brahmin, one is with unguarded doors.” “Wonderful, Venerable Kaccāna! Marvelous, Venerable Kaccāna! How exceedingly well has the Venerable Kaccāna declared one who is truly unguarded at the doors to be ‘one with unguarded doors’!”

“‘Guttadvāro’ti [M 2.0337] bhavaṃ kaccāno āha. Kittāvatā nu kho, bho kaccāna, guttadvāro hotī”ti? “Idha, brāhmaṇa, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā piyarūpe rūpe nādhimuccati, appiyarūpe rūpe na byāpajjati, upaṭṭhitakāyassati ca viharati, appamāṇacetaso tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya piyarūpe dhamme [V 2.0126] nādhimuccati, appiyarūpe dhamme na byāpajjati, upaṭṭhitakāyassati ca viharati, appamāṇacetaso tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Evaṃ kho, brāhmaṇa, guttadvāro hotī”ti.

“‘One with guarded doors’—so says the Venerable Kaccāna. But in what way, Venerable Kaccāna, is one with guarded doors?” “Here, brahmin, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, is not infatuated with an agreeable form, nor does he feel aversion toward a disagreeable form. He dwells with established mindfulness and with a boundless mind, and he understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states that have arisen for him cease without remainder. Having heard a sound with the ear… having smelled an odor with the nose… having tasted a flavor with the tongue… having felt a tangible object with the body… having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is not infatuated with an agreeable mental object, nor does he feel aversion toward a disagreeable mental object. He dwells with established mindfulness and with a boundless mind, and he understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states that have arisen for him cease without remainder. In this way, brahmin, one is with guarded doors.”

“Acchariyaṃ, bho kaccāna; abbhutaṃ, bho kaccāna! Yāvañcidaṃ [P 4.0121] bhotā kaccānena guttadvārova samāno guttadvāroti akkhāto. Abhikkantaṃ, bho kaccāna; abhikkantaṃ, bho kaccāna! Seyyathāpi, bho kaccāna, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya, paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantīti; evamevaṃ bhotā kaccānena anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ, bho kaccāna, taṃ bhagavantaṃ [T 4.0152] saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, dhammañca, bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ kaccāno dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gataṃ. Yathā ca bhavaṃ kaccāno makkarakate upāsakakulāni upasaṅkamati; evameva lohiccakulaṃ upasaṅkamatu. Tattha ye māṇavakā vā māṇavikā vā bhavantaṃ kaccānaṃ abhivādessanti paccuṭṭhissanti āsanaṃ vā udakaṃ vā dassanti, tesaṃ taṃ bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti. Navamaṃ.

“Wonderful, Venerable Kaccāna! Marvelous, Venerable Kaccāna! How exceedingly well has the Venerable Kaccāna declared one who is truly guarded at the doors to be ‘one with guarded doors’! Excellent, Venerable Kaccāna! Excellent, Venerable Kaccāna! Just as, Venerable Kaccāna, one might set upright what has been overturned, or reveal what has been hidden, or show the path to one who is lost, or hold up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes may see forms—so too has the Dhamma been made clear in many ways by the Venerable Kaccāna. I, Venerable Kaccāna, go for refuge to that Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Venerable Kaccāna remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts. And just as the Venerable Kaccāna visits the families of lay followers in Makkarakaṭa, so too may he visit the family of Lohicca. There, whatever young men or young women pay homage to the Venerable Kaccāna, rise to greet him, or offer him a seat or water, that will be for their long-term welfare and happiness.”

10. Verahaccānisuttaṃ

10. The Verahaccāni Sutta

133. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā udāyī kāmaṇḍāyaṃ viharati todeyyassa brāhmaṇassa ambavane. Atha kho verahaccānigottāya brāhmaṇiyā antevāsī māṇavako yenāyasmā udāyī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā udāyinā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho taṃ māṇavakaṃ [M 2.0338] āyasmā udāyī dhammiyā kathāya sandassesi samādapesi samuttejesi sampahaṃsesi. Atha kho so māṇavako āyasmatā udāyinā dhammiyā kathāya sandassito samādapito samuttejito sampahaṃsito uṭṭhāyāsanā yena verahaccānigottā brāhmaṇī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā verahaccānigottaṃ brāhmaṇiṃ etadavoca – “yagghe, bhoti, jāneyyāsi bhoti jāneyya (sī. pī. ka.), bhotī jāneyya (syā. kaṃ.)! Samaṇo udāyī dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ[P 4.0122], sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetī”ti.

133. On one occasion, the Venerable Udāyī was dwelling at Kāmaṇḍā, in the mango grove of the brahmin Todeyya. Then a young student of the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan approached the Venerable Udāyī. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Udāyī. When their courteous and memorable talk was concluded, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting to one side, the Venerable Udāyī instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened that young student with a Dhamma talk. Then that young student, having been instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the Venerable Udāyī with a Dhamma talk, rose from his seat and approached the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan. Having approached, he said to the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan: “If you please, madam, you should know! The recluse Udāyī teaches the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with its meaning and phrasing; and he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.”

“Tena hi tvaṃ, māṇavaka, mama vacanena samaṇaṃ udāyiṃ nimantehi svātanāya bhattenā”ti[V 2.0127]. “Evaṃ bhotī”ti kho [T 4.0153] so māṇavako verahaccānigottāya brāhmaṇiyā paṭissutvā yenāyasmā udāyī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ etadavoca – “adhivāsetu kira, bhavaṃ, udāyi, amhākaṃ ācariyabhariyāya verahaccānigottāya brāhmaṇiyā svātanāya bhatta”nti. Adhivāsesi kho āyasmā udāyī tuṇhībhāvena. Atha kho āyasmā udāyī tassā rattiyā accayena pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena verahaccānigottāya brāhmaṇiyā nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Atha kho verahaccānigottā brāhmaṇī āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena sahatthā santappesi sampavāresi. Atha kho verahaccānigottā brāhmaṇī āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ bhuttāviṃ onītapattapāṇiṃ pādukā ārohitvā ucce āsane nisīditvā sīsaṃ oguṇṭhitvā āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ etadavoca – “bhaṇa, samaṇa, dhamma”nti. “Bhavissati, bhagini, samayo”ti vatvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkami pakkāmi (syā. kaṃ. pī.).

“Then, young man, in my name invite the recluse Udāyī for tomorrow’s meal.” “Yes, madam,” that young man replied, and having assented to the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan, he approached the Venerable Udāyī. Having approached, he said to the Venerable Udāyī: “Venerable Udāyī, may you please consent to a meal tomorrow from our teacher’s wife, the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan.” The Venerable Udāyī consented by remaining silent. Then, when that night had passed, the Venerable Udāyī, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and went to the residence of the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan. Having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan, with her own hands, served and satisfied the Venerable Udāyī with fine hard and soft food until he indicated he was content. Then, knowing that the Venerable Udāyī had finished eating and had removed his hand from the bowl, the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan, putting on her sandals, sitting on a high seat, and covering her head, said to the Venerable Udāyī: “Speak the Dhamma, recluse.” “There will be a time for that, sister,” he said, and rising from his seat, he departed.

Dutiyampi kho so māṇavako yenāyasmā udāyī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā udāyinā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho taṃ māṇavakaṃ āyasmā udāyī dhammiyā kathāya sandassesi samādapesi samuttejesi sampahaṃsesi. Dutiyampi kho so māṇavako āyasmatā udāyinā dhammiyā kathāya sandassito samādapito samuttejito [T 4.0154] sampahaṃsito uṭṭhāyāsanā yena verahaccānigottā brāhmaṇī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā [M 2.0339] verahaccānigottaṃ brāhmaṇiṃ etadavoca – “yagghe, bhoti, jāneyyāsi! Samaṇo udāyī dhammaṃ deseti ādikalyāṇaṃ majjhekalyāṇaṃ pariyosānakalyāṇaṃ[P 4.0123], sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ kevalaparipuṇṇaṃ parisuddhaṃ brahmacariyaṃ pakāsetī”ti.

For a second time, that young student approached the Venerable Udāyī. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Udāyī. When their courteous and memorable talk was concluded, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting to one side, the Venerable Udāyī instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened that young student with a Dhamma talk. For a second time, that young student, having been instructed, urged, roused, and gladdened by the Venerable Udāyī with a Dhamma talk, rose from his seat and approached the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan. Having approached, he said to the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan: “If you please, madam, you should know! The recluse Udāyī teaches the Dhamma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with its meaning and phrasing; and he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.”

“Evamevaṃ pana tvaṃ, māṇavaka, samaṇassa udāyissa vaṇṇaṃ bhāsasi. Samaṇo panudāyī ‘bhaṇa, samaṇa, dhamma’nti vutto samāno ‘bhavissati, bhagini, samayo’ti vatvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkanto”ti. “Tathā hi pana tvaṃ, bhoti, pādukā ārohitvā ucce āsane nisīditvā sīsaṃ oguṇṭhitvā etadavoca – ‘bhaṇa, samaṇa, dhamma’nti. Dhammagaruno hi te bhavanto dhammagāravā”ti. “Tena hi tvaṃ, māṇavaka, mama vacanena samaṇaṃ udāyiṃ nimantehi svātanāya bhattenā”ti. “Evaṃ, bhotī”ti kho so māṇavako verahaccānigottāya brāhmaṇiyā paṭissutvā yenāyasmā udāyī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ etadavoca – “adhivāsetu kira [V 2.0128] bhavaṃ udāyī amhākaṃ ācariyabhariyāya verahaccānigottāya brāhmaṇiyā svātanāya bhatta”nti. Adhivāsesi kho āyasmā udāyī tuṇhībhāvena.

“Yet, young man, you praise the recluse Udāyī in this way. But when I told the recluse Udāyī, ‘Speak the Dhamma, recluse,’ he said, ‘There will be a time for that, sister,’ and then rose from his seat and departed.” “That is because you, madam, had put on sandals, sat on a high seat, covered your head, and then said, ‘Speak the Dhamma, recluse.’ For those venerable ones hold the Dhamma as their teacher and are respectful towards the Dhamma.” “Then, young man, in my name invite the recluse Udāyī for tomorrow’s meal.” “Yes, madam,” that young man replied, and having assented to the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan, he approached the Venerable Udāyī. Having approached, he said to the Venerable Udāyī: “Venerable Udāyī, may you please consent to a meal tomorrow from our teacher’s wife, the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan.” The Venerable Udāyī consented by remaining silent.

Atha kho āyasmā udāyī tassā rattiyā accayena pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya yena verahaccānigottāya brāhmaṇiyā nivesanaṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Atha kho verahaccānigottā brāhmaṇī āyasmantaṃ [T 4.0155] udāyiṃ paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena sahatthā santappesi sampavāresi. Atha kho verahaccānigottā brāhmaṇī āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ bhuttāviṃ onītapattapāṇiṃ pādukā orohitvā nīce āsane nisīditvā sīsaṃ vivaritvā āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ etadavoca – “kismiṃ nu kho, bhante, sati arahanto sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti, kismiṃ asati arahanto sukhadukkhaṃ na paññapentī”ti?

Then, when that night had passed, the Venerable Udāyī, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe and went to the residence of the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan. Having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan, with her own hands, served and satisfied the Venerable Udāyī with fine hard and soft food until he indicated he was content. When the Venerable Udāyī had finished eating and had removed his hand from the bowl, the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan, having taken off her sandals, sat on a low seat, uncovered her head, and said to the Venerable Udāyī: “Venerable sir, when what exists do the arahants designate pleasure and pain, and when what does not exist do the arahants not designate pleasure and pain?”

“Cakkhusmiṃ kho, bhagini, sati arahanto sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti, cakkhusmiṃ asati arahanto sukhadukkhaṃ [P 4.0124] na paññapenti…pe… jivhāya sati arahanto sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti, jivhāya asati arahanto sukhadukkhaṃ na paññapenti…pe…. Manasmiṃ sati arahanto sukhadukkhaṃ paññapenti, manasmiṃ asati arahanto sukhadukkhaṃ na paññapentī”ti.

“Sister, when the eye exists, arahants designate pleasure and pain; when the eye does not exist, arahants do not designate pleasure and pain… When the tongue exists, arahants designate pleasure and pain; when the tongue does not exist, arahants do not designate pleasure and pain… When the mind exists, arahants designate pleasure and pain; when the mind does not exist, arahants do not designate pleasure and pain.”

Evaṃ vutte, verahaccānigottā brāhmaṇī āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bhante; abhikkantaṃ, bhante! Seyyathāpi, bhante, nikkujjitaṃ vā ukkujjeyya[M 2.0340], paṭicchannaṃ vā vivareyya, mūḷhassa vā maggaṃ ācikkheyya, andhakāre vā telapajjotaṃ dhāreyya, cakkhumanto rūpāni dakkhantīti; evamevaṃ ayyena udāyinā anekapariyāyena dhammo pakāsito. Esāhaṃ, ayya udāyi, taṃ bhagavantaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchāmi, dhammañca, bhikkhusaṅghañca. Upāsikaṃ maṃ ayyo udāyī dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti. Dasamaṃ.

When this was said, the brahmin woman of the Verahaccāni clan said to the Venerable Udāyī: “Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent, venerable sir! Just as, venerable sir, one might set upright what was overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the path to one who is lost, or hold up an oil lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms—in the very same way, the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by the noble Udāyī. I go for refuge to that Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha. May the noble Udāyī remember me as a female lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts.” The Tenth.

Gahapativaggo terasamo.

The Householder Chapter, the thirteenth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of it:

Vesālī [T 4.0156] vajji nāḷandā, bhāradvāja soṇo ca ghosito;

Hāliddiko nakulapitā, lohicco verahaccānīti.

Vesālī, Vajjī, Nāḷandā, Bhāradvāja, Soṇa, and Ghosita; Hāliddika, Nakulapitā, Lohicca, and Verahaccāni.

14. Devadahavaggo

14. The Devadaha Chapter

1. Devadahasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse at Devadaha

134. Ekaṃ [T 4.0157][V 2.0129] samayaṃ bhagavā sakkesu viharati devadahaṃ nāma sakyānaṃ nigamo. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbesaṃyeva bhikkhūnaṃ chasu phassāyatanesu appamādena karaṇīyanti vadāmi, na ca panāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbesaṃyeva bhikkhūnaṃ chasu phassāyatanesu [P 4.0125] nāppamādena karaṇīyanti vadāmi. Ye te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū arahanto khīṇāsavā vusitavanto katakaraṇīyā ohitabhārā anuppattasadatthā parikkhīṇabhavasaṃyojanā sammadaññā vimuttā, tesāhaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhūnaṃ chasu phassāyatanesu nāppamādena karaṇīyanti vadāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Kataṃ tesaṃ appamādena, abhabbā te pamajjituṃ. Ye ca kho te, bhikkhave, bhikkhū sekkhā sekhā (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) appattamānasā anuttaraṃ yogakkhemaṃ patthayamānā viharanti, tesāhaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhūnaṃ chasu phassāyatanesu appamādena karaṇīyanti vadāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Santi, bhikkhave, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā manoramāpi, amanoramāpi. Tyāssa phussa phussa cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Cetaso apariyādānā āraddhaṃ hoti vīriyaṃ asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā apammuṭṭhā (sī.), appamuṭṭhā (syā. kaṃ.), passaddho kāyo asāraddho, samāhitaṃ cittaṃ ekaggaṃ. Imaṃ khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, appamādaphalaṃ [M 2.0341] sampassamāno tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ chasu [T 4.0158] phassāyatanesu appamādena karaṇīyanti vadāmi…pe… santi, bhikkhave, manoviññeyyā dhammā manoramāpi amanoramāpi. Tyāssa phussa phussa cittaṃ na pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti. Cetaso apariyādānā āraddhaṃ hoti vīriyaṃ asallīnaṃ, upaṭṭhitā sati asammuṭṭhā, passaddho kāyo asāraddho, samāhitaṃ cittaṃ ekaggaṃ. Imaṃ khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, appamādaphalaṃ sampassamāno tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ chasu chassu (sī.) phassāyatanesu appamādena karaṇīyanti vadāmī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

134. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans in a town of the Sakyans named Devadaha. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, I do not say for all bhikkhus whatsoever that there is something to be done with heedfulness in regard to the six bases for contact. Nor, bhikkhus, do I say for all bhikkhus whatsoever that they should act with heedlessness in regard to the six bases for contact. Bhikkhus, as to those bhikkhus who are arahants, whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and are liberated through perfect, final knowledge—for those bhikkhus, I do not say that there is something to be done with heedfulness in regard to the six bases for contact. For what reason? It has been done by them with heedfulness; they are incapable of being heedless. But, bhikkhus, as to those bhikkhus who are trainees, who have not attained the goal of their minds, who dwell aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage—for those bhikkhus, I say that there is something to be done with heedfulness in regard to the six bases for contact. For what reason? There are, bhikkhus, forms cognizable by the eye that are pleasing and also unpleasing. Those forms, having repeatedly made contact, do not persist in taking over his mind. Because his mind is not taken over, his energy is aroused and unflagging, his mindfulness is established and unconfused, his body is tranquil and undisturbed, and his mind is concentrated and one-pointed. Seeing this fruit of heedfulness, bhikkhus, I say that for those bhikkhus there is something to be done with heedfulness in regard to the six bases for contact… There are, bhikkhus, mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are pleasing and also unpleasing. Those phenomena, having repeatedly made contact, do not persist in taking over his mind. Because his mind is not taken over, his energy is aroused and unflagging, his mindfulness is established and unconfused, his body is tranquil and undisturbed, and his mind is concentrated and one-pointed. Seeing this fruit of heedfulness, bhikkhus, I say that for those bhikkhus there is something to be done with heedfulness in regard to the six bases for contact.” The First.

2. Khaṇasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on the Opportunity

135. “Lābhā [P 4.0126] vo, bhikkhave, suladdhaṃ vo, bhikkhave, khaṇo vo paṭiladdho brahmacariyavāsāya. Diṭṭhā mayā, bhikkhave, chaphassāyatanikā nāma nirayā. Tattha yaṃ kiñci cakkhunā [V 2.0130] rūpaṃ passati aniṭṭharūpaṃyeva passati, no iṭṭharūpaṃ; akantarūpaṃyeva passati, no kantarūpaṃ; amanāparūpaṃyeva passati, no manāparūpaṃ. Yaṃ kiñci sotena saddaṃ suṇāti…pe… yaṃ kiñci ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyati…pe… yaṃ kiñci jivhāya rasaṃ sāyati…pe… yaṃ kiñci kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusati…pe… yaṃ [T 4.0159] kiñci manasā dhammaṃ vijānāti aniṭṭharūpaṃyeva vijānāti, no iṭṭharūpaṃ; akantarūpaṃyeva vijānāti, no kantarūpaṃ; amanāparūpaṃyeva vijānāti, no manāparūpaṃ. Lābhā vo, bhikkhave, suladdhaṃ vo, bhikkhave, khaṇo vo paṭiladdho brahmacariyavāsāya. Diṭṭhā mayā, bhikkhave, chaphassāyatanikā nāma saggā. Tattha yaṃ kiñci cakkhunā rūpaṃ passati iṭṭharūpaṃyeva passati, no aniṭṭharūpaṃ; kantarūpaṃyeva passati, no akantarūpaṃ; manāparūpaṃyeva passati, no amanāparūpaṃ…pe… yaṃ kiñci jivhāya rasaṃ sāyati…pe… yaṃ kiñci manasā dhammaṃ vijānāti iṭṭharūpaṃyeva vijānāti, no aniṭṭharūpaṃ; kantarūpaṃyeva vijānāti, no akantarūpaṃ; manāparūpaṃyeva vijānāti, no amanāparūpaṃ. Lābhā vo, bhikkhave, suladdhaṃ vo, bhikkhave, khaṇo vo paṭiladdho brahmacariyavāsāyā”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

135. “A gain for you, bhikkhus! A great gain for you, bhikkhus! You have obtained the opportunity for the practice of the holy life. I have seen, bhikkhus, the hells of the six bases for contact. There, whatever form one sees with the eye, one sees only an undesirable form, not a desirable one; one sees only an unlovely form, not a lovely one; one sees only an unappealing form, not an appealing one. Whatever sound one hears with the ear… whatever odor one smells with the nose… whatever taste one savors with the tongue… whatever tangible object one feels with the body… whatever mental object one cognizes with the mind, one cognizes only an undesirable mental object, not a desirable one; one cognizes only an unlovely mental object, not a lovely one; one cognizes only an unappealing mental object, not an appealing one. A gain for you, bhikkhus! A great gain for you, bhikkhus! You have obtained the opportunity for the practice of the holy life. I have seen, bhikkhus, the heavens of the six bases for contact. There, whatever form one sees with the eye, one sees only a desirable form, not an undesirable one; one sees only a lovely form, not an unlovely one; one sees only an appealing form, not an unappealing one… whatever taste one savors with the tongue… whatever mental object one cognizes with the mind, one cognizes only a desirable mental object, not an undesirable one; one cognizes only a lovely mental object, not an unlovely one; one cognizes only an appealing mental object, not an unappealing one. A gain for you, bhikkhus! A great gain for you, bhikkhus! You have obtained the opportunity for the practice of the holy life.” The Second.

3. Paṭhamarūpārāmasuttaṃ

3. The First Discourse on Delighting in Forms

136. “Rūpārāmā, bhikkhave, devamanussā rūparatā rūpasammuditā. Rūpavipariṇāmavirāganirodhā dukkhā, bhikkhave, devamanussā viharanti. Saddārāmā, bhikkhave[M 2.0342], devamanussā saddaratā saddasammuditā. Saddavipariṇāmavirāganirodhā dukkhā, bhikkhave, devamanussā viharanti. Gandhārāmā… rasārāmā… phoṭṭhabbārāmā… dhammārāmā, bhikkhave, devamanussā [P 4.0127] dhammaratā dhammasammuditā. Dhammavipariṇāmavirāganirodhā dukkhā, bhikkhave, devamanussā viharanti. Tathāgato ca kho, bhikkhave, arahaṃ sammāsambuddho [T 4.0160] rūpānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavaṃ ca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā na rūpārāmo na rūparato na rūpasammudito. Rūpavipariṇāmavirāganirodhā sukho, bhikkhave, tathāgato viharati. Saddānaṃ… gandhānaṃ… rasānaṃ… phoṭṭhabbānaṃ… dhammānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā na dhammārāmo, na dhammarato, na dhammasammudito. Dhammavipariṇāmavirāganirodhā sukho, bhikkhave, tathāgato viharati”. Idamavoca bhagavā. Idaṃ vatvāna sugato athāparaṃ etadavoca satthā –

136. “Bhikkhus, devas and humans delight in forms, are fond of forms, and rejoice in forms. With the change, fading away, and cessation of forms, bhikkhus, devas and humans dwell in suffering. Bhikkhus, devas and humans delight in sounds, are fond of sounds, and rejoice in sounds. With the change, fading away, and cessation of sounds, bhikkhus, devas and humans dwell in suffering. They delight in odors... tastes... tangible objects... Bhikkhus, devas and humans delight in mental objects, are fond of mental objects, and rejoice in mental objects. With the change, fading away, and cessation of mental objects, bhikkhus, devas and humans dwell in suffering. But, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having understood as they truly are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to forms, does not delight in forms, is not fond of forms, and does not rejoice in forms. With the change, fading away, and cessation of forms, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata dwells in happiness. Having understood as they truly are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to sounds... odors... tastes... tangible objects... mental objects, he does not delight in mental objects, is not fond of mental objects, and does not rejoice in mental objects. With the change, fading away, and cessation of mental objects, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata dwells in happiness.” The Blessed One said this. Having said this, the Well-Farer, the Teacher, further said this:

“Rūpā [V 2.0131] saddā rasā gandhā, phassā dhammā ca kevalā;

Iṭṭhā kantā manāpā ca, yāvatatthīti vuccati.

“Forms, sounds, tastes, odors, tangible objects, and mental objects—all of them, desirable, lovely, and appealing—are spoken of only to the extent that they exist.

“Sadevakassa lokassa, ete vo sukhasammatā;

Yattha cete nirujjhanti, taṃ tesaṃ dukkhasammataṃ.

For the world with its devas, these are considered happiness; but where these cease, that is considered suffering by them.

“Sukhaṃ sukhanti (sī.) diṭṭhamariyebhi, sakkāyassa nirodhanaṃ;

Paccanīkamidaṃ hoti, sabbalokena passataṃ.

The cessation of embodiment is seen as happiness by the noble ones; this is contrary to the view of the entire world.

“Yaṃ pare sukhato āhu, tadariyā āhu dukkhato;

Yaṃ pare dukkhato āhu, tadariyā sukhato vidū.

What others call happiness, that the noble ones call suffering; what others call suffering, that the noble ones know as happiness.

“Passa dhammaṃ durājānaṃ, sammūḷhettha aviddasu;

Nivutānaṃ tamo hoti, andhakāro apassataṃ.

Behold this Dhamma, so difficult to understand; herein the unwise are bewildered. For those who are veiled it is darkness, pitch darkness for those who do not see.

“Satañca [P 4.0128] vivaṭaṃ hoti, āloko passatāmi;

Santike na vijānanti, maggā magā (sī.) dhammassa akovidā.

But for the virtuous it is open, a light for those who see. Though it is near, those unskilled in the Dhamma do not understand it.

“Bhavarāgaparetebhi[T 4.0161], bhavarāgānusārībhi bhavasotānusāribhi (syā. kaṃ. pī.), bhavasotānusārihi (sī.);

Māradheyyānupannehi, nāyaṃ dhammo susambudho.

This Dhamma is not well understood by those overcome by the passion for existence, who follow the passion for existence, and who have fallen into Māra’s domain.

“Ko [M 2.0343] nu aññatra mariyebhi, padaṃ sambuddhumarahati;

Yaṃ padaṃ sammadaññāya, parinibbanti anāsavā”ti. tatiyaṃ;

Who else but the noble ones is capable of awakening to that state? Having rightly understood that state, the taintless attain final Nibbāna.” The Third.

4. Dutiyarūpārāmasuttaṃ

4. The Second Discourse on Delighting in Forms

137. “Rūpārāmā, bhikkhave, devamanussā rūparatā rūpasammuditā. Rūpavipariṇāmavirāganirodhā dukkhā, bhikkhave, devamanussā viharanti. Saddārāmā… gandhārāmā… rasārāmā [V 2.0132]… phoṭṭhabbārāmā… dhammārāmā, bhikkhave, devamanussā dhammaratā dhammasammuditā. Dhammavipariṇāmavirāganirodhā dukkhā, bhikkhave, devamanussā viharanti. Tathāgato ca, bhikkhave, arahaṃ sammāsambuddho rūpānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā na rūpārāmo na rūparato na rūpasammudito. Rūpavipariṇāmavirāganirodhā sukho, bhikkhave, tathāgato viharati. Saddānaṃ… gandhānaṃ… rasānaṃ… phoṭṭhabbānaṃ… dhammānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ viditvā na dhammārāmo na dhammarato na dhammasammudito. Dhammavipariṇāmavirāganirodhā sukho, bhikkhave, tathāgato viharatī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

137. “Bhikkhus, devas and humans delight in forms, are fond of forms, and rejoice in forms. With the change, fading away, and cessation of forms, bhikkhus, devas and humans dwell in suffering. They delight in sounds… odors… tastes… tangible objects… Bhikkhus, devas and humans delight in mental objects, are fond of mental objects, and rejoice in mental objects. With the change, fading away, and cessation of mental objects, bhikkhus, devas and humans dwell in suffering. And the Tathāgata, bhikkhus, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having understood as they truly are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to forms, does not delight in forms, is not fond of forms, and does not rejoice in forms. With the change, fading away, and cessation of forms, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata dwells in happiness. Having understood as they truly are the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to sounds… odors… tastes… tangible objects… mental objects, he does not delight in mental objects, is not fond of mental objects, and does not rejoice in mental objects. With the change, fading away, and cessation of mental objects, bhikkhus, the Tathāgata dwells in happiness.” The Fourth.

5. Paṭhamanatumhākaṃsuttaṃ

5. The First Discourse on What Is Not Yours

138. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Kiñca, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ; taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati…pe… [T 4.0162] jivhā na tumhākaṃ[P 4.0129]; taṃ pajahatha. Sā vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissati…pe… mano na tumhākaṃ; taṃ pajahatha. So vo pahīno hitāya sukhāya bhavissati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yaṃ imasmiṃ jetavane tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṃ taṃ jano hareyya vā ḍaheyya vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā kareyya, api nu tumhākaṃ evamassa – ‘amhe jano harati vā ḍahati vā yathāpaccayaṃ vā karotī’”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Na hi no etaṃ, bhante, attā vā attaniyaṃ vā”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, cakkhu na tumhākaṃ; taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati…pe… jivhā na tumhākaṃ; taṃ pajahatha. Sā vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissati…pe… mano na tumhākaṃ[M 2.0344]; taṃ pajahatha. So vo pahīno hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

138. “Bhikkhus, abandon what is not yours. That, being abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. And what, bhikkhus, is not yours? The eye, bhikkhus, is not yours; abandon it. That, being abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness… The tongue is not yours; abandon it. That, being abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness… The mind is not yours; abandon it. That, being abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness. Just as, bhikkhus, if people were to carry away, burn, or do with as they please the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in this Jeta's Grove, would you think, ‘People are carrying us away, burning us, or doing with us as they please’?” “No, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “Because, venerable sir, that is neither our self nor what belongs to our self.” “In the same way, bhikkhus, the eye is not yours; abandon it. That, being abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness… The tongue is not yours; abandon it. That, being abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness… The mind is not yours; abandon it. That, being abandoned, will be for your welfare and happiness.” The fifth.

6. Dutiyanatumhākaṃsuttaṃ

6. The Second Discourse on What Is Not Yours

139. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ, taṃ pajahatha. Taṃ vo pahīnaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissati[V 2.0133]. Kiñca, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ? Rūpā, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ; te pajahatha. Te vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissanti. Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā [T 4.0163] na tumhākaṃ; te pajahatha. Te vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissanti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, yaṃ imasmiṃ jetavane…pe… evameva kho, bhikkhave, rūpā na tumhākaṃ; te pajahatha. Te vo pahīnā hitāya sukhāya bhavissantī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

139. “Bhikkhus, whatever is not yours, abandon it. When you have abandoned it, that will lead to your welfare and happiness. And what, bhikkhus, is not yours? Forms, bhikkhus, are not yours; abandon them. When you have abandoned them, they will lead to your welfare and happiness. Sounds… odors… tastes… tangibles… mental objects are not yours; abandon them. When you have abandoned them, they will lead to your welfare and happiness. Just as, bhikkhus, whatever grass, sticks, branches, and leaves are in this Jeta's Grove… so too, bhikkhus, forms are not yours; abandon them. When you have abandoned them, they will lead to your welfare and happiness.” Sixth.

7. Ajjhattāniccahetusuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on the Cause of Internal Impermanence

140. “Cakkhuṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ. Yopi hetu, yopi paccayo cakkhussa uppādāya, sopi anicco. Aniccasambhūtaṃ, bhikkhave, cakkhu kuto niccaṃ bhavissati…pe… [P 4.0130] jivhā aniccā. Yopi hetu, yopi paccayo jivhāya uppādāya sopi anicco. Aniccasambhūtā, bhikkhave, jivhā kuto niccā bhavissati…pe… mano anicco. Yopi, bhikkhave, hetu yopi paccayo manassa uppādāya, sopi anicco. Aniccasambhūto, bhikkhave, mano kuto nicco bhavissati! Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati…pe… jivhāyapi nibbindati…pe… nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

140. “The eye, bhikkhus, is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of the eye, that too is impermanent. The eye, bhikkhus, having arisen from what is impermanent, how could it be permanent? … The tongue is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of the tongue, that too is impermanent. The tongue, bhikkhus, having arisen from what is impermanent, how could it be permanent? … The mind is impermanent. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of the mind, that too is impermanent. The mind, bhikkhus, having arisen from what is impermanent, how could it be permanent? Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye… becomes disenchanted with the tongue… becomes disenchanted with the mind. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’” Seventh.

8. Ajjhattadukkhahetusuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on the Cause of Internal Suffering

141. “Cakkhuṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ. Yopi hetu yopi paccayo cakkhussa uppādāya, sopi dukkho. Dukkhasambhūtaṃ, bhikkhave, cakkhu kuto sukhaṃ bhavissati…pe… jivhā dukkhā. Yopi hetu, yopi paccayo jivhāya uppādāya, sopi dukkho. Dukkhasambhūtā, bhikkhave, jivhā kuto sukhā bhavissati…pe… mano dukkho. Yopi hetu yopi paccayo manassa uppādāya, sopi dukkho. Dukkhasambhūto, bhikkhave, mano kuto sukho bhavissati! Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

141. “The eye, bhikkhus, is suffering. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of the eye, that too is suffering. The eye, bhikkhus, having arisen from suffering, how could it be pleasant? … The tongue is suffering. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of the tongue, that too is suffering. The tongue, bhikkhus, having arisen from suffering, how could it be pleasant? … The mind is suffering. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of the mind, that too is suffering. The mind, bhikkhus, having arisen from suffering, how could it be pleasant? Seeing thus… he understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’” Eighth.

9. Ajjhattānattahetusuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on the Cause of Internal Not-self

142. “Cakkhuṃ[T 4.0164][V 2.0134][M 2.0345], bhikkhave, anattā. Yopi hetu, yopi paccayo cakkhussa uppādāya, sopi anattā. Anattasambhūtaṃ, bhikkhave, cakkhu kuto attā bhavissati…pe… jivhā anattā. Yopi hetu yopi paccayo jivhāya uppādāya, sopi anattā. Anattasambhūtā, bhikkhave, jivhā kuto attā bhavissati…pe… mano anattā. Yopi hetu yopi paccayo manassa uppādāya[P 4.0131], sopi anattā. Anattasambhūto, bhikkhave, mano kuto attā bhavissati! Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Navamaṃ.

142. “Bhikkhus, the eye is not-self. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of the eye, that too is not-self. Bhikkhus, the eye having arisen from what is not-self, how could it be self? … The tongue is not-self. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of the tongue, that too is not-self. Bhikkhus, the tongue having arisen from what is not-self, how could it be self? … The mind is not-self. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of the mind, that too is not-self. Bhikkhus, the mind having arisen from what is not-self, how could it be self? Seeing thus… he understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’ ” Ninth.

10. Bāhirāniccahetusuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on the External Cause of Impermanence

143. “Rūpā, bhikkhave, aniccā. Yopi hetu, yopi paccayo rūpānaṃ uppādāya, sopi anicco. Aniccasambhūtā, bhikkhave, rūpā kuto niccā bhavissanti! Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā aniccā. Yopi hetu, yopi paccayo dhammānaṃ uppādāya, sopi anicco. Aniccasambhūtā, bhikkhave, dhammā kuto niccā bhavissanti! Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

143. “Bhikkhus, forms are impermanent. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of forms, that too is impermanent. Bhikkhus, forms having arisen from what is impermanent, how could they be permanent? Sounds… odors… tastes… tangibles… mental objects are impermanent. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of mental objects, that too is impermanent. Bhikkhus, mental objects having arisen from what is impermanent, how could they be permanent? Seeing thus… he understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’ ” Tenth.

11. Bāhiradukkhahetusuttaṃ

11. The Discourse on the External Cause of Suffering

144. “Rūpā, bhikkhave, dukkhā. Yopi hetu, yopi paccayo rūpānaṃ uppādāya, sopi dukkho. Dukkhasambhūtā, bhikkhave, rūpā kuto sukhā bhavissanti! Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā dukkhā. Yopi hetu, yopi paccayo dhammānaṃ uppādāya, sopi dukkho. Dukkhasambhūtā, bhikkhave, dhammā kuto sukhā bhavissanti! Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Ekādasamaṃ.

144. “Bhikkhus, forms are suffering. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of forms, that too is suffering. Bhikkhus, forms having arisen from suffering, how could they be pleasant? Sounds… odors… tastes… tangibles… mental objects are suffering. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of mental objects, that too is suffering. Bhikkhus, mental objects having arisen from suffering, how could they be pleasant? Seeing thus… he understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’ ” Eleventh.

12. Bāhirānattahetusuttaṃ

12. The Discourse on the External Cause of Not-Self

145. “Rūpā[T 4.0165][V 2.0135], bhikkhave, anattā. Yopi hetu, yopi paccayo rūpānaṃ uppādāya, sopi anattā. Anattasambhūtā, bhikkhave, rūpā kuto attā bhavissanti! Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā anattā. Yopi hetu, yopi paccayo dhammānaṃ uppādāya, sopi anattā. Anattasambhūtā, bhikkhave, dhammā [M 2.0346] kuto attā bhavissanti! Evaṃ passaṃ[P 4.0132], bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako rūpesupi nibbindati, saddesupi… gandhesupi… rasesupi… phoṭṭhabbesupi… dhammesupi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Dvādasamaṃ.

145. “Bhikkhus, forms are not-self. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of forms, that too is not-self. Bhikkhus, forms having arisen from what is not-self, how could they be self? Sounds… odors… tastes… tangibles… mental objects are not-self. Whatever cause and condition there is for the arising of mental objects, that too is not-self. Bhikkhus, mental objects having arisen from what is not-self, how could they be self? Seeing thus, Bhikkhus, an instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with forms, with sounds, with odors, with tastes, with tangibles, and with mental objects. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’ ” Twelfth.

Devadahavaggo cuddasamo.

The Devadaha Chapter, the fourteenth, is concluded.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of that chapter:
