Devadaho khaṇo rūpā, dve natumhākameva ca;

Hetunāpi tayo vuttā, duve ajjhattabāhirāti.

Devadaha, Khaṇa, Saṃgayha, and Agayha; the two suttas Palāsina and Na Tumhākaṃ; three are taught with a cause, and two as internal and external.

15. Navapurāṇavaggo

15. The Chapter on the New and the Old

1. Kammanirodhasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on the Cessation of Kamma

146. “Navapurāṇāni[T 4.0166], bhikkhave, kammāni desessāmi kammanirodhaṃ kammanirodhagāminiñca paṭipadaṃ. Taṃ suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha; bhāsissāmīti. Katamañca, bhikkhave, purāṇakammaṃ? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, purāṇakammaṃ abhisaṅkhataṃ abhisañcetayitaṃ vedaniyaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ…pe… jivhā purāṇakammā abhisaṅkhatā abhisañcetayitā vedaniyā daṭṭhabbā…pe… mano purāṇakammo abhisaṅkhato abhisañcetayito vedaniyo daṭṭhabbo. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, purāṇakammaṃ. Katamañca, bhikkhave, navakammaṃ? Yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, etarahi [V 2.0136] kammaṃ karoti kāyena vācāya manasā, idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, navakammaṃ. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, kammanirodho? Yo kho, bhikkhave, kāyakammavacīkammamanokammassa nirodhā vimuttiṃ [P 4.0133] phusati, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, kammanirodho. Katamā ca, bhikkhave, kammanirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi, sammāsaṅkappo, sammāvācā, sammākammanto, sammāājīvo, sammāvāyāmo, sammāsati, sammāsamādhi – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, kammanirodhagāminī paṭipadā. Iti kho, bhikkhave, desitaṃ mayā purāṇakammaṃ, desitaṃ [M 2.0347] navakammaṃ, desito kammanirodho, desitā kammanirodhagāminī paṭipadā. Yaṃ [T 4.0167] kho, bhikkhave, satthārā karaṇīyaṃ sāvakānaṃ hitesinā anukampakena anukampaṃ upādāya, kataṃ vo taṃ mayā. Etāni, bhikkhave, rukkhamūlāni, etāni suññāgārāni. Jhāyatha, bhikkhave, mā pamādattha; mā pacchāvippaṭisārino ahuvattha. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

146. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you new and old kamma, the cessation of kamma, and the practice leading to the cessation of kamma. Listen to that, attend to it well; I will speak. And what, bhikkhus, is old kamma? The eye, bhikkhus, should be seen as old kamma, as formed, as willed, as to be experienced. … The tongue should be seen as old kamma, as formed, as willed, as to be experienced. … The mind should be seen as old kamma, as formed, as willed, as to be experienced. This, bhikkhus, is called old kamma. And what, bhikkhus, is new kamma? Whatever kamma one now performs by body, speech, or mind—this, bhikkhus, is called new kamma. And what, bhikkhus, is the cessation of kamma? When, bhikkhus, one attains liberation through the cessation of bodily kamma, verbal kamma, and mental kamma, this is called the cessation of kamma. And what, bhikkhus, is the practice leading to the cessation of kamma? It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called the practice leading to the cessation of kamma. Thus, bhikkhus, old kamma has been taught by me, new kamma has been taught, the cessation of kamma has been taught, and the practice leading to the cessation of kamma has been taught. Whatever should be done by a teacher for his disciples, seeking their welfare and out of compassion for them, that has been done by me for you. Here, bhikkhus, are the roots of trees; here are empty dwellings. Meditate, bhikkhus, do not be heedless; do not be regretful later. This is our instruction to you.” First.

2. Aniccanibbānasappāyasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on Impermanence Conducive to Nibbāna

147. “Nibbānasappāyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, paṭipadaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha…pe… katamā ca sā, bhikkhave, nibbānasappāyā paṭipadā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhuṃ aniccanti passati, rūpā aniccāti passati, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ aniccanti passati, cakkhusamphasso aniccoti passati. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccanti passati…pe… jivhā aniccāti passati, rasā aniccāti passati, jivhāviññāṇaṃ aniccanti passati, jivhāsamphasso aniccoti passati[P 4.0134], yampidaṃ jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccanti passati…pe… mano aniccoti passati, dhammā aniccāti passati, manoviññāṇaṃ aniccanti passati, manosamphasso aniccoti passati, yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccanti passati. Ayaṃ kho sā, bhikkhave, nibbānasappāyā paṭipadā”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

147. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the practice conducive to Nibbāna. Listen to it… And what, bhikkhus, is that practice conducive to Nibbāna? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu sees the eye as impermanent, forms as impermanent, eye-consciousness as impermanent, eye-contact as impermanent. Whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too he sees as impermanent. … He sees the tongue as impermanent, tastes as impermanent, tongue-consciousness as impermanent, tongue-contact as impermanent. Whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too he sees as impermanent. … He sees the mind as impermanent, mental objects as impermanent, mind-consciousness as impermanent, mind-contact as impermanent. Whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too he sees as impermanent. This, bhikkhus, is that practice conducive to Nibbāna.” Second.

3. Dukkhanibbānasappāyasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on Suffering Conducive to Nibbāna

148. “Nibbānasappāyaṃ [V 2.0137][T 4.0168] vo, bhikkhave, paṭipadaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha…pe… katamā ca sā, bhikkhave, nibbānasappāyā paṭipadā? Idha, bhikkhave, cakkhuṃ dukkhanti passati, rūpā dukkhāti passati, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dukkhanti passati, cakkhusamphasso dukkhoti passati, yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi dukkhanti passati…pe… jivhā dukkhāti passati…pe… mano dukkhoti passati, dhammā dukkhāti passati, manoviññāṇaṃ dukkhanti passati, manosamphasso dukkhoti passati, yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi [M 2.0348] dukkhanti passati. Ayaṃ kho sā, bhikkhave, nibbānasappāyā paṭipadā”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

148. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the practice conducive to Nibbāna. Listen to it... And what, bhikkhus, is that practice conducive to Nibbāna? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu sees the eye as suffering, he sees forms as suffering, he sees eye-consciousness as suffering, he sees eye-contact as suffering. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too he sees as suffering... He sees the tongue as suffering... He sees the mind as suffering, he sees mental objects as suffering, he sees mind-consciousness as suffering, he sees mind-contact as suffering. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too he sees as suffering. This, bhikkhus, is that practice conducive to Nibbāna.” Third.

4. Anattanibbānasappāyasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on Not-Self Conducive to Nibbāna

149. “Nibbānasappāyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, paṭipadaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha…pe… katamā ca sā, bhikkhave, nibbānasappāyā paṭipadā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhuṃ anattāti passati, rūpā anattāti passati, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ anattāti passati, cakkhusamphasso anattāti passati, yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā [P 4.0135] uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi anattāti passati…pe… mano anattāti passati, dhammā anattāti passati, manoviññāṇaṃ anattāti passati, manosamphasso anattāti passati, yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ [T 4.0169] vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi anattāti passati. Ayaṃ kho sā, bhikkhave, nibbānasappāyā paṭipadā”ti. Catutthaṃ.

149. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the practice conducive to Nibbāna. Listen to it... And what, bhikkhus, is that practice conducive to Nibbāna? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu sees the eye as not-self, he sees forms as not-self, he sees eye-consciousness as not-self, he sees eye-contact as not-self. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too he sees as not-self... He sees the mind as not-self, he sees mental objects as not-self, he sees mind-consciousness as not-self, he sees mind-contact as not-self. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too he sees as not-self. This, bhikkhus, is that practice conducive to Nibbāna.” Fourth.

5. Nibbānasappāyapaṭipadāsuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on the Practice Conducive to Nibbāna

150. “Nibbānasappāyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, paṭipadaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha…pe… katamā ca sā, bhikkhave, nibbānasappāyā paṭipadā? Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, cakkhu niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

150. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the practice conducive to Nibbāna. Listen to it... And what, bhikkhus, is that practice conducive to Nibbāna? What do you think, bhikkhus, is the eye permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ[V 2.0138], bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“Now, that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“It is suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti?

“Now, that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Indeed, it is not, venerable sir.”

“Rūpā niccā vā aniccā vā”ti?

“Are forms permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccā, bhante”…pe….

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”…pe…

“Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ… cakkhusamphasso…pe… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vā”ti?

“Is eye-consciousness… eye-contact…pe… and whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—is that too permanent or impermanent?”

“Aniccaṃ, bhante”.

“Impermanent, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vā”ti?

“Now, that which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?”

“Dukkhaṃ, bhante”.

“It is suffering, venerable sir.”

“Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ – ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”ti?

“Now, that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it fitting to regard it thus: ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?”

“No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Indeed, it is not, venerable sir.”

“Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati, rūpesupi nibbindati, cakkhuviññāṇepi nibbindati, cakkhusamphassepi nibbindati…pe… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tasmimpi nibbindati[P 4.0136]. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati [V 2.0139] …pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānāti. Ayaṃ kho sā, bhikkhave, nibbānasappāyā paṭipadā”ti[T 4.0170]. Pañcamaṃ.

“Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, disenchanted with eye-contact…pe… and with whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—with that too he becomes disenchanted. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated…pe… He understands: ‘…there is nothing further for this state of being.’ This, bhikkhus, is that practice conducive to Nibbāna.” The fifth.

6. Antevāsikasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on the Resident Pupil

151. “Anantevāsikamidaṃ[M 2.0349], bhikkhave, brahmacariyaṃ vussati anācariyakaṃ. Santevāsiko, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sācariyako dukkhaṃ na phāsu phāsuṃ (sī. pī.) viharati. Anantevāsiko, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anācariyako sukhaṃ phāsu viharati. Kathañca, bhikkhu, santevāsiko sācariyako dukkhaṃ na phāsu viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā dhammā sarasaṅkappā saṃyojaniyā. Tyāssa anto vasanti, antassa vasanti pāpakā akusalā dhammāti. Tasmā santevāsikoti vuccati. Te naṃ samudācaranti, samudācaranti naṃ pāpakā akusalā dhammāti. Tasmā sācariyakoti vuccati…pe….

151. “Bhikkhus, this holy life is lived without a resident pupil, without a teacher. A bhikkhu, bhikkhus, who has a resident pupil and a teacher dwells in suffering, not at ease. A bhikkhu, bhikkhus, who is without a resident pupil and without a teacher dwells happily, at ease. And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu who has a resident pupil and a teacher dwell in suffering, not at ease? Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu sees a form with the eye, evil, unwholesome states—thoughts that rush, conducive to fetters—arise. They dwell within him; because evil, unwholesome states dwell within him, he is therefore called ‘one with a resident pupil.’ They assail him; because evil, unwholesome states assail him, he is therefore called ‘one with a teacher.’…pe…

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā dhammā sarasaṅkappā saṃyojaniyā. Tyāssa anto vasanti, antassa vasanti pāpakā akusalā dhammāti. Tasmā santevāsikoti vuccati. Te naṃ samudācaranti, samudācaranti naṃ pāpakā akusalā dhammāti. Tasmā sācariyakoti vuccati…pe….

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has tasted a flavor with the tongue, evil, unwholesome states—thoughts that rush, conducive to fetters—arise. They dwell within him; because evil, unwholesome states dwell within him, he is therefore called ‘one with a resident pupil.’ They assail him; because evil, unwholesome states assail him, he is therefore called ‘one with a teacher.’…pe…

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno manasā dhammaṃ viññāya uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā dhammā sarasaṅkappā saṃyojaniyā. Tyāssa anto vasanti, antassa vasanti [P 4.0137] pāpakā akusalā dhammāti. Tasmā santevāsikoti vuccati. Te naṃ samudācaranti, samudācaranti naṃ pāpakā akusalā dhammāti. Tasmā sācariyakoti vuccati. Evaṃ kho[T 4.0171], bhikkhave, bhikkhu santevāsiko sācariyako dukkhaṃ, na phāsu viharati.

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has cognized a mental object with the mind, evil, unwholesome states—thoughts that rush, conducive to fetters—arise. They dwell within him; because evil, unwholesome states dwell within him, he is therefore called ‘one with a resident pupil.’ They assail him; because evil, unwholesome states assail him, he is therefore called ‘one with a teacher.’ Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who has a resident pupil and a teacher dwells in suffering, not at ease.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anantevāsiko anācariyako sukhaṃ phāsu viharati? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā na uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā dhammā sarasaṅkappā saṃyojaniyā. Tyāssa na anto vasanti, nāssa anto vasanti pāpakā akusalā dhammāti[V 2.0140]. Tasmā anantevāsikoti vuccati. Te naṃ na samudācaranti, na samudācaranti naṃ pāpakā akusalā dhammāti. Tasmā anācariyakoti vuccati…pe….

“And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu who is without a resident pupil and without a teacher dwell happily, at ease? Here, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu sees a form with the eye, evil, unwholesome states—thoughts that rush, conducive to fetters—do not arise. They do not dwell within him; because evil, unwholesome states do not dwell within him, he is therefore called ‘one without a resident pupil.’ They do not assail him; because evil, unwholesome states do not assail him, he is therefore called ‘one without a teacher.’…pe…

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā na uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā dhammā sarasaṅkappā saṃyojaniyā. Tyāssa na anto vasanti, nāssa [M 2.0350] anto vasanti pāpakā akusalā dhammāti. Tasmā anantevāsikoti vuccati. Te naṃ na samudācaranti, na samudācaranti naṃ pāpakā akusalā dhammāti. Tasmā anācariyakoti vuccati…pe….

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has tasted a flavor with the tongue, evil, unwholesome states—thoughts that rush, conducive to fetters—do not arise. They do not dwell within him; because evil, unwholesome states do not dwell within him, he is therefore called ‘one without a resident pupil.’ They do not assail him; because evil, unwholesome states do not assail him, he is therefore called ‘one without a teacher.’…pe…

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno manasā dhammaṃ viññāya na uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā dhammā sarasaṅkappā saṃyojaniyā. Tyāssa na anto vasanti, nāssa anto vasanti pāpakā akusalā dhammāti. Tasmā anantevāsikoti vuccati. Te naṃ na samudācaranti, na samudācaranti naṃ pāpakā akusalā dhammāti. Tasmā anācariyakoti vuccati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anantevāsiko anācariyako sukhaṃ phāsu viharati. Anantevāsikamidaṃ, bhikkhave, brahmacariyaṃ vussati[T 4.0172]. Anācariyakaṃ santevāsiko[P 4.0138], bhikkhave, bhikkhu sācariyako dukkhaṃ, na phāsu viharati. Anantevāsiko, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anācariyako sukhaṃ phāsu viharatī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu has cognized a mental object with the mind, evil, unwholesome states—thoughts that rush, conducive to fetters—do not arise. They do not dwell within him; because evil, unwholesome states do not dwell within him, he is therefore called ‘one without a resident pupil.’ They do not assail him; because evil, unwholesome states do not assail him, he is therefore called ‘one without a teacher.’ Thus, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is without a resident pupil and without a teacher dwells happily, at ease. This holy life, bhikkhus, is lived without a resident pupil and without a teacher. A bhikkhu, bhikkhus, who has a resident pupil and a teacher dwells in suffering, not at ease. A bhikkhu, bhikkhus, who is without a resident pupil and without a teacher dwells happily, at ease.” The sixth.

7. Kimatthiyabrahmacariyasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on the Purpose of the Holy Life

152. “Sace vo, bhikkhave, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ puccheyyuṃ – ‘kimatthiyaṃ, āvuso, samaṇe gotame brahmacariyaṃ vussatī’ti? Evaṃ puṭṭhā tumhe, bhikkhave, tesaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ evaṃ byākareyyātha – ‘dukkhassa kho, āvuso, pariññāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussatī’ti. Sace pana vo, bhikkhave, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ puccheyyuṃ – ‘katamaṃ panāvuso, dukkhaṃ, yassa pariññāya samaṇe gotame brahmacariyaṃ vussatī’ti? Evaṃ puṭṭhā tumhe, bhikkhave, tesaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ evaṃ byākareyyātha –

152. “Bhikkhus, if wanderers of other sects should ask you: ‘For what purpose, friends, is the holy life lived under the ascetic Gotama?’—being asked thus, bhikkhus, you should answer those wanderers of other sects thus: ‘For the full understanding of suffering, friends, the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.’ If then, bhikkhus, wanderers of other sects should ask you: ‘But what, friends, is that suffering for the full understanding of which the holy life is lived under the ascetic Gotama?’—being asked thus, bhikkhus, you should answer those wanderers of other sects thus:

“Cakkhu kho, āvuso, dukkhaṃ; tassa pariññāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati. Rūpā dukkhā[V 2.0141]; tesaṃ pariññāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dukkhaṃ; tassa pariññāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati. Cakkhusamphasso dukkho; tassa pariññāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi dukkhaṃ; tassa pariññāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati…pe… jivhā dukkhā… mano dukkho; tassa pariññāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati…pe… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ [T 4.0173] vā tampi dukkhaṃ; tassa pariññāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussati. Idaṃ kho, āvuso[M 2.0351], dukkhaṃ; yassa pariññāya bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussatī’ti. Evaṃ puṭṭhā tumhe, bhikkhave, tesaṃ aññatitthiyānaṃ paribbājakānaṃ evaṃ byākareyyāthā”ti. Sattamaṃ.

‘Friends, the eye is suffering; for its full understanding the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. Forms are suffering; for their full understanding the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. Eye-consciousness is suffering; for its full understanding the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. Eye-contact is suffering; for its full understanding the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. Whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is suffering; for its full understanding the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. … The tongue is suffering … the mind is suffering; for its full understanding the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. … Whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is suffering; for its full understanding the holy life is lived under the Blessed One. This, friends, is the suffering for the full understanding of which the holy life is lived under the Blessed One.’ Being asked thus, bhikkhus, you should answer those wanderers of other sects in this way.”

8. Atthinukhopariyāyasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on Whether There Is a Method

153. “Atthi nu kho, bhikkhave, pariyāyo yaṃ pariyāyaṃ āgamma bhikkhu aññatreva saddhāya, aññatra ruciyā, aññatra anussavā, aññatra ākāraparivitakkā, aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā [P 4.0139] aññaṃ byākareyya – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāmī”ti pajānātīti (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.)? “Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā, bhagavaṃnettikā bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā. Sādhu vata, bhante, bhagavantaṃyeva paṭibhātu etassa bhāsitassa attho. Bhagavato sutvā bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti. “Tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha; bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho te bhikkhū bhagavato paccassosuṃ. Bhagavā etadavoca – “atthi, bhikkhave, pariyāyo yaṃ pariyāyaṃ āgamma bhikkhu aññatreva saddhāya, aññatra ruciyā, aññatra anussavā, aññatra ākāraparivitakkā, aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā aññaṃ byākareyya – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāmī”ti.

153. “Is there, bhikkhus, a method, relying on which a bhikkhu—apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoning about appearances, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration—might declare final knowledge: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being, I know’?” “Venerable sir, our teachings have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, the Blessed One as their recourse. It would be good if the Blessed One himself would illuminate the meaning of this statement. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will remember it.” “Then listen, bhikkhus, and pay close attention. I will speak.” “Yes, venerable sir,” the bhikkhus replied. The Blessed One said: “There is, bhikkhus, a method, relying on which a bhikkhu—apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoning about appearances, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration—might declare final knowledge: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being, I know’.”

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, pariyāyo, yaṃ pariyāyaṃ āgamma bhikkhu aññatreva saddhāya…pe… aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā aññaṃ [T 4.0174] byākaroti – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānāmī’ti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohaṃ, atthi me ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohoti pajānāti[V 2.0142]; asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohaṃ, natthi me ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohoti pajānāti. Yaṃ taṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohaṃ, atthi me ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohoti pajānāti; asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohaṃ, natthi me ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohoti pajānāti. Api nume, bhikkhave, dhammā saddhāya vā veditabbā, ruciyā vā veditabbā, anussavena vā veditabbā, ākāraparivitakkena vā veditabbā, diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā vā veditabbā”ti? “No hetaṃ[M 2.0352], bhante”. “Nanume, bhikkhave, dhammā paññāya disvā veditabbā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, pariyāyo yaṃ pariyāyaṃ āgamma bhikkhu aññatreva saddhāya, aññatra ruciyā, aññatra anussavā, aññatra ākāraparivitakkā, aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā aññaṃ byākaroti – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāmī”ti…pe….

“And what, bhikkhus, is that method, relying on which a bhikkhu—apart from faith… apart from acceptance of a view after consideration—declares final knowledge: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being, I know’? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, if there is internal lust, hatred, and delusion, knows: ‘There is internal lust, hatred, and delusion in me.’ If there is no internal lust, hatred, and delusion, he knows: ‘There is no internal lust, hatred, and delusion in me.’ That a bhikkhu, bhikkhus, having seen a form with the eye, knows ‘There is internal lust, hatred, and delusion in me’ when it is present, and knows ‘There is no internal lust, hatred, and delusion in me’ when it is absent—should these matters be known through faith? Should they be known through inclination? Should they be known through oral tradition? Should they be known through reasoning about appearances? Should they be known through acceptance of a view after consideration?” “No, venerable sir.” “Bhikkhus, should these matters not be known by seeing them with wisdom?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “This, bhikkhus, is the method, relying on which a bhikkhu—apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoning about appearances, apart from acceptance of a view after consideration—declares final knowledge: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being, I know’.”

“Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ…pe… rāgadosamohoti pajānāti; asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohaṃ, natthi me ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohoti pajānāti[T 4.0175]. Yaṃ taṃ, bhikkhave, jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohaṃ, atthi me ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohoti pajānāti; asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohaṃ, natthi me ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohoti pajānāti; api nume, bhikkhave, dhammā saddhāya vā veditabbā, ruciyā vā veditabbā, anussavena vā veditabbā, ākāraparivitakkena vā veditabbā, diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā vā veditabbā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Nanume, bhikkhave, dhammā paññāya disvā veditabbā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Ayampi kho, bhikkhave, pariyāyo yaṃ pariyāyaṃ āgamma bhikkhu aññatreva saddhāya, aññatra ruciyā, aññatra anussavā, aññatra ākāraparivitakkā, aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā aññaṃ byākaroti – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāmī”ti pajānātīti (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) …pe….

“Furthermore, monks, a monk, having tasted a flavor with the tongue, knows of the existing internal… lust, hatred, and delusion, thus: ‘There is internal lust, hatred, and delusion in me’; or he knows of the non-existent internal lust, hatred, and delusion, thus: ‘There is no internal lust, hatred, and delusion in me.’ Monks, that which he knows—having tasted a flavor with the tongue, he knows of the existing internal lust, hatred, and delusion, thus: ‘There is internal lust, hatred, and delusion in me,’ or he knows of the non-existent internal lust, hatred, and delusion, thus: ‘There is no internal lust, hatred, and delusion in me’—should these things, monks, be known through faith, through inclination, through oral tradition, through reasoned contemplation, or through the acceptance of a view after consideration?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Monks, should not these things be known by seeing them with wisdom?” “Indeed, venerable sir.” “This, monks, is the way by which a monk—apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned contemplation, and apart from the acceptance of a view after consideration—declares final knowledge: ‘I know that birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, and there is nothing further for this state of being.’”… and so on…

“Puna [P 4.0140] caparaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu manasā dhammaṃ viññāya santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohaṃ, atthi me ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohoti pajānāti; asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohaṃ, natthi me ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohoti pajānāti. Yaṃ taṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu manasā [V 2.0143] dhammaṃ viññāya santaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohaṃ, atthi me ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohoti pajānāti; asantaṃ vā ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohaṃ, natthi me ajjhattaṃ rāgadosamohoti pajānāti; api nume, bhikkhave, dhammā saddhāya vā veditabbā, ruciyā vā veditabbā, anussavena [T 4.0176] vā veditabbā, ākāraparivitakkena vā veditabbā, diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā vā veditabbā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Nanume, bhikkhave, dhammā paññāya disvā veditabbā”ti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Ayampi kho, bhikkhave, pariyāyo yaṃ pariyāyaṃ āgamma bhikkhu [M 2.0353] aññatreva saddhāya, aññatra ruciyā, aññatra anussavā, aññatra ākāraparivitakkā, aññatra diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiyā aññaṃ byākaroti – ‘khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāmī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Furthermore, monks, a monk, having cognized a mental object with the mind, knows of the existing internal lust, hatred, and delusion, thus: ‘There is internal lust, hatred, and delusion in me’; or he knows of the non-existent internal lust, hatred, and delusion, thus: ‘There is no internal lust, hatred, and delusion in me.’ Monks, that which he knows—having cognized a mental object with the mind, he knows of the existing internal lust, hatred, and delusion, thus: ‘There is internal lust, hatred, and delusion in me,’ or he knows of the non-existent internal lust, hatred, and delusion, thus: ‘There is no internal lust, hatred, and delusion in me’—should these things, monks, be known through faith, through inclination, through oral tradition, through reasoned contemplation, or through the acceptance of a view after consideration?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “Monks, should not these things be known by seeing them with wisdom?” “Indeed, venerable sir.” “This, monks, is the way by which a monk—apart from faith, apart from inclination, apart from oral tradition, apart from reasoned contemplation, and apart from the acceptance of a view after consideration—declares final knowledge: ‘I know that birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, and there is nothing further for this state of being.’” The eighth.

9. Indriyasampannasuttaṃ

9. 9. The Discourse on Being Endowed with Faculties

154. Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “‘indriyasampanno, indriyasampanno’ti, bhante, vuccati. Kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, indriyasampanno hotī”ti?

154. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One… and so on… Seated to one side, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘one endowed with faculties, one endowed with faculties.’ To what extent, venerable sir, is one endowed with faculties?”

“Cakkhundriye ce, bhikkhu, udayabbayānupassī viharanto cakkhundriye nibbindati…pe… jivhindriye ce, bhikkhu, udayabbayānupassī viharanto jivhindriye nibbindati…pe… manindriye ce, bhikkhu, udayabbayānupassī viharanto manindriye nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati…pe… vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti. Ettāvatā kho, bhikkhu, indriyasampanno hotī”ti. Navamaṃ.

“Bhikkhu, if, while dwelling contemplating arising and passing away in the eye faculty, one becomes disenchanted with the eye faculty… and so on… if, while dwelling contemplating arising and passing away in the tongue faculty, one becomes disenchanted with the tongue faculty… and so on… if, while dwelling contemplating arising and passing away in the mind faculty, one becomes disenchanted with the mind faculty. Being disenchanted, one becomes dispassionate… and so on… When liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ One knows: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, and there is nothing further for this state of being.’ It is to this extent, bhikkhu, that one is endowed with faculties.” The ninth.

10. Dhammakathikapucchasuttaṃ

10. 10. The Discourse on the Question about the Dhamma-preacher

155. Atha [P 4.0141] kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “‘dhammakathiko[T 4.0177], dhammakathiko’ti, bhante, vuccati. Kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, dhammakathiko hotī”ti?

155. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One… and so on… Seated to one side, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is said, ‘a Dhamma-preacher, a Dhamma-preacher.’ To what extent, venerable sir, is one a Dhamma-preacher?”

“Cakkhussa [V 2.0144] ce, bhikkhu nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya dhammaṃ deseti, ‘dhammakathiko bhikkhū’ti alaṃvacanāya. Cakkhussa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti, ‘dhammānudhammappaṭipanno bhikkhū’ti alaṃvacanāya. Cakkhussa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidā virāgā nirodhā anupādāvimutto hoti, ‘diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto bhikkhū’ti alaṃvacanāya…pe… jivhāya ce, bhikkhu, nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya dhammaṃ deseti, ‘dhammakathiko bhikkhū’ti alaṃvacanāya…pe… manassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya dhammaṃ deseti, ‘dhammakathiko bhikkhū’ti alaṃvacanāya. Manassa ce, bhikkhu, nibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya paṭipanno hoti, ‘dhammānudhammappaṭipanno bhikkhū’ti alaṃvacanāya. Manassa [M 2.0354] ce, bhikkhu, nibbidā virāgā nirodhā anupādāvimutto hoti, ‘diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto bhikkhū’ti alaṃvacanāyā”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“Bhikkhu, if one teaches the Dhamma for disenchantment with the eye, for its dispassion, for its cessation, it is fitting to say, ‘a Dhamma-preacher bhikkhu.’ If, bhikkhu, one is practicing for disenchantment with the eye, for its dispassion, for its cessation, it is fitting to say, ‘a bhikkhu practicing in accordance with the Dhamma.’ If, bhikkhu, through disenchantment with the eye, dispassion, and cessation, one is liberated without clinging, it is fitting to say, ‘a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life.’ …and so on… If, bhikkhu, one teaches the Dhamma for disenchantment with the tongue, for its dispassion, for its cessation, it is fitting to say, ‘a Dhamma-preacher bhikkhu.’ …and so on… If, bhikkhu, one teaches the Dhamma for disenchantment with the mind, for its dispassion, for its cessation, it is fitting to say, ‘a Dhamma-preacher bhikkhu.’ If, bhikkhu, one is practicing for disenchantment with the mind, for its dispassion, for its cessation, it is fitting to say, ‘a bhikkhu practicing in accordance with the Dhamma.’ If, bhikkhu, through disenchantment with the mind, dispassion, and cessation, one is liberated without clinging, it is fitting to say, ‘a bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna in this very life.’” The tenth.

Navapurāṇavaggo pañcadasamo.

The fifth chapter, the Navapurāṇavagga, is concluded.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Kammaṃ cattāri sappāyā, anantevāsi kimatthiyā;

Atthi nu kho pariyāyo, indriyakathikena cāti.

Kamma, four Sappāyas, Anantevāsi, Kimatthiya; Atthi Nu Kho Pariyāyo, Indriya, and with the Kathika.

Saḷāyatanavagge tatiyapaṇṇāsako samatto.

The Third Fifty in the Chapter on the Six Sense Bases is completed.

Tassa vagguddānaṃ –

The chapter summary thereof:

Yogakkhemi [T 4.0178] ca loko ca, gahapati devadahena ca;

Navapurāṇena paṇṇāso, tatiyo tena vuccatīti.

Yogakkhema and Loka, Gahapati and Devadaha; with Navapurāṇa, it is therefore called the Third Fifty.

16. Nandikkhayavaggo

16. The Chapter on the Destruction of Delight

1. Ajjhattanandikkhayasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on the Internal Destruction of Delight

156. “Aniccaṃyeva[T 4.0179][P 4.0142], bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhuṃ aniccanti passati, sāssa sāyaṃ (pī. ka.) hoti sammādiṭṭhi[V 2.0145]. Sammā passaṃ nibbindati. Nandikkhayā rāgakkhayo; rāgakkhayā nandikkhayo. Nandirāgakkhayā cittaṃ suvimuttanti vuccati…pe… aniccaṃyeva, bhikkhave, bhikkhu jivhaṃ aniccanti passati, sāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhi. Sammā passaṃ nibbindati. Nandikkhayā rāgakkhayo; rāgakkhayā…pe… cittaṃ suvimuttanti vuccati…pe… aniccaṃyeva, bhikkhave, bhikkhu manaṃ aniccanti passati, sāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhi. Sammā passaṃ nibbindati. Nandikkhayā rāgakkhayo; rāgakkhayā nandikkhayo. Nandirāgakkhayā cittaṃ suvimuttanti vuccatī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

156. “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu sees the eye, which is indeed impermanent, as ‘impermanent’; that is his right view. Seeing rightly, he becomes disenchanted. From the exhaustion of delight, there is the exhaustion of passion; from the exhaustion of passion, there is the exhaustion of delight. Through the exhaustion of delight and passion, the mind is said to be well liberated. … Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu sees the tongue, which is indeed impermanent, as ‘impermanent’; that is his right view. Seeing rightly, he becomes disenchanted. From the exhaustion of delight, there is the exhaustion of passion; from the exhaustion of passion… the mind is said to be well liberated. … Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu sees the mind, which is indeed impermanent, as ‘impermanent’; that is his right view. Seeing rightly, he becomes disenchanted. From the exhaustion of delight, there is the exhaustion of passion; from the exhaustion of passion, there is the exhaustion of delight. Through the exhaustion of delight and passion, the mind is said to be well liberated.” First.

2. Bāhiranandikkhayasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on the Exhaustion of External Delight

157. “Anicceyeva, bhikkhave, bhikkhu rūpe aniccāti passati, sāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhi. Sammā passaṃ nibbindati. Nandikkhayā rāgakkhayo; rāgakkhayā nandikkhayo[M 2.0355]. Nandirāgakkhayā cittaṃ suvimuttanti vuccati. Anicceyeva, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sadde… gandhe… rase… phoṭṭhabbe… dhamme aniccāti passati, sāssa hoti sammādiṭṭhi. Sammā passaṃ nibbindati. Nandikkhayā rāgakkhayo; rāgakkhayā nandikkhayo. Nandirāgakkhayā cittaṃ suvimuttanti vuccatī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

157. “Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu sees forms, which are indeed impermanent, as ‘impermanent’; that is his right view. Seeing rightly, he becomes disenchanted. From the exhaustion of delight, there is the exhaustion of passion; from the exhaustion of passion, there is the exhaustion of delight. Through the exhaustion of delight and passion, the mind is said to be well liberated. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu sees sounds... odors... tastes... tactile objects... mental phenomena, which are indeed impermanent, as ‘impermanent’; that is his right view. Seeing rightly, he becomes disenchanted. From the exhaustion of delight, there is the exhaustion of passion; from the exhaustion of passion, there is the exhaustion of delight. Through the exhaustion of delight and passion, the mind is said to be well liberated.” Second.

3. Ajjhattaaniccanandikkhayasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on Internal Impermanence and the Exhaustion of Delight

158. “Cakkhuṃ, bhikkhave, yoniso manasi karotha; cakkhāniccatañca yathābhūtaṃ [T 4.0180] samanupassatha. Cakkhuṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yoniso manasikaronto, cakkhāniccatañca yathābhūtaṃ samanupassanto cakkhusmimpi nibbindati. Nandikkhayā rāgakkhayo; rāgakkhayā nandikkhayo. Nandirāgakkhayā cittaṃ suvimuttanti vuccati. Sotaṃ[P 4.0143], bhikkhave, yoniso manasi karotha… ghānaṃ… jivhaṃ, bhikkhave, yoniso manasi karotha; jivhāniccatañca yathābhūtaṃ samanupassatha. Jivhaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yoniso manasikaronto, jivhāniccatañca yathābhūtaṃ samanupassanto jivhāyapi nibbindati. Nandikkhayā rāgakkhayo; rāgakkhayā nandikkhayo. Nandirāgakkhayā cittaṃ suvimuttanti vuccati. Kāyaṃ… manaṃ, bhikkhave, yoniso manasi karotha; manāniccatañca yathābhūtaṃ samanupassatha. Manaṃ, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yoniso manasikaronto[V 2.0146], manāniccatañca yathābhūtaṃ samanupassanto manasmimpi nibbindati. Nandikkhayā rāgakkhayo; rāgakkhayā nandikkhayo. Nandirāgakkhayā cittaṃ suvimuttanti vuccatī”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

158. “Bhikkhus, attend to the eye properly, and see the impermanence of the eye as it really is. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, attending to the eye properly and seeing its impermanence as it really is, becomes disenchanted with the eye. From the exhaustion of delight, there is the exhaustion of passion; from the exhaustion of passion, there is the exhaustion of delight. Through the exhaustion of delight and passion, the mind is said to be well liberated. Bhikkhus, attend to the ear properly... the nose... Bhikkhus, attend to the tongue properly, and see the impermanence of the tongue as it really is. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, attending to the tongue properly and seeing its impermanence as it really is, becomes disenchanted with the tongue. From the exhaustion of delight, there is the exhaustion of passion; from the exhaustion of passion, there is the exhaustion of delight. Through the exhaustion of delight and passion, the mind is said to be well liberated. ...the body... Bhikkhus, attend to the mind properly, and see the impermanence of the mind as it really is. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, attending to the mind properly and seeing its impermanence as it really is, becomes disenchanted with the mind. From the exhaustion of delight, there is the exhaustion of passion; from the exhaustion of passion, there is the exhaustion of delight. Through the exhaustion of delight and passion, the mind is said to be well liberated.” Third.

4. Bāhiraaniccanandikkhayasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on External Impermanence and the Exhaustion of Delight

159. “Rūpe, bhikkhave, yoniso manasi karotha; rūpāniccatañca yathābhūtaṃ samanupassatha. Rūpe, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yoniso manasikaronto, rūpāniccatañca yathābhūtaṃ samanupassanto rūpesupi nibbindati. Nandikkhayā rāgakkhayo; rāgakkhayā nandikkhayo. Nandirāgakkhayā cittaṃ suvimuttanti vuccati. Sadde… gandhe… rase… phoṭṭhabbe… dhamme, bhikkhave, yoniso manasi karotha; dhammāniccatañca yathābhūtaṃ samanupassatha. Dhamme, bhikkhave, bhikkhu yoniso manasikaronto, dhammāniccatañca yathābhūtaṃ samanupassanto dhammesupi nibbindati. Nandikkhayā rāgakkhayo; rāgakkhayā nandikkhayo[T 4.0181]. Nandirāgakkhayā cittaṃ suvimuttanti vuccatī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

159. “Bhikkhus, attend to forms properly, and see the impermanence of forms as it really is. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, attending to forms properly and seeing their impermanence as it really is, becomes disenchanted with forms. From the exhaustion of delight, there is the exhaustion of passion; from the exhaustion of passion, there is the exhaustion of delight. Through the exhaustion of delight and passion, the mind is said to be well liberated. ...sounds... odors... tastes... tactile objects... Bhikkhus, attend to mental phenomena properly, and see the impermanence of mental phenomena as it really is. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, attending to mental phenomena properly and seeing their impermanence as it really is, becomes disenchanted with mental phenomena. From the exhaustion of delight, there is the exhaustion of passion; from the exhaustion of passion, there is the exhaustion of delight. Through the exhaustion of delight and passion, the mind is said to be well liberated.” Fourth.

5. Jīvakambavanasamādhisuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Concentration at Jīvaka’s Mango Grove

160. Ekaṃ [M 2.0356] samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati jīvakambavane. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi – “bhikkhavo”ti…pe… “samādhiṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvetha. Samāhitassa, bhikkhave[P 4.0144], bhikkhuno yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati. Kiñca yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati? Cakkhuṃ aniccanti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati, rūpā aniccāti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ aniccanti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati, cakkhusamphasso aniccoti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati, yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccanti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati…pe… jivhā aniccāti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati…pe… mano aniccoti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati, dhammā aniccāti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati…pe… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccanti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati. Samādhiṃ, bhikkhave, bhāvetha. Samāhitassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyatī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

160. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus…” … “Develop concentration, bhikkhus. For a bhikkhu who is concentrated, it is discerned as it really is. And what is discerned as it really is? ‘The eye is impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is. ‘Forms are impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is. ‘Eye-consciousness is impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is. ‘Eye-contact is impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is. ‘Whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is… ‘The tongue is impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is… ‘The mind is impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is. ‘Mental phenomena are impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is… ‘Whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is. Develop concentration, bhikkhus. For a bhikkhu who is concentrated, it is discerned as it really is.” Fifth.

6. Jīvakambavanapaṭisallānasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Seclusion at Jīvaka’s Mango Grove

161. Ekaṃ [V 2.0147] samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati jīvakambavane. Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi…pe… “paṭisallāne, bhikkhave, yogamāpajjatha. Paṭisallīnassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati. Kiñca yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati? Cakkhuṃ aniccanti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati, rūpā aniccāti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ aniccanti [T 4.0182] yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati, cakkhusamphasso aniccoti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati, yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccanti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati…pe… mano aniccoti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati, dhammā… manoviññāṇaṃ… manosamphasso… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā [P 4.0145] adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccanti yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyati. Paṭisallāne bhikkhave, yogamāpajjatha. Paṭisallīnassa, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno yathābhūtaṃ okkhāyatī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

161. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: … “Bhikkhus, apply yourselves to seclusion. For a bhikkhu who is in seclusion, bhikkhus, it is discerned as it really is. And what is discerned as it really is? ‘The eye is impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is. ‘Forms are impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is. ‘Eye-consciousness is impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is. ‘Eye-contact is impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is. ‘Whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is… ‘The mind is impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is. ‘Mental phenomena… mind-consciousness… mind-contact… whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent,’ is discerned as it really is. Bhikkhus, apply yourselves to seclusion. For a bhikkhu who is in seclusion, bhikkhus, it is discerned as it really is.”

7. Koṭṭhikaaniccasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on Impermanence to Koṭṭhika

162. Atha kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā koṭṭhiko bhagavantaṃ etadavoca [M 2.0357] – “sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetu, yamahaṃ bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto vihareyya”nti.

162. Then the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika approached the Blessed One … Having sat down to one side, the Venerable Koṭṭhika said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.”

“Yaṃ kho, koṭṭhika, aniccaṃ tatra te chando pahātabbo. Kiñca, koṭṭhika, aniccaṃ? Cakkhu kho, koṭṭhika, aniccaṃ; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Rūpā aniccā; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Cakkhusamphasso anicco; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccaṃ; tatra te chando pahātabbo…pe… jivhā aniccā; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Rasā [T 4.0183] aniccā; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Jivhāviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Jivhāsamphasso anicco; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Yampidaṃ [V 2.0148] jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccaṃ; tatra te chando pahātabbo…pe… mano anicco; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Dhammā aniccā; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Manoviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Manosamphasso anicco; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccaṃ; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Yaṃ kho, koṭṭhika, aniccaṃ tatra te chando pahātabbo”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Koṭṭhika, whatever is impermanent, in that you should abandon desire. And what, Koṭṭhika, is impermanent? The eye, Koṭṭhika, is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire. Forms are impermanent; in them you should abandon desire. Eye-consciousness is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire. Eye-contact is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire. Whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire… The tongue is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire. Flavors are impermanent; in them you should abandon desire. Tongue-consciousness is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire. Tongue-contact is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire. Whatever feeling arises with tongue-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire… The mind is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire. Mental objects are impermanent; in them you should abandon desire. Mind-consciousness is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire. Mind-contact is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire. Whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is impermanent; in that you should abandon desire. Koṭṭhika, whatever is impermanent, in that you should abandon desire.”

8. Koṭṭhikadukkhasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on Suffering to Koṭṭhika

163. Atha [P 4.0146] kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko…pe… bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “sādhu me, bhante…pe… vihareyya”nti. “Yaṃ kho, koṭṭhika, dukkhaṃ tatra te chando pahātabbo. Kiñca, koṭṭhika, dukkhaṃ? Cakkhu kho, koṭṭhika, dukkhaṃ; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Rūpā dukkhā; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dukkhaṃ; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Cakkhusamphasso dukkho; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi dukkhaṃ; tatra te chando pahātabbo…pe… jivhā dukkhā; tatra te chando pahātabbo…pe… mano dukkho; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Dhammā dukkhā; tatra te chando pahātabbo[T 4.0184]. Manoviññāṇaṃ dukkhaṃ[M 2.0358]; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Manosamphasso dukkho; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi dukkhaṃ; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Yaṃ kho, koṭṭhika, dukkhaṃ tatra te chando pahātabbo”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

163. Then the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika… said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir… I might dwell.” “Koṭṭhika, whatever is suffering, in that you should abandon desire. And what, Koṭṭhika, is suffering? The eye, Koṭṭhika, is suffering; in that you should abandon desire. Forms are suffering; in them you should abandon desire. Eye-consciousness is suffering; in that you should abandon desire. Eye-contact is suffering; in that you should abandon desire. Whatever feeling arises with eye-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is suffering; in that you should abandon desire… The tongue is suffering; in that you should abandon desire… The mind is suffering; in that you should abandon desire. Mental objects are suffering; in them you should abandon desire. Mind-consciousness is suffering; in that you should abandon desire. Mind-contact is suffering; in that you should abandon desire. Whatever feeling arises with mind-contact as its condition—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is suffering; in that you should abandon desire. Koṭṭhika, whatever is suffering, in that you should abandon desire.”

9. Koṭṭhikaanattasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on Not-Self to Koṭṭhika

164. Ekamantaṃ…pe… vihareyyanti. “Yo kho, koṭṭhika, anattā tatra te chando pahātabbo. Ko ca, koṭṭhika, anattā? Cakkhu kho, koṭṭhika, anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Rūpā anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Cakkhusamphasso anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo [V 2.0149] …pe… jivhā anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo…pe… mano anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Dhammā anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Manoviññāṇaṃ… manosamphasso… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā [P 4.0147] uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi anattā; tatra te chando pahātabbo. Yo kho, koṭṭhika, anattā, tatra te chando pahātabbo”ti. Navamaṃ.

164. …to one side… he would dwell. “Koṭṭhika, whatever is not-self, desire for it should be abandoned by you. And what, Koṭṭhika, is not-self? The eye, Koṭṭhika, is not-self; desire for it should be abandoned by you. Forms are not-self; desire for them should be abandoned by you. Eye-consciousness is not-self; desire for it should be abandoned by you. Eye-contact is not-self; desire for it should be abandoned by you. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is not-self; desire for it should be abandoned by you. … The tongue is not-self; desire for it should be abandoned by you. … The mind is not-self; desire for it should be abandoned by you. Mental objects are not-self; desire for them should be abandoned by you. Mind-consciousness… mind-contact… And whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is not-self; desire for it should be abandoned by you. Koṭṭhika, whatever is not-self, desire for it should be abandoned by you.” The Ninth.

10. Micchādiṭṭhipahānasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on Abandoning Wrong View

165. Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami…pe… ekamantaṃ [T 4.0185] nisinno so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “kathaṃ nu kho, bhante, jānato kathaṃ passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyatī”ti?

165. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One… and, having approached, sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how for one who knows, how for one who sees, is wrong view abandoned?”

“Cakkhuṃ kho, bhikkhu, aniccato jānato passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyati. Rūpe aniccato jānato passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyati. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ aniccato jānato passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyati. Cakkhusamphassaṃ aniccato jānato passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyati…pe… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccato jānato passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, jānato evaṃ passato micchādiṭṭhi pahīyatī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“Bhikkhu, for one who knows and sees the eye as impermanent, wrong view is abandoned. For one who knows and sees forms as impermanent, wrong view is abandoned. For one who knows and sees eye-consciousness as impermanent, wrong view is abandoned. For one who knows and sees eye-contact as impermanent, wrong view is abandoned… And whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—for one who knows and sees that too as impermanent, wrong view is abandoned. Bhikkhu, it is for one who knows thus and sees thus that wrong view is abandoned.” The Tenth.

11. Sakkāyadiṭṭhipahānasuttaṃ

11. The Discourse on Abandoning Identity View

166. Atha [M 2.0359][V 2.0150] kho aññataro bhikkhu…pe… etadavoca – “kathaṃ nu kho, bhante, jānato kathaṃ passato sakkāyadiṭṭhi pahīyatī”ti? “Cakkhuṃ kho, bhikkhu, dukkhato jānato passato sakkāyadiṭṭhi pahīyati. Rūpe dukkhato jānato passato sakkāyadiṭṭhi pahīyati. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ dukkhato jānato passato sakkāyadiṭṭhi pahīyati. Cakkhusamphassaṃ dukkhato jānato passato sakkāyadiṭṭhi pahīyati…pe… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi dukkhato jānato passato sakkāyadiṭṭhi pahīyati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhu, jānato evaṃ passato sakkāyadiṭṭhi pahīyatī”ti. Ekādasamaṃ.

166. Then a certain bhikkhu… said this: “Venerable sir, how for one who knows, how for one who sees, is identity view abandoned?” “Bhikkhu, for one who knows and sees the eye as suffering, identity view is abandoned. For one who knows and sees forms as suffering, identity view is abandoned. For one who knows and sees eye-consciousness as suffering, identity view is abandoned. For one who knows and sees eye-contact as suffering, identity view is abandoned… And whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—for one who knows and sees that too as suffering, identity view is abandoned. It is in this way, bhikkhu, for one who knows thus and sees thus, that identity view is abandoned.” The Eleventh.

12. Attānudiṭṭhipahānasuttaṃ

12. The Discourse on Abandoning Self-View

167. Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu…pe… etadavoca [P 4.0148] – “kathaṃ nu kho[T 4.0186], bhante, jānato kathaṃ passato attānudiṭṭhi pahīyatī”ti? “Cakkhuṃ kho, bhikkhu, anattato jānato passato attānudiṭṭhi pahīyati. Rūpe anattato jānato passato attānudiṭṭhi pahīyati. Cakkhuviññāṇaṃ anattato jānato passato attānudiṭṭhi pahīyati. Cakkhusamphassaṃ anattato jānato passato attānudiṭṭhi pahīyati. Yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi anattato jānato passato attānudiṭṭhi pahīyati…pe… jivhaṃ anattato jānato passato attānudiṭṭhi pahīyati…pe… manaṃ anattato [V 2.0151] jānato passato attānudiṭṭhi pahīyati. Dhamme… manoviññāṇaṃ… manosamphassaṃ… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi anattato jānato passato attānudiṭṭhi pahīyatī”ti. Dvādasamaṃ.

167. Then a certain bhikkhu… said this: “Venerable sir, how for one who knows, how for one who sees, is self-view abandoned?” “Bhikkhu, for one who knows and sees the eye as not-self, self-view is abandoned. For one who knows and sees forms as not-self, self-view is abandoned. For one who knows and sees eye-consciousness as not-self, self-view is abandoned. For one who knows and sees eye-contact as not-self, self-view is abandoned. And whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—for one who knows and sees that too as not-self, self-view is abandoned. … For one who knows and sees the tongue as not-self, self-view is abandoned. … For one who knows and sees the mind as not-self, self-view is abandoned. For one who knows and sees mental phenomena… mind-consciousness… mind-contact… And whatever feeling arises conditioned by mind-contact—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—for one who knows and sees that too as not-self, self-view is abandoned.” The Twelfth.

Nandikkhayavaggo soḷasamo.

The Sixteenth Chapter on the Exhaustion of Delight.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Nandikkhayena cattāro, jīvakambavane duve;

Koṭṭhikena tayo vuttā, micchā sakkāya attanoti.

Four on the exhaustion of delight, two in Jīvaka's Mango Grove; with Koṭṭhika, three are spoken: Wrong View, Identity View, and Self-view.

17. Saṭṭhipeyyālavaggo

17. The Chapter of Sixty Repetitions

1. Ajjhattaaniccachandasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on Desire regarding the Internal and Impermanent

168. “Yaṃ[T 4.0187][M 2.0360], bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, tatra vo chando pahātabbo. Kiñca, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ? Cakkhu[P 4.0149], bhikkhave, aniccaṃ; tatra vo chando pahātabbo…pe… jivhā aniccā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo…pe… mano anicco; tatra vo chando pahātabbo. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, tatra vo chando pahātabbo”ti.

168. “Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, therein you should abandon desire. And what, bhikkhus, is impermanent? The eye, bhikkhus, is impermanent; therein you should abandon desire… The tongue is impermanent; therein you should abandon desire… The mind is impermanent; therein you should abandon desire. Whatever, bhikkhus, is impermanent, therein you should abandon desire.”

2. Ajjhattaaniccarāgasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on Lust regarding the Internal and Impermanent

169. “Yaṃ[V 2.0152], bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo. Kiñca, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ; tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo…pe… jivhā aniccā; tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo…pe… mano anicco; tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, tatra vo rāgo pahātabbo”ti.

169. “Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, therein you should abandon lust. And what, bhikkhus, is impermanent? The eye, bhikkhus, is impermanent; therein you should abandon lust… The tongue is impermanent; therein you should abandon lust… The mind is impermanent; therein you should abandon lust. Whatever, bhikkhus, is impermanent, therein you should abandon lust.”

3. Ajjhattaaniccachandarāgasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on Desire and Lust regarding the Internal and Impermanent

170. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo. Kiñca, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ; tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo…pe… jivhā aniccā; tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo…pe… mano anicco; tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, tatra vo chandarāgo pahātabbo”ti.

170. “Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, therein you should abandon desire and lust. And what, bhikkhus, is impermanent? The eye, bhikkhus, is impermanent; therein you should abandon desire and lust… The tongue is impermanent; therein you should abandon desire and lust… The mind is impermanent; therein you should abandon desire and lust. Whatever, bhikkhus, is impermanent, therein you should abandon desire and lust.”

4-6. Dukkhachandādisuttaṃ

4–6. The Discourse on Suffering, Desire, and So On

171-173. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ, tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Kiñca, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo…pe… jivhā dukkhā…pe… [T 4.0188] mano dukkho; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Yaṃ[P 4.0150], bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo”ti.

171–173. “Bhikkhus, whatever is suffering, therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. And what, bhikkhus, is suffering? The eye, bhikkhus, is suffering; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust… The tongue is suffering… The mind is suffering; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. Whatever, bhikkhus, is suffering, therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust.”

7-9. Anattachandādisuttaṃ

7–9. The Discourse on Not-Self, Desire, and So On

174-176. “Yo[M 2.0361], bhikkhave, anattā, tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Ko ca, bhikkhave, anattā? Cakkhu, bhikkhave, anattā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo…pe… jivhā anattā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo…pe… mano anattā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Yo, bhikkhave, anattā tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo”ti.

174–176. “Bhikkhus, whatever is not-self, therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. And what, bhikkhus, is not-self? The eye, bhikkhus, is not-self; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust… The tongue is not-self; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust… The mind is not-self; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. Whatever, bhikkhus, is not-self, therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust.”

10-12. Bāhirāniccachandādisuttaṃ

10–12. The Discourse on the External, Impermanence, Desire, and So On

177-179. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ, tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Kiñca, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ? Rūpā, bhikkhave, aniccā; tatra vo chando [V 2.0153] pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Saddā aniccā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Gandhā aniccā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo [T 4.0189] pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Rasā aniccā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Phoṭṭhabbā aniccā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Dhammā aniccā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo”ti.

177–179. “Bhikkhus, whatever is impermanent, therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. And what, bhikkhus, is impermanent? Forms, bhikkhus, are impermanent; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. Sounds are impermanent; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. Odors are impermanent; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. Tastes are impermanent; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. Tangibles are impermanent; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. Mental objects are impermanent; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. Whatever, bhikkhus, is impermanent, therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust.”

13-15. Bāhiradukkhachandādisuttaṃ

13–15. The Discourse on the External, Suffering, Desire, and So On

180-182. “Yaṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ, tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Kiñca, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ? Rūpā, bhikkhave, dukkhā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā dukkhā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ, tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo”ti.

180–182. “Bhikkhus, whatever is suffering, therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. And what, bhikkhus, is suffering? Forms, bhikkhus, are suffering; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. Sounds… odors… tastes… tangibles… mental objects are suffering; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. Whatever, bhikkhus, is suffering, therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust.”

16-18. Bāhirānattachandādisuttaṃ

16–18. The Discourse on the External, Not-Self, Desire, and So On

183-185. “Yo[M 2.0362][P 4.0151], bhikkhave, anattā, tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Ko ca, bhikkhave, anattā? Rūpā, bhikkhave, anattā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā anattā; tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo. Yo, bhikkhave, anattā [T 4.0190] tatra vo chando pahātabbo, rāgo pahātabbo, chandarāgo pahātabbo”ti.

183–185. “Bhikkhus, whatever is not-self, therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. And what, bhikkhus, is not-self? Forms, bhikkhus, are not-self; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. Sounds… odors… tastes… tangibles… mental objects are not-self; therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust. Whatever, bhikkhus, is not-self, therein you should abandon desire, abandon lust, and abandon desire and lust.”

19. Ajjhattātītāniccasuttaṃ

19. 19. The Discourse on Internal Past Impermanence

186. “Cakkhu[V 2.0154], bhikkhave, aniccaṃ atītaṃ…pe… jivhā aniccā atītā…pe… mano anicco atīto. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati…pe… jivhāyapi nibbindati…pe… manasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti.

186. “The past eye, bhikkhus, is impermanent… the past tongue is impermanent… the past mind is impermanent. Seeing thus, bhikkhus, the learned noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye… becomes disenchanted with the tongue… becomes disenchanted with the mind. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. Upon liberation, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is nothing further for this state of being.’”

20. Ajjhattānāgatāniccasuttaṃ

20. 20. The Discourse on Internal Future Impermanence

187. “Cakkhu, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ anāgataṃ…pe… jivhā aniccā anāgatā…pe… mano anicco anāgato. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

187. “The future eye, bhikkhus, is impermanent… the future tongue is impermanent… the future mind is impermanent. Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state of being.’”

21. Ajjhattapaccuppannāniccasuttaṃ

21. 21. The Discourse on Internal Present Impermanence

188. “Cakkhu, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ paccuppannaṃ…pe… jivhā aniccā paccuppannā…pe… mano anicco paccuppanno. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

188. “The present eye, bhikkhus, is impermanent… the present tongue is impermanent… the present mind is impermanent. Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state of being.’”

22-24. Ajjhattātītādidukkhasuttaṃ

22–24. The Discourse on Internal Past, etc., Suffering

189-191. “Cakkhu[P 4.0152], bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ atītaṃ anāgataṃ paccuppannaṃ…pe… jivhā dukkhā atītā anāgatā paccuppannā…pe… mano dukkho atīto anāgato paccuppanno. Evaṃ passaṃ[V 2.0155], bhikkhave…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

189–191. “The eye, bhikkhus, whether past, future, or present, is suffering… the tongue, whether past, future, or present, is suffering… the mind, whether past, future, or present, is suffering. Seeing thus, bhikkhus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state of being.’”

25-27. Ajjhattātītādianattasuttaṃ

25–27. The Discourse on Internal Past, etc., Not-Self

192-194. “Cakkhu[M 2.0363], bhikkhave, anattā atītaṃ anāgataṃ paccuppannaṃ…pe… jivhā anattā…pe… mano anattā atīto anāgato paccuppanno[T 4.0191]. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

“Bhikkhus, the eye is not-self, whether past, future, or present... the tongue is not-self... the mind is not-self, whether past, future, or present. Seeing thus... he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state.’”

28-30. Bāhirātītādianiccasuttaṃ

28-30. The Discourse on the External, Past, etc., and Impermanence

195-197. “Rūpā, bhikkhave, aniccā atītā anāgatā paccuppannā. Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā aniccā atītā anāgatā paccuppannā. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

“Bhikkhus, forms are impermanent, whether past, future, or present. Sounds… odors… tastes… tangibles… mental objects are impermanent, whether past, future, or present. Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state.’”

31-33. Bāhirātītādidukkhasuttaṃ

31-33. The Discourse on the External, Past, etc., and Suffering

198-200. “Rūpā, bhikkhave, dukkhā atītā anāgatā paccuppannā. Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā dukkhā atītā anāgatā paccuppannā. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

“Bhikkhus, forms are suffering, whether past, future, or present. Sounds… odors… tastes… tangibles… mental objects are suffering, whether past, future, or present. Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state.’”

34-36. Bāhirātītādianattasuttaṃ

34-36. The Discourse on the External, Past, etc., and Not-Self

201-203. “Rūpā[V 2.0156], bhikkhave, anattā atītā anāgatā paccuppannā. Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā anattā atītā anāgatā paccuppannā. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

“Bhikkhus, forms are not-self, whether past, future, or present. Sounds… odors… tastes… tangibles… mental objects are not-self, whether past, future, or present. Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state.’”

37. Ajjhattātītayadaniccasuttaṃ

37. 37. The Discourse on the Internal and Past: What is Impermanent

204. “Cakkhu, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ atītaṃ. Yadaniccaṃ, taṃ [P 4.0153] dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ…pe… jivhā aniccā atītā. Yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ…pe… mano anicco atīto. Yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi[T 4.0192], na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

204. “Bhikkhus, the past eye is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ … The past tongue is impermanent… What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ … The past mind is impermanent… What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state.’”

38. Ajjhattānāgatayadaniccasuttaṃ

38. 38. The Discourse on the Internal and Future: What is Impermanent

205. “Cakkhu[M 2.0364], bhikkhave, aniccaṃ anāgataṃ. Yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā. Yadanattā taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ…pe… jivhā aniccā anāgatā. Yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ…pe… mano anicco anāgato. Yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā[V 2.0157]. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

205. “Bhikkhus, the future eye is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ … The future tongue is impermanent… What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ … The future mind is impermanent… What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus, Bhikkhus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state.’”

39. Ajjhattapaccuppannayadaniccasuttaṃ

39. 39. The Discourse on the Internal and Present: What is Impermanent

206. “Cakkhu, bhikkhave, aniccaṃ paccuppannaṃ. Yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā. Yadanattā taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ…pe… jivhā aniccā paccuppannā. Yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ…pe… mano anicco paccuppanno. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

206. “Bhikkhus, the present eye is impermanent. What is impermanent is suffering. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ … The present tongue is impermanent… What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ … The present mind is impermanent… What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state.’”

40-42. Ajjhattātītādiyaṃdukkhasuttaṃ

40-42. The Discourse on the Internal, Past, etc.: What is Suffering

207-209. “Cakkhu[P 4.0154], bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ atītaṃ anāgataṃ paccuppannaṃ. Yaṃ [T 4.0193] dukkhaṃ, tadanattā. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ…pe… jivhā dukkhā…pe… mano dukkho atīto anāgato paccuppanno. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… [V 2.0158] nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

“Bhikkhus, the eye is suffering, whether past, future, or present. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ … The tongue is suffering… … The mind is suffering, whether past, future, or present. What is suffering is not-self. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state.’”

43-45. Ajjhattātītādiyadanattasuttaṃ

43-45. The Discourse on the Internal, Past, etc.: What is Not-Self

210-212. “Cakkhu, bhikkhave, anattā atītaṃ anāgataṃ paccuppannaṃ. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ [M 2.0365] yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ…pe… jivhā anattā…pe… mano anattā atīto anāgato paccuppanno. Yadanattā taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

“Bhikkhus, the eye is not-self, whether past, future, or present. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ … The tongue is not-self… … The mind is not-self, whether past, future, or present. What is not-self should be seen as it really is with right wisdom thus: ‘This is not mine, I am not this, this is not my self.’ Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state.’”

46-48. Bāhirātītādiyadaniccasuttaṃ
