46-48. The Discourse on the External, Past, etc.: What is Impermanent

213-215. “Rūpā, bhikkhave, aniccā atītā anāgatā paccuppannā. Yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā aniccā atītā anāgatā paccuppannā. Yadaniccaṃ taṃ dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ tadanattā. Yadanattā taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ [T 4.0194] itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

Bhikkhus, visual objects that are past, future, or present are impermanent. Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering. Whatever is suffering, that is not-self. Whatever is not-self, that should be seen as it truly is with right wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.” Sounds... smells... tastes... tactile objects... mental objects that are past, future, or present are impermanent. Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering. Whatever is suffering, that is not-self. Whatever is not-self, that should be seen as it truly is with right wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.” Seeing thus... and so on... he understands that there is nothing further for this state of existence.

49-51. Bāhirātītādiyaṃdukkhasuttaṃ

49-51. The Discourse on the External, Past, etc., as Suffering.

216-218. “Rūpā[P 4.0155], bhikkhave, dukkhā atītā anāgatā paccuppannā. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā[V 2.0159]. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā dukkhā atītā anāgatā paccuppannā. Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

Bhikkhus, visual objects that are past, future, or present are suffering. Whatever is suffering, that is not-self. Whatever is not-self, that should be seen as it truly is with right wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.” Sounds... smells... tastes... tactile objects... mental objects that are past, future, or present are suffering. Whatever is suffering, that is not-self. Whatever is not-self, that should be seen as it truly is with right wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.” Seeing thus... and so on... he understands that there is nothing further for this state of existence.

52-54. Bāhirātītādiyadanattasuttaṃ

52-54. The Discourse on the External, Past, etc., as Not-self.

219-221. “Rūpā, bhikkhave, anattā atītā anāgatā paccuppannā. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā anattā atītā anāgatā paccuppannā. Yadanattā, taṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

Bhikkhus, visual objects that are past, future, or present are not-self. Whatever is not-self, that should be seen as it truly is with right wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.” Sounds... smells... tastes... tactile objects... mental objects that are past, future, or present are not-self. Whatever is not-self, that should be seen as it truly is with right wisdom thus: “This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.” Seeing thus... and so on... he understands that there is nothing further for this state of existence.

55. Ajjhattāyatanaaniccasuttaṃ

55. The Discourse on the Impermanence of the Internal Sense Bases

222. “Cakkhu[M 2.0366], bhikkhave, aniccaṃ…pe… jivhā aniccā…pe… mano anicco. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

222. Bhikkhus, the eye is impermanent... and so on... the tongue is impermanent... and so on... the mind is impermanent. Seeing thus... and so on... he understands that there is nothing further for this state of existence.

56. Ajjhattāyatanadukkhasuttaṃ

56. The Discourse on the Suffering of the Internal Sense Bases

223. “Cakkhu, bhikkhave, dukkhaṃ…pe… jivhā dukkhā…pe… mano dukkho. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… [V 2.0160] nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

223. Bhikkhus, the eye is suffering… the tongue is suffering… the mind is suffering. Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state of existence.’”

57. Ajjhattāyatanaanattasuttaṃ

57. The Discourse on the Not-Self of the Internal Sense Bases

224. “Cakkhu[T 4.0195][P 4.0156], bhikkhave, anattā…pe… jivhā anattā…pe… mano anattā. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

224. Bhikkhus, the eye is not-self… the tongue is not-self… the mind is not-self. Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state of existence.’”

58. Bāhirāyatanaaniccasuttaṃ

58. The Discourse on the Impermanence of the External Sense Bases

225. “Rūpā, bhikkhave, aniccā. Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā aniccā. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

225. Bhikkhus, forms are impermanent. Sounds… smells… tastes… tactile objects… mental phenomena are impermanent. Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state of existence.’”

59. Bāhirāyatanadukkhasuttaṃ

59. The Discourse on the Suffering of the External Sense Bases

226. “Rūpā, bhikkhave, dukkhā. Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā dukkhā. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

226. Bhikkhus, forms are suffering. Sounds… smells… tastes… tactile objects… mental phenomena are suffering. Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state of existence.’”

60. Bāhirāyatanaanattasuttaṃ

60. The Discourse on the Not-Self of the External Sense Bases

227. “Rūpā[V 2.0161], bhikkhave, anattā. Saddā… gandhā… rasā… phoṭṭhabbā… dhammā anattā. Evaṃ passaṃ…pe… nāparaṃ itthattāyāti pajānātī”ti.

227. Bhikkhus, forms are not-self. Sounds… smells… tastes… tactile objects… mental phenomena are not-self. Seeing thus… he understands: ‘There is nothing further for this state of existence.’”

Saṭṭhipeyyālavaggo sattarasamo.

The Seventeenth Chapter, the Section of Sixty Abbreviated Texts, is concluded.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Chandenaṭṭhārasa honti, atītena ca dve nava;

Yadaniccāṭṭhārasa vuttā, tayo ajjhattabāhirā;

Peyyālo saṭṭhiko vutto, buddhenādiccabandhunāti.

Eighteen with desire, and two nines with the past; eighteen are spoken of as ‘what is impermanent,’ and three as internal and external. The abbreviated section of sixty was spoken by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun.

Suttantāni saṭṭhi.

There are sixty discourses.

18. Samuddavaggo

18. The Chapter on the Ocean

1. Paṭhamasamuddasuttaṃ

1. The First Discourse on the Ocean

228. “‘Samuddo[T 4.0196][M 2.0367][P 4.0157], samuddo’ti, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano bhāsati. Neso, bhikkhave, ariyassa vinaye samuddo. Mahā eso, bhikkhave, udakarāsi mahāudakaṇṇavo. Cakkhu, bhikkhave, purisassa samuddo; tassa rūpamayo vego. Yo taṃ rūpamayaṃ vegaṃ sahati, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, atari cakkhusamuddaṃ saūmiṃ sāvaṭṭaṃ sagāhaṃ sarakkhasaṃ; tiṇṇo pāraṅgato [V 2.0162] thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇo…pe… jivhā, bhikkhave, purisassa samuddo; tassa rasamayo vego. Yo taṃ rasamayaṃ vegaṃ sahati, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, atari jivhāsamuddaṃ saūmiṃ sāvaṭṭaṃ sagāhaṃ sarakkhasaṃ; tiṇṇo pāraṅgato thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇo…pe… mano, bhikkhave, purisassa samuddo; tassa dhammamayo vego. Yo taṃ dhammamayaṃ vegaṃ sahati, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, atari manosamuddaṃ saūmiṃ sāvaṭṭaṃ sagāhaṃ sarakkhasaṃ; tiṇṇo pāraṅgato thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇo”ti. Idamavoca…pe… satthā –

228. “Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling says, ‘The ocean, the ocean.’ But in the discipline of the noble one, that is not the ocean. That, bhikkhus, is a great mass of water, a great watery expanse. The eye, bhikkhus, is the ocean for a person; its current is made of forms. Whoever can withstand that current made of forms is said, bhikkhus, to have crossed over the ocean of the eye with its waves, whirlpools, crocodiles, and demons. Having crossed over and gone to the other shore, he stands on high ground, a brahmin… The tongue, bhikkhus, is the ocean for a person; its current is made of tastes. Whoever can withstand that current made of tastes is said, bhikkhus, to have crossed over the ocean of the tongue with its waves, whirlpools, crocodiles, and demons. Having crossed over and gone to the other shore, he stands on high ground, a brahmin… The mind, bhikkhus, is the ocean for a person; its current is made of mental phenomena. Whoever can withstand that current made of mental phenomena is said, bhikkhus, to have crossed over the ocean of the mind with its waves, whirlpools, crocodiles, and demons. Having crossed over and gone to the other shore, he stands on high ground, a brahmin.” The Teacher spoke these words.

“Yo imaṃ samuddaṃ sagāhaṃ sarakkhasaṃ,

Saūmiṃ sāvaṭṭaṃ sabhayaṃ duttaraṃ accatari;

Sa vedagū vusitabrahmacariyo,

Lokantagū pāragatoti vuccatī”ti. paṭhamaṃ;

“Whoever has crossed this ocean—with its crocodiles and demons, with its waves, whirlpools, and dangers, so difficult to cross; that one who has attained wisdom, who has lived the holy life, who has gone to the end of the world, is called ‘one who has gone to the other shore.’”

2. Dutiyasamuddasuttaṃ

2. The Second Discourse on the Ocean

229. “Samuddo, samuddo’ti, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano bhāsati[P 4.0158]. Neso, bhikkhave, ariyassa vinaye samuddo. Mahā eso, bhikkhave, udakarāsi mahāudakaṇṇavo. Santi, bhikkhave, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā [T 4.0197] iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ariyassa vinaye samuddo. Etthāyaṃ sadevako loko samārako sabrahmako sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī pajā sadevamanussā yebhuyyena samunnā tantākulakajātā kulagaṇṭhikajātā guḷāguṇṭhikajātā (sī.), kulaguṇḍikajātā (syā. kaṃ.), guṇaguṇikajātā (pī.), kulāguṇḍikajātā (ka.) muñjapabbajabhūtā, apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ saṃsāraṃ nātivattati…pe….

229. “Bhikkhus, the uninstructed worldling says, ‘The ocean, the ocean.’ But that, bhikkhus, is not the ocean in the discipline of the noble one. That, bhikkhus, is a great mass of water, a great expanse of water. There are, bhikkhus, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, pleasing, gladdening, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and passion-arousing. This, bhikkhus, is called the ocean in the discipline of the noble one. Herein, this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, is for the most part submerged, has become like a tangled skein, has become like a knotted ball, has become like muñja and babbaja grass, and does not transcend the state of loss, the bad destination, the downfall, saṃsāra.

“Santi[M 2.0368], bhikkhave, jivhāviññeyyā rasā…pe… santi, bhikkhave, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ariyassa vinaye samuddo. Etthāyaṃ sadevako loko samārako sabrahmako sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī pajā sadevamanussā yebhuyyena samunnā tantākulakajātā kulagaṇṭhikajātā muñjapabbajabhūtā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ saṃsāraṃ nātivattatī”ti.

“Bhikkhus, there are tastes cognizable by the tongue… Bhikkhus, there are mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and passion-arousing. This, bhikkhus, is called the ocean in the discipline of the noble one. Herein, this world with its devas, Māra, and Brahmā, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, is for the most part submerged, has become like a tangled skein, like a knotted ball of thread, has become like muñja and babbaja grass, and does not transcend the plane of misery, the bad destination, the downfall, saṃsāra.”

“Yassa [V 2.0163] rāgo ca doso ca, avijjā ca virājitā;

So imaṃ samuddaṃ sagāhaṃ sarakkhasaṃ, saūmibhayaṃ duttaraṃ accatari.

“One for whom lust, hatred, and ignorance have been dispelled; he has crossed over this ocean, with its grasping creatures and demons, with its waves and dangers, so difficult to cross.”

“Saṅgātigo maccujaho nirupadhi, pahāsi dukkhaṃ apunabbhavāya;

Atthaṅgato so na puneti na pamāṇameti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), amohayī, maccurājanti brūmī”ti. dutiyaṃ;

“Having gone beyond attachment, having abandoned death, without acquisitions, having abandoned suffering for the sake of no-further-becoming; he who has gone to his setting does not come again; he has bewildered the King of Death, thus I declare.”

3. Bāḷisikopamasuttaṃ

3. The Simile of the Fisherman

230. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, bāḷisiko āmisagatabaḷisaṃ gambhīre udakarahade pakkhipeyya. Tamenaṃ aññataro [P 4.0159] āmisacakkhu maccho gileyya. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, maccho gilitabaḷiso bāḷisikassa anayaṃ [T 4.0198] āpanno byasanaṃ āpanno yathākāmakaraṇīyo bāḷisikassa.

230. “Suppose, bhikkhus, a fisherman were to cast a baited hook into a deep lake. A certain fish with an eye for bait would swallow it. Thus, bhikkhus, that fish, having swallowed the hook, would have met with misfortune, would have met with disaster, and would be subject to the fisherman’s will.”

Evameva kho, bhikkhave, chayime baḷisā lokasmiṃ anayāya sattānaṃ vadhāya byābādhāya (sī. pī.) pāṇinaṃ. Katame cha? Santi, bhikkhave, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce, bhikkhu, abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gilitabaḷiso, mārassa anayaṃ āpanno byasanaṃ āpanno yathākāmakaraṇīyo pāpimato…pe… santi, bhikkhave, jivhāviññeyyā rasā…pe….

“So too, bhikkhus, these six hooks exist in the world for the misfortune of beings, for the slaughter of living beings. What six? There are, bhikkhus, forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and passion-arousing. If a bhikkhu delights in it, welcomes it, and abides attached to it, that bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is called one who has swallowed Māra’s hook, who has met with misfortune, who has met with disaster, and is subject to the will of the Evil One… There are, bhikkhus, tastes cognizable by the tongue…”

Santi, bhikkhave, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce, bhikkhu, abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu gilitabaḷiso mārassa anayaṃ āpanno byasanaṃ āpanno yathākāmakaraṇīyo pāpimato.

“Bhikkhus, there are mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and passion-arousing. If a bhikkhu delights in it, welcomes it, and abides attached to it, that bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is called one who has swallowed Māra’s hook, who has met with misfortune, who has met with disaster, and is subject to the will of the Evil One.”

“Santi [M 2.0369] ca, bhikkhave, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya tiṭṭhati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu na gilitabaḷiso mārassa abhedi baḷisaṃ paribhedi baḷisaṃ na anayaṃ āpanno na byasanaṃ āpanno na yathākāmakaraṇīyo pāpimato…pe….

“Bhikkhus, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and passion-arousing. If a bhikkhu does not delight in it, does not welcome it, and does not abide attached to it, that bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is called one who has not swallowed Māra’s hook, who has broken the hook, who has shattered the hook, who has not met with misfortune, who has not met with disaster, and is not subject to the will of the Evil One…”

“Santi[V 2.0164], bhikkhave, jivhāviññeyyā rasā…pe…. Santi, bhikkhave, manoviññeyyā dhammā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Tañce bhikkhu nābhinandati nābhivadati nājjhosāya [T 4.0199] tiṭṭhati, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, bhikkhu na gilitabaḷiso mārassa abhedi baḷisaṃ paribhedi baḷisaṃ na anayaṃ āpanno na byasanaṃ āpanno na yathākāmakaraṇīyo pāpimato”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, there are tastes cognizable by the tongue… Bhikkhus, there are mental phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, pleasing, agreeable, of a lovely nature, connected with sensual desire, and passion-arousing. If a bhikkhu does not delight in it, does not welcome it, and does not abide attached to it, that bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is called one who has not swallowed Māra’s hook, who has broken the hook, who has shattered the hook, who has not met with misfortune, who has not met with disaster, and is not subject to the will of the Evil One.”

4. Khīrarukkhopamasuttaṃ

4. The Simile of the Sap-Tree

231. “Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā [P 4.0160] cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu yo rāgo so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno tassa parittā cepi cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā cakkhussa āpāthaṃ āgacchanti pariyādiyantevassa cittaṃ; ko pana vādo adhimattānaṃ! Taṃ kissa hetu? Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo, so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno…pe….

231. “Bhikkhus, for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī in whom, regarding forms cognizable by the eye, there is lust, there is hatred, and there is delusion; whose lust is unabandoned, whose hatred is unabandoned, and whose delusion is unabandoned—even if only a few forms cognizable by the eye come into the range of the eye, they indeed overwhelm their mind. What then is to be said of many? For what reason is that? Because, bhikkhus, there is lust, there is hatred, and there is delusion; whose lust is unabandoned, whose hatred is unabandoned, and whose delusion is unabandoned.”

“Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu yo rāgo so atthi…pe….

“Bhikkhus, for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī in whom, regarding tastes cognizable by the tongue, there is lust… and so on.”

“Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā manoviññeyyesu dhammesu yo rāgo so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno, tassa parittā cepi manoviññeyyā dhammā manassa āpāthaṃ āgacchanti pariyādiyantevassa cittaṃ; ko pana vādo adhimattānaṃ! Taṃ kissa hetu? Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo, so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so [M 2.0370] atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno.

“Bhikkhus, for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī in whom, regarding mental phenomena cognizable by the mind, there is lust, there is hatred, and there is delusion; whose lust is unabandoned, whose hatred is unabandoned, and whose delusion is unabandoned—even if only a few mental phenomena cognizable by the mind come into the range of the mind, they indeed overwhelm their mind. What then is to be said of many? For what reason is that? Because, bhikkhus, there is lust, there is hatred, and there is delusion; whose lust is unabandoned, whose hatred is unabandoned, and whose delusion is unabandoned.”

“Seyyathāpi[T 4.0200], bhikkhave, khīrarukkho assattho vā nigrodho vā pilakkho vā udumbaro vā daharo taruṇo komārako. Tamenaṃ puriso tiṇhāya kuṭhāriyā yato yato ābhindeyya bhindeyya (syā. kaṃ. sī. aṭṭha.), abhindeyya (katthaci) āgaccheyya [V 2.0165] khīra”nti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Yañhi, bhante, khīraṃ taṃ atthī”ti.

“Suppose, bhikkhus, there were a sap-tree—an assattha tree, a banyan tree, a pilakkha tree, or an udumbara tree—young, tender, and a sapling. If a man were to strike it here and there with a sharp axe, would sap come out?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “For what reason is that?” “Because, venerable sir, the sap is in it.”

“Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yassa kassaci bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu yo rāgo so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno, tassa parittā cepi cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā cakkhussa āpāthaṃ āgacchanti pariyādiyantevassa cittaṃ; ko pana vādo adhimattānaṃ! Taṃ kissa hetu? Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo so atthi, yo doso so atthi[P 4.0161], yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno…pe….

“In this very way, monks, for any monk or nun in whom, regarding forms cognizable by the eye, there is passion, there is aversion, and there is delusion; whose passion is unabandoned, whose aversion is unabandoned, and whose delusion is unabandoned—even if only a few forms cognizable by the eye come into the range of the eye, they indeed overwhelm their mind. What is to be said of excessive ones? For what reason is that? Because, monks, there is passion, there is aversion, and there is delusion; whose passion is unabandoned, whose aversion is unabandoned, and whose delusion is unabandoned… and so on.”

“Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu yo rāgo so atthi…pe….

“Monks, for any monk or nun in whom, regarding tastes cognizable by the tongue, there is passion… and so on.”

“Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā manoviññeyyesu dhammesu yo rāgo so atthi, yo doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno, tassa parittā cepi manoviññeyyā dhammā manassa āpāthaṃ āgacchanti pariyādiyantevassa cittaṃ; ko pana vādo adhimattānaṃ! Taṃ kissa hetu? Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo so atthi, yo [T 4.0201] doso so atthi, yo moho so atthi, yo rāgo so appahīno, yo doso so appahīno, yo moho so appahīno.

“Monks, for any monk or nun in whom, regarding mental objects cognizable by the mind, there is passion, there is aversion, and there is delusion; whose passion is unabandoned, whose aversion is unabandoned, and whose delusion is unabandoned—even if only a few mental objects cognizable by the mind come into the range of the mind, they indeed overwhelm their mind. What is to be said of excessive ones? For what reason is that? Because, monks, there is passion, there is aversion, and there is delusion; whose passion is unabandoned, whose aversion is unabandoned, and whose delusion is unabandoned.”

“Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu yo rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so [M 2.0371] pahīno, tassa adhimattā cepi cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā cakkhussa āpāthaṃ āgacchanti nevassa cittaṃ pariyādiyanti; ko pana vādo parittānaṃ! Taṃ kissa hetu? Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno…pe….

“Monks, for any monk or nun in whom, regarding forms cognizable by the eye, there is no passion, no aversion, and no delusion; whose passion is abandoned, whose aversion is abandoned, and whose delusion is abandoned—even if excessive forms cognizable by the eye come into the range of the eye, they do not overwhelm their mind. What is to be said of lesser ones? For what reason is that? Because, monks, there is no passion, no aversion, and no delusion; whose passion is abandoned, whose aversion is abandoned, and whose delusion is abandoned… and so on.”

“Yassa [V 2.0166] kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu…pe… manoviññeyyesu dhammesu yo rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno, tassa adhimattā cepi manoviññeyyā dhammā manassa āpāthaṃ āgacchanti nevassa cittaṃ pariyādiyanti; ko pana vādo parittānaṃ! Taṃ kissa hetu? Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno. Seyyathāpi[T 4.0202], bhikkhave, khīrarukkho assattho vā nigrodho vā pilakkho vā udumbaro vā sukkho kolāpo terovassiko. Tamenaṃ puriso tiṇhāya kuṭhāriyā yato yato ābhindeyya āgaccheyya khīra”nti? “No [P 4.0162] hetaṃ, bhante”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Yañhi, bhante, khīraṃ taṃ natthī”ti.

“Monks, for any monk or nun in whom, regarding tastes cognizable by the tongue… and so on… and regarding mental objects cognizable by the mind, there is no passion, no aversion, and no delusion; whose passion is abandoned, whose aversion is abandoned, and whose delusion is abandoned—even if excessive mental objects cognizable by the mind come into the range of the mind, they do not overwhelm their mind. What is to be said of lesser ones? For what reason is that? Because, monks, there is no passion, no aversion, and no delusion; whose passion is abandoned, whose aversion is abandoned, and whose delusion is abandoned. Suppose, monks, there were a milk-tree—an assattha, a banyan, a pilakkha, or an udumbara—that was dry, decayed, and long-dead. If a man were to cut it here and there with a sharp axe, would sap come out?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “For what reason is that?” “Because, venerable sir, what sap there was is no more.”

“Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yassa kassaci bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu yo rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno, tassa adhimattā cepi cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā cakkhussa āpāthaṃ āgacchanti nevassa cittaṃ pariyādiyanti; ko pana vādo parittānaṃ! Taṃ kissa hetu? Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno…pe….

“Just so, monks, for any monk or nun in whom, regarding forms cognizable by the eye, there is no passion, no aversion, and no delusion; whose passion is abandoned, whose aversion is abandoned, and whose delusion is abandoned—even if excessive forms cognizable by the eye come into the range of the eye, they do not overwhelm their mind. What is to be said of lesser ones? For what reason is that? Because, monks, there is no passion, no aversion, and no delusion; whose passion is abandoned, whose aversion is abandoned, and whose delusion is abandoned… and so on.”

“Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu…pe….

“Monks, for any monk or nun in whom, regarding tastes cognizable by the tongue… and so on.”

“Yassa [M 2.0372] kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā manoviññeyyesu dhammesu yo rāgo so natthi, yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno, tassa adhimattā cepi manoviññeyyā dhammā manassa āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, nevassa cittaṃ pariyādiyanti; ko pana vādo parittānaṃ! Taṃ kissa hetu? Yo, bhikkhave, rāgo so natthi[T 4.0203], yo doso so natthi, yo moho so natthi, yo rāgo so pahīno, yo doso so pahīno, yo moho so pahīno”ti. Catutthaṃ.

“Monks, for any monk or nun in whom, regarding mind-objects cognizable by the mind, there is no passion, no aversion, and no delusion; whose passion is abandoned, whose aversion is abandoned, and whose delusion is abandoned—even if excessive mind-objects cognizable by the mind come into the range of the mind, they do not overwhelm their mind. What is to be said of lesser ones? For what reason is that? Because, monks, there is no passion, no aversion, and no delusion; whose passion is abandoned, whose aversion is abandoned, and whose delusion is abandoned.” The Fourth.

5. Koṭṭhikasuttaṃ

5. The Sutta on Koṭṭhika

232. Ekaṃ [V 2.0167] samayaṃ āyasmā ca sāriputto āyasmā ca mahākoṭṭhiko bārāṇasiyaṃ viharanti isipatane migadāye. Atha kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā sāriputto tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā sāriputtena saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā mahākoṭṭhiko āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ etadavoca –

232. On one occasion, the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika were dwelling at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika, having arisen from solitary meditation, approached the Venerable Sāriputta. Having approached, he exchanged pleasant and memorable greetings with the Venerable Sāriputta. Having concluded this conversation, he sat down at a suitable place. Having sat down at a suitable place, the Venerable Mahākoṭṭhika said this to the Venerable Sāriputta:

“Kiṃ nu kho, āvuso sāriputta, cakkhu rūpānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, rūpā cakkhussa saṃyojanaṃ…pe… jivhā rasānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, rasā jivhāya saṃyojanaṃ [P 4.0163]…pe… mano dhammānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, dhammā manassa saṃyojana”nti?

“Friend Sāriputta, is the eye a fetter to forms, or are forms a fetter to the eye? … Is the tongue a fetter to tastes, or are tastes a fetter to the tongue? … Is the mind a fetter to mind-objects, or are mind-objects a fetter to the mind?”

“Na kho, āvuso koṭṭhika, cakkhu rūpānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na rūpā cakkhussa saṃyojanaṃ. Yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ…pe… na jivhā rasānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na rasā jivhāya saṃyojanaṃ. Yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ…pe… na mano dhammānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na dhammā manassa saṃyojanaṃ. Yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ.

“Friend Koṭṭhika, the eye is not a fetter to forms, nor are forms a fetter to the eye. But whatever passionate desire arises in dependence on both, that is the fetter there... The tongue is not a fetter to tastes, nor are tastes a fetter to the tongue. But whatever passionate desire arises in dependence on both, that is the fetter there... The mind is not a fetter to mind-objects, nor are mind-objects a fetter to the mind. But whatever passionate desire arises in dependence on both, that is the fetter there.”

“Seyyathāpi[T 4.0204], āvuso, kāḷo ca balībaddo balivaddo (sī. pī.), balibaddo (syā. kaṃ. ka.) odāto ca balībaddo ekena dāmena vā yottena vā saṃyuttā assu. Yo nu kho evaṃ [M 2.0373] vadeyya – ‘kāḷo balībaddo odātassa balībaddassa saṃyojanaṃ, odāto balībaddo kāḷassa balībaddassa saṃyojana’nti, sammā nu kho so vadamāno vadeyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”. “Na kho, āvuso, kāḷo balībaddo odātassa balībaddassa saṃyojanaṃ, na odāto balībaddo kāḷassa balībaddassa saṃyojanaṃ. Yena ca kho te ekena dāmena vā yottena vā saṃyuttā taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ.

“Suppose, friend, a black ox and a white ox were yoked together by a single harness or rope. If someone were to say, ‘The black ox is the fetter of the white ox, and the white ox is the fetter of the black ox,’ would one who says so be speaking correctly?” “Indeed not, friend.” “Friend, the black ox is not the fetter of the white ox, nor is the white ox the fetter of the black ox. But the single harness or rope by which they are yoked, that is the fetter there.”

“Evameva kho, āvuso, na cakkhu rūpānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na rūpā cakkhussa saṃyojanaṃ. Yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ…pe… na jivhā rasānaṃ [V 2.0168] saṃyojanaṃ…pe… na mano dhammānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na dhammā manassa saṃyojanaṃ. Yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ.

“In the same way, friend, the eye is not a fetter to forms, nor are forms a fetter to the eye. But whatever passionate desire arises in dependence on both, that is the fetter there… The tongue is not a fetter to tastes… The mind is not a fetter to mind-objects, nor are mind-objects a fetter to the mind. But whatever passionate desire arises in dependence on both, that is the fetter there.”

“Cakkhu vā, āvuso, rūpānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ abhavissa, rūpā vā cakkhussa saṃyojanaṃ, nayidaṃ brahmacariyavāso paññāyetha paññāyati (ka.) sammā dukkhakkhayāya. Yasmā ca kho, āvuso, na cakkhu rūpānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na rūpā cakkhussa saṃyojanaṃ[P 4.0164]; yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ, tasmā brahmacariyavāso paññāyati sammā [T 4.0205] dukkhakkhayāya…pe….

“If, friend, the eye were a fetter to forms, or forms were a fetter to the eye, this living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be apparent. But because, friend, the eye is not a fetter to forms, nor are forms a fetter to the eye, and whatever passionate desire arises in dependence on both—that is the fetter there—therefore the living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is apparent...”

“Jivhā, āvuso, rasānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ abhavissa, rasā vā jivhāya saṃyojanaṃ, nayidaṃ brahmacariyavāso paññāyetha sammā dukkhakkhayāya. Yasmā ca kho, āvuso, na jivhā rasānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na rasā jivhāya saṃyojanaṃ; yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ, tasmā brahmacariyavāso paññāyati sammā dukkhakkhayāya…pe….

“If, friend, the tongue were a fetter to tastes, or tastes were a fetter to the tongue, this living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be apparent. But because, friend, the tongue is not a fetter to tastes, nor are tastes a fetter to the tongue, and whatever passionate desire arises in dependence on both—that is the fetter there—therefore the living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is apparent...”

“Mano vā, āvuso, dhammānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ abhavissa, dhammā vā manassa saṃyojanaṃ, nayidaṃ brahmacariyavāso paññāyetha sammā dukkhakkhayāya. Yasmā ca kho, āvuso, na mano dhammānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na dhammā manassa saṃyojanaṃ; yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ, tasmā brahmacariyavāso paññāyati sammā dukkhakkhayāya.

“If, friend, the mind were a fetter to mind-objects, or mind-objects were a fetter to the mind, this living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering would not be apparent. But because, friend, the mind is not a fetter to mind-objects, nor are mind-objects a fetter to the mind, and whatever passionate desire arises in dependence on both—that is the fetter there—therefore the living of the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering is apparent.”

“Imināpetaṃ[M 2.0374], āvuso, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā na cakkhu rūpānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na rūpā cakkhussa saṃyojanaṃ. Yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ…pe… na jivhā rasānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ…pe… na mano dhammānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na dhammā manassa saṃyojanaṃ. Yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ.

“By this line of reasoning, friend, it should be understood how the eye is not a fetter to forms, nor are forms a fetter to the eye. But whatever passionate desire arises there in dependence on both, that is the fetter there... the tongue is not a fetter to tastes... the mind is not a fetter to mind-objects, nor are mind-objects a fetter to the mind. But whatever passionate desire arises there in dependence on both, that is the fetter there.”

“Saṃvijjati kho, āvuso, bhagavato cakkhu. Passati bhagavā cakkhunā rūpaṃ. Chandarāgo bhagavato natthi. Suvimuttacitto bhagavā. Saṃvijjati kho, āvuso, bhagavato sotaṃ. Suṇāti bhagavā sotena saddaṃ. Chandarāgo [T 4.0206] bhagavato natthi. Suvimuttacitto bhagavā. Saṃvijjati kho, āvuso, bhagavato ghānaṃ. Ghāyati bhagavā ghānena gandhaṃ. Chandarāgo bhagavato natthi. Suvimuttacitto [V 2.0169] bhagavā. Saṃvijjati kho, āvuso, bhagavato jivhā. Sāyati bhagavā jivhāya rasaṃ. Chandarāgo bhagavato natthi. Suvimuttacitto bhagavā. Saṃvijjati kho, āvuso, bhagavato kāyo. Phusati bhagavā kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ. Chandarāgo bhagavato natthi. Suvimuttacitto bhagavā. Saṃvijjati kho, āvuso, bhagavato mano. Vijānāti bhagavā manasā [P 4.0165] dhammaṃ. Chandarāgo bhagavato natthi. Suvimuttacitto bhagavā.

“Friend, the Blessed One indeed has an eye. The Blessed One sees a form with the eye. The Blessed One has no passionate desire. The Blessed One has a well-liberated mind. Friend, the Blessed One indeed has an ear. The Blessed One hears a sound with the ear. The Blessed One has no passionate desire. The Blessed One has a well-liberated mind. Friend, the Blessed One indeed has a nose. The Blessed One smells an odor with the nose. The Blessed One has no passionate desire. The Blessed One has a well-liberated mind. Friend, the Blessed One indeed has a tongue. The Blessed One tastes a flavor with the tongue. The Blessed One has no passionate desire. The Blessed One has a well-liberated mind. Friend, the Blessed One indeed has a body. The Blessed One feels a tangible object with the body. The Blessed One has no passionate desire. The Blessed One has a well-liberated mind. Friend, the Blessed One indeed has a mind. The Blessed One cognizes a mind-object with the mind. The Blessed One has no passionate desire. The Blessed One has a well-liberated mind.”

“Iminā kho etaṃ, āvuso, pariyāyena veditabbaṃ yathā na cakkhu rūpānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na rūpā cakkhussa saṃyojanaṃ; yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ. Na sotaṃ… na ghānaṃ… na jivhā rasānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na rasā jivhāya saṃyojanaṃ; yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ. Na kāyo… na mano dhammānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na dhammā manassa saṃyojanaṃ; yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojana”nti. Pañcamaṃ.

“By this line of reasoning, friend, it should be understood how the eye is not a fetter to forms, nor are forms a fetter to the eye; but whatever passionate desire arises there in dependence on both, that is the fetter there. The ear is not… the nose is not… the tongue is not a fetter to tastes, nor are tastes a fetter to the tongue; but whatever passionate desire arises there in dependence on both, that is the fetter there. The body is not… the mind is not a fetter to mind-objects, nor are mind-objects a fetter to the mind; but whatever passionate desire arises there in dependence on both, that is the fetter there.” The fifth.

6. Kāmabhūsuttaṃ

6. The Discourse with Kāmabhū

233. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā ca ānando āyasmā ca kāmabhū kosambiyaṃ viharanti ghositārāme. Atha kho āyasmā kāmabhū sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā [T 4.0207] āyasmatā ānandena saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ [M 2.0375] kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā kāmabhū āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca –

233. On one occasion, the Venerable Ānanda and the Venerable Kāmabhū were dwelling in Kosambī at Ghosita’s monastery. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Kāmabhū, having risen from seclusion, approached the Venerable Ānanda. Having approached, he exchanged pleasantries with the Venerable Ānanda. Having concluded this pleasant and memorable conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Kāmabhū said this to the Venerable Ānanda:

“Kiṃ nu kho, āvuso ānanda, cakkhu rūpānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, rūpā cakkhussa saṃyojanaṃ…pe… jivhā rasānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, rasā jivhāya saṃyojanaṃ…pe… mano dhammānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, dhammā manassa saṃyojana”nti?

“Friend Ānanda, is the eye a fetter of forms, or are forms a fetter of the eye? … Is the tongue a fetter of tastes, or are tastes a fetter of the tongue? … Is the mind a fetter of mental phenomena, or are mental phenomena a fetter of the mind?”

“Na kho, āvuso kāmabhū kāmabhu (sī.) moggallāne 65-ge vāti suttaṃ passitabbaṃ, cakkhu rūpānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na rūpā cakkhussa saṃyojanaṃ. Yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ…pe… na jivhā rasānaṃ [V 2.0170] saṃyojanaṃ, na rasā jivhāya saṃyojanaṃ…pe… na mano dhammānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na dhammā manassa saṃyojanaṃ. Yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ.

“Friend Kāmabhū, the eye is not a fetter of forms, nor are forms a fetter of the eye. And whatever desire and lust arises there in dependence on both, that is the fetter there. … The tongue is not a fetter of tastes, nor are tastes a fetter of the tongue. … The mind is not a fetter of mental phenomena, nor are mental phenomena a fetter of the mind. And whatever desire and lust arises there in dependence on both, that is the fetter there.

“Seyyathāpi[P 4.0166], āvuso, kāḷo ca balībaddo odāto ca balībaddo ekena dāmena vā yottena vā saṃyuttā assu. Yo nu kho evaṃ vadeyya – ‘kāḷo balībaddo odātassa balībaddassa saṃyojanaṃ, odāto balībaddo kāḷassa balībaddassa saṃyojana’nti, sammā nu kho so vadamāno vadeyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”. “Na kho, āvuso, kāḷo balībaddo odātassa balībaddassa saṃyojanaṃ, napi odāto balībaddo kāḷassa balībaddassa saṃyojanaṃ. Yena ca kho te ekena dāmena vā yottena vā saṃyuttā, taṃ tattha saṃyojanaṃ. Evameva kho[T 4.0208], āvuso, na cakkhu rūpānaṃ saṃyojanaṃ, na rūpā cakkhussa saṃyojanaṃ…pe… na jivhā…pe… na mano…pe… yañca tattha tadubhayaṃ paṭicca uppajjati chandarāgo, taṃ tattha saṃyojana”nti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

“Suppose, friend, a black ox and a white ox were yoked together with a single strap or rope. If someone were to say, ‘The black ox is the fetter of the white ox, and the white ox is the fetter of the black ox,’ would they be speaking correctly?” “Certainly not, friend.” “Friend, the black ox is not the fetter of the white ox, nor is the white ox the fetter of the black ox. But by whatever single strap or rope they are yoked, that is the fetter there. In the same way, friend, the eye is not a fetter of forms, nor are forms a fetter of the eye… the tongue… the mind… and whatever desire and lust arises there in dependence on both, that is the fetter there.” Sixth.

7. Udāyīsuttaṃ

7. The Discourse with Udāyī

234. Ekaṃ samayaṃ āyasmā ca ānando āyasmā ca udāyī kosambiyaṃ viharanti ghositārāme. Atha kho āyasmā udāyī sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yenāyasmā ānando tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmatā ānandena saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā udāyī āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca –

234. On one occasion, the Venerable Ānanda and the Venerable Udāyī were dwelling in Kosambī at Ghosita’s monastery. Then, in the evening, the Venerable Udāyī, having risen from seclusion, approached the Venerable Ānanda. Having approached, he exchanged pleasantries with the Venerable Ānanda. Having concluded this pleasant and memorable conversation, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Udāyī said this to the Venerable Ānanda:

“Yatheva [M 2.0376] nu kho, āvuso ānanda, ayaṃ kāyo bhagavatā anekapariyāyena akkhāto vivaṭo pakāsito – ‘itipāyaṃ kāyo anattā’ti, sakkā evameva viññāṇaṃ pidaṃ ācikkhituṃ desetuṃ paññapetuṃ paṭṭhapetuṃ vivarituṃ vibhajituṃ uttānīkātuṃ – ‘itipidaṃ viññāṇaṃ anattā’”ti?

“Friend Ānanda, just as this body has been declared, revealed, and made plain by the Blessed One in many ways—that ‘thus this body is not-self’—is it possible in the very same way to declare, teach, proclaim, establish, reveal, analyze, and make plain this consciousness—that ‘thus this consciousness is not-self’?”

“Yatheva kho, āvuso udāyī, ayaṃ kāyo bhagavatā anekapariyāyena akkhāto vivaṭo pakāsito – ‘itipāyaṃ kāyo anattā’ti, sakkā evameva viññāṇaṃ pidaṃ ācikkhituṃ [V 2.0171] desetuṃ paññapetuṃ paṭṭhapetuṃ vivarituṃ vibhajituṃ uttānīkātuṃ – ‘itipidaṃ viññāṇaṃ anattā’”ti.

“Friend Udāyī, just as this body has been declared, revealed, and made plain by the Blessed One in many ways—that ‘thus this body is not-self’—so too can this consciousness be declared, taught, proclaimed, established, revealed, analyzed, and made plain—that ‘thus this consciousness is not-self.’”

“Cakkhuñca, āvuso, paṭicca rūpe ca uppajjati cakkhuviññāṇa”nti? “Evamāvuso”ti[P 4.0167]. “Yo cāvuso, hetu, yo ca paccayo cakkhuviññāṇassa uppādāya, so ca hetu, so ca paccayo sabbena sabbaṃ [T 4.0209] sabbathā sabbaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjheyya. Api nu kho cakkhuviññāṇaṃ paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”. “Imināpi kho etaṃ, āvuso, pariyāyena bhagavatā akkhātaṃ vivaṭaṃ pakāsitaṃ – ‘itipidaṃ viññāṇaṃ anattā’”ti…pe….

“Friend, dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises, does it not?” “Yes, friend.” “Friend, if the cause and condition for the arising of eye-consciousness were to cease completely, in every way, without remainder, would eye-consciousness be discerned?” “No, friend.” “By this line of reasoning also, friend, it has been declared, revealed, and made plain by the Blessed One that ‘thus this consciousness is not-self.’”…

“Jivhañcāvuso, paṭicca rase ca uppajjati jivhāviññāṇa”nti? “Evamāvuso”ti. “Yo cāvuso, hetu yo ca paccayo jivhāviññāṇassa uppādāya, so ca hetu, so ca paccayo sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjheyya, api nu kho jivhāviññāṇaṃ paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”. “Imināpi kho etaṃ, āvuso, pariyāyena bhagavatā akkhātaṃ vivaṭaṃ pakāsitaṃ – ‘itipidaṃ viññāṇaṃ anattā’”ti…pe….

“Friend, dependent on the tongue and tastes, tongue-consciousness arises, does it not?” “Yes, friend.” “Friend, if the cause and condition for the arising of tongue-consciousness were to cease completely, in every way, without remainder, would tongue-consciousness be discerned?” “No, friend.” “By this line of reasoning also, friend, it has been declared, revealed, and made plain by the Blessed One that ‘thus this consciousness is not-self.’”…

“Manañcāvuso, paṭicca dhamme ca uppajjati manoviññāṇa”nti? “Evamāvuso”ti. “Yo cāvuso, hetu, yo ca paccayo manoviññāṇassa uppādāya, so ca hetu, so ca paccayo sabbena sabbaṃ sabbathā sabbaṃ aparisesaṃ nirujjheyya, api nu kho manoviññāṇaṃ paññāyethā”ti? “No hetaṃ, āvuso”. “Imināpi kho etaṃ, āvuso, pariyāyena bhagavatā akkhātaṃ vivaṭaṃ pakāsitaṃ – ‘itipidaṃ viññāṇaṃ anattā’”ti.

“Friend, dependent on the mind and mental phenomena, mind-consciousness arises, does it not?” “Yes, friend.” “Friend, if the cause and condition for the arising of mind-consciousness were to cease completely, in every way, without remainder, would mind-consciousness be discerned?” “No, friend.” “By this line of reasoning also, friend, it has been declared, revealed, and made plain by the Blessed One that ‘thus this consciousness is not-self.’”

“Seyyathāpi, āvuso, puriso sāratthiko sāragavesī sārapariyesanaṃ caramāno tiṇhaṃ kuṭhāriṃ ādāya vanaṃ paviseyya. So tattha [M 2.0377] passeyya mahantaṃ kadalikkhandhaṃ ujuṃ navaṃ akukkukajātaṃ akukkuṭakajātaṃ (syā. kaṃ.), akukkajaṭajātaṃ (ka.). Tamenaṃ mūle chindeyya[T 4.0210][P 4.0168]; mūle chetvā agge chindeyya; agge chetvā pattavaṭṭiṃ vinibbhujeyya vinibbhujjeyya (pī.), vinibbhajjeyya (syā. kaṃ.). So tattha pheggumpi nādhigaccheyya, kuto sāraṃ! Evameva kho, āvuso, bhikkhu chasu phassāyatanesu nevattānaṃ na attaniyaṃ samanupassati. So evaṃ asamanupassanto evaṃ samanupassanto (syā. kaṃ. ka.) na kiñci loke [V 2.0172] upādiyati. Anupādiyaṃ na paritassati. Aparitassaṃ paccattaññeva parinibbāyati. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānātī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Suppose, friend, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood, wandering in search of heartwood, might take a sharp axe and enter a forest. There he might see a large banana trunk, straight, new, and without decay. He would cut it at the root; having cut it at the root, he would cut off the top; having cut off the top, he would peel away the leaf sheaths. He would not find even pith-wood there, let alone heartwood. In the very same way, friend, a bhikkhu does not perceive a self or what belongs to a self in the six bases for contact. Not perceiving thus, he does not cling to anything in the world. Not clinging, he is not agitated. Being unagitated, he personally attains Parinibbāna. He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.’” Seventh.

8. Ādittapariyāyasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on the All-Ablaze

235. “Ādittapariyāyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dhammapariyāyaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, ādittapariyāyo, dhammapariyāyo? Varaṃ, bhikkhave, tattāya ayosalākāya ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya sañjotibhūtāya (syā. kaṃ.) cakkhundriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭhaṃ, na tveva cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho. Nimittassādagathitaṃ nimittassādagadhitaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) ma. ni. 3.316-317 vā, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhamānaṃ tiṭṭheyya, anubyañjanassādagathitaṃ vā tasmiñce samaye kālaṃ kareyya, ṭhānametaṃ vijjati, yaṃ dvinnaṃ gatīnaṃ aññataraṃ gatiṃ gaccheyya – nirayaṃ vā, tiracchānayoniṃ vā. Imaṃ khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, ādīnavaṃ disvā evaṃ vadāmi.

235. “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you a discourse on the all-ablaze, a discourse on the Dhamma. Listen to it. And what, bhikkhus, is that discourse on the all-ablaze? It is better, bhikkhus, for the eye faculty to be struck with a heated iron stake, blazing, aflame, and glowing, than to grasp the signs and features in forms cognizable by the eye. For if, bhikkhus, consciousness were to persist while attached to the delight in the signs or attached to the delight in the features, and if one were to pass away at that moment, it is possible that one would go to one of two destinations: either to hell or to the animal realm. Seeing this danger, bhikkhus, I speak thus.

“Varaṃ, bhikkhave, tiṇhena ayosaṅkunā ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena sotindriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭhaṃ, na tveva sotaviññeyyesu saddesu anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho. Nimittassādagathitaṃ vā, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhamānaṃ tiṭṭheyya[T 4.0211], anubyañjanassādagathitaṃ vā tasmiñce samaye kālaṅkareyya, ṭhānametaṃ vijjati, yaṃ dvinnaṃ gatīnaṃ aññataraṃ gatiṃ gaccheyya – nirayaṃ vā tiracchānayoniṃ vā. Imaṃ khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, ādīnavaṃ disvā evaṃ vadāmi[P 4.0169].

“It is better, bhikkhus, for the ear faculty to be struck with a sharp iron spike, blazing, aflame, and glowing, than to grasp the signs and features in sounds cognizable by the ear. For if, bhikkhus, consciousness were to persist while attached to the delight in the signs or attached to the delight in the features, and if one were to pass away at that moment, it is possible that one would go to one of two destinations: either to hell or to the animal realm. Seeing this danger, bhikkhus, I speak thus.

“Varaṃ[M 2.0378], bhikkhave, tiṇhena nakhacchedanena ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena ghānindriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭhaṃ, na tveva ghānaviññeyyesu gandhesu anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho. Nimittassādagathitaṃ vā, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhamānaṃ tiṭṭheyya, anubyañjanassādagathitaṃ vā tasmiñce samaye kālaṃ kareyya. Ṭhānametaṃ vijjati, yaṃ dvinnaṃ gatīnaṃ aññataraṃ gatiṃ gaccheyya – nirayaṃ vā tiracchānayoniṃ vā. Imaṃ khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, ādīnavaṃ disvā evaṃ vadāmi.

“It is better, bhikkhus, for the nose faculty to be struck with a sharp nail-cutter, blazing, aflame, and glowing, than to grasp the signs and features in odors cognizable by the nose. For if, bhikkhus, consciousness were to persist while attached to the delight in the signs or attached to the delight in the features, and if one were to pass away at that moment, it is possible that one would go to one of two destinations: either to hell or to the animal realm. Seeing this danger, bhikkhus, I speak thus.

“Varaṃ, bhikkhave, tiṇhena khurena ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena jivhindriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭhaṃ, na tveva jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho. Nimittassādagathitaṃ [V 2.0173] vā, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhamānaṃ tiṭṭheyya, anubyañjanassādagathitaṃ vā tasmiñce samaye kālaṃ kareyya. Ṭhānametaṃ vijjati, yaṃ dvinnaṃ gatīnaṃ aññataraṃ gatiṃ gaccheyya – nirayaṃ vā tiracchānayoniṃ vā. Imaṃ khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, ādīnavaṃ disvā evaṃ vadāmi.

“It is better, bhikkhus, for the tongue faculty to be struck with a sharp razor, blazing, aflame, and glowing, than to grasp the signs and features in tastes cognizable by the tongue. For if, bhikkhus, consciousness were to persist while attached to the delight in the signs or attached to the delight in the features, and if one were to pass away at that moment, it is possible that one would go to one of two destinations: either to hell or to the animal realm. Seeing this danger, bhikkhus, I speak thus.

“Varaṃ, bhikkhave, tiṇhāya sattiyā ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya kāyindriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭhaṃ, na tveva kāyaviññeyyesu phoṭṭhabbesu anubyañjanaso nimittaggāho. Nimittassādagathitaṃ vā, bhikkhave, viññāṇaṃ tiṭṭhamānaṃ tiṭṭheyya, anubyañjanassādagathitaṃ vā tasmiñce [T 4.0212] samaye kālaṃ kareyya. Ṭhānametaṃ vijjati, yaṃ dvinnaṃ gatīnaṃ aññataraṃ gatiṃ gaccheyya – nirayaṃ vā tiracchānayoniṃ vā. Imaṃ khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, ādīnavaṃ disvā evaṃ vadāmi.

“It is better, bhikkhus, for the body faculty to be struck with a sharp spear, blazing, aflame, and glowing, than to grasp the signs and features in tangible objects cognizable by the body. For if, bhikkhus, consciousness were to persist while attached to the delight in the signs or attached to the delight in the features, and if one were to pass away at that moment, it is possible that one would go to one of two destinations: either to hell or to the animal realm. Seeing this danger, bhikkhus, I speak thus.

“Varaṃ, bhikkhave, sottaṃ. Sottaṃ kho panāhaṃ, bhikkhave, vañjhaṃ jīvitānaṃ vadāmi, aphalaṃ jīvitānaṃ vadāmi, momūhaṃ jīvitānaṃ vadāmi, na tveva tathārūpe vitakke vitakkeyya yathārūpānaṃ vitakkānaṃ vasaṃ gato saṅghaṃ bhindeyya. Imaṃ khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave[P 4.0170], vañjhaṃ jīvitānaṃ ādīnavaṃ disvā evaṃ vadāmi.

“It is better, bhikkhus, to be asleep. For I say, bhikkhus, that for the living, sleep is barren, for the living it is fruitless, for the living it is bewildering. But one should not think such thoughts that, having come under their influence, one would cause a schism in the Saṅgha. Seeing this danger, bhikkhus, I speak thus.

“Tattha, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘tiṭṭhatu tāva tattāya ayosalākāya ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya cakkhundriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭhaṃ. Handāhaṃ idameva manasi karomi – iti cakkhu aniccaṃ, rūpā aniccā, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ, cakkhusamphasso anicco, yampidaṃ cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccaṃ’” anicca”nti (?).

“Therein, bhikkhus, the instructed noble disciple reflects thus: ‘Let alone the eye faculty being struck with a heated iron stake, blazing, aflame, and glowing. Come now, I shall attend only to this: the eye is impermanent, forms are impermanent, eye-consciousness is impermanent, eye-contact is impermanent, and whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by eye-contact, that too is impermanent.’”

“Tiṭṭhatu [M 2.0379] tāva tiṇhena ayosaṅkunā ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena sotindriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭhaṃ. Handāhaṃ idameva manasi karomi – iti sotaṃ aniccaṃ, saddā aniccā, sotaviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ, sotasamphasso anicco, yampidaṃ sotasamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccaṃ.

‘Let the piercing of the ear faculty by a sharp iron spike—ablaze, blazing brightly, and with flames—be for now. Now, I shall attend only to this: the ear is impermanent, sounds are impermanent, ear-consciousness is impermanent, ear-contact is impermanent, and whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by ear-contact, that too is impermanent.’

“Tiṭṭhatu [V 2.0174] tāva tiṇhena nakhacchedanena ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena ghānindriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭhaṃ. Handāhaṃ idameva manasi karomi – iti [T 4.0213] ghānaṃ aniccaṃ, gandhā aniccā, ghānaviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ, ghānasamphasso anicco, yampidaṃ ghānasamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ…pe… tampi aniccaṃ.

‘Let the piercing of the nose faculty by a sharp nail-cutting knife—ablaze, blazing brightly, and with flames—be for now. Now, I shall attend only to this: the nose is impermanent, odors are impermanent, nose-consciousness is impermanent, nose-contact is impermanent, and whatever feeling arises conditioned by nose-contact… that too is impermanent.’

“Tiṭṭhatu tāva tiṇhena khurena ādittena sampajjalitena sajotibhūtena jivhindriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭhaṃ. Handāhaṃ idameva manasi karomi – iti jivhā aniccā, rasā aniccā, jivhāviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ, jivhāsamphasso anicco, yampidaṃ jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati…pe… tampi aniccaṃ.

‘Let the piercing of the tongue faculty by a sharp razor—ablaze, blazing brightly, and with flames—be for now. Now, I shall attend only to this: the tongue is impermanent, tastes are impermanent, tongue-consciousness is impermanent, tongue-contact is impermanent, and whatever feeling arises conditioned by tongue-contact… that too is impermanent.’

“Tiṭṭhatu tāva tiṇhāya sattiyā ādittāya sampajjalitāya sajotibhūtāya kāyindriyaṃ sampalimaṭṭhaṃ. Handāhaṃ idameva manasi karomi – iti kāyo anicco, phoṭṭhabbā aniccā[P 4.0171], kāyaviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ, kāyasamphasso anicco, yampidaṃ kāyasamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ…pe… tampi aniccaṃ.

‘Let the piercing of the body faculty by a sharp spear—ablaze, blazing brightly, and with flames—be for now. Now, I shall attend only to this: the body is impermanent, tactile objects are impermanent, body-consciousness is impermanent, body-contact is impermanent, and whatever feeling arises conditioned by body-contact… that too is impermanent.’

“Tiṭṭhatu tāva sottaṃ. Handāhaṃ idameva manasi karomi – iti mano anicco, dhammā aniccā, manoviññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ, manosamphasso anicco, yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tampi aniccaṃ”.

‘Let sleeping be for now. Now, I shall attend only to this: the mind is impermanent, mental phenomena are impermanent, mind-consciousness is impermanent, mind-contact is impermanent, and whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises conditioned by mind-contact, that too is impermanent.’

“Evaṃ passaṃ, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako cakkhusmimpi nibbindati, rūpesupi nibbindati, cakkhuviññāṇepi nibbindati, cakkhusamphassepi nibbindati…pe… yampidaṃ manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati vedayitaṃ sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā tasmimpi nibbindati. Nibbindaṃ virajjati; virāgā vimuccati; vimuttasmiṃ vimuttamiti ñāṇaṃ hoti. ‘Khīṇā jāti, vusitaṃ brahmacariyaṃ, kataṃ [T 4.0214] karaṇīyaṃ, nāparaṃ itthattāyā’ti pajānāti. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, ādittapariyāyo, dhammapariyāyo”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Seeing thus, monks, the instructed noble disciple becomes disenchanted with the eye, disenchanted with forms, disenchanted with eye-consciousness, disenchanted with eye-contact… and with whatever feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by mind-contact, with that too he becomes disenchanted. Being disenchanted, he becomes dispassionate. Through dispassion, he is liberated. When liberated, the knowledge arises: ‘I am liberated.’ He understands: ‘Birth is destroyed, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more for this state of being.’ This, monks, is the discourse on that which is burning, the discourse on the Dhamma.” The eighth.

9. Paṭhamahatthapādopamasuttaṃ

9. The First Discourse on the Simile of Hands and Feet

236. “Hatthesu[V 2.0175][M 2.0380], bhikkhave, sati ādānanikkhepanaṃ paññāyati; pādesu sati abhikkamapaṭikkamo paññāyati; pabbesu sati samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ paññāyati; kucchismiṃ sati jighacchā pipāsā paññāyati. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, cakkhusmiṃ sati cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ…pe… jivhāya sati jivhāsamphassapaccayā uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ…pe… manasmiṃ sati manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ…pe….

236. “Monks, when there are hands, taking up and putting down are discerned. When there are feet, advancing and retreating are discerned. When there are joints, bending and stretching are discerned. When there is a belly, hunger and thirst are discerned. In the same way, monks, when there is the eye, pleasure and pain arise internally, conditioned by eye-contact… when there is the tongue, pleasure and pain arise internally, conditioned by tongue-contact… when there is the mind, pleasure and pain arise internally, conditioned by mind-contact…”

“Hatthesu, bhikkhave, asati ādānanikkhepanaṃ na paññāyati; pādesu asati abhikkamapaṭikkamo na paññāyati; pabbesu asati samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ na paññāyati; kucchismiṃ asati jighacchā pipāsā na paññāyati. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, cakkhusmiṃ asati cakkhusamphassapaccayā [P 4.0172] nuppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ…pe… jivhāya asati jivhāsamphassapaccayā nuppajjati…pe… manasmiṃ asati manosamphassapaccayā nuppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkha”nti. Navamaṃ.

“Monks, when there are no hands, taking up and putting down are not discerned. When there are no feet, advancing and retreating are not discerned. When there are no joints, bending and stretching are not discerned. When there is no belly, hunger and thirst are not discerned. In the same way, monks, when there is no eye, pleasure and pain do not arise internally, conditioned by eye-contact… when there is no tongue… do not arise… when there is no mind, pleasure and pain do not arise internally, conditioned by mind-contact.” The ninth.

10. Dutiyahatthapādopamasuttaṃ

10. The Second Discourse on the Simile of Hands and Feet

237. “Hatthesu, bhikkhave, sati ādānanikkhepanaṃ hoti; pādesu sati abhikkamapaṭikkamo hoti; pabbesu sati samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ hoti; kucchismiṃ sati jighacchā pipāsā hoti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, cakkhusmiṃ sati cakkhusamphassapaccayā uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ…pe… [T 4.0215] jivhāya sati…pe… manasmiṃ sati manosamphassapaccayā uppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ…pe….

237. “Monks, when there are hands, taking up and putting down occurs. When there are feet, advancing and retreating occur. When there are joints, bending and stretching occur. When there is a belly, hunger and thirst occur. In the same way, monks, when there is the eye, pleasure and pain arise internally, conditioned by eye-contact… when there is the tongue… when there is the mind, pleasure and pain arise internally, conditioned by mind-contact…”

“Hatthesu, bhikkhave, asati ādānanikkhepanaṃ na hoti; pādesu asati abhikkamapaṭikkamo na hoti; pabbesu asati samiñjanapasāraṇaṃ na hoti; kucchismiṃ asati jighacchā pipāsā na hoti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, cakkhusmiṃ asati cakkhusamphassapaccayā nuppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkhaṃ…pe… jivhāya asati jivhāsamphassapaccayā [V 2.0176] nuppajjati…pe… manasmiṃ asati manosamphassapaccayā nuppajjati ajjhattaṃ sukhaṃ dukkha”nti. Dasamaṃ.

“Monks, when there are no hands, taking up and putting down do not occur. When there are no feet, advancing and retreating do not occur. When there are no joints, bending and stretching do not occur. When there is no belly, hunger and thirst do not occur. In the same way, monks, when there is no eye, pleasure and pain do not arise internally, conditioned by eye-contact… when there is no tongue… do not arise… when there is no mind, pleasure and pain do not arise internally, conditioned by mind-contact.” The tenth.

Samuddavaggo aṭṭharasamo.

The Chapter on the Ocean, the Eighteenth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of that:

Dve [M 2.0381] samuddā bāḷisiko, khīrarukkhena koṭṭhiko;

Kāmabhū udāyī ceva, ādittena ca aṭṭhamaṃ;

Hatthapādūpamā dveti, vaggo tena pavuccatīti.

Two on the Ocean, the Fisherman, the Milk-tree, and Koṭṭhika; Kāmabhū and Udāyī, and the eighth on the Burning; two Similes of Hands and Feet—thus is the chapter called.

19. Āsīvisavaggo

The Chapter on the Venomous Snake

1. Āsīvisopamasuttaṃ

The Discourse on the Simile of the Venomous Snake

238. “Seyyathāpi[T 4.0216], bhikkhave, cattāro āsīvisā uggatejā ghoravisā. Atha puriso āgaccheyya jīvitukāmo amaritukāmo sukhakāmo dukkhappaṭikūlo. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘ime te, ambho purisa, cattāro āsīvisā uggatejā ghoravisā kālena [P 4.0173] kālaṃ vuṭṭhāpetabbā, kālena kālaṃ nhāpetabbā, kālena kālaṃ bhojetabbā, kālena kālaṃ saṃvesetabbā pavesetabbā (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.). Yadā ca kho te, ambho purisa, imesaṃ catunnaṃ āsīvisānaṃ uggatejānaṃ ghoravisānaṃ aññataro vā aññataro vā kuppissati, tato tvaṃ, ambho purisa, maraṇaṃ vā nigacchasi, maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhaṃ. Yaṃ te, ambho purisa, karaṇīyaṃ taṃ karohī’”ti.

238. “Suppose, bhikkhus, there were four venomous snakes of fierce potency and terrible venom. Then a man would come along, desiring to live, not desiring to die, desiring happiness and averse to suffering. They would say to him: ‘Good man, these four venomous snakes of fierce potency and terrible venom must be roused from time to time, bathed from time to time, fed from time to time, and put to rest from time to time. Whenever, good man, any one of these four venomous snakes of fierce potency and terrible venom becomes angry, you will then meet with death or suffering equivalent to death. Whatever you have to do, good man, do it.’”

“Atha kho so, bhikkhave, puriso bhīto catunnaṃ āsīvisānaṃ uggatejānaṃ ghoravisānaṃ yena vā tena vā palāyetha. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘ime kho, ambho purisa, pañca vadhakā paccatthikā piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhā, yattheva naṃ passissāma tattheva jīvitā voropessāmāti. Yaṃ te, ambho purisa, karaṇīyaṃ taṃ karohī’”ti.

“Then, bhikkhus, that man, frightened of the four venomous snakes of fierce potency and terrible venom, would flee in one direction or another. They would say to him: ‘Good man, five murderous enemies are following close behind you, thinking, “Wherever we see him, we will take his life.” Whatever you have to do, good man, do it!’”

“Atha [V 2.0177] kho so, bhikkhave, puriso bhīto catunnaṃ āsīvisānaṃ uggatejānaṃ ghoravisānaṃ, bhīto pañcannaṃ vadhakānaṃ paccatthikānaṃ yena vā [T 4.0217] tena vā palāyetha. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘ayaṃ te, ambho purisa, chaṭṭho antaracaro vadhako ukkhittāsiko piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandho yattheva naṃ passissāmi tattheva siro pātessāmīti. Yaṃ te, ambho purisa, karaṇīyaṃ taṃ karohī’”ti.

“Then, bhikkhus, that man, frightened of the four venomous snakes of fierce potency and terrible venom, and frightened of the five murderous enemies, would flee in one direction or another. They would say to him: ‘Good man, a sixth murderer, an intimate, with sword upraised, is following close behind you, thinking, “Wherever I see him, I will cut off his head.” Whatever you have to do, good man, do it!’”

“Atha [M 2.0382] kho so, bhikkhave, puriso bhīto catunnaṃ āsīvisānaṃ uggatejānaṃ ghoravisānaṃ, bhīto pañcannaṃ vadhakānaṃ paccatthikānaṃ, bhīto chaṭṭhassa antaracarassa vadhakassa ukkhittāsikassa yena vā tena vā palāyetha. So passeyya suññaṃ gāmaṃ. Yaññadeva gharaṃ paviseyya rittakaññeva paviseyya tucchakaññeva paviseyya suññakaññeva paviseyya. Yaññadeva bhājanaṃ parimaseyya rittakaññeva parimaseyya tucchakaññeva parimaseyya suññakaññeva parimaseyya. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘idāni, ambho purisa, imaṃ suññaṃ gāmaṃ corā gāmaghātakā pavisanti vadhissanti (sī. pī.). Yaṃ te, ambho purisa, karaṇīyaṃ taṃ karohī’”ti.

“Then, bhikkhus, that man, frightened of the four venomous snakes of fierce potency and terrible venom, frightened of the five murderous enemies, and frightened of the sixth murderer, an intimate, with sword upraised, would flee in one direction or another. He would see a deserted village. Whatever house he were to enter, he would enter it only to find it empty, void, and deserted. Whatever vessel he were to touch, he would touch it only to find it empty, void, and deserted. They would say to him: ‘Good man, village-plundering thieves are now entering this deserted village. Whatever you have to do, good man, do it!’”

“Atha [P 4.0174] kho so, bhikkhave, puriso bhīto catunnaṃ āsīvisānaṃ uggatejānaṃ ghoravisānaṃ, bhīto pañcannaṃ vadhakānaṃ paccatthikānaṃ, bhīto chaṭṭhassa antaracarassa vadhakassa ukkhittāsikassa, bhīto corānaṃ gāmaghātakānaṃ yena vā tena vā palāyetha. So passeyya mahantaṃ udakaṇṇavaṃ orimaṃ tīraṃ sāsaṅkaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ, pārimaṃ tīraṃ khemaṃ appaṭibhayaṃ. Na cassa nāvā santāraṇī uttarasetu vā apārā pāraṃ gamanāya. Atha [T 4.0218] kho, bhikkhave, tassa purisassa evamassa – ‘ayaṃ kho mahāudakaṇṇavo orimaṃ tīraṃ sāsaṅkaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ, pārimaṃ tīraṃ khemaṃ appaṭibhayaṃ, natthi ca na cassa (sī. ka.), natthassa (syā. kaṃ.) nāvā santāraṇī uttarasetu vā apārā pāraṃ gamanāya. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṃ saṃkaḍḍhitvā kullaṃ bandhitvā taṃ kullaṃ nissāya hatthehi ca pādehi ca vāyamamāno sotthinā pāraṃ gaccheyya’”nti.

“Then, bhikkhus, that man, frightened of the four venomous snakes of fierce potency and terrible venom, frightened of the five murderous enemies, frightened of the sixth murderer, an intimate, with sword upraised, and frightened of the village-plundering thieves, would flee in one direction or another. He would see a great expanse of water, with the near shore perilous and fearful, and the far shore safe and free from fear. But there would be no boat for crossing, nor a bridge for going from the one shore to the other. Then, bhikkhus, it would occur to that man: ‘Here is this great expanse of water, with the near shore perilous and fearful, and the far shore safe and free from fear. But there is no boat for crossing, nor a bridge for going from the one shore to the other. What if I were to gather grass, wood, branches, and leaves and, having bound them into a raft, relying on that raft and striving with my hands and feet, I might safely cross to the far shore?’”

“Atha kho so, bhikkhave, puriso tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṃ saṃkaḍḍhitvā kullaṃ bandhitvā taṃ kullaṃ nissāya hatthehi ca pādehi ca vāyamamāno sotthinā pāraṃ gaccheyya, tiṇṇo pāraṅgato pāragato (sī. syā. kaṃ.) thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇo.

“Then, bhikkhus, that man would gather grass, wood, branches, and leaves and, having bound them into a raft, relying on that raft and striving with his hands and feet, he would safely cross to the far shore. Having crossed over and gone to the other shore, the brahmin stands on high ground.”

“Upamā [V 2.0178] kho myāyaṃ, bhikkhave, katā atthassa viññāpanāya. Ayañcettha ayaṃ cevettha (sī.) attho – cattāro āsīvisā uggatejā ghoravisāti kho, bhikkhave, catunnetaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ adhivacanaṃ – pathavīdhātuyā, āpodhātuyā, tejodhātuyā, vāyodhātuyā.

“Bhikkhus, this simile was made by me to convey the meaning. And this is the meaning here: ‘The four venomous snakes of fierce potency and terrible venom’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the four great elements: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element.”

“Pañca [M 2.0383] vadhakā paccatthikāti kho, bhikkhave, pañcannetaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ adhivacanaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – rūpupādānakkhandhassa, vedanupādānakkhandhassa, saññupādānakkhandhassa, saṅkhārupādānakkhandhassa, viññāṇupādānakkhandhassa.

“‘The five murderous enemies’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the five aggregates subject to clinging; that is, the form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging.”

“Chaṭṭho antaracaro vadhako ukkhittāsikoti kho, bhikkhave, nandīrāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

“‘The sixth murderer, an intimate, with sword upraised’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for delight and lust.”

“Suñño gāmoti kho, bhikkhave, channetaṃ ajjhattikānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Cakkhuto cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto medhāvī upaparikkhati rittakaññeva khāyati, tucchakaññeva [P 4.0175] khāyati, suññakaññeva [T 4.0219] khāyati…pe… jivhāto cepi naṃ, bhikkhave…pe… manato cepi naṃ, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto medhāvī upaparikkhati rittakaññeva khāyati, tucchakaññeva khāyati, suññakaññeva khāyati.

“‘The empty village’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the six internal sense bases. If, bhikkhus, a wise, competent, and intelligent bhikkhu examines it with respect to the eye, it appears to be empty, void, and desolate… If, bhikkhus… with respect to the tongue… If, bhikkhus, a wise, competent, and intelligent bhikkhu examines it with respect to the mind, it appears to be empty, void, and desolate.”

“Corā gāmaghātakāti kho, bhikkhave, channetaṃ bāhirānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Cakkhu, bhikkhave, haññati manāpāmanāpesu rūpesu; sotaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… ghānaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… jivhā, bhikkhave, haññati manāpāmanāpesu rasesu; kāyo, bhikkhave…pe… mano, bhikkhave, haññati manāpāmanāpesu dhammesu.

“‘The village-plundering thieves’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the six external sense bases. The eye, bhikkhus, is assailed by agreeable and disagreeable forms; the ear, bhikkhus… the nose, bhikkhus… the tongue, bhikkhus, is assailed by agreeable and disagreeable tastes; the body, bhikkhus… the mind, bhikkhus, is assailed by agreeable and disagreeable mental phenomena.”

“Mahā udakaṇṇavoti kho, bhikkhave, catunnetaṃ oghānaṃ adhivacanaṃ – kāmoghassa, bhavoghassa, diṭṭhoghassa, avijjoghassa.

“‘The great ocean’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the four floods: the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.”

“Orimaṃ tīraṃ sāsaṅkaṃ sappaṭibhayanti kho, bhikkhave, sakkāyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

“‘The near shore, perilous and fearful’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the existing body.”

“Pārimaṃ tīraṃ khemaṃ appaṭibhayanti kho, bhikkhave, nibbānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

“‘The far shore, safe and fearless’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for Nibbāna.”

“Kullanti [V 2.0179] kho, bhikkhave, ariyassetaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa adhivacanaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi.

“‘The raft’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view… right concentration.”

“Tassa hatthehi ca pādehi ca vāyāmoti kho, bhikkhave, vīriyārambhassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

“‘Striving with hands and feet’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the arousal of energy.”

“Tiṇṇo pāraṅgato thale tiṭṭhati brāhmaṇoti kho, bhikkhave, arahato etaṃ adhivacana”nti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“‘Crossed over, gone to the far shore, a brahmin stands on high ground’—this, bhikkhus, is a designation for the Arahant.”

2. Rathopamasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on the Simile of the Chariot

239. “Tīhi[T 4.0220][M 2.0384], bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu diṭṭheva dhamme sukhasomanassabahulo viharati, yoni cassa āraddhā hoti āsavānaṃ khayāya. Katamehi tīhi? Indriyesu guttadvāro hoti, bhojane mattaññū, jāgariyaṃ anuyutto.

239. “Bhikkhus, a monk endowed with three qualities dwells with an abundance of happiness and joy in this very life, and the foundation for the destruction of the taints has been laid by him. With which three? He guards the doors of the sense faculties, knows the proper measure in eating, and is devoted to wakefulness.”

“Kathañca[P 4.0176], bhikkhave, bhikkhu indriyesu guttadvāro hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā na nimittaggāhī hoti, nānubyañjanaggāhī; yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ. Tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjati; rakkhati cakkhundriyaṃ; cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjati. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya na nimittaggāhī hoti nānubyañjanaggāhī; yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ manindriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjati; rakkhati manindriyaṃ; manindriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjati. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, subhūmiyaṃ cātumahāpathe ājaññaratho yutto assa ṭhito odhastapatodo odhatapatodo (syā. kaṃ.), odhasatapatodo (pī.). Tamenaṃ dakkho yoggācariyo assadammasārathi abhiruhitvā vāmena hatthena rasmiyo gahetvā, dakkhiṇena hatthena patodaṃ gahetvā, yenicchakaṃ yadicchakaṃ sāreyyapi paccāsāreyyapi. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu imesaṃ channaṃ indriyānaṃ ārakkhāya [T 4.0221] sikkhati[V 2.0180], saṃyamāya sikkhati, damāya sikkhati, upasamāya sikkhati. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu indriyesu guttadvāro hoti.

“And how, bhikkhus, does a monk guard the doors of the sense faculties? Here, bhikkhus, having seen a form with the eye, a monk does not grasp the general appearance or the secondary characteristics. Inasmuch as, if he were to dwell with the eye faculty unrestrained, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure would assail him, he practices for its restraint; he guards the eye faculty; he undertakes the restraint of the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear… having smelled an odor with the nose… having tasted a flavor with the tongue… having felt a tangible object with the body… having cognized a mental object with the mind, he does not grasp the general appearance or the secondary characteristics. Inasmuch as, if he were to dwell with the mind faculty unrestrained, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure would assail him, he practices for its restraint; he guards the mind faculty; he undertakes the restraint of the mind faculty. Suppose, bhikkhus, on level ground at a four-way crossroads, a chariot drawn by thoroughbreds might stand harnessed, with the goad placed ready. Then a skilled trainer, a horse-taming charioteer, having mounted it, taking the reins with his left hand and the goad with his right hand, might drive it forward and back wherever he wishes, to whatever destination he desires. In the same way, bhikkhus, a monk trains for the protection of these six sense faculties, for their restraint, for their taming, and for their calming. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a monk guards the doors of the sense faculties.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bhojane mattaññū hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṃ āhāreti – ‘neva davāya, na madāya, na maṇḍanāya, na vibhūsanāya, yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā, yāpanāya, vihiṃsūparatiyā, brahmacariyānuggahāya, iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi, navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmi, yātrā ca me bhavissati, anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro cā’ti. Seyyathāpi[P 4.0177], bhikkhave, puriso vaṇaṃ ālimpeyya [M 2.0385] yāvadeva rohanatthāya ropanatthāya (sī. pī.), sevanatthāya (syā. kaṃ.), gopanatthāya (ka.), seyyathā vā pana akkhaṃ abbhañjeyya yāvadeva bhārassa nittharaṇatthāya; evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṃ āhāreti – ‘neva davāya, na madāya, na maṇḍanāya, na vibhūsanāya, yāvadeva imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā, yāpanāya, vihiṃsūparatiyā, brahmacariyānuggahāya, iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi, navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmi, yātrā ca me bhavissati, anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro cā’ti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bhojane mattaññū hoti.

“And how, bhikkhus, does a monk know the proper measure in eating? Here, bhikkhus, a monk, reflecting appropriately, partakes of food: not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for physical embellishment, not for beautification, but only for the maintenance and sustenance of this body, for the cessation of discomfort, and for the support of the holy life, thinking: ‘Thus I will eliminate the old feeling and not give rise to a new feeling. I will maintain myself, be blameless, and dwell in comfort.’ Just as a person might anoint a wound only for the sake of its healing, or as one might grease an axle only for the sake of conveying a load; in the same way, bhikkhus, a monk, reflecting appropriately, partakes of food: not for amusement, not for intoxication, not for physical embellishment, not for beautification, but only for the maintenance and sustenance of this body, for the cessation of discomfort, and for the support of the holy life, thinking: ‘Thus I will eliminate the old feeling and not give rise to a new feeling. I will maintain myself, be blameless, and dwell in comfort.’ It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a monk knows the proper measure in eating.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu jāgariyaṃ anuyutto hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodheti. Rattiyā paṭhamaṃ yāmaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodheti. Rattiyā majjhimaṃ yāmaṃ dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ [T 4.0222] kappeti pāde pādaṃ accādhāya sato sampajāno uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasi karitvā. Rattiyā pacchimaṃ yāmaṃ paccuṭṭhāya caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodheti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu jāgariyaṃ anuyutto hoti. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, tīhi dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu diṭṭheva dhamme sukhasomanassabahulo viharati, yoni cassa āraddhā hoti āsavānaṃ khayāyā”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

“And how, bhikkhus, is a monk devoted to wakefulness? Here, bhikkhus, during the day, a monk purifies his mind from obstructive states by walking back and forth and by sitting. During the first watch of the night, he purifies his mind from obstructive states by walking back and forth and by sitting.
