During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side in the lion’s posture, with one foot placed slightly over the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having established in his mind the perception of rising. During the last watch of the night, having arisen, he purifies his mind from obstructive states by walking back and forth and by sitting. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a monk is devoted to wakefulness. Bhikkhus, endowed with these three qualities, a monk dwells with an abundance of happiness and joy in this very life, and the foundation for the destruction of the taints has been laid by him.”

3. Kummopamasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on the Simile of the Turtle

240. “Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, kummo kacchapo sāyanhasamayaṃ anunadītīre gocarapasuto ahosi. Siṅgālopi sigālopi (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) kho, bhikkhave, sāyanhasamayaṃ anunadītīre gocarapasuto ahosi. Addasā [V 2.0181] kho, bhikkhave, kummo kacchapo siṅgālaṃ dūratova gocarapasutaṃ. Disvāna soṇḍipañcamāni aṅgāni [P 4.0178] sake kapāle samodahitvā appossukko tuṇhībhūto saṅkasāyati. Siṅgālopi kho, bhikkhave, addasa kummaṃ kacchapaṃ dūratova gocarapasutaṃ. Disvāna yena kummo kacchapo tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā kummaṃ kacchapaṃ paccupaṭṭhito ahosi – ‘yadāyaṃ kummo kacchapo soṇḍipañcamānaṃ aṅgānaṃ aññataraṃ vā aññataraṃ vā aṅgaṃ abhininnāmessati, tattheva naṃ gahetvā uddālitvā khādissāmī’ti. Yadā kho, bhikkhave, kummo kacchapo [M 2.0386] soṇḍipañcamānaṃ aṅgānaṃ aññataraṃ vā aññataraṃ vā aṅgaṃ na abhininnāmi, atha siṅgālo kummamhā nibbijja pakkāmi, otāraṃ alabhamāno.

240. Once upon a time, monks, a tortoise was foraging along a river bank in the evening. A jackal, too, was foraging along a river bank in the evening. The tortoise saw the jackal from afar as it was foraging. Seeing it, the tortoise withdrew its five limbs, including its head, into its own shell, and remained still, unconcerned and silent. The jackal also saw the tortoise from afar as it was foraging. Seeing it, the jackal approached the tortoise and stood waiting, thinking: ‘When this tortoise extends one or another of its five limbs, including its head, I will grab it right there, break it open, and eat it.’ But, monks, when the tortoise did not extend any of its five limbs, including its head, the jackal, finding no opportunity, became disheartened and departed from the tortoise.

“Evameva kho, bhikkhave, tumhepi māro pāpimā satataṃ samitaṃ paccupaṭṭhito – ‘appeva nāmāhaṃ imesaṃ cakkhuto [T 4.0223] vā otāraṃ labheyyaṃ…pe… jivhāto vā otāraṃ labheyyaṃ…pe… manato vā otāraṃ labheyya’nti. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, indriyesu guttadvārā viharatha. Cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā mā nimittaggāhino ahuvattha, mā anubyañjanaggāhino. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ cakkhundriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjatha, rakkhatha cakkhundriyaṃ, cakkhundriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatha. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya mā nimittaggāhino ahuvattha, mā anubyañjanaggāhino. Yatvādhikaraṇamenaṃ manindriyaṃ asaṃvutaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāssaveyyuṃ, tassa saṃvarāya paṭipajjatha, rakkhatha manindriyaṃ, manindriye saṃvaraṃ āpajjatha. Yato tumhe, bhikkhave, indriyesu guttadvārā viharissatha, atha tumhehipi māro pāpimā nibbijja pakkamissati, otāraṃ alabhamāno – kummamhāva siṅgālo”ti.

In the same way, monks, Māra the Evil One is constantly and continuously present before you, thinking: ‘Perhaps I can find an opening through their eye… or through their tongue… or through their mind.’ Therefore, monks, you should dwell with the doors of your sense faculties guarded. Having seen a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs or its features. Since, if you dwell with the eye faculty unguarded, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might overcome you, you should practice for its restraint, guard the eye faculty, and achieve restraint of the eye faculty. Having heard a sound with the ear… Having smelled an odor with the nose… Having tasted a flavor with the tongue… Having touched a tangible object with the body… Having cognized a mental object with the mind, do not grasp at its signs or its features. Since, if you dwell with the mind faculty unguarded, evil, unwholesome states of covetousness and displeasure might overcome you, you should practice for its restraint, guard the mind faculty, and achieve restraint of the mind faculty. When you, monks, dwell with the doors of your sense faculties guarded, then Māra the Evil One, finding no opening, will become disheartened and depart from you, just like the jackal from the tortoise.

“Kummo [P 4.0179] aṅgāni sake kapāle,

Samodahaṃ bhikkhu manovitakke;

Anissito aññamaheṭhayāno,

Parinibbuto nūpavadeyya kañcī”ti. tatiyaṃ;

As a tortoise withdraws its limbs into its own shell, so a monk should withdraw his mental thoughts. Unreliant, not harming another, fully extinguished, he would not disparage anyone.

4. Paṭhamadārukkhandhopamasuttaṃ

4. The First Discourse on the Simile of the Log of Wood

241. Ekaṃ [V 2.0182] samayaṃ bhagavā kosambiyaṃ viharati gaṅgāya nadiyā tīre. Addasā kho bhagavā mahantaṃ dārukkhandhaṃ gaṅgāya nadiyā sotena vuyhamānaṃ. Disvāna bhikkhū āmantesi – “passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, amuṃ [T 4.0224] mahantaṃ dārukkhandhaṃ gaṅgāya nadiyā sotena vuyhamāna”nti? “Evaṃ, bhante”. “Sace so, bhikkhave, dārukkhandho na orimaṃ tīraṃ upagacchati, na pārimaṃ tīraṃ upagacchati, na majjhe saṃsīdissati, na thale ussīdissati, na manussaggāho gahessati, na [M 2.0387] amanussaggāho gahessati, na āvaṭṭaggāho gahessati, na antopūti bhavissati; evañhi so, bhikkhave, dārukkhandho samuddaninno bhavissati samuddapoṇo samuddapabbhāro. Taṃ kissa hetu? Samuddaninno, bhikkhave, gaṅgāya nadiyā soto samuddapoṇo samuddapabbhāro.

241. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kosambī on the bank of the river Ganges. The Blessed One saw a great log of wood being carried along by the current of the river Ganges. Having seen it, he addressed the monks: “Do you see, monks, that great log of wood being carried along by the current of the river Ganges?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “If, monks, that log of wood does not ground on the near shore, does not ground on the far shore, does not sink in the middle, is not stranded on high ground, is not seized by humans, is not seized by non-humans, is not caught in a whirlpool, and does not become rotten within, then that log of wood, monks, will slant, slope, and incline towards the ocean. For what reason? Because the current of the river Ganges, monks, slants, slopes, and inclines towards the ocean.

“Evameva kho, bhikkhave, sace tumhepi na orimaṃ tīraṃ upagacchatha, na pārimaṃ tīraṃ upagacchatha; na majjhe saṃsīdissatha, na thale ussīdissatha, na manussaggāho gahessati, na amanussaggāho gahessati, na āvaṭṭaggāho gahessati, na antopūtī bhavissatha; evaṃ tumhe[P 4.0180], bhikkhave, nibbānaninnā bhavissatha nibbānapoṇā nibbānapabbhārā. Taṃ kissa hetu? Nibbānaninnā, bhikkhave, sammādiṭṭhi nibbānapoṇā nibbānapabbhārā”ti. Evaṃ vutte, aññataro bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “kiṃ nu kho, bhante, orimaṃ tīraṃ, kiṃ pārimaṃ tīraṃ, ko majjhe saṃsādo saṃsīdo (ka.), saṃsīdito (syā. kaṃ.), ko thale ussādo, ko manussaggāho, ko amanussaggāho, ko āvaṭṭaggāho, ko antopūtibhāvo”ti?

In the same way, monks, if you do not ground on the near shore, do not ground on the far shore, do not sink in the middle, are not stranded on high ground, are not seized by humans, are not seized by non-humans, are not caught in a whirlpool, and do not become rotten within, then you, monks, will slant, slope, and incline towards Nibbāna. For what reason? Because right view, monks, slants, slopes, and inclines towards Nibbāna.” When this was said, a certain monk said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is the near shore? What is the far shore? What is sinking in the middle? What is being stranded on high ground? What is seizure by humans? What is seizure by non-humans? What is being caught in a whirlpool? What is the state of being rotten within?”

“‘Orimaṃ tīra’nti kho, bhikkhu, channetaṃ ajjhattikānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. ‘Pārimaṃ tīra’nti kho[T 4.0225], bhikkhu, channetaṃ bāhirānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. ‘Majjhe saṃsādo’ti kho, bhikkhu, nandīrāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. ‘Thale ussādo’ti kho, bhikkhu, asmimānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

“‘The near shore,’ monk, is a designation for the six internal sense bases. ‘The far shore,’ monk, is a designation for the six external sense bases. ‘Sinking in the middle,’ monk, is a designation for delight and lust. ‘Being stranded on high ground,’ monk, is a designation for the conceit ‘I am.’”

“Katamo ca, bhikkhu, manussaggāho? Idha, bhikkhu, gihīhi saṃsaṭṭho gihisaṃsaṭṭho (ka.) viharati, sahanandī [V 2.0183] sahasokī, sukhitesu sukhito, dukkhitesu dukkhito, uppannesu kiccakaraṇīyesu attanā tesu yogaṃ āpajjati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhu, manussaggāho.

“And what, monk, is seizure by humans? Here, monk, a monk dwells associated with householders; he rejoices with them and sorrows with them, is happy when they are happy and suffers when they suffer, and he personally involves himself in their duties and affairs when they arise. This, monk, is called seizure by humans.

“Katamo ca, bhikkhu, amanussaggāho? Idha, bhikkhu, ekacco aññataraṃ devanikāyaṃ paṇidhāya brahmacariyaṃ carati – ‘imināhaṃ sīlena vā vatena vā tapena vā brahmacariyena vā devo vā bhavissāmi devaññataro vā’ti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhu, amanussaggāho. ‘Āvaṭṭaggāho’ti kho, bhikkhu, pañcannetaṃ kāmaguṇānaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

“And what, monk, is seizure by non-humans? Here, monk, a certain person practices the holy life aspiring to a certain group of deities, thinking, ‘By this virtue or observance or austerity or holy life, I will become a deva or one of the devas.’ This, monk, is called seizure by non-humans. ‘Seizure by a whirlpool,’ monk, is a designation for the five cords of sensual pleasure.

“Katamo ca, bhikkhu, antopūtibhāvo? Idha, bhikkhu, ekacco dussīlo hoti pāpadhammo asucisaṅkassarasamācāro paṭicchannakammanto assamaṇo [M 2.0388] samaṇapaṭiñño abrahmacārī [P 4.0181] brahmacāripaṭiñño antopūti avassuto kasambujāto. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhu, ‘antopūtibhāvo’”ti.

“And what, monk, is the state of being rotten inside? Here, monk, a certain person is immoral, of evil character, impure, of suspect conduct, of concealed actions; not an ascetic, he claims to be an ascetic; not a practitioner of the holy life, he claims to be a practitioner of the holy life; he is rotten inside, oozing with defilements, and has become like a heap of refuse. This, monk, is called the state of being rotten inside.”

Tena kho pana samayena nando gopālako bhagavato avidūre ṭhito hoti. Atha kho nando gopālako bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ahaṃ kho, bhante, na orimaṃ tīraṃ upagacchāmi, na pārimaṃ tīraṃ upagacchāmi, na majjhe saṃsīdissāmi, na [T 4.0226] thale ussīdissāmi, na maṃ manussaggāho gahessati, na amanussaggāho gahessati, na āvaṭṭaggāho gahessati, na antopūti bhavissāmi. Labheyyāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ, labheyyaṃ upasampada”nti. “Tena hi tvaṃ, nanda, sāmikānaṃ gāvo niyyātehī”ti nīyyādehīti (sī.), niyyādehīti (syā. kaṃ. pī.). “Gamissanti, bhante, gāvo vacchagiddhiniyo”ti. “Niyyāteheva tvaṃ, nanda, sāmikānaṃ gāvo”ti. Atha kho nando gopālako sāmikānaṃ gāvo niyyātetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “niyyātitā niyyātā (syā. kaṃ. ka. sī. aṭṭha.), bhante, sāmikānaṃ gāvo. Labheyyāhaṃ, bhante, bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ, labheyyaṃ upasampada”nti. Alattha kho nando gopālako bhagavato santike pabbajjaṃ, alattha upasampadaṃ. Acirūpasampanno ca panāyasmā nando eko vūpakaṭṭho…pe… aññataro ca panāyasmā nando arahataṃ ahosīti. Catutthaṃ.

At that time, the cowherd Nanda was standing not far from the Blessed One. Then the cowherd Nanda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, I will not approach the near shore, I will not approach the far shore, I will not sink in the middle, I will not be stranded on dry land, I will not be seized by humans, I will not be seized by non-humans, I will not be seized by a whirlpool, and I will not become rotten inside. Venerable sir, may I receive the going forth in the Blessed One’s presence, may I receive the higher ordination.” “In that case, Nanda, return the cows to their owners.” “Venerable sir, the cows will go on their own, longing for their calves.” “You must return the cows to their owners, Nanda.” Then the cowherd Nanda, having returned the cows to their owners, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the cows have been returned to their owners. Venerable sir, may I receive the going forth in the Blessed One’s presence, may I receive the higher ordination.” The cowherd Nanda indeed received the going forth in the Blessed One’s presence, he received the higher ordination. And not long after his higher ordination, the venerable Nanda, dwelling alone, secluded… the venerable Nanda became one of the arahants. The fourth.

5. Dutiyadārukkhandhopamasuttaṃ

5. The Second Discourse on the Simile of the Log

242. Ekaṃ [V 2.0184] samayaṃ bhagavā kimilāyaṃ kimbilāyaṃ (sī. pī.), kimmilāyaṃ (syā. kaṃ.) viharati gaṅgāya nadiyā tīre. Addasā kho bhagavā mahantaṃ dārukkhandhaṃ gaṅgāya nadiyā sotena vuyhamānaṃ. Disvāna bhikkhū āmantesi – “passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, amuṃ mahantaṃ [P 4.0182] dārukkhandhaṃ gaṅgāya nadiyā sotena vuyhamāna”nti? “Evaṃ bhante”…pe… evaṃ vutte, āyasmā kimilo bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – kiṃ nu kho, bhante, orimaṃ tīraṃ…pe… katamo ca, kimila, antopūtibhāvo. Idha, kimila, bhikkhu aññataraṃ saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ āpattiṃ [T 4.0227] āpanno hoti yathārūpāya āpattiyā na vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati. Ayaṃ vuccati, kimila, antopūtibhāvoti. Pañcamaṃ.

242. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Kimilā on the bank of the Ganges River. The Blessed One saw a great log being carried along by the current of the Ganges River. Having seen it, he addressed the monks: “Do you see, monks, that great log being carried along by the current of the Ganges River?” “Yes, venerable sir.” … When this was said, the Venerable Kimila said this to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, is the near shore? … And what, Kimila, is being inwardly rotten? Here, Kimila, a monk has committed a certain defiled offense of such a kind that emergence from that offense is not apparent. This, Kimila, is called being inwardly rotten.” The fifth.

6. Avassutapariyāyasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Being Drenched by Defilements

243. Ekaṃ [M 2.0389] samayaṃ bhagavā sakkesu viharati kapilavatthusmiṃ nigrodhārāme. Tena kho pana samayena kāpilavatthavānaṃ sakyānaṃ navaṃ santhāgāraṃ sandhāgāraṃ (ka.) acirakāritaṃ hoti anajjhāvuṭṭhaṃ anajjhāvutthaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā kenaci vā manussabhūtena. Atha kho kāpilavatthavā sakyā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho kāpilavatthavā sakyā bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “idha, bhante, kāpilavatthavānaṃ sakyānaṃ navaṃ santhāgāraṃ acirakāritaṃ acirakāritaṃ hoti (ka.) anajjhāvuṭṭhaṃ samaṇena vā brāhmaṇena vā kenaci vā manussabhūtena[P 4.0183]. Taṃ, bhante, bhagavā paṭhamaṃ paribhuñjatu. Bhagavatā paṭhamaṃ paribhuttaṃ pacchā kāpilavatthavā sakyā paribhuñjissanti. Tadassa kāpilavatthavānaṃ sakyānaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti. Adhivāsesi bhagavā tuṇhībhāvena.

243. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at Kapilavatthu in the Nigrodha Park. Now at that time, the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu had a new assembly hall that had been recently built and was as yet uninhabited by any ascetic, brahmin, or any human being. Then the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu said this to the Blessed One: “Here, venerable sir, the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu have a new assembly hall that has been recently built and is as yet uninhabited by any ascetic, brahmin, or any human being. Venerable sir, may the Blessed One be the first to use it. After the Blessed One has used it first, the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu will then use it. That would be for the long-term welfare and happiness of the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu.” The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

Atha kho kāpilavatthavā sakyā bhagavato adhivāsanaṃ viditvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā yena navaṃ santhāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā sabbasanthariṃ sabbasanthariṃ santhataṃ (ka.) santhāgāraṃ santharitvā āsanāni paññāpetvā udakamaṇikaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā telappadīpaṃ āropetvā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “sabbasantharisanthataṃ sabbasanthariṃ santhataṃ (sī. pī. ka.), bhante, santhāgāraṃ, āsanāni paññattāni, udakamaṇiko patiṭṭhāpito, telappadīpo [T 4.0228] āropito. Yassa dāni[V 2.0185], bhante, bhagavā kālaṃ maññatī”ti. Atha kho bhagavā nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena yena navaṃ santhāgāraṃ tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā pāde pakkhāletvā santhāgāraṃ pavisitvā majjhimaṃ thambhaṃ nissāya puratthābhimukho nisīdi. Bhikkhusaṅghopi kho pāde pakkhāletvā santhāgāraṃ pavisitvā pacchimaṃ bhittiṃ nissāya puratthābhimukho nisīdi bhagavantaṃyeva purakkhatvā. Kāpilavatthavā sakyā pāde pakkhāletvā santhāgāraṃ pavisitvā puratthimaṃ bhittiṃ nissāya pacchimābhimukhā nisīdiṃsu bhagavantaṃyeva purakkhatvā. Atha kho bhagavā kāpilavatthave sakye bahudeva rattiṃ dhammiyā kathāya sandassetvā samādapetvā samuttejetvā sampahaṃsetvā uyyojesi – “abhikkantā kho, gotamā, ratti. Yassa dāni kālaṃ maññathā”ti[M 2.0390]. “Evaṃ[P 4.0184], bhante”ti kho kāpilavatthavā sakyā bhagavato paṭissutvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkamiṃsu.

Then the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him respectfully, and went to the new assembly hall. Having arrived, they spread coverings throughout the entire assembly hall, arranged the seats, set up a water vessel, and lit an oil lamp. Then they approached the Blessed One and said this: “Venerable sir, the assembly hall is entirely spread with coverings, the seats are arranged, the water vessel is set up, and the oil lamp is lit. Now, venerable sir, it is the time the Blessed One deems fit.” Then the Blessed One, having adjusted his lower robe and taken his bowl and outer robe, went to the new assembly hall together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Upon arrival, he washed his feet, entered the assembly hall, and sat down facing east, leaning against the central pillar. The Saṅgha of bhikkhus also washed their feet, entered the assembly hall, and sat down facing east, leaning against the western wall, with the Blessed One before them. The Sakyans of Kapilavatthu also washed their feet, entered the assembly hall, and sat down facing west, leaning against the eastern wall, with the Blessed One before them. Then, for much of the night, the Blessed One instructed, roused, inspired, and gladdened the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu with a Dhamma talk. Then he dismissed them, saying: “The night is far advanced, Gotamas. Now is the time for you to do as you think fit.” “Yes, venerable sir,” the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu replied to the Blessed One. They rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him respectfully, and departed.

Atha kho bhagavā acirapakkantesu kāpilavatthavesu sakyesu āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ āmantesi – “vigatathinamiddho kho, moggallāna, bhikkhusaṅgho. Paṭibhātu taṃ, moggallāna, bhikkhūnaṃ dhammī kathā. Piṭṭhi me āgilāyati; tamahaṃ āyamissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhagavato paccassosi. Atha kho bhagavā catugguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paññapetvā dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ kappesi[T 4.0229], pāde pādaṃ accādhāya, sato sampajāno uṭṭhānasaññaṃ manasi karitvā. Tatra kho āyasmā mahāmoggallāno bhikkhū āmantesi – “āvuso bhikkhave”ti. “Āvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa paccassosuṃ. Āyasmā mahāmoggallāno etadavoca – “avassutapariyāyañca vo, āvuso, desessāmi, anavassutapariyāyañca. Taṃ suṇātha, sādhukaṃ manasi karotha; bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evamāvuso”ti kho te bhikkhū āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa paccassosuṃ. Āyasmā mahāmoggallāno etadavoca –

Then, soon after the Sakyans of Kapilavatthu had departed, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: “Moggallāna, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is free from sloth and torpor. Let a Dhamma talk occur to you, Moggallāna, for the bhikkhus. My back is aching; I will stretch it.” “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, having arranged his outer robe folded in four, took up the lion’s posture on his right side, placing one foot on the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having established in his mind the perception of rising. There, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna addressed the bhikkhus: “Friends, bhikkhus.” “Friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this: “Friends, I will teach you the discourse on being drenched and the discourse on not being drenched. Listen to it and pay close attention. I will speak.” “Yes, friend,” those bhikkhus replied to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna said this:

“Kathaṃ, āvuso, avassuto hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā piyarūpe rūpe adhimuccati, appiyarūpe rūpe byāpajjati, anupaṭṭhitakāyassati viharati parittacetaso, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti [P 4.0185]…pe… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya piyarūpe dhamme adhimuccati, appiyarūpe dhamme byāpajjati, anupaṭṭhitakāyassati ca viharati [V 2.0186] parittacetaso, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Ayaṃ vuccati, āvuso, bhikkhu avassuto cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu…pe… avassuto jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu…pe… avassuto manoviññeyyesu dhammesu. Evaṃvihāriñcāvuso, bhikkhuṃ cakkhuto cepi naṃ māro upasaṅkamati [T 4.0230] labhateva māro otāraṃ, labhati māro ārammaṇaṃ…pe… jivhāto cepi naṃ māro upasaṅkamati, labhateva labhetha (ka.) māro otāraṃ[M 2.0391], labhati labhetha (ka.) māro ārammaṇaṃ…pe… manato cepi naṃ māro upasaṅkamati, labhateva māro otāraṃ, labhati māro ārammaṇaṃ.

“How, friends, is one drenched? Here, friends, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, becomes intensely attached to a pleasing form and is angered by an unpleasing form. He dwells with mindfulness of the body unestablished and with a limited mind, and he does not understand as it truly is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil, unwholesome states of his cease without remainder... having tasted a flavor with the tongue... having cognized a mental object with the mind, he becomes intensely attached to a pleasing mental object and is angered by an unpleasing mental object. He dwells with mindfulness of the body unestablished and with a limited mind, and he does not understand as it truly is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil, unwholesome states of his cease without remainder. This, friends, is called a bhikkhu drenched in regard to forms cognizable by the eye... drenched in regard to flavors cognizable by the tongue... drenched in regard to mental objects cognizable by the mind. Friends, if Māra approaches a bhikkhu dwelling thus through the eye, Māra gains access, Māra finds a foothold... through the tongue... through the mind, Māra gains access, Māra finds a foothold.”

“Seyyathāpi, āvuso, naḷāgāraṃ vā tiṇāgāraṃ vā sukkhaṃ kolāpaṃ terovassikaṃ. Puratthimāya cepi naṃ disāya puriso ādittāya tiṇukkāya upasaṅkameyya, labhetheva labhetha (ka.) aggi otāraṃ, labhetha aggi ārammaṇaṃ; pacchimāya cepi naṃ disāya puriso ādittāya tiṇukkāya upasaṅkameyya…pe… uttarāya cepi naṃ disāya…pe… dakkhiṇāya cepi naṃ disāya…pe… heṭṭhimato cepi naṃ…pe… uparimato cepi naṃ… yato kutoci cepi naṃ puriso ādittāya tiṇukkāya upasaṅkameyya, labhetheva aggi otāraṃ labhetha aggi ārammaṇaṃ. Evameva kho, āvuso, evaṃvihāriṃ bhikkhuṃ cakkhuto cepi naṃ māro upasaṅkamati, labhateva māro otāraṃ, labhati māro ārammaṇaṃ…pe… jivhāto cepi naṃ māro upasaṅkamati…pe… manato cepi naṃ māro upasaṅkamati, labhateva māro otāraṃ, labhati māro ārammaṇaṃ. Evaṃvihāriñcāvuso, bhikkhuṃ rūpā adhibhaṃsu, na bhikkhu rūpe adhibhosi; saddā bhikkhuṃ adhibhaṃsu, na bhikkhu [P 4.0186] sadde adhibhosi; gandhā bhikkhuṃ adhibhaṃsu, na bhikkhu gandhe adhibhosi; rasā bhikkhuṃ adhibhaṃsu, na bhikkhu rase adhibhosi; phoṭṭhabbā bhikkhuṃ adhibhaṃsu, na bhikkhu phoṭṭhabbe adhibhosi[T 4.0231]; dhammā bhikkhuṃ adhibhaṃsu, na bhikkhu dhamme adhibhosi. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, bhikkhu rūpādhibhūto, saddādhibhūto, gandhādhibhūto, rasādhibhūto, phoṭṭhabbādhibhūto, dhammādhibhūto, adhibhūto, anadhibhū, anadhibhūto (sī. syā. kaṃ. ka.) adhibhaṃsu naṃ pāpakā akusalā dhammā saṃkilesikā ponobbhavikā sadarā dukkhavipākā āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiyā. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, avassuto hoti.

“Just as, friends, there might be a reed hut or a grass hut, dry, decayed, and long exposed to the rains. If a person were to approach it from the eastern direction with a blazing grass torch, the fire would find an opening, the fire would find a support. If a person were to approach it from the western direction with a blazing grass torch… from the northern direction… from the southern direction… from below… from above… from whatever direction a person were to approach it with a blazing grass torch, the fire would find an opening, the fire would find a support. In the same way, friends, when a bhikkhu dwells thus, if Māra approaches him through the eye, Māra finds an opening, Māra finds a support… if Māra approaches him through the tongue… if Māra approaches him through the mind, Māra finds an opening, Māra finds a support. When a bhikkhu dwells thus, friends, forms overpower him, he does not overpower forms; sounds overpower him, he does not overpower sounds; odors overpower him, he does not overpower odors; tastes overpower him, he does not overpower tastes; tangibles overpower him, he does not overpower tangibles; mental phenomena overpower him, he does not overpower mental phenomena. This, friends, is called a bhikkhu who is overpowered by forms, overpowered by sounds, overpowered by odors, overpowered by tastes, overpowered by tangibles, overpowered by mental phenomena—overpowered, not an overcomer. The evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, troublesome, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death overpower him. Thus, friends, one is drenched.”

“Kathañcāvuso, anavassuto hoti? Idhāvuso, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā piyarūpe rūpe nādhimuccati, appiyarūpe rūpe na byāpajjati, upaṭṭhitakāyassati ca viharati appamāṇacetaso[V 2.0187], tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti…pe… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā…pe… manasā [M 2.0392] dhammaṃ viññāya piyarūpe dhamme nādhimuccati, appiyarūpe dhamme na byāpajjati, upaṭṭhitakāyassati ca viharati appamāṇacetaso, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, bhikkhu anavassuto cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu…pe… anavassuto manoviññeyyesu dhammesu. Evaṃvihāriñcāvuso, bhikkhuṃ cakkhuto cepi naṃ māro upasaṅkamati, neva labhati māro otāraṃ, na labhati māro ārammaṇaṃ…pe… jivhāto cepi naṃ māro upasaṅkamati…pe… manato cepi [T 4.0232] naṃ māro upasaṅkamati, neva labhati māro otāraṃ, na labhati māro ārammaṇaṃ.

“And how, friends, is one not drenched? Here, friends, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, is not captivated by a pleasing form and does not resent an unpleasing form. He dwells with mindfulness of the body established and with a boundless mind, and he understands as it truly is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil, unwholesome states of his cease without remainder… having tasted a flavor with the tongue… having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is not captivated by a pleasing mental object and does not resent an unpleasing mental object. He dwells with mindfulness of the body established and with a boundless mind, and he understands as it truly is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those arisen evil, unwholesome states of his cease without remainder. This, friends, is called a bhikkhu who is not drenched in regard to forms cognizable by the eye… not drenched in regard to mental objects cognizable by the mind. Friends, if Māra approaches a bhikkhu dwelling thus through the eye, Māra gains no access, Māra finds no foothold… through the tongue… through the mind, Māra gains no access, Māra finds no foothold.”

“Seyyathāpi, āvuso, kūṭāgāraṃ vā sālā vā bahalamattikā [P 4.0187] addāvalepanā. Puratthimāya cepi naṃ disāya puriso ādittāya tiṇukkāya upasaṅkameyya, neva labhetha aggi otāraṃ, na labhetha aggi ārammaṇaṃ…pe… pacchimāya cepi naṃ… uttarāya cepi naṃ… dakkhiṇāya cepi naṃ… heṭṭhimato cepi naṃ… uparimato cepi naṃ… yato kutoci cepi naṃ puriso ādittāya tiṇukkāya upasaṅkameyya, neva labhetha aggi otāraṃ, na labhetha aggi ārammaṇaṃ. Evameva kho, āvuso, evaṃvihāriṃ bhikkhuṃ cakkhuto cepi naṃ māro upasaṅkamati, neva labhati māro otāraṃ, na labhati māro ārammaṇaṃ…pe… manato cepi naṃ māro upasaṅkamati, neva labhati māro otāraṃ, na labhati māro ārammaṇaṃ. Evaṃvihārī cāvuso, bhikkhu rūpe adhibhosi, na rūpā bhikkhuṃ adhibhaṃsu; sadde bhikkhu adhibhosi, na saddā bhikkhuṃ adhibhaṃsu; gandhe bhikkhu adhibhosi, na gandhā bhikkhuṃ adhibhaṃsu; rase bhikkhu adhibhosi, na rasā bhikkhuṃ adhibhaṃsu; phoṭṭhabbe bhikkhu adhibhosi, na phoṭṭhabbā bhikkhuṃ adhibhaṃsu; dhamme bhikkhu adhibhosi, na dhammā bhikkhuṃ adhibhaṃsu. Ayaṃ vuccatāvuso, bhikkhu rūpādhibhū, saddādhibhū, gandhādhibhū, rasādhibhū, phoṭṭhabbādhibhū, dhammādhibhū, adhibhū, anadhibhūto anadhibhūto kehici kilesehi (ka.), adhibhosi te pāpake akusale dhamme saṃkilesike ponobbhavike sadare [T 4.0233] dukkhavipāke āyatiṃ jātijarāmaraṇiye. Evaṃ kho, āvuso, anavassuto hotī”ti.

“Just as, friends, there might be a gabled house or a hall, well-plastered with thick clay. If a person were to approach it from the eastern direction with a blazing grass torch, the fire would find no opening, the fire would find no support… from the western direction… from the northern direction… from the southern direction… from below… from above… from whatever direction a person were to approach it with a blazing grass torch, the fire would find no opening, the fire would find no support. In the same way, friends, when a bhikkhu dwells thus, if Māra approaches him through the eye, Māra gains no entry, Māra gains no foothold… if Māra approaches him through the mind, Māra gains no entry, Māra gains no foothold. A bhikkhu dwelling thus, friends, has mastered forms; forms have not mastered the bhikkhu. He has mastered sounds; sounds have not mastered the bhikkhu. He has mastered odors; odors have not mastered the bhikkhu. He has mastered tastes; tastes have not mastered the bhikkhu. He has mastered tangibles; tangibles have not mastered the bhikkhu. He has mastered mental phenomena; mental phenomena have not mastered the bhikkhu. This, friends, is called a bhikkhu who has mastered forms, mastered sounds, mastered odors, mastered tastes, mastered tangibles, mastered mental phenomena—a master, unmastered. He has mastered those evil, unwholesome states that are defiling, leading to renewed existence, troublesome, resulting in suffering, and leading to future birth, aging, and death. Thus, friends, one is not drenched.”

Atha [M 2.0393][V 2.0188] kho bhagavā vuṭṭhahitvā āyasmantaṃ mahāmoggallānaṃ āmantesi – “sādhu sādhu, moggallāna! Sādhu kho tvaṃ, moggallāna, bhikkhūnaṃ avassutapariyāyañca anavassutapariyāyañca abhāsī”ti.

Then the Blessed One, having risen, addressed the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna: ‘Good, good, Moggallāna! Well have you, Moggallāna, spoken to the bhikkhus about the exposition on being drenched and the exposition on not being drenched.’”

Idamavoca āyasmā mahāmoggallāno. Samanuñño satthā [P 4.0188] ahosi. Attamanā te bhikkhū āyasmato mahāmoggallānassa bhāsitaṃ abhinandunti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

This was said by the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. The Teacher approved. Those bhikkhus, delighted, rejoiced at the words of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna.

7. Dukkhadhammasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on States of Suffering

244. Yato kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbesaṃyeva dukkhadhammānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tathā kho panassa kāmā diṭṭhā honti, yathāssa kāme passato, yo kāmesu kāmacchando kāmasneho kāmamucchā kāmapariḷāho, so nānuseti. Tathā kho panassa cāro ca vihāro ca anubuddho hoti, yathā carantaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā nānusenti.

244. Monks, when a monk understands as it actually is the origin and disappearance of all phenomena of suffering, sensual pleasures are seen by him in such a way that for him who sees sensual pleasures, the sensual desire, affection, infatuation, and fever for sensual pleasures do not lie latent. Furthermore, his conduct and abiding are understood in such a way that as he conducts himself and abides, covetousness and displeasure—evil, unwholesome states—do not lie latent in him.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbesaṃyeva dukkhadhammānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti? ‘Iti rūpaṃ, iti rūpassa samudayo, iti rūpassa atthaṅgamo; iti vedanā… iti saññā… iti saṅkhārā… iti viññāṇaṃ, iti viññāṇassa samudayo, iti viññāṇassa atthaṅgamo’ti – evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sabbesaṃyeva dukkhadhammānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti.

And how, monks, does a monk understand as it actually is the origin and disappearance of all phenomena of suffering? ‘Such is form, such is the origin of form, such is the disappearance of form; such is feeling... such is perception... such are volitional formations... such is consciousness, such is the origin of consciousness, such is the disappearance of consciousness.’ It is in this way, monks, that a monk understands as it actually is the origin and disappearance of all phenomena of suffering.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno kāmā diṭṭhā honti? Yathāssa kāme [T 4.0234] passato, yo kāmesu kāmacchando kāmasneho kāmamucchā kāmapariḷāho, so nānuseti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, aṅgārakāsu sādhikaporisā puṇṇā aṅgārānaṃ vītaccikānaṃ vītadhūmānaṃ. Atha puriso āgaccheyya jīvitukāmo amaritukāmo sukhakāmo dukkhapaṭikūlo. Tamenaṃ dve balavanto purisā nānābāhāsu gahetvā, taṃ aṅgārakāsuṃ upakaḍḍheyyuṃ. So iticīticeva kāyaṃ sannāmeyya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Ñāta ñāṇaṃ (ka.) ñhi, bhikkhave, tassa [P 4.0189] purisassa purisassa hoti (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.), purisassa hetu hoti (ka.) ma. ni. 2.45 imaṃ cāhaṃ aṅgārakāsuṃ papatissāmi, tatonidānaṃ maraṇaṃ vā nigacchissāmi maraṇamattaṃ vā dukkhanti. Evameva kho[M 2.0394], bhikkhave[V 2.0189], bhikkhuno aṅgārakāsūpamā kāmā diṭṭhā honti, yathāssa kāme passato, yo kāmesu kāmacchando kāmasneho kāmamucchā kāmapariḷāho, so nānuseti.

And how, monks, are sensual pleasures seen by a monk in such a way that for him who sees sensual pleasures, the sensual desire, affection, infatuation, and fever for sensual pleasures do not lie latent? Suppose, monks, there were a pit of glowing coals, more than a man’s height, full of coals without flame or smoke. Then a man would come along, desiring to live, not desiring to die, desiring happiness and averse to suffering. Then two strong men would seize him by both arms and drag him towards that pit of coals. He would twist his body this way and that. For what reason? Because that man knows: ‘If I fall into this pit of coals, then because of that I shall meet either death or suffering equivalent to death.’ In the same way, monks, sensual pleasures are seen by a monk as like a pit of coals, in such a way that for him who sees sensual pleasures, the sensual desire, affection, infatuation, and fever for sensual pleasures do not lie latent.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno cāro ca vihāro ca anubuddho hoti, yathā carantaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā nānussavanti nānusenti (ka.)? Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso bahukaṇṭakaṃ dāyaṃ paviseyya. Tassa puratopi kaṇṭako, pacchatopi kaṇṭako, uttaratopi kaṇṭako, dakkhiṇatopi kaṇṭako, heṭṭhatopi kaṇṭako, uparitopi kaṇṭako. So satova abhikkameyya, satova paṭikkameyya – ‘mā maṃ kaṇṭako’ti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yaṃ loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ, ayaṃ vuccati ariyassa vinaye kaṇṭako”ti. Iti viditvā kaṇḍako. taṃ kaṇḍakoti iti viditvā (sī.) saṃvaro ca asaṃvaro ca [T 4.0235] veditabbo.

And how, monks, are a monk’s conduct and abiding understood, so that as he conducts himself and abides, covetousness and displeasure—evil, unwholesome states—do not pursue him? Suppose, monks, a man were to enter a thorny jungle. There would be thorns in front of him, thorns behind him, thorns to the north, thorns to the south, thorns below him, thorns above him. He would advance mindfully, he would retreat mindfully, thinking: ‘May no thorn prick me!’ In the same way, monks, whatever in the world is agreeable and pleasing is called a thorn in the Noble One’s discipline. Having understood this, restraint and non-restraint should be known.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, asaṃvaro hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā piyarūpe rūpe adhimuccati, appiyarūpe rūpe byāpajjati, anupaṭṭhitakāyassati ca viharati parittacetaso, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti…pe… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya piyarūpe dhamme adhimuccati, appiyarūpe dhamme byāpajjati, anupaṭṭhitakāyassati ca viharati parittacetaso, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, asaṃvaro hoti.

And how, monks, is there lack of restraint? Here, monks, a monk, seeing a form with the eye, is attached to agreeable forms and feels aversion towards disagreeable forms; and he dwells with mindfulness of the body unestablished and with a constricted mind. And he does not understand as it actually is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states that have arisen in him cease without remainder… having tasted a flavour with the tongue… having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is attached to agreeable mental phenomena and feels aversion towards disagreeable mental phenomena; and he dwells with mindfulness of the body unestablished and with a constricted mind. And he does not understand as it actually is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states that have arisen in him cease without remainder. It is in this way, monks, that there is lack of restraint.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, saṃvaro hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā piyarūpe rūpe nādhimuccati, appiyarūpe rūpe na byāpajjati, upaṭṭhitakāyassati ca viharati appamāṇacetaso, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā [P 4.0190] akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti…pe… jivhā rasaṃ sāyitvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya piyarūpe dhamme nādhimuccati, appiyarūpe dhamme na byāpajjati, upaṭṭhitakāyassati ca viharati appamāṇacetaso, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā [M 2.0395] akusalā dhammā [T 4.0236] aparisesā nirujjhanti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, saṃvaro hoti.

And how, monks, is there restraint? Here, monks, a monk, seeing a form with the eye, is not attached to agreeable forms, nor does he feel aversion towards disagreeable forms. He dwells with mindfulness of the body established and with an immeasurable mind. And he understands as it actually is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states that have arisen in him cease without remainder… having tasted a flavour with the tongue… having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, he is not attached to agreeable mental phenomena, nor does he feel aversion towards disagreeable mental phenomena. He dwells with mindfulness of the body established and with an immeasurable mind. And he understands as it actually is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein those evil, unwholesome states that have arisen in him cease without remainder. It is in this way, monks, that there is restraint.

“Tassa [V 2.0190] ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno evaṃ carato evaṃ viharato kadāci karahaci satisammosā uppajjanti, pāpakā akusalā sarasaṅkappā saṃyojaniyā, dandho, bhikkhave, satuppādo. Atha kho naṃ khippameva pajahati vinodeti byantīkaroti anabhāvaṃ gameti.

If, monks, for a monk conducting himself and abiding in this way, there should occasionally arise, due to a lapse of mindfulness, evil, unwholesome, discursive thoughts connected with the fetters, then, monks, the arising of mindfulness is slow. But indeed, he quickly abandons them, dispels them, brings them to termination, and causes them to go to non-existence.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso divasaṃsantatte divasasantatte (sī.) ayokaṭāhe dve vā tīṇi vā udakaphusitāni nipāteyya. Dandho, bhikkhave, udakaphusitānaṃ nipāto, atha kho naṃ khippameva parikkhayaṃ pariyādānaṃ gaccheyya. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, tassa ce bhikkhuno evaṃ carato, evaṃ viharato kadāci karahaci satisammosā uppajjanti pāpakā akusalā sarasaṅkappā saṃyojaniyā, dandho, bhikkhave, satuppādo. Atha kho naṃ khippameva pajahati vinodeti byantīkaroti anabhāvaṃ gameti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno cāro ca vihāro ca anubuddho hoti; yathā carantaṃ viharantaṃ abhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā nānussavanti. Tañce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuṃ evaṃ carantaṃ evaṃ viharantaṃ rājāno vā rājamahāmattā vā mittā vā amaccā vā ñātī vā sālohitā vā, bhogehi abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyyuṃ – ‘ehi evaṃ (sī.), bho purisa, kiṃ te ime kāsāvā anudahanti, kiṃ muṇḍo kapālamanucarasi, ehi hīnāyāvattitvā bhoge ca bhuñjassu, puññāni ca karohī’ti. So vata, bhikkhave, bhikkhu [T 4.0237] evaṃ caranto evaṃ viharanto sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati.

“Just as, monks, if a man were to drop two or three drops of water onto an iron pan heated all day long, slow, monks, is the falling of those drops, yet they would quickly be exhausted and come to an end. In the same way, monks, for a monk who is conducting himself and dwelling thus, if occasionally, due to a lapse of mindfulness, there arise evil, unwholesome, discursive thoughts connected with the fetters, then, monks, the arising of mindfulness is slow. Yet he would quickly abandon them, dispel them, bring them to termination, and cause them to go to non-existence. It is in this way, monks, that a monk’s conduct and dwelling are properly understood; in such a way that as he conducts himself and dwells, covetousness and displeasure—evil, unwholesome states—do not flow in upon him. If, monks, kings or royal ministers, friends or associates, relatives or blood relatives were to invite that monk—who is conducting himself and dwelling in this way—and offer him wealth, saying: ‘Come, good man, why are you afflicted by these saffron robes? Why do you wander with a shaven head and a bowl? Come, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and make merit,’ it is impossible, monks, that that monk—who is conducting himself and dwelling in this way—would renounce the training and return to the lower life.”

“Seyyathāpi[P 4.0191], bhikkhave, gaṅgā nadī pācīnaninnā pācīnapoṇā pācīnapabbhārā. Atha mahājanakāyo āgaccheyya kuddāla-piṭakaṃ ādāya – ‘mayaṃ imaṃ gaṅgaṃ nadiṃ pacchāninnaṃ karissāma pacchāpoṇaṃ pacchāpabbhāra’nti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, api nu kho so mahājanakāyo gaṅgaṃ nadiṃ pacchāninnaṃ kareyya pacchāpoṇaṃ pacchāpabbhāra”nti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Taṃ kissa hetu”? “Gaṅgā, bhante, nadī pācīnaninnā pācīnapoṇā pācīnapabbhārā; sā na sukarā pacchāninnā kātuṃ pacchāpoṇā pacchāpabbhārā. Yāvadeva ca pana so mahājanakāyo kilamathassa vighātassa bhāgī assā”ti. “Evameva kho, bhikkhave, tañce bhikkhuṃ evaṃ carantaṃ evaṃ viharantaṃ rājāno vā rājamahāmattā [M 2.0396] vā mittā vā amaccā vā ñātī vā sālohitā vā bhogehi abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyyuṃ – ‘ehi, bho purisa, kiṃ te ime kāsāvā anudahanti, kiṃ muṇḍo kapālamanucarasi, ehi hīnāyāvattitvā bhoge ca bhuñjassu, puññāni [V 2.0191] ca karohī’ti. So vata, bhikkhave, bhikkhu evaṃ caranto evaṃ viharanto sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Yañhi taṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ dīgharattaṃ vivekaninnaṃ vivekapoṇaṃ vivekapabbhāraṃ, tathā kañca (syā. kaṃ. ka.) hīnāyāvattissatīti netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Just as, monks, the Ganges river slopes, inclines, and tends to the east. Then a great crowd of people might come taking spades and baskets, thinking, ‘We will make this Ganges river slope to the west, incline to the west, and tend to the west.’ What do you think, monks, would that great crowd of people be able to make the Ganges river slope, incline, and tend to the west?” “No, venerable sir.” “For what reason?” “Because, venerable sir, the Ganges river slopes, inclines, and tends to the east; it is not easy to make it slope, incline, and tend to the west. That great crowd of people would only become partakers of fatigue and vexation.” “Just so, monks, if kings or royal ministers, friends or associates, relatives or blood relatives were to invite a monk who is conducting himself and dwelling in such a way, and offer him wealth, saying, ‘Come, good man, why are you afflicted by these saffron robes? Why do you wander with a shaven head and a bowl? Come, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and make merit.’ It is impossible, monks, that a monk conducting himself and dwelling thus would renounce the training and return to the lower life. For what reason? Because, monks, that mind has for a long time sloped, inclined, and tended towards seclusion, that it would return to the lower life is impossible.”

8. Kiṃsukopamasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on the Simile of the Kiṃsuka Tree

245. Atha [T 4.0238] kho aññataro bhikkhu yenaññataro bhikkhu tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavoca – “kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hotī”ti? “Yato kho, āvuso, bhikkhu channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayañca [P 4.0192] atthaṅgamañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ettāvatā kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hotī”ti.

245. Then, a certain bhikkhu approached another bhikkhu. Having approached, he said this to that bhikkhu: 'Friend, to what extent is a bhikkhu's vision thoroughly purified?' 'Friend, when a bhikkhu distinctly knows, as it really is, the arising and cessation of the six bases for contact, to that extent, friend, a bhikkhu's vision is thoroughly purified.'

Atha kho so bhikkhu asantuṭṭho tassa bhikkhussa pañhaveyyākaraṇena pañhāveyyākaraṇena (syā. kaṃ. ka.), yenaññataro bhikkhu tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavoca – “kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hotī”ti? “Yato kho, āvuso, bhikkhu pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ettāvatā kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hotī”ti.

Then that bhikkhu, being dissatisfied with that bhikkhu's answer to the question, approached another bhikkhu. Having approached, he said this to that bhikkhu: 'Friend, to what extent is a bhikkhu's vision thoroughly purified?' 'Friend, when a bhikkhu distinctly knows, as it really is, the arising and cessation of the five aggregates of clinging, to that extent, friend, a bhikkhu's vision is thoroughly purified.'

Atha kho so bhikkhu asantuṭṭho tassa bhikkhussa pañhaveyyākaraṇena, yenaññataro bhikkhu tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavoca – “kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hotī”ti? “Yato kho, āvuso, bhikkhu catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ettāvatā kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hotī”ti.

Then that bhikkhu, being dissatisfied with that bhikkhu's answer to the question, approached another bhikkhu. Having approached, he said this to that bhikkhu: 'Friend, to what extent is a bhikkhu's vision thoroughly purified?' 'Friend, when a bhikkhu distinctly knows, as it really is, the arising and cessation of the four great elements, to that extent, friend, a bhikkhu's vision is thoroughly purified.'

Atha kho so bhikkhu asantuṭṭho tassa bhikkhussa pañhaveyyākaraṇena, yenaññataro bhikkhu tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavoca – “kittāvatā [M 2.0397] nu kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hotī”ti? “Yato kho, āvuso, bhikkhu yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ[V 2.0192], sabbaṃ taṃ [T 4.0239] nirodhadhammanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ettāvatā, kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hotī”ti.

Then that bhikkhu, being dissatisfied with that bhikkhu's answer to the question, approached another bhikkhu. Having approached, he said this to that bhikkhu: 'Friend, to what extent is a bhikkhu's vision thoroughly purified?' 'Friend, when a bhikkhu knows, as it really is, that 'Whatever is of a nature to arise, all that is of a nature to cease,' to that extent, friend, a bhikkhu's vision is thoroughly purified.'

Atha kho so bhikkhu asantuṭṭho tassa bhikkhussa pañhaveyyākaraṇena, yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “idhāhaṃ, bhante, yenaññataro bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavocaṃ – kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hotī’ti? Evaṃ vutte, bhante, so bhikkhu maṃ etadavoca – ‘yato kho, āvuso, bhikkhu channaṃ phassāyatanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ettāvatā kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hotī’ti. Atha khvāhaṃ, bhante, asantuṭṭho tassa bhikkhussa pañhaveyyākaraṇena[P 4.0193], yenaññataro bhikkhu tenupasaṅkamiṃ; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavocaṃ – ‘kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hotī’ti? Evaṃ vutte, bhante, so bhikkhu maṃ etadavoca – ‘yato kho, āvuso, bhikkhu pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhānaṃ…pe… catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti…pe… yaṃ kiñci samudayadhammaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ nirodhadhammanti yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, ettāvatā kho, āvuso, bhikkhuno dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hotī’ti. Atha khvāhaṃ, bhante, asantuṭṭho tassa bhikkhussa pañhaveyyākaraṇena yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃ ( ) (upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ etadavocaṃ) (ka.). Kittāvatā [T 4.0240] nu kho, bhante, bhikkhuno dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hotī”ti?

Then that bhikkhu, dissatisfied with that bhikkhu's answer to the question, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable Sir, I approached a certain bhikkhu. Having approached, I said this to that bhikkhu: "To what extent, friend, is a bhikkhu's vision thoroughly purified?" When this was said, Venerable Sir, that bhikkhu said this to me: "When, friend, a bhikkhu knows as it truly is the arising and cessation of the six bases for contact, to that extent, friend, a bhikkhu's vision is thoroughly purified." Then, Venerable Sir, dissatisfied with that bhikkhu's answer to the question, I approached another bhikkhu. Having approached, I said this to that bhikkhu: "To what extent, friend, is a bhikkhu's vision thoroughly purified?" When this was said, Venerable Sir, that bhikkhu said this to me: "When, friend, a bhikkhu knows as it truly is the arising and cessation of the five aggregates of clinging... of the four great elements... that 'Whatever is of a nature to arise, all that is of a nature to cease,' to that extent, friend, a bhikkhu's vision is thoroughly purified." Then, Venerable Sir, dissatisfied with that bhikkhu's answer to the question, I approached the Blessed One and said: "To what extent, Venerable Sir, is a bhikkhu's vision thoroughly purified?"'

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhu, purisassa kiṃsuko adiṭṭhapubbo assa. So yenaññataro puriso kiṃsukassa dassāvī tenupasaṅkameyya. Upasaṅkamitvā taṃ purisaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘kīdiso, bho purisa, kiṃsuko’ti? So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘kāḷako kho, ambho purisa, kiṃsuko – seyyathāpi jhāmakhāṇū’ti. Tena kho pana, bhikkhu, samayena tādisovassa kiṃsuko yathāpi yathā (sī. syā. kaṃ.) dutiyavārādīsu pana “yathāpi”tveva dissati tassa purisassa dassanaṃ. Atha kho, so bhikkhu, puriso asantuṭṭho tassa purisassa pañhaveyyākaraṇena, yenaññataro puriso kiṃsukassa dassāvī tenupasaṅkameyya; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ purisaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘kīdiso[M 2.0398], bho purisa, kiṃsuko’ti? So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘lohitako kho, ambho purisa, kiṃsuko – seyyathāpi maṃsapesī’ti. Tena kho pana, bhikkhu, samayena tādisovassa kiṃsuko yathāpi tassa purisassa dassanaṃ. Atha kho so bhikkhu puriso asantuṭṭho tassa purisassa pañhaveyyākaraṇena, yenaññataro puriso kiṃsukassa dassāvī tenupasaṅkameyya[V 2.0193]; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ purisaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘kīdiso, bho purisa, kiṃsuko’ti? So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ocīrakajāto ojīrakajāto (sī.), odīrakajāto (pī.) kho, ambho purisa, kiṃsuko ādinnasipāṭiko – seyyathāpi sirīso’ti. Tena kho pana, bhikkhu, samayena tādisovassa kiṃsuko, yathāpi tassa purisassa dassanaṃ. Atha kho so bhikkhu puriso asantuṭṭho tassa purisassa pañhaveyyākaraṇena[P 4.0194], yenaññataro puriso kiṃsukassa dassāvī tenupasaṅkameyya; upasaṅkamitvā taṃ [T 4.0241] purisaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘kīdiso, bho purisa, kiṃsuko’ti? So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘bahalapattapalāso sandacchāyo saṇḍacchāyo (syā. kaṃ.) kho, ambho purisa, kiṃsuko – seyyathāpi nigrodho’ti. Tena kho pana, bhikkhu, samayena tādisovassa kiṃsuko, yathāpi tassa purisassa dassanaṃ. Evameva kho, bhikkhu, yathā yathā adhimuttānaṃ tesaṃ sappurisānaṃ dassanaṃ suvisuddhaṃ hoti, tathā tathā kho tehi sappurisehi byākataṃ.

“Suppose, bhikkhu, a man had never before seen a kiṃsuka tree. He might approach another man who had seen a kiṃsuka tree and ask him, ‘Good man, what is a kiṃsuka tree like?’ That man might reply, ‘Good man, the kiṃsuka tree is black, like a charred stump.’ And at that time, bhikkhu, the kiṃsuka tree would be just as that man had seen it. Then that man, dissatisfied with the other's explanation, might approach another man who had seen a kiṃsuka tree and ask, ‘Good man, what is a kiṃsuka tree like?’ That man might reply, ‘Good man, the kiṃsuka tree is red, like a piece of meat.’ And at that time, bhikkhu, the kiṃsuka tree would be just as that man had seen it. Then that man, dissatisfied with the other's explanation, might approach another man who had seen a kiṃsuka tree and ask, ‘Good man, what is a kiṃsuka tree like?’ That man might reply, ‘Good man, the kiṃsuka tree has hanging clusters and pods like a sirīsa tree.’ And at that time, bhikkhu, the kiṃsuka tree would be just as that man had seen it. Then that man, dissatisfied with the other's explanation, might approach another man who had seen a kiṃsuka tree and ask, ‘Good man, what is a kiṃsuka tree like?’ That man might reply, ‘Good man, the kiṃsuka tree has thick leaves and foliage and provides dense shade, like a banyan tree.’ And at that time, bhikkhu, the kiṃsuka tree would be just as that man had seen it. In this very way, bhikkhu, just as the vision of those good men is thoroughly pure according to their respective inclinations, so was it declared by those good men.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhu, rañño paccantimaṃ nagaraṃ daḷhuddhāpaṃ daḷhuddāpaṃ (sī. pī.) daḷhapākāratoraṇaṃ chadvāraṃ. Tatrassa dovāriko paṇḍito byatto medhāvī, aññātānaṃ nivāretā, ñātānaṃ pavesetā. Puratthimāya disāya āgantvā sīghaṃ dūtayugaṃ taṃ dovārikaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘kahaṃ, bho purisa, imassa nagarassa nagarassāmī’ti? So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘eso, bhante, majjhe siṅghāṭake nisinno’ti. Atha kho taṃ sīghaṃ dūtayugaṃ nagarassāmikassa yathābhūtaṃ vacanaṃ niyyātetvā yathāgatamaggaṃ paṭipajjeyya. Pacchimāya disāya āgantvā sīghaṃ dūtayugaṃ…pe… uttarāya disāya… dakkhiṇāya disāya āgantvā sīghaṃ dūtayugaṃ taṃ dovārikaṃ evaṃ vadeyya – ‘kahaṃ, bho purisa, imassa nagarassāmī’ti? So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘eso, bhante, majjhe siṅghāṭake nisinno’ti. Atha kho taṃ sīghaṃ dūtayugaṃ nagarassāmikassa yathābhūtaṃ vacanaṃ niyyātetvā yathāgatamaggaṃ paṭipajjeyya.

“Suppose, bhikkhu, there were a king’s frontier city with strong ramparts, strong walls and archways, and six gates. There would be a gatekeeper—wise, competent, and intelligent—who would keep out those who are unknown and let in those who are known. A swift pair of messengers might arrive from the eastern direction and ask the gatekeeper, ‘Where, good man, is the lord of this city?’ He would reply, ‘There he is, sirs, sitting in the middle of the crossroads.’ Then the swift pair of messengers would deliver their message as it truly is to the city lord and depart by the path on which they came. A swift pair of messengers might arrive from the western direction… from the northern direction… from the southern direction and ask the gatekeeper, ‘Where, good man, is the lord of this city?’ He would reply, ‘There he is, sirs, sitting in the middle of the crossroads.’ Then the swift pair of messengers would deliver their message as it truly is to the city lord and depart by the path on which they came.

“Upamā [M 2.0399] kho myāyaṃ, bhikkhu, katā atthassa viññāpanāya. Ayañcettha attho [T 4.0242] – ‘nagara’nti kho, bhikkhu, imassetaṃ cātumahābhūtikassa kāyassa adhivacanaṃ mātāpettikasambhavassa odanakummāsūpacayassa aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammassa. ‘Cha dvārā’ti kho, bhikkhu, channetaṃ ajjhattikānaṃ āyatanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ. ‘Dovāriko’ti kho, bhikkhu, satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. ‘Sīghaṃ [P 4.0195] dūtayuga’nti kho, bhikkhu, samathavipassanānetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. ‘Nagarassāmī’ti kho, bhikkhu, viññāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. ‘Majjhe siṅghāṭako’ti kho[V 2.0194], bhikkhu, catunnetaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ adhivacanaṃ – pathavīdhātuyā, āpodhātuyā, tejodhātuyā, vāyodhātuyā. ‘Yathābhūtaṃ vacana’nti kho, bhikkhu, nibbānassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. ‘Yathāgatamaggo’ti kho, bhikkhu, ariyassetaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa adhivacanaṃ, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhiyā…pe… sammāsamādhissā”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Bhikkhu, I have made this simile to make the meaning known. And this is the meaning here: ‘City’ is a designation for this body, composed of the four great elements, born from mother and father, built up of rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, to being rubbed, pressed, broken, and dispersed. ‘Six gates’ is a designation for the six internal sense bases. ‘Gatekeeper’ is a designation for mindfulness. ‘A swift pair of messengers’ is a designation for serenity and insight. ‘Lord of the city’ is a designation for consciousness. ‘Crossroads in the middle’ is a designation for the four great elements: the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element. ‘The statement as it truly is’ is a designation for Nibbāna. ‘The path as it has been trodden’ is a designation for the Noble Eightfold Path, that is: right view… right concentration.”

9. Vīṇopamasuttaṃ

9. The Simile of the Lute

246. “Yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā cakkhuviññeyyesu rūpesu uppajjeyya chando vā rāgo vā doso vā moho vā paṭighaṃ vāpi paṭighaṃ vā (sī.) cetaso, tato cittaṃ nivāreyya. Sabhayo ceso maggo sappaṭibhayo ca sakaṇṭako ca sagahano ca ummaggo ca kummaggo ca duhitiko ca. Asappurisasevito ceso maggo, na ceso maggo sappurisehi sevito. Na tvaṃ etaṃ arahasīti. Tato cittaṃ nivāraye cakkhuviññeyyehi rūpehi…pe… yassa kassaci, bhikkhave, bhikkhussa vā bhikkhuniyā vā jivhāviññeyyesu rasesu…pe… manoviññeyyesu dhammesu uppajjeyya chando vā rāgo vā doso vā [T 4.0243] moho vā paṭighaṃ vāpi cetaso tato cittaṃ nivāreyya. Sabhayo ceso maggo sappaṭibhayo ca sakaṇṭako ca sagahano ca ummaggo ca kummaggo ca duhitiko ca. Asappurisasevito ceso maggo, na ceso maggo sappurisehi sevito. Na tvaṃ etaṃ arahasīti. Tato cittaṃ nivāraye manoviññeyyehi dhammehi.

246. “Bhikkhus, if for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī there should arise desire, lust, hatred, delusion, or mental aversion toward forms cognizable by the eye, one should restrain the mind from them. For this path is with fear, with peril, with thorns, and with thickets; it is a side-track, a wrong path, and a difficult passage. This path is frequented by the ignoble, and it is not frequented by the noble. Thinking, ‘You are not worthy of this,’ one should restrain the mind from forms cognizable by the eye… and so on… if for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī there should arise desire, lust, hatred, delusion, or mental aversion toward mental phenomena cognizable by the mind, one should restrain the mind from them. For this path is with fear, with peril, with thorns, and with thickets; it is a side-track, a wrong path, and a difficult passage. This path is frequented by the ignoble, and it is not frequented by the noble. Thinking, ‘You are not worthy of this,’ one should restrain the mind from mental phenomena cognizable by the mind.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kiṭṭhaṃ sampannaṃ. Kiṭṭhārakkho kiṭṭhārakkhako (sī.) ca pamatto, goṇo ca kiṭṭhādo aduṃ kiṭṭhaṃ otaritvā [P 4.0196] yāvadatthaṃ madaṃ āpajjeyya pamādaṃ āpajjeyya[M 2.0400]; evameva kho, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano chasu phassāyatanesu asaṃvutakārī pañcasu kāmaguṇesu yāvadatthaṃ madaṃ āpajjati pamādaṃ āpajjati.

“Just as, bhikkhus, a field of grain is flourishing, but the field guard is negligent, and a grain-eating bull enters that field and would indulge to its heart’s content, becoming intoxicated and negligent; in the same way, bhikkhus, an uninstructed ordinary person, acting without restraint in the six bases for contact, indulges to their heart’s content in the five strands of sensual pleasure, becoming intoxicated and negligent.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, kiṭṭhaṃ sampannaṃ kiṭṭhārakkho ca appamatto goṇo ca kiṭṭhādo aduṃ kiṭṭhaṃ otareyya. Tamenaṃ kiṭṭhārakkho nāsāyaṃ suggahitaṃ gaṇheyya. Nāsāyaṃ suggahitaṃ gahetvā uparighaṭāyaṃ suniggahitaṃ niggaṇheyya. Uparighaṭāyaṃ suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā daṇḍena sutāḷitaṃ tāḷeyya. Daṇḍena sutāḷitaṃ tāḷetvā osajjeyya. Dutiyampi kho, bhikkhave [V 2.0195] …pe… tatiyampi kho, bhikkhave, goṇo kiṭṭhādo aduṃ kiṭṭhaṃ otareyya. Tamenaṃ kiṭṭhārakkho nāsāyaṃ suggahitaṃ gaṇheyya. Nāsāyaṃ suggahitaṃ gahetvā uparighaṭāyaṃ suniggahitaṃ niggaṇheyya. Uparighaṭāyaṃ suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā daṇḍena sutāḷitaṃ tāḷeyya. Daṇḍena sutāḷitaṃ tāḷetvā osajjeyya. Evañhi [T 4.0244] so, bhikkhave, goṇo kiṭṭhādo gāmagato vā araññagato vā, ṭhānabahulo vā assa nisajjabahulo vā na taṃ kiṭṭhaṃ puna otareyya – tameva purimaṃ daṇḍasamphassaṃ samanussaranto. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yato kho bhikkhuno chasu phassāyatanesu cittaṃ udujitaṃ hoti sudujitaṃ, ajjhattameva santiṭṭhati, sannisīdati, ekodi hoti, samādhiyati.

“Just as, bhikkhus, when a field of grain is flourishing and the field guard is diligent, a grain-eating bull might enter that field. The field guard would seize it firmly by the nose. Having seized it firmly by the nose, he would press it down firmly between the horns. Having pressed it down firmly between the horns, he would strike it soundly with a stick. Having struck it soundly with a stick, he would let it go. For a second time, bhikkhus… For a third time, bhikkhus, that grain-eating bull might enter the field. The field guard would seize it firmly by the nose. Having seized it firmly by the nose, he would press it down firmly between the horns. Having pressed it down firmly between the horns, he would strike it soundly with a stick. Having struck it soundly with a stick, he would let it go. In this way, bhikkhus, that grain-eating bull—whether it goes to the village or to the forest, whether it stands much or sits much—would not enter that field again, remembering that former contact with the stick. In the same way, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu’s mind is subdued and well-subdued regarding the six bases for contact, it becomes inwardly steady, settles down, becomes unified, and concentrated.”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, rañño vā rājamahāmattassa vā vīṇāya saddo assutapubbo assa. So vīṇāsaddaṃ suṇeyya. So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘ambho, kassa kissa (sī. pī.) nu kho eso saddo evaṃrajanīyo evaṃkamanīyo evaṃmadanīyo [P 4.0197] evaṃmucchanīyo evaṃbandhanīyo’ti? Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘esā, kho, bhante, vīṇā nāma, yassā eso saddo evaṃrajanīyo evaṃkamanīyo evaṃmadanīyo evaṃmucchanīyo evaṃbandhanīyo’ti. So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘gacchatha me, bho, taṃ vīṇaṃ āharathā’ti. Tassa taṃ vīṇaṃ āhareyyuṃ. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘ayaṃ kho sā, bhante, vīṇā yassā eso saddo evaṃrajanīyo evaṃkamanīyo evaṃmadanīyo evaṃmucchanīyo evaṃbandhanīyo’ti. So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘alaṃ me, bho, tāya vīṇāya, tameva me saddaṃ āharathā’ti. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘ayaṃ kho, bhante, vīṇā nāma anekasambhārā mahāsambhārā. Anekehi sambhārehi samāraddhā vadati[M 2.0401], seyyathidaṃ – doṇiñca paṭicca cammañca paṭicca daṇḍañca paṭicca upadhāraṇe ca [T 4.0245] paṭicca tantiyo ca paṭicca koṇañca paṭicca purisassa ca tajjaṃ vāyāmaṃ paṭicca evāyaṃ, bhante, vīṇā nāma anekasambhārā mahāsambhārā. Anekehi sambhārehi samāraddhā vadatī’ti. So taṃ vīṇaṃ dasadhā vā satadhā vā phāleyya, dasadhā vā satadhā vā taṃ phāletvā sakalikaṃ sakalikaṃ kareyya. Sakalikaṃ sakalikaṃ karitvā agginā ḍaheyya, agginā ḍahitvā masiṃ kareyya. Masiṃ karitvā mahāvāte vā ophuneyya opuneyya (sī. pī.), ophuṇeyya (?), nadiyā vā sīghasotāya pavāheyya. So evaṃ vadeyya – ‘asatī kirāyaṃ, bho, vīṇā nāma, yathevaṃ yaṃ yathevāyaṃ (sī.), yathevayaṃ (pī.) kiñci vīṇā nāma ettha ca panāyaṃ jano ettha panāyaṃ jano (syā. kaṃ.), ettha ca mahājano (pī. ka.) ativelaṃ pamatto palaḷito’ti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu rūpaṃ samanvesati samannesati (sī. syā. kaṃ.), samanesati (pī.) yāvatā rūpassa gati, vedanaṃ samanvesati yāvatā vedanāya gati, saññaṃ samanvesati yāvatā saññāya gati, saṅkhāre samanvesati yāvatā saṅkhārānaṃ gati, viññāṇaṃ samanvesati [V 2.0196] yāvatā viññāṇassa gati. Tassa rūpaṃ samanvesato yāvatā rūpassa gati, vedanaṃ samanvesato…pe… saññaṃ… saṅkhāre… viññāṇaṃ samanvesato yāvatā viññāṇassa gati. Yampissa taṃ hoti [P 4.0198] ahanti vā mamanti vā asmīti vā tampi tassa na hotī”ti. Navamaṃ.

“Suppose, bhikkhus, a king or a royal minister had never before heard the sound of a lute. He might hear the sound of a lute and say, ‘Good sirs, what is this sound, so enchanting, so desirable, so intoxicating, so bewildering, so binding?’ They would say to him, ‘Sir, that is called a lute, whose sound is so enchanting, so desirable, so intoxicating, so bewildering, so binding.’ He would say, ‘Go, my good men, fetch me that lute.’ They would bring him the lute and say, ‘Sir, this is that lute whose sound is so enchanting, so desirable, so intoxicating, so bewildering, so binding.’ He would say, ‘Enough of that lute, my good men. Just bring me that sound.’ They would say to him, ‘Sir, this thing called a lute has many components, a great many components. It produces sound when played with its full complement of components; that is, dependent on the soundbox, the skin, the neck, the tuning pegs, the strings, and the plectrum, and dependent on the appropriate effort of the person. Thus, sir, this thing called a lute has many components, a great many components, and produces sound when played with its full complement of components.’ Then he would split that lute into ten or a hundred pieces. Having split it, he would reduce it to splinters. Having reduced it to splinters, he would burn it in a fire and reduce it to ashes. Having reduced it to ashes, he would winnow them in a strong wind or let them be carried away by the swift current of a river. He would then say, ‘My good sirs, a worthless thing, it seems, is this so-called lute, and so is any so-called lute whatsoever, about which this populace has been so long heedless and infatuated!’ In the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu investigates form as far as the range of form extends, he investigates feeling as far as the range of feeling extends, he investigates perception as far as the range of perception extends, he investigates volitional formations as far as the range of volitional formations extends, he investigates consciousness as far as the range of consciousness extends. For him, while investigating form as far as the range of form extends, while investigating feeling… perception… volitional formations… while investigating consciousness as far as the range of consciousness extends, whatever conceiving there is of ‘I’ or ‘mine’ or ‘I am’—that no longer occurs.”

10. Chappāṇakopamasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on the Simile of the Six Animals

247. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso arugatto pakkagatto saravanaṃ paviseyya. Tassa kusakaṇṭakā ceva pāde vijjheyyuṃ, sarapattāni ca gattāni [T 4.0246] sarapattāni pakkagattāni (syā. kaṃ.), arupakkāni gattāni (pī. ka.) vilekheyyuṃ. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, puriso bhiyyosomattāya tatonidānaṃ dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvediyetha. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco bhikkhu gāmagato vā araññagato vā labhati vattāraṃ – ‘ayañca so ayañca kho (pī. ka.), ayaṃ so (?) āyasmā evaṃkārī evaṃsamācāro asucigāmakaṇṭako’ti. Taṃ kaṇṭakoti taṃ “asucigāmakaṇḍato”ti (ka.) iti viditvā saṃvaro ca asaṃvaro ca veditabbo.

247. “Bhikkhus, suppose a man with a body of sores, with a festering body, were to enter a thorn-thicket. The kusa thorns would pierce his feet, and the thorn-leaves would scrape his limbs. Thus, bhikkhus, that man would, on that account, experience pain and displeasure all the more. In the same way, bhikkhus, here some bhikkhu, having gone to a village or to the wilderness, finds one who would say: ‘This venerable one is one who acts in such a way, who behaves in such a way; he is an impure village-thorn.’ He being thus known as a ‘thorn,’ restraint and lack of restraint are to be understood.

“Kathañca[M 2.0402], bhikkhave, asaṃvaro hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā piyarūpe rūpe adhimuccati, appiyarūpe rūpe byāpajjati, anupaṭṭhitakāyassati ca viharati parittacetaso. Tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti. Sotena saddaṃ sutvā… ghānena gandhaṃ ghāyitvā… jivhāya rasaṃ sāyitvā… kāyena phoṭṭhabbaṃ phusitvā… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya piyarūpe dhamme adhimuccati, appiyarūpe dhamme byāpajjati, anupaṭṭhitakāyassati ca viharati parittacetaso, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti, yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti.

“And how, bhikkhus, is there lack of restraint? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having seen a form with the eye, is greatly attached to a pleasing form and is angered by a displeasing form. He dwells with mindfulness of the body unestablished and with a limited mind. And he does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein for him those arisen evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder. Having heard a sound with the ear… having smelled an odor with the nose… having tasted a flavor with the tongue… having touched a tangible with the body… having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is greatly attached to a pleasing mental object and is angered by a displeasing mental object. He dwells with mindfulness of the body unestablished and with a limited mind, and he does not understand as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein for him those arisen evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso chappāṇake gahetvā nānāvisaye nānāgocare daḷhāya rajjuyā bandheyya. Ahiṃ gahetvā daḷhāya [T 4.0247] rajjuyā bandheyya. Susumāraṃ suṃsumāraṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) gahetvā daḷhāya rajjuyā bandheyya. Pakkhiṃ gahetvā daḷhāya rajjuyā bandheyya. Kukkuraṃ gahetvā daḷhāya rajjuyā bandheyya[P 4.0199]. Siṅgālaṃ gahetvā daḷhāya rajjuyā bandheyya. Makkaṭaṃ gahetvā daḷhāya rajjuyā bandheyya. Daḷhāya rajjuyā bandhitvā majjhe gaṇṭhiṃ karitvā ossajjeyya. Atha kho, te, bhikkhave[V 2.0197], chappāṇakā nānāvisayā nānāgocarā sakaṃ sakaṃ gocaravisayaṃ āviñcheyyuṃ āviñjeyyuṃ (sī.) – ahi āviñcheyya ‘vammikaṃ pavekkhāmī’ti, susumāro āviñcheyya ‘udakaṃ pavekkhāmī’ti, pakkhī āviñcheyya ‘ākāsaṃ ḍessāmī’ti, kukkuro āviñcheyya ‘gāmaṃ pavekkhāmī’ti, siṅgālo āviñcheyya ‘sīvathikaṃ sivathikaṃ (ka.) pavekkhāmī’ti, makkaṭo āviñcheyya ‘vanaṃ pavekkhāmī’ti. Yadā kho te, bhikkhave, chappāṇakā jhattā assu kilantā, atha kho yo nesaṃ pāṇakānaṃ balavataro assa tassa te anuvatteyyuṃ, anuvidhāyeyyuṃ vasaṃ gaccheyyuṃ. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yassa kassaci bhikkhuno kāyagatāsati abhāvitā abahulīkatā, taṃ cakkhu āviñchati manāpiyesu rūpesu, amanāpiyā rūpā paṭikūlā honti…pe… mano āviñchati manāpiyesu dhammesu, amanāpiyā dhammā paṭikūlā honti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, asaṃvaro hoti.

Monks, suppose a man, having caught six animals of different domains and different feeding grounds, were to tie them with a strong rope. He would catch a snake and tie it with a strong rope. He would catch a crocodile and tie it with a strong rope. He would catch a bird and tie it with a strong rope. He would catch a dog and tie it with a strong rope. He would catch a jackal and tie it with a strong rope. He would catch a monkey and tie it with a strong rope. Having tied them with a strong rope and made a knot in the middle, he would release them. Then, monks, those six animals of different domains and different feeding grounds would each pull toward its own feeding ground and domain. The snake would pull, thinking, ‘I will enter an anthill.’ The crocodile would pull, thinking, ‘I will enter the water.’ The bird would pull, thinking, ‘I will fly into the sky.’ The dog would pull, thinking, ‘I will enter the village.’ The jackal would pull, thinking, ‘I will enter the charnel ground.’ The monkey would pull, thinking, ‘I will enter the forest.’ When, monks, those six animals are hungry and tired, then whichever animal among them is the stronger, they would follow after it, conform to it, and come under its power. In the same way, monks, for any monk for whom mindfulness directed to the body is undeveloped and uncultivated, the eye pulls him toward pleasing forms, and unpleasing forms are repulsive... the mind pulls him toward pleasing mental objects, and unpleasing mental objects are repulsive. Thus, monks, there is lack of restraint.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, saṃvaro hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā [T 4.0248] rūpaṃ disvā piyarūpe rūpe nādhimuccati, appiyarūpe rūpe na byāpajjati, upaṭṭhitakāyassati ca [M 2.0403] viharati appamāṇacetaso, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti, yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti…pe… jivhā rasaṃ sāyitvā…pe… manasā dhammaṃ viññāya piyarūpe dhamme nādhimuccati, appiyarūpe dhamme [P 4.0200] na byāpajjati, upaṭṭhitakāyassati ca viharati appamāṇacetaso, tañca cetovimuttiṃ paññāvimuttiṃ yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti yatthassa te uppannā pāpakā akusalā dhammā aparisesā nirujjhanti.

And how, monks, is there restraint? Here, monks, a monk, having seen a form with the eye, is not captivated by a pleasing form and is not repelled by a displeasing form. He dwells with mindfulness directed to the body established and with a measureless mind. And he understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein for him those arisen evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder... Having tasted a flavor with the tongue... Having cognized a mental object with the mind, he is not captivated by a pleasing mental object and is not repelled by a displeasing mental object. He dwells with mindfulness directed to the body established and with a measureless mind, and he understands as it really is that liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom wherein for him those arisen evil, unwholesome states cease without remainder.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso chappāṇake gahetvā nānāvisaye nānāgocare daḷhāya rajjuyā bandheyya. Ahiṃ gahetvā daḷhāya rajjuyā bandheyya. Susumāraṃ gahetvā daḷhāya rajjuyā bandheyya. Pakkhiṃ gahetvā…pe… kukkuraṃ gahetvā… siṅgālaṃ gahetvā… makkaṭaṃ gahetvā daḷhāya rajjuyā bandheyya. Daḷhāya rajjuyā bandhitvā daḷhe khīle vā thambhe vā upanibandheyya. Atha kho te, bhikkhave, chappāṇakā nānāvisayā nānāgocarā sakaṃ sakaṃ gocaravisayaṃ āviñcheyyuṃ – ahi āviñcheyya ‘vammikaṃ pavekkhāmī’ti, susumāro āviñcheyya ‘udakaṃ pavekkhāmī’ti, pakkhī āviñcheyya ‘ākāsaṃ ḍessāmī’ti, kukkuro āviñcheyya ‘gāmaṃ pavekkhāmī’ti, siṅgālo āviñcheyya ‘sīvathikaṃ pavekkhāmī’ti, makkaṭo āviñcheyya ‘vanaṃ pavekkhāmī’ti[T 4.0249]. Yadā kho te, bhikkhave, chappāṇakā jhattā assu kilantā[V 2.0198], atha tameva khīlaṃ vā thambhaṃ vā upatiṭṭheyyuṃ, upanisīdeyyuṃ, upanipajjeyyuṃ. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, yassa kassaci bhikkhuno kāyagatāsati bhāvitā bahulīkatā, taṃ cakkhu nāviñchati manāpiyesu rūpesu, amanāpiyā rūpā nappaṭikūlā honti…pe… jivhā nāviñchati manāpiyesu rasesu…pe… mano nāviñchati manāpiyesu dhammesu, amanāpiyā dhammā nappaṭikūlā honti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, saṃvaro hoti.

Monks, suppose a man were to catch six animals—each with different domains and different feeding grounds—and tie them with a strong rope. He would catch a snake and tie it with a strong rope. He would catch a crocodile and tie it with a strong rope. He would catch a bird… and so on… a dog… a jackal… a monkey and tie it with a strong rope. Having tied them with a strong rope, he would fasten them to a strong stake or pillar. Then, monks, those six animals with different domains and different feeding grounds would each pull toward their own domain: the snake would pull, thinking, ‘I will enter an anthill’; the crocodile would pull, thinking, ‘I will enter the water’; the bird would pull, thinking, ‘I will fly into the sky’; the dog would pull, thinking, ‘I will enter the village’; the jackal would pull, thinking, ‘I will enter the charnel ground’; the monkey would pull, thinking, ‘I will enter the forest.’ But when, monks, those six animals become hungry and exhausted, they would stand by, sit by, or lie down by that very stake or pillar. In the same way, monks, for any monk who has developed and cultivated mindfulness of the body: the eye does not pull him toward pleasing forms, and unpleasing forms are not repulsive… the tongue does not pull him toward pleasing flavors… the mind does not pull him toward pleasing mental objects, and unpleasing mental objects are not repulsive. Thus, monks, there is restraint.

“‘Daḷhe khīle vā thambhe vā’ti kho, bhikkhave, kāyagatāya satiyā etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tasmātiha vo, bhikkhave, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ – ‘kāyagatā no sati bhāvitā bhavissati bahulīkatā yānīkatā vatthukatā anuṭṭhitā paricitā susamāraddhā’ti. Evañhi kho, bhikkhave, sikkhitabba”nti. Dasamaṃ.

‘A strong stake or pillar,’ monks, is a designation for mindfulness directed to the body. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘For us, mindfulness directed to the body will be developed, frequently practiced, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, familiarized, and well undertaken.’ Thus, monks, should you train yourselves.

11. Yavakalāpisuttaṃ

11. The Discourse on the Sheaf of Barley

248. “Seyyathāpi[M 2.0404][P 4.0201], bhikkhave, yavakalāpī cātumahāpathe nikkhittā assa. Atha cha purisā āgaccheyyuṃ byābhaṅgihatthā. Te yavakalāpiṃ chahi byābhaṅgīhi haneyyuṃ. Evañhi sā, bhikkhave, yavakalāpī suhatā assa chahi byābhaṅgīhi haññamānā. Atha sattamo puriso āgaccheyya byābhaṅgihattho. So taṃ yavakalāpiṃ sattamāya byābhaṅgiyā haneyya. Evañhi sā bhikkhave, yavakalāpī suhatatarā assa, sattamāya byābhaṅgiyā haññamānā. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano cakkhusmiṃ haññati manāpāmanāpehi rūpehi…pe… jivhāya haññati manāpāmanāpehi rasehi…pe… manasmiṃ haññati [T 4.0250] manāpāmanāpehi dhammehi. Sace so, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano āyatiṃ punabbhavāya ceteti, evañhi so, bhikkhave, moghapuriso suhatataro hoti, seyyathāpi sā yavakalāpī sattamāya byābhaṅgiyā haññamānā.

248. Monks, suppose a sheaf of barley were placed at a crossroads. Then six men with flails in their hands were to come along and strike that sheaf of barley with six flails. In this way, monks, that sheaf of barley would be well struck, being struck by six flails.
