Then a seventh man with a flail in his hand were to come along and strike that sheaf of barley with a seventh flail. In this way, monks, that sheaf of barley would be even more thoroughly struck, being struck by the seventh flail. Just so, monks, an uninstructed ordinary person is struck in the eye by pleasant and unpleasant forms… struck in the tongue by pleasant and unpleasant tastes… struck in the mind by pleasant and unpleasant mental objects. If, monks, that uninstructed ordinary person directs his thought towards future rebirth, then indeed, monks, that foolish person is even more thoroughly struck—just like that sheaf of barley being struck by the seventh flail.

“Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhikkhave, devāsurasaṅgāmo samupabyūḷho samupabbūḷho (sī. pī.) ahosi. Atha kho, bhikkhave, vepacitti asurindo asure āmantesi – ‘sace, mārisā, devāsurasaṅgāme samupabyūḷhe asurā jineyyuṃ devā parājineyyuṃ, yena naṃ sakkaṃ devānamindaṃ kaṇṭhapañcamehi bandhanehi bandhitvā mama santike āneyyātha asurapura’nti. Sakkopi kho, bhikkhave, devānamindo deve tāvatiṃse āmantesi – ‘sace, mārisā, devāsurasaṅgāme samupabyūḷhe devā jineyyuṃ asurā parājineyyuṃ, yena [V 2.0199] naṃ vepacittiṃ asurindaṃ kaṇṭhapañcamehi bandhanehi bandhitvā mama santike āneyyātha sudhammaṃ devasabha’nti. Tasmiṃ kho pana, bhikkhave, saṅgāme devā jiniṃsu, asurā parājiniṃsu[P 4.0202]. Atha kho, bhikkhave, devā tāvatiṃsā vepacittiṃ asurindaṃ kaṇṭhapañcamehi bandhanehi bandhitvā sakkassa devānamindassa santike ānesuṃ sudhammaṃ devasabhaṃ. Tatra sudaṃ, bhikkhave, vepacitti asurindo kaṇṭhapañcamehi bandhanehi baddho bandho (sī. syā. kaṃ. ka.) hoti. Yadā kho, bhikkhave, vepacittissa asurindassa evaṃ hoti – ‘dhammikā kho devā, adhammikā asurā[M 2.0405], idheva dānāhaṃ [T 4.0251] devapuraṃ gacchāmī’ti. Atha kaṇṭhapañcamehi bandhanehi muttaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati, dibbehi ca pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappito samaṅgībhūto paricāreti. Yadā ca kho, bhikkhave, vepacittissa asurindassa evaṃ hoti – ‘dhammikā kho asurā, adhammikā devā, tattheva dānāhaṃ asurapuraṃ gamissāmī’ti, atha kaṇṭhapañcamehi bandhanehi baddhaṃ attānaṃ samanupassati. Dibbehi ca pañcahi kāmaguṇehi parihāyati. Evaṃ sukhumaṃ kho, bhikkhave, vepacittibandhanaṃ. Tato sukhumataraṃ mārabandhanaṃ. Maññamāno kho, bhikkhave, baddho mārassa, amaññamāno mutto pāpimato.

“Once upon a time, monks, a battle was arrayed between the devas and the asuras. Then, monks, Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, addressed the asuras: ‘If, sirs, in the battle arrayed between the devas and the asuras, the asuras should win and the devas be defeated, bind Sakka, the lord of the devas, with bonds on his four limbs and neck and bring him to me in the city of the asuras.’ Sakka too, monks, the lord of the devas, addressed the Tāvatiṃsa devas: ‘If, sirs, in the battle arrayed between the devas and the asuras, the devas should win and the asuras be defeated, bind Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, with bonds on his four limbs and neck and bring him to me in the Sudhamma assembly hall of the devas.’ In that battle, monks, the devas won and the asuras were defeated. Then, monks, the Tāvatiṃsa devas bound Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, with bonds on his four limbs and neck and brought him to Sakka, the lord of the devas, in the Sudhamma assembly hall. There, monks, Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, was bound with bonds on his four limbs and neck. Whenever, monks, Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, thought: ‘The devas are righteous, the asuras are unrighteous; now I shall go to the realm of the devas,’ then he saw himself freed from the bonds on his four limbs and neck and indulged, fully equipped and provided, in the five divine strands of sensual pleasure. But whenever, monks, Vepacitti, the lord of the asuras, thought: ‘The asuras are righteous, the devas are unrighteous; now I shall return to the city of the asuras,’ then he saw himself bound by the bonds on his four limbs and neck and was deprived of the five divine strands of sensual pleasure. So subtle, monks, is the bondage of Vepacitti. Even subtler is the bondage of Māra. One who conceives is bound by Māra; one who does not conceive is freed from the Evil One.”

“‘Asmī’ti, bhikkhave, maññitametaṃ, ‘ayamahamasmī’ti maññitametaṃ, ‘bhavissa’nti maññitametaṃ, ‘na bhavissa’nti maññitametaṃ, ‘rūpī bhavissa’nti maññitametaṃ, ‘arūpī bhavissa’nti maññitametaṃ, ‘saññī bhavissa’nti maññitametaṃ, ‘asaññī bhavissa’nti maññitametaṃ, ‘nevasaññīnāsaññī bhavissa’nti maññitametaṃ. Maññitaṃ, bhikkhave, rogo, maññitaṃ gaṇḍo, maññitaṃ sallaṃ. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘amaññamānena amaññitamānena (pī. ka.) cetasā viharissāmā’ti – evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ.

“‘I am,’ monks, this is a conceiving. ‘This I am,’ this is a conceiving. ‘I shall be,’ this is a conceiving. ‘I shall not be,’ this is a conceiving. ‘I shall be with form,’ this is a conceiving. ‘I shall be formless,’ this is a conceiving. ‘I shall be percipient,’ this is a conceiving. ‘I shall be non-percipient,’ this is a conceiving. ‘I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient,’ this is a conceiving. Conceiving, monks, is a disease, conceiving is a tumor, conceiving is a dart. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will dwell with a mind that does not conceive.’”

“‘Asmī’ti, bhikkhave, iñjitametaṃ, ‘ayamahamasmī’ti iñjitametaṃ, ‘bhavissa’nti iñjitametaṃ, ‘na bhavissa’nti iñjitametaṃ, ‘rūpī bhavissa’nti iñjitametaṃ, ‘arūpī bhavissa’nti iñjitametaṃ, ‘saññī bhavissa’nti iñjitametaṃ, ‘asaññī bhavissa’nti iñjitametaṃ, ‘nevasaññīnāsaññī bhavissa’nti [T 4.0252] iñjitametaṃ. Iñjitaṃ, bhikkhave[P 4.0203], rogo, iñjitaṃ gaṇḍo, iñjitaṃ sallaṃ. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘aniñjamānena aniñjiyamānena (syā. kaṃ. ka.) cetasā viharissāmā’ti – evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ.

“‘I am,’ monks, this is an agitation. ‘This I am,’ this is an agitation. ‘I shall be,’ this is an agitation. ‘I shall not be,’ this is an agitation. ‘I shall be with form,’ this is an agitation. ‘I shall be formless,’ this is an agitation. ‘I shall be percipient,’ this is an agitation. ‘I shall be non-percipient,’ this is an agitation. ‘I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient,’ this is an agitation. Agitation, monks, is a disease, agitation is a tumor, agitation is a dart. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will dwell with an unagitated mind.’”

“‘Asmī’ti[V 2.0200], bhikkhave, phanditametaṃ, ‘ayamahamasmī’ti phanditametaṃ, ‘bhavissa’nti…pe… ‘na bhavissa’nti… ‘rūpī bhavissa’nti… ‘arūpī bhavissa’nti… ‘saññī bhavissa’nti… ‘asaññī bhavissa’nti… ‘nevasaññīnāsaññī bhavissa’nti phanditametaṃ. Phanditaṃ, bhikkhave, rogo, phanditaṃ gaṇḍo, phanditaṃ sallaṃ. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘aphandamānena aphandiyamānena (syā. kaṃ. ka.) cetasā viharissāmā’ti – evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ.

“‘I am,’ monks, this is a quivering. ‘This I am,’ this is a quivering. ‘I shall be’… and so on … ‘I shall not be’… ‘I shall be with form’… ‘I shall be formless’… ‘I shall be percipient’… ‘I shall be non-percipient’… ‘I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient,’ this is a quivering. Quivering, monks, is a disease, quivering is a tumor, quivering is a dart. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will dwell with an unquivering mind.’”

“‘Asmī’ti, bhikkhave, papañcitametaṃ, ‘ayamahamasmī’ti papañcitametaṃ, ‘bhavissa’nti…pe… ‘na bhavissa’nti… ‘rūpī bhavissa’nti… ‘arūpī bhavissa’nti… ‘saññī bhavissa’nti… ‘asaññī bhavissa’nti… ‘nevasaññīnāsaññī bhavissa’nti papañcitametaṃ[M 2.0406]. Papañcitaṃ, bhikkhave, rogo, papañcitaṃ gaṇḍo, papañcitaṃ sallaṃ. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘nippapañcena cetasā viharissāmā’ti – evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabbaṃ.

“‘I am,’ monks, this is a proliferation. ‘This I am,’ this is a proliferation. ‘I shall be’… and so on … ‘I shall not be’… ‘I shall be with form’… ‘I shall be formless’… ‘I shall be percipient’… ‘I shall be non-percipient’… ‘I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient,’ this is a proliferation. Proliferation, monks, is a disease, proliferation is a tumor, proliferation is a dart. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will dwell with a mind free from proliferation.’”

“‘Asmī’ti, bhikkhave, mānagatametaṃ, ‘ayamahamasmī’ti mānagatametaṃ, ‘bhavissa’nti mānagatametaṃ, ‘na bhavissa’nti mānagatametaṃ, ‘rūpī bhavissa’nti mānagatametaṃ, ‘arūpī bhavissa’nti mānagatametaṃ, ‘saññī bhavissa’nti mānagatametaṃ, ‘asaññī bhavissa’nti mānagatametaṃ, ‘nevasaññīnāsaññī bhavissa’nti [T 4.0253] mānagatametaṃ. Mānagataṃ, bhikkhave, rogo, mānagataṃ gaṇḍo, mānagataṃ sallaṃ. Tasmātiha, bhikkhave, ‘nihatamānena cetasā viharissāmā’ti – evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabba”nti. Ekādasamaṃ.

“‘I am,’ monks, this is a matter of conceit. ‘This I am,’ this is a matter of conceit. ‘I shall be,’ this is a matter of conceit. ‘I shall not be,’ this is a matter of conceit. ‘I shall be with form,’ this is a matter of conceit. ‘I shall be formless,’ this is a matter of conceit. ‘I shall be percipient,’ this is a matter of conceit. ‘I shall be non-percipient,’ this is a matter of conceit. ‘I shall be neither percipient nor non-percipient,’ this is a matter of conceit. A matter of conceit, monks, is a disease, a matter of conceit is a tumor, a matter of conceit is a dart. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We will dwell with a mind devoid of conceit.’” The eleventh.

Āsīvisavaggo ekūnavīsatimo.

The Section on the Viper, the nineteenth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary:

Āsīviso [P 4.0204] ratho kummo, dve dārukkhandhā avassuto;

Dukkhadhammā kiṃsukā vīṇā, chappāṇā yavakalāpīti.

The Viper, the Chariot, the Tortoise, the two Logs of Wood, the Leaky; the States of Suffering, the Kiṃsuka Tree, the Lute, the Six Animals, and the Sheaf of Barley.

Saḷāyatanavagge catutthapaṇṇāsako samatto.

The Fourth Fifty in the Chapter on the Six Sense Bases is completed.

Tassa [V 2.0201] vagguddānaṃ –

The summary of its sections:

Nandikkhayo saṭṭhinayo, samuddo uragena ca;

Catupaṇṇāsakā ete, nipātesu pakāsitāti.

The Destruction of Delight, the Sixtyfold Method, the Ocean, and the Serpent; these fifty-fours are well proclaimed in the collections. This is the summary of the chapters.

Saḷāyatanasaṃyuttaṃ samattaṃ.

The Connected Discourses on the Six Sense Bases is completed.

2. Vedanāsaṃyuttaṃ

2. The Connected Discourses on Feeling

1. Sagāthāvaggo

1. The Chapter with Verses

1. Samādhisuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on Concentration

249. “Tisso [T 4.0254][V 2.0202][M 2.0407] imā, bhikkhave, vedanā. Katamā tisso? Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā kho, bhikkhave, tisso vedanāti.

249. “Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings. What are the three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, bhikkhus, are the three feelings.”

“Samāhito sampajāno, sato buddhassa sāvako;

Vedanā ca pajānāti, vedanānañca sambhavaṃ.

“A disciple of the Buddha, concentrated, fully comprehending, and mindful, distinctly knows feelings and the origin of feelings,

“Yattha cetā nirujjhanti, maggañca khayagāminaṃ;

Vedanānaṃ khayā bhikkhu, nicchāto parinibbuto”ti. paṭhamaṃ;

where they cease, and the path leading to their destruction. Through the destruction of feelings, a bhikkhu, free from craving, is fully extinguished.”

2. Sukhasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on the Pleasant

250. “Tisso imā, bhikkhave, vedanā. Katamā tisso? Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā kho, bhikkhave, tisso vedanāti.

250. “Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings. What are the three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, bhikkhus, are the three feelings.”

“Sukhaṃ [P 4.0205] vā yadi vā dukkhaṃ, adukkhamasukhaṃ saha;

Ajjhattañca bahiddhā ca, yaṃ kiñci atthi veditaṃ.

“Whether pleasant or painful, together with the neither-painful-nor-pleasant, both internally and externally, whatever feeling there is,

“Etaṃ [V 2.0203] dukkhanti ñatvāna, mosadhammaṃ palokinaṃ;

Phussa phussa vayaṃ passaṃ, evaṃ tattha virajjatī”ti. dutiyaṃ;

having known this as suffering, of a deceptive and perishable nature, repeatedly contacting its passing away, one thus becomes dispassionate towards it.”

3. Pahānasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on Abandonment

251. “Tisso imā, bhikkhave, vedanā. Katamā tisso? Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Sukhāya, bhikkhave, vedanāya rāgānusayo pahātabbo, dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo pahātabbo, adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo pahātabbo. Yato [T 4.0255] kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo pahīno hoti, dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo pahīno hoti, adukkhamasukhāya [M 2.0408] vedanāya avijjānusayo pahīno hoti, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘bhikkhu niranusayo sammaddaso acchecchi acchejji (bahūsu) taṇhaṃ, vivattayi vāvattayi (sī.) saṃyojanaṃ, sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā’”ti.

251. “Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings. What are the three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. For a pleasant feeling, bhikkhus, the underlying tendency to lust is to be abandoned. For a painful feeling, the underlying tendency to aversion is to be abandoned. For a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, the underlying tendency to ignorance is to be abandoned. When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu’s underlying tendency to lust for a pleasant feeling has been abandoned, his underlying tendency to aversion for a painful feeling has been abandoned, and his underlying tendency to ignorance for a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling has been abandoned, this one is called, bhikkhus, ‘a bhikkhu without underlying tendencies, one who sees rightly, who has cut off craving, has turned away the fetter, and through the right penetration of conceit has made an end of suffering.’”

“Sukhaṃ vedayamānassa vediyamānassa (sī. pī.), vedanaṃ appajānato;

So rāgānusayo hoti, anissaraṇadassino.

“For one experiencing a pleasant feeling, not distinctly knowing that feeling, not seeing an escape from it, the underlying tendency to lust arises.

“Dukkhaṃ vedayamānassa, vedanaṃ appajānato;

Paṭighānusayo hoti, anissaraṇadassino.

For one experiencing a painful feeling, not distinctly knowing that feeling, not seeing an escape from it, the underlying tendency to aversion arises.

“Adukkhamasukhaṃ santaṃ, bhūripaññena desitaṃ;

Tañcāpi abhinandati, neva dukkhā pamuccati.

The peaceful neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling was taught by the one of vast wisdom. If one delights even in that, one is not freed from suffering.

“Yato [P 4.0206] ca bhikkhu ātāpī, sampajaññaṃ na riñcati;

Tato so vedanā sabbā, parijānāti paṇḍito.

When a bhikkhu is ardent and does not neglect full comprehension, then that wise one fully understands all feelings.

“So vedanā pariññāya, diṭṭhe dhamme anāsavo;

Kāyassa bhedā dhammaṭṭho, saṅkhyaṃ nopeti vedagū”ti. tatiyaṃ;

Having fully understood feelings, being without taints in this very life, established in the Dhamma, one who has attained knowledge, after the breakup of the body, does not enter into designation.”

4. Pātālasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on the Abyss

252. “Assutavā[V 2.0204], bhikkhave, puthujjano yaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati – ‘atthi mahāsamudde pātālo’ti. Taṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano asantaṃ avijjamānaṃ evaṃ vācaṃ bhāsati – ‘atthi mahāsamudde pātālo’ti. Sārīrikānaṃ kho etaṃ, bhikkhave, dukkhānaṃ vedanānaṃ adhivacanaṃ yadidaṃ ‘pātālo’ti. Assutavā, bhikkhave, puthujjano sārīrikāya dukkhāya vedanāya [T 4.0256] phuṭṭho samāno socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohaṃ āpajjati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘assutavā puthujjano pātāle na paccuṭṭhāsi, gādhañca nājjhagā’. Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako sārīrikāya dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno neva socati, na kilamati, na paridevati, na urattāḷiṃ kandati, na sammohaṃ āpajjati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘sutavā ariyasāvako pātāle paccuṭṭhāsi, gādhañca ajjhagā’”ti.

252. “Bhikkhus, the uninstructed ordinary person speaks this word: ‘There is an abyss in the great ocean.’ But this, bhikkhus, is the uninstructed ordinary person speaking of what is non-existent, not manifest, when they say: ‘There is an abyss in the great ocean.’ ‘Abyss,’ bhikkhus, is a designation for painful bodily feelings. When the uninstructed ordinary person is afflicted by a painful bodily feeling, they sorrow, become weary, lament, beat their breast and wail, and fall into bewilderment. This, bhikkhus, is called ‘the uninstructed ordinary person who cannot stand firm in the abyss and has not found a foothold.’ But the instructed noble disciple, bhikkhus, when afflicted by a painful bodily feeling, does not sorrow, does not become weary, does not lament, does not beat their breast and wail, and does not fall into bewilderment. This, bhikkhus, is called ‘the instructed noble disciple who stands firm in the abyss and has found a foothold.’”

“Yo [M 2.0409] etā nādhivāseti, uppannā vedanā dukhā;

Sārīrikā pāṇaharā, yāhi phuṭṭho pavedhati.

“One who does not endure these painful feelings that have arisen, bodily and life-taking, afflicted by which, they tremble.

“Akkandati parodati, dubbalo appathāmako;

Na so pātāle paccuṭṭhāsi, atho gādhampi nājjhagā.

They wail and cry, weak, of feeble strength; they cannot stand firm in the abyss, and furthermore, do not find a foothold.

“Yo [P 4.0207] cetā adhivāseti, uppannā vedanā dukhā;

Sārīrikā pāṇaharā, yāhi phuṭṭho na vedhati;

Sa ve pātāle paccuṭṭhāsi, atho gādhampi ajjhagā”ti. catutthaṃ;

But one who endures these painful feelings that have arisen, bodily and life-taking, afflicted by which, they do not tremble; they indeed stand firm in the abyss, and furthermore, have found a foothold.”

5. Daṭṭhabbasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on What Should Be Seen

253. “Tisso imā, bhikkhave, vedanā. Katamā tisso? Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Sukhā, bhikkhave, vedanā dukkhato daṭṭhabbā, dukkhā vedanā sallato daṭṭhabbā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā aniccato daṭṭhabbā. Yato kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno sukhā vedanā dukkhato diṭṭhā hoti, dukkhā vedanā sallato diṭṭhā hoti, adukkhamasukhā vedanā aniccato [V 2.0205] diṭṭhā hoti [T 4.0257] – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘bhikkhu sammaddaso acchecchi taṇhaṃ, vivattayi saṃyojanaṃ, sammā mānābhisamayā antamakāsi dukkhassā’”ti.

253. “Bhikkhus, there are these three feelings. What are the three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Bhikkhus, pleasant feeling should be seen as suffering; painful feeling should be seen as a dart; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling should be seen as impermanent. When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has seen pleasant feeling as suffering, painful feeling as a dart, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as impermanent—this bhikkhu, bhikkhus, is called one who sees rightly, who has cut off craving, has removed the fetter, and who, through the right comprehension of conceit, has made an end of suffering.”

“Yo sukhaṃ dukkhato adda, dukkhamaddakkhi sallato;

Adukkhamasukhaṃ santaṃ, addakkhi naṃ aniccato.

“One who has seen the pleasant as suffering, has seen the painful as a dart, and has seen the peaceful neither-painful-nor-pleasant as impermanent.

“Sa ve sammaddaso bhikkhu, parijānāti vedanā;

So vedanā pariññāya, diṭṭhe dhamme anāsavo;

Kāyassa bhedā dhammaṭṭho, saṅkhyaṃ nopeti vedagū”ti. pañcamaṃ;

Indeed, that bhikkhu who sees rightly fully understands feelings. Having fully understood feelings, in this very life he is without taints. Established in the Dhamma, one who has attained knowledge, after the breaking up of the body, does not enter into designation.”

6. Sallasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on the Dart

254. “Assutavā, bhikkhave, puthujjano sukhampi vedanaṃ vedayati vediyati (sī. pī.), dukkhampi vedanaṃ vedayati, adukkhamasukhampi vedanaṃ vedayati. Sutavā, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako sukhampi vedanaṃ vedayati[P 4.0208], dukkhampi vedanaṃ vedayati, adukkhamasukhampi [M 2.0410] vedanaṃ vedayati. Tatra, bhikkhave, ko viseso ko adhippayāso adhippāyo (sī. ka.), adhippāyaso (syā. kaṃ.), adhippāyoso (pī.) kiṃ nānākaraṇaṃ sutavato ariyasāvakassa assutavatā puthujjanenā”ti? Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā…pe… assutavā. Bhikkhave, puthujjano dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno socati kilamati [T 4.0258] paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohaṃ āpajjati. So dve vedanā vedayati – kāyikañca, cetasikañca. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, purisaṃ sallena vijjheyya sallena anuvijjheyyuṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.). Tamenaṃ dutiyena sallena anuvedhaṃ vijjheyya sallena anuvijjheyyuṃ (sī.), sallena anuvedhaṃ vijjheyyuṃ (syā. kaṃ.), sallena vijjheyyuṃ (pī.). Evañhi so, bhikkhave, puriso dvisallena vedanaṃ vedayati. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, assutavā puthujjano dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno socati kilamati paridevati urattāḷiṃ kandati sammohaṃ āpajjati. So dve vedanā vedayati – kāyikañca, cetasikañca. Tassāyeva kho pana dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno paṭighavā hoti. Tamenaṃ dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighavantaṃ, yo dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo, so anuseti. So dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno kāmasukhaṃ abhinandati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Na hi so, bhikkhave, pajānāti assutavā puthujjano aññatra kāmasukhā dukkhāya vedanāya nissaraṇaṃ, tassa kāmasukhañca abhinandato, yo sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo, so anuseti. So tāsaṃ vedanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca [V 2.0206] nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānāti. Tassa tāsaṃ vedanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ appajānato, yo adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo, so anuseti. So sukhañce vedanaṃ vedayati, saññutto naṃ vedayati. Dukkhañce vedanaṃ vedayati, saññutto naṃ vedayati. Adukkhamasukhañce [P 4.0209] vedanaṃ vedayati, saññutto naṃ vedayati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘assutavā puthujjano saññutto jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi, saññutto dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi.

254. “Monks, the uninstructed ordinary person feels pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling. The instructed noble disciple also feels pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling. Here, monks, what is the distinction, what is the superiority, what is the disparity between the instructed noble disciple and the uninstructed ordinary person?” “Venerable sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One… Monks, the uninstructed ordinary person, when touched by painful feeling, sorrows, becomes weary, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion. He feels two feelings—a bodily one and a mental one. Suppose, monks, a man were pierced by a dart. Then they would pierce him with a second dart in succession. Thus, monks, that man feels the feeling from two darts. In the same way, monks, when an uninstructed ordinary person is touched by painful feeling, he sorrows, becomes weary, laments, beats his breast, and falls into confusion. He feels two feelings—a bodily one and a mental one. Being touched by that very painful feeling, he has aversion. For him who has aversion to that painful feeling, the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling lies dormant. Being touched by painful feeling, he delights in sensual pleasure. For what reason? Because, monks, the uninstructed ordinary person does not know any escape from painful feeling other than sensual pleasure. For him who delights in sensual pleasure, the underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feeling lies dormant. He does not know as it really is the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to those feelings. For him who does not know as it really is the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to those feelings, the underlying tendency to ignorance toward neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling lies dormant. If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it conjoined. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it conjoined. If he feels a neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, he feels it conjoined. This, monks, is called ‘the uninstructed ordinary person conjoined with birth, aging, and death; with sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, and despairs; conjoined with suffering,’ I say.”

“Sutavā ca kho, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno na socati, na kilamati, na paridevati, na urattāḷiṃ kandati, na [M 2.0411] sammohaṃ āpajjati. So ekaṃ vedanaṃ vedayati – kāyikaṃ, na cetasikaṃ.

“But, monks, the instructed noble disciple, when touched by painful feeling, does not sorrow, does not become weary, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion. He feels one feeling—a bodily one, not a mental one.

“Seyyathāpi[T 4.0259], bhikkhave, purisaṃ sallena vijjheyya. Tamenaṃ dutiyena sallena anuvedhaṃ na vijjheyya. Evañhi so, bhikkhave, puriso ekasallena vedanaṃ vedayati. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno na socati, na kilamati, na paridevati, na urattāḷiṃ kandati, na sammohaṃ āpajjati. So ekaṃ vedanaṃ vedayati – kāyikaṃ, na cetasikaṃ. Tassāyeva kho pana dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno paṭighavā na hoti. Tamenaṃ dukkhāya vedanāya appaṭighavantaṃ, yo dukkhāya vedanāya paṭighānusayo, so nānuseti. So dukkhāya vedanāya phuṭṭho samāno kāmasukhaṃ nābhinandati. Taṃ kissa hetu? Pajānāti hi so, bhikkhave, sutavā ariyasāvako aññatra kāmasukhā dukkhāya vedanāya nissaraṇaṃ. Tassa kāmasukhaṃ nābhinandato yo sukhāya vedanāya rāgānusayo, so nānuseti. So tāsaṃ vedanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavaṃ ca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānāti. Tassa tāsaṃ vedanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānato, yo adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya avijjānusayo, so nānuseti. So sukhañce vedanaṃ vedayati, visaññutto naṃ vedayati. Dukkhañce vedanaṃ vedayati[P 4.0210], visaññutto naṃ vedayati. Adukkhamasukhañce vedanaṃ vedayati, visaññutto naṃ vedayati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, ‘sutavā ariyasāvako visaññutto jātiyā jarāya maraṇena sokehi paridevehi dukkhehi domanassehi upāyāsehi[T 4.0260][V 2.0207], visaññutto dukkhasmā’ti vadāmi. Ayaṃ kho, bhikkhave, viseso, ayaṃ adhippayāso, idaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ sutavato ariyasāvakassa assutavatā puthujjanenā”ti.

“Suppose, monks, a man were pierced by a dart. Then they would not pierce him with a second dart in succession. Thus, monks, that man feels the feeling from one dart. In the same way, monks, when an instructed noble disciple is touched by painful feeling, he does not sorrow, does not become weary, does not lament, does not beat his breast, and does not fall into confusion. He feels one feeling—a bodily one, not a mental one. Being touched by that very painful feeling, he does not have aversion. For him who does not have aversion to that painful feeling, the underlying tendency to aversion toward painful feeling does not lie dormant. Being touched by painful feeling, he does not delight in sensual pleasure. For what reason? Because, monks, the instructed noble disciple knows the escape from painful feeling apart from sensual pleasure. For him who does not delight in sensual pleasure, the underlying tendency to lust for pleasant feeling does not lie dormant. He knows as it really is the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to those feelings. For him who knows as it really is the origin, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape in regard to those feelings, the underlying tendency to ignorance toward neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling does not lie dormant. If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it disjoined. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it disjoined. If he feels a neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling, he feels it disjoined. This, monks, is called ‘the instructed noble disciple disjoined from birth, aging, and death; from sorrows, lamentations, pains, distresses, and despairs; disjoined from suffering,’ I say. This, monks, is the distinction, this is the superiority, this is the disparity between the instructed noble disciple and the uninstructed ordinary person.”

“Na vedanaṃ vedayati sapañño,

Sukhampi dukkhampi bahussutopi;

Ayañca dhīrassa puthujjanena,

Mahā ayaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) viseso kusalassa hoti.

“The wise, the very learned one, does not experience feeling, whether pleasant or painful. This is the great distinction of the steadfast and skilled one from the ordinary person.”

“Saṅkhātadhammassa [M 2.0412] bahussutassa,

Vipassato sampassato (sī. pī.) lokamimaṃ parañca;

Iṭṭhassa dhammā na mathenti cittaṃ,

Aniṭṭhato no paṭighātameti.

“For one who has comprehended the Dhamma, is very learned, and who sees this world and the next, desirable things do not agitate his mind, and he does not come to aversion from the undesirable.”

“Tassānurodhā athavā virodhā,

Vidhūpitā atthagatā na santi;

Padañca ñatvā virajaṃ asokaṃ,

Sammā pajānāti bhavassa pāragū”ti. chaṭṭhaṃ;

“For him, attraction and opposition are dispelled, have vanished, and do not exist. Having known the stainless, sorrowless state, he, the one who has gone beyond becoming, understands rightly.”

7. Paṭhamagelaññasuttaṃ

7. The First Discourse on Illness

255. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ. Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena gilānasālā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Nisajja kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi [P 4.0211] –

255. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī, in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then, in the evening, the Blessed One emerged from seclusion and went to the sick ward. Having approached, he sat down on the seat that was prepared. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:

“Sato, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajāno kālaṃ āgameyya. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī.

“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, being mindful and clearly comprehending, should await his time. This is our instruction to you.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sato hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu vedanānupassī [V 2.0208] viharati…pe… citte cittānupassī viharati…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ[T 4.0261]. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sato hoti.

“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu mindful? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... he dwells contemplating mind in mind... he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in the world. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is mindful.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajāno hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hoti, ālokite vilokite sampajānakārī hoti, samiñjite pasārite sampajānakārī hoti, saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe sampajānakārī hoti, asite pīte khāyite sāyite sampajānakārī hoti, uccārapassāvakamme sampajānakārī hoti, gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite bhāsite tuṇhībhāve [M 2.0413] sampajānakārī hoti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajānakārī hoti. Sato, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajāno kālaṃ āgameyya. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī.

“And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu clearly comprehending? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who acts with clear comprehension in going forward and in returning; in looking ahead and in looking aside; in bending and in stretching; in carrying the double-robe, bowl, and outer robe; in eating, drinking, chewing, and savoring; in the act of defecating and urinating; in walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and in keeping silent. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a bhikkhu is one who acts with clear comprehension. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, being mindful and clearly comprehending, should await his time. This is our instruction to you.”

“Tassa ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno evaṃ satassa sampajānassa appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati sukhā vedanā, so evaṃ pajānāti – ‘uppannā kho myāyaṃ sukhā vedanā. Sā ca kho paṭicca, no appaṭicca. Kiṃ paṭicca? Imameva kāyaṃ paṭicca. Ayaṃ kho pana kāyo anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno. Aniccaṃ kho pana saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ kāyaṃ paṭicca uppannā sukhā vedanā kuto niccā bhavissatī’ti! So kāye ca sukhāya ca vedanāya aniccānupassī viharati, vayānupassī viharati, virāgānupassī viharati, nirodhānupassī viharati, paṭinissaggānupassī viharati. Tassa kāye ca sukhāya ca vedanāya aniccānupassino viharato, vayānupassino viharato, virāgānupassino viharato, nirodhānupassino viharato, paṭinissaggānupassino [T 4.0262][P 4.0212] viharato, yo kāye ca sukhāya ca vedanāya rāgānusayo, so pahīyati.

“If, bhikkhus, while a bhikkhu is dwelling thus—mindful, clearly comprehending, diligent, ardent, and resolute—a pleasant feeling arises, he understands thus: ‘This pleasant feeling has arisen in me. And it has arisen dependently, not independently. Dependent on what? Dependent on this very body. But this body is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. How could a pleasant feeling that has arisen dependent on a body that is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen be permanent?’ He dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in the pleasant feeling, he dwells contemplating vanishing, he dwells contemplating dispassion, he dwells contemplating cessation, he dwells contemplating relinquishment. For him who dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in the pleasant feeling, contemplating vanishing, contemplating dispassion, contemplating cessation, and contemplating relinquishment, whatever underlying tendency to lust there is in regard to the body and the pleasant feeling, that is abandoned.”

“Tassa ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno evaṃ satassa sampajānassa appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati dukkhā vedanā. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘uppannā kho myāyaṃ dukkhā vedanā. Sā ca kho paṭicca, no appaṭicca. Kiṃ paṭicca? Imameva kāyaṃ paṭicca. Ayaṃ kho pana kāyo anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno. Aniccaṃ kho pana saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ kāyaṃ paṭicca uppannā dukkhā vedanā kuto niccā bhavissatī’ti! So kāye ca dukkhāya vedanāya [V 2.0209] aniccānupassī viharati, vayānupassī viharati, virāgānupassī viharati, nirodhānupassī viharati, paṭinissaggānupassī viharati. Tassa kāye ca dukkhāya ca vedanāya aniccānupassino viharato…pe… paṭinissaggānupassino viharato, yo kāye ca dukkhāya ca vedanāya paṭighānusayo, so pahīyati.

“If, bhikkhus, while a bhikkhu is dwelling thus—mindful, clearly comprehending, diligent, ardent, and resolute—a painful feeling arises, he understands thus: ‘This painful feeling has arisen in me. And it has arisen dependently, not independently. Dependent on what? Dependent on this very body. But this body is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. How could a painful feeling that has arisen dependent on a body that is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen be permanent?’ He dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in the painful feeling, he dwells contemplating vanishing, he dwells contemplating dispassion, he dwells contemplating cessation, he dwells contemplating relinquishment. For him who dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in the painful feeling... contemplating relinquishment, whatever underlying tendency to aversion there is in regard to the body and the painful feeling, that is abandoned.”

“Tassa ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno evaṃ satassa sampajānassa appamattassa ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati adukkhamasukhā vedanā, so evaṃ pajānāti – ‘uppannā kho myāyaṃ adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Sā ca kho paṭicca, no appaṭicca. Kiṃ paṭicca? Imameva kāyaṃ paṭicca. Ayaṃ kho pana kāyo anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno. Aniccaṃ kho pana saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ kāyaṃ [M 2.0414] paṭicca uppannā [T 4.0263] adukkhamasukhā vedanā kuto niccā bhavissatī’ti! So kāye ca adukkhamasukhāya ca vedanāya aniccānupassī viharati, vayānupassī viharati, virāgānupassī viharati, nirodhānupassī viharati, paṭinissaggānupassī viharati. Tassa kāye ca adukkhamasukhāya ca vedanāya aniccānupassino viharato…pe… paṭinissaggānupassino viharato, yo kāye ca adukkhamasukhāya ca vedanāya avijjānusayo, so pahīyati.

“If, bhikkhus, while a bhikkhu is dwelling thus—mindful, clearly comprehending, diligent, ardent, and resolute—a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises, he understands thus: ‘This neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling has arisen in me. And it has arisen dependently, not independently. Dependent on what? Dependent on this very body. But this body is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. How could a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that has arisen dependent on a body that is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen be permanent?’ He dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he dwells contemplating vanishing, he dwells contemplating dispassion, he dwells contemplating cessation, he dwells contemplating relinquishment. For him who dwells contemplating impermanence in the body and in the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling... contemplating relinquishment, whatever underlying tendency to ignorance there is in regard to the body and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, that is abandoned.”

“So [P 4.0213] sukhañce vedanaṃ vedayati, sā aniccāti pajānāti, anajjhositāti pajānāti, anabhinanditāti pajānāti; dukkhañce vedanaṃ vedayati, sā aniccāti pajānāti, anajjhositāti pajānāti, anabhinanditāti pajānāti; adukkhamasukhañce vedanaṃ vedayati, sā aniccāti pajānāti, anajjhositāti pajānāti, anabhinanditāti pajānāti. So sukhañce vedanaṃ vedayati, visaññutto naṃ vedayati; dukkhañce vedanaṃ vedayati, visaññutto naṃ vedayati; adukkhamasukhañce vedanaṃ vedayati, visaññutto naṃ vedayati. So kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti, jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. ‘Kāyassa bhedā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissantī’ti sītibhavissantīti (sī. pī. ka.) pajānāti.

“If he feels a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not to be clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not to be delighted in.’ If he feels a painful feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not to be clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not to be delighted in.’ If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not to be clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not to be delighted in.’ If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it detached. If he feels a painful feeling, he feels it detached. If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it detached. Feeling a feeling limited to the body, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited to the body.’ Feeling a feeling limited to life, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited to life.’ He understands: ‘After the breaking up of the body, on account of the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here.’”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, telañca paṭicca vaṭṭiñca paṭicca telappadīpo jhāyeyya, tasseva telassa ca vaṭṭiyā ca pariyādānā anāhāro nibbāyeyya; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāyapariyantikaṃ [V 2.0210] vedanaṃ vedayamāno [T 4.0264] ‘kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. ‘Kāyassa bhedā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissantī’ti pajānātī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Just as, monks, an oil lamp would burn in dependence on oil and a wick, and on account of the exhaustion of that very oil and wick, being without fuel, it would be extinguished; even so, monks, a monk, feeling a feeling limited to the body, understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited to the body.’ Feeling a feeling limited to life, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited to life.’ He understands: ‘After the breaking up of the body, on account of the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here.’” The seventh.

8. Dutiyagelaññasuttaṃ

8. The Second Discourse on Sickness

256. Ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ. Atha kho bhagavā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṭisallānā vuṭṭhito yena gilānasālā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā paññatte āsane nisīdi. Nisajja kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi –

256. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof. Then, in the evening, the Blessed One, having arisen from seclusion, went to the sick ward. Having gone there, he sat down on the prepared seat. Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the monks:

“Sato[M 2.0415], bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajāno kālaṃ āgameyya. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī.

“Monks, a monk should await the time, mindful and clearly comprehending. This is our instruction to you.”

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sato hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ; vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati… citte cittānupassī viharati… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā, vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sato hoti.

“And how, monks, is a monk mindful? Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings… the mind in the mind… phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. Thus, monks, a monk is mindful.”

“Kathañca[P 4.0214], bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajāno hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hoti…pe… bhāsite tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī hoti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajāno hoti. Sato, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sampajāno kālaṃ āgameyya. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī.

“And how, monks, is a monk clearly comprehending? Here, monks, a monk is one who acts with clear comprehension in going forward and returning… in speaking and in keeping silent. Thus, monks, a monk is clearly comprehending. Monks, a monk should await the time, mindful and clearly comprehending. This is our instruction to you.”

“Tassa ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno evaṃ satassa sampajānassa appamattassa [T 4.0265] ātāpino pahitattassa viharato uppajjati sukhā vedanā. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘uppannā kho myāyaṃ sukhā vedanā; sā ca kho paṭicca, no appaṭicca. Kiṃ paṭicca? Imameva phassaṃ paṭicca. Ayaṃ kho [V 2.0211] pana phasso anicco saṅkhato paṭiccasamuppanno. Aniccaṃ kho pana saṅkhataṃ paṭiccasamuppannaṃ phassaṃ paṭicca uppannā sukhā vedanā kuto niccā bhavissatī’ti! So phasse ca sukhāya ca vedanāya aniccānupassī viharati, vayānupassī viharati, virāgānupassī viharati, nirodhānupassī viharati, paṭinissaggānupassī viharati. Tassa phasse ca sukhāya ca vedanāya aniccānupassino viharato, vayānupassino viharato, virāgānupassino viharato, nirodhānupassino viharato, paṭinissaggānupassino viharato yo phasse ca sukhāya ca vedanāya rāgānusayo, so pahīyati.

“If, monks, for a monk dwelling thus—mindful, clearly comprehending, diligent, ardent, and resolute—a pleasant feeling arises, he understands thus: ‘This pleasant feeling has arisen in me; and that has arisen dependently, not independently. Dependent on what? Dependent on this very contact. But this contact is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. A pleasant feeling that has arisen in dependence on an impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen contact—how could it be permanent?’ He dwells contemplating impermanence in contact and in the pleasant feeling, dwells contemplating vanishing, dwells contemplating dispassion, dwells contemplating cessation, and dwells contemplating relinquishment. As he dwells contemplating impermanence, vanishing, dispassion, cessation, and relinquishment in contact and in the pleasant feeling, whatever underlying tendency to lust there is in regard to them is abandoned.”

“Tassa ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno evaṃ satassa…pe… viharato uppajjati dukkhā vedanā…pe… uppajjati adukkhamasukhā vedanā. So evaṃ pajānāti – ‘uppannā kho myāyaṃ adukkhamasukhā vedanā; sā ca kho paṭicca, no appaṭicca. Kiṃ paṭicca? Imameva phassaṃ paṭicca…pe… kāyassa [M 2.0416] bhedā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissantī’ti pajānāti”.

“If, monks, for a monk dwelling thus… a painful feeling arises… a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises, he understands thus: ‘This neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling has arisen in me; and that has arisen dependently, not independently. Dependent on what? Dependent on this very contact…’ He understands: ‘After the breaking up of the body, on account of the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here.’”

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, telañca paṭicca vaṭṭiñca paṭicca telappadīpo jhāyeyya[T 4.0266], tasseva telassa ca vaṭṭiyā ca pariyādānā anāhāro nibbāyeyya; evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘kāyapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. Jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayamāno ‘jīvitapariyantikaṃ vedanaṃ vedayāmī’ti pajānāti. ‘Kāyassa bhedā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā idheva sabbavedayitāni anabhinanditāni sītībhavissantī’ti pajānātī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

“Just as, monks, an oil lamp would burn in dependence on oil and a wick, and on account of the exhaustion of that very oil and wick, being without fuel, it would be extinguished; even so, monks, a monk, feeling a feeling limited to the body, understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited to the body.’ Feeling a feeling limited to life, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling limited to life.’ He understands: ‘After the breaking up of the body, on account of the exhaustion of life, all that is felt, not being delighted in, will become cool right here.’” The eighth.

9. Aniccasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on Impermanence

257. “Tisso imā, bhikkhave, vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā. Katamā tisso? Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā kho, bhikkhave, tisso vedanā aniccā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā”ti. Navamaṃ.

257. “Bhikkhus, these three feelings are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation. Which three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, bhikkhus, are the three feelings that are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation.”

10. Phassamūlakasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse Rooted in Contact

258. “Tisso [V 2.0212][P 4.0215] imā, bhikkhave, vedanā phassajā phassamūlakā phassanidānā phassapaccayā. Katamā tisso? Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Sukhavedaniyaṃ, bhikkhave, phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhā vedanā. Tasseva sukhavedaniyassa phassassa nirodhā, yaṃ tajjaṃ vedayitaṃ sukhavedaniyaṃ phassaṃ paṭicca uppannā sukhā vedanā, sā nirujjhati, sā vūpasammati. Dukkhavedaniyaṃ, bhikkhave, phassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati dukkhā vedanā. Tasseva dukkhavedaniyassa phassassa nirodhā, yaṃ tajjaṃ vedayitaṃ dukkhavedaniyaṃ phassaṃ paṭicca uppannā dukkhā vedanā, sā nirujjhati, sā vūpasammati. Adukkhamasukhavedaniyaṃ, bhikkhave, phassaṃ paṭicca [T 4.0267] uppajjati adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Tasseva adukkhamasukhavedaniyassa phassassa nirodhā, yaṃ tajjaṃ vedayitaṃ adukkhamasukhavedaniyaṃ phassaṃ paṭicca uppannā adukkhamasukhā vedanā, sā nirujjhati, sā vūpasammati. Seyyathāpi[M 2.0417], bhikkhave, dvinnaṃ kaṭṭhānaṃ saṅghaṭṭanasamodhānā saṅkhattā tassa samodhānā (syā. kaṃ.) saṅghattā tassa samodhānā (ka.) saṃ. ni. 2.62 passitabbaṃ usmā jāyati, tejo abhinibbattati. Tesaṃyeva kaṭṭhānaṃ nānābhāvā vinikkhepā, yā tajjā usmā, sā nirujjhati, sā vūpasammati. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, imā tisso vedanā phassajā phassamūlakā phassanidānā phassapaccayā. Tajjaṃ phassaṃ paṭicca tajjā vedanā uppajjanti. Tajjassa phassassa nirodhā tajjā vedanā nirujjhantī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

258. “Bhikkhus, these three feelings are born of contact, have contact as their root, have contact as their origin, and are conditioned by contact. Which three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Bhikkhus, dependent on a contact to be felt as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very contact to be felt as pleasant, the corresponding feeling that arose—the pleasant feeling dependent on the contact to be felt as pleasant—ceases and is stilled. Bhikkhus, dependent on a contact to be felt as painful, a painful feeling arises. With the cessation of that very contact to be felt as painful, the corresponding feeling that arose—the painful feeling dependent on the contact to be felt as painful—ceases and is stilled. Bhikkhus, dependent on a contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. With the cessation of that very contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, the corresponding feeling that arose—the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling dependent on the contact to be felt as neither-painful-nor-pleasant—ceases and is stilled. Just as, bhikkhus, from the friction and coming together of two sticks of wood, heat is born and fire is produced; and from the separation and parting of those same sticks of wood, the corresponding heat ceases and is stilled. Even so, bhikkhus, these three feelings are born of contact, have contact as their root, have contact as their origin, and are conditioned by contact. Dependent on a corresponding contact, a corresponding feeling arises. With the cessation of the corresponding contact, the corresponding feeling ceases.”

Sagāthāvaggo paṭhamo[P 4.0216].

The First Chapter with Verses.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary for that is:

Samādhi sukhaṃ pahānena, pātālaṃ daṭṭhabbena ca;

Sallena ceva gelaññā, anicca phassamūlakāti.

Samādhi, Sukha, and Pahāna, Pātāla, and Daṭṭhabba; Sallena and Gelañña, Anicca and Phassamūlaka.

2. Rahogatavaggo

2. The Chapter on Seclusion

1. Rahogatasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on Seclusion

259. Atha [V 2.0213][T 4.0268] kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “idha mayhaṃ, bhante, rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi – ‘tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā. Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā. Vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ bhagavatā – ‘yaṃ kiñci vedayitaṃ taṃ dukkhasmi’nti. Kiṃ nu kho etaṃ bhagavatā sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘yaṃ kiñci vedayitaṃ taṃ dukkhasmi’”nti?

259. Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Here, venerable sir, as I was alone in seclusion, this thought arose in my mind: ‘The Blessed One has spoken of three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These three feelings have been spoken of by the Blessed One. Yet this has also been said by the Blessed One: “Whatever is felt is within suffering.” With reference to what was this said by the Blessed One: “Whatever is felt is within suffering”?’”

“Sādhu sādhu, bhikkhu! Tisso imā, bhikkhu, vedanā vuttā mayā. Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā tisso vedanā vuttā mayā. Vuttaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhu, mayā – ‘yaṃ kiñci vedayitaṃ, taṃ dukkhasmi’nti. Taṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhu, mayā saṅkhārānaṃyeva aniccataṃ sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘yaṃ kiñci vedayitaṃ taṃ dukkhasmi’nti[M 2.0418]. Taṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhu, mayā saṅkhārānaṃyeva khayadhammataṃ…pe… vayadhammataṃ…pe… virāgadhammataṃ [P 4.0217]…pe… nirodhadhammataṃ…pe… vipariṇāmadhammataṃ sandhāya bhāsitaṃ – ‘yaṃ kiñci vedayitaṃ taṃ dukkhasmi’nti. Atha kho pana, bhikkhu, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṃ nirodho akkhāto. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vācā niruddhā hoti. Dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ [T 4.0269] samāpannassa vitakkavicārā niruddhā honti. Tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa pīti niruddhā hoti. Catutthaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa assāsapassāsā niruddhā honti. Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samāpannassa rūpasaññā niruddhā hoti. Viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samāpannassa ākāsānañcāyatanasaññā niruddhā hoti. Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpannassa viññāṇañcāyatanasaññā niruddhā hoti. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpannassa ākiñcaññāyatanasaññā niruddhā hoti. Saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca niruddhā honti. Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo niruddho hoti, doso niruddho hoti, moho niruddho hoti. Atha kho, bhikkhu, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṃ vūpasamo akkhāto. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa [V 2.0214] vācā vūpasantā hoti. Dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vitakkavicārā vūpasantā honti…pe… saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca vūpasantā honti. Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo vūpasanto hoti, doso vūpasanto hoti, moho vūpasanto hoti. Chayimā, bhikkhu, passaddhiyo. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vācā paṭippassaddhā hoti. Dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vitakkavicārā paṭippassaddhā honti. Tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa pīti paṭippassaddhā hoti. Catutthaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa assāsapassāsā paṭippassaddhā [T 4.0270] honti[P 4.0218]. Saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca paṭippassaddhā honti. Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo paṭippassaddho hoti, doso paṭippassaddho hoti, moho paṭippassaddho hotī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“Good, good, monk! These three feelings, monk, have been spoken of by me: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling. These three feelings have been spoken of by me. Yet this has also been said by me, monk: ‘Whatever is felt is within suffering.’ That, monk, was said by me with reference to the impermanence of formations: ‘Whatever is felt is within suffering.’ That, monk, was said by me with reference to the nature of formations to be subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation, and subject to change: ‘Whatever is felt is within suffering.’ Furthermore, monk, I have taught the gradual cessation of formations. For one who has attained the first jhāna, speech has ceased. For one who has attained the second jhāna, initial application and sustained application have ceased. For one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture has ceased. For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, in-breathing and out-breathing have ceased. For one who has attained the base of infinite space, the perception of form has ceased. For one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, the perception of the base of infinite space has ceased. For one who has attained the base of nothingness, the perception of the base of infinite consciousness has ceased. For one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the base of nothingness has ceased. For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have ceased. For a monk whose taints are destroyed, lust has ceased, hatred has ceased, and delusion has ceased. Furthermore, monk, I have taught the gradual subsiding of formations. For one who has attained the first jhāna, speech has subsided. For one who has attained the second jhāna, initial application and sustained application have subsided... For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have subsided. For a monk whose taints are destroyed, lust has subsided, hatred has subsided, and delusion has subsided. There are these six tranquilities, monk. For one who has attained the first jhāna, speech is stilled. For one who has attained the second jhāna, initial application and sustained application are stilled. For one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture is stilled. For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, in-breathing and out-breathing are stilled. For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling are stilled. For a monk whose taints are destroyed, lust is stilled, hatred is stilled, and delusion is stilled.”

2. Paṭhamaākāsasuttaṃ

2. The First Discourse on the Sky

260. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ākāse vividhā vātā vāyanti. Puratthimāpi vātā vāyanti, pacchimāpi vātā vāyanti, uttarāpi vātā vāyanti, dakkhiṇāpi vātā vāyanti, sarajāpi vātā vāyanti, arajāpi vātā vāyanti, sītāpi vātā vāyanti, uṇhāpi vātā vāyanti, parittāpi vātā vāyanti, adhimattāpi vātā [M 2.0419] vāyanti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, imasmiṃ kāyasmiṃ vividhā vedanā uppajjanti, sukhāpi vedanā uppajjati, dukkhāpi vedanā uppajjati, adukkhamasukhāpi vedanā uppajjatī”ti.

260. “Bhikkhus, it is like the various winds that blow in the sky: winds from the east blow, winds from the west blow, winds from the north blow, winds from the south blow, dusty winds blow, dustless winds blow, cold winds blow, hot winds blow, gentle winds blow, and strong winds blow. In the same way, bhikkhus, various feelings arise in this body: a pleasant feeling arises, a painful feeling arises, and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.”

“Yathāpi vātā ākāse, vāyanti vividhā puthū;

Puratthimā pacchimā cāpi, uttarā atha dakkhiṇā.

“Just as in the sky, various and many winds blow; from the east and the west, from the north and then the south.

“Sarajā arajā capi, sītā uṇhā ca ekadā;

Adhimattā parittā ca, puthū vāyanti mālutā.

“Dusty and dustless, cold and at times hot; strong and slight, and many winds blow.

“Tathevimasmiṃ kāyasmiṃ, samuppajjanti vedanā;

Sukhadukkhasamuppatti, adukkhamasukhā ca yā.

“In the same way, in this body, feelings arise; the arising of pleasure and pain, and that which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.

“Yato [V 2.0215] ca bhikkhu ātāpī, sampajaññaṃ na riñcati sampajāno nirūpadhi (ka.);

Tato so vedanā sabbā, parijānāti paṇḍito.

“And when a bhikkhu is ardent and does not neglect clear comprehension, then that wise one fully understands all feelings.

“So [T 4.0271] vedanā pariññāya, diṭṭhe dhamme anāsavo;

Kāyassa bhedā dhammaṭṭho, saṅkhyaṃ nopeti vedagū”ti. dutiyaṃ;

“Having fully understood feelings, taintless in this very life; established in the Dhamma, upon the body’s breaking up, the one who has reached knowledge does not go to reckoning.”

3. Dutiyaākāsasuttaṃ

3. The Second Discourse on the Sky

261. “Seyyathāpi[P 4.0219], bhikkhave, ākāse vividhā vātā vāyanti. Puratthimāpi vātā vāyanti…pe… adhimattāpi vātā vāyanti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, imasmiṃ kāyasmiṃ vividhā vedanā uppajjanti, sukhāpi vedanā uppajjati, dukkhāpi vedanā uppajjati, adukkhamasukhāpi vedanā uppajjatī”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

261. “Bhikkhus, it is like the various winds that blow in the sky: winds from the east blow… and strong winds blow. In the same way, bhikkhus, various feelings arise in this body: a pleasant feeling arises, a painful feeling arises, and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.”

4. Agārasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on the Guesthouse

262. “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, āgantukāgāraṃ. Tattha puratthimāyapi disāya āgantvā vāsaṃ kappenti, pacchimāyapi disāya āgantvā vāsaṃ kappenti, uttarāyapi disāya āgantvā vāsaṃ kappenti, dakkhiṇāyapi disāya āgantvā vāsaṃ kappenti. Khattiyāpi āgantvā vāsaṃ kappenti, brāhmaṇāpi āgantvā vāsaṃ kappenti, vessāpi āgantvā vāsaṃ kappenti, suddāpi āgantvā vāsaṃ kappenti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, imasmiṃ kāyasmiṃ vividhā vedanā [M 2.0420] uppajjanti. Sukhāpi vedanā uppajjati, dukkhāpi vedanā uppajjati, adukkhamasukhāpi vedanā uppajjati. Sāmisāpi sukhā vedanā uppajjati, sāmisāpi dukkhā vedanā uppajjati, sāmisāpi adukkhamasukhā vedanā uppajjati. Nirāmisāpi sukhā vedanā uppajjati, nirāmisāpi dukkhā vedanā uppajjati, nirāmisāpi adukkhamasukhā vedanā uppajjatī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

262. “Bhikkhus, it is like a guesthouse. People come from the eastern direction and take up lodging, people come from the western direction and take up lodging, people come from the northern direction and take up lodging, people come from the southern direction and take up lodging. Nobles come and take up lodging, brahmins come and take up lodging, merchants come and take up lodging, and commoners come and take up lodging. In the same way, Bhikkhus, various feelings arise in this body. A pleasant feeling arises, a painful feeling arises, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. A worldly pleasant feeling arises, a worldly painful feeling arises, a worldly neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises. A spiritual pleasant feeling arises, a spiritual painful feeling arises, and a spiritual neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arises.”

5. Paṭhamaānandasuttaṃ

5. The First Discourse to Ānanda

263. Atha [T 4.0272] kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi[V 2.0216], ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “katamā nu kho, bhante, vedanā, katamo vedanāsamudayo, katamo vedanānirodho, katamā vedanānirodhagāminī [P 4.0220] paṭipadā? Ko vedanāya assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇanti? Tisso imā, ānanda, vedanā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā vuccanti, ānanda, vedanā. Phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayo; phassanirodhā vedanānirodho. Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi. Yaṃ vedanaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ vedanāya assādo. Yā vedanā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā, ayaṃ vedanāya ādīnavo. Yo vedanāya chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ, idaṃ vedanāya nissaraṇaṃ. Atha kho panānanda, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṃ nirodho akkhāto. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vācā niruddhā hoti…pe… saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ [T 4.0273] samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca niruddhā honti. Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo niruddho hoti, doso niruddho hoti, moho niruddho hoti. Atha kho panānanda, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṃ vūpasamo akkhāto. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vācā vūpasantā hoti…pe… saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca vūpasantā honti. Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo vūpasanto hoti, doso vūpasanto hoti, moho vūpasanto hoti. Atha kho panānanda, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṃ paṭippassaddhi akkhātā. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vācā paṭippassaddhā hoti…pe… ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samāpannassa rūpasaññā paṭippassaddhā hoti. Viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samāpannassa ākāsānañcāyatanasaññā paṭippassaddhā hoti. Ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samāpannassa [M 2.0421] viññāṇañcāyatanasaññā paṭippassaddhā hoti. Nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samāpannassa ākiñcaññāyatanasaññā paṭippassaddhā hoti. Saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca paṭippassaddhā honti. Khīṇāsavassa [P 4.0221] bhikkhuno rāgo paṭippassaddho hoti, doso paṭippassaddho hoti, moho paṭippassaddho hotī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

263. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the practice that is the way leading to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification of feeling? What is the danger? What is the escape?”

“Ānanda, there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, Ānanda, are called feelings. From the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling; from the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the practice that is the way leading to the cessation of feeling, that is: right view … to … right concentration. Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on feeling, this is the gratification of feeling. That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, this is the danger of feeling. Whatever is the removal of desire and lust, the abandonment of desire and lust for feeling, this is the escape from feeling.

Furthermore, Ānanda, I have declared the sequential cessation of formations. For one who has attained the first jhāna, speech has ceased. … to … For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have ceased. For a monk whose taints are destroyed, lust has ceased, hatred has ceased, and delusion has ceased.

Furthermore, Ānanda, I have declared the sequential stilling of formations. For one who has attained the first jhāna, speech has been stilled. … to … For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have been stilled. For a monk whose taints are destroyed, lust has been stilled, hatred has been stilled, and delusion has been stilled.

Furthermore, Ānanda, I have declared the sequential subsiding of formations. For one who has attained the first jhāna, speech has subsided. … to … For one who has attained the base of infinite space, the perception of form has subsided. For one who has attained the base of infinite consciousness, the perception of the base of infinite space has subsided. For one who has attained the base of nothingness, the perception of the base of infinite consciousness has subsided. For one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the perception of the base of nothingness has subsided. For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling have subsided. For a monk whose taints are destroyed, lust has subsided, hatred has subsided, and delusion has subsided.”

6. Dutiyaānandasuttaṃ

6. The Second Discourse to Ānanda

264. Atha kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinnaṃ kho āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ bhagavā etadavoca – “katamā nu kho, ānanda, vedanā, katamo vedanāsamudayo, katamo vedanānirodho[V 2.0217], katamā vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Ko vedanāya assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇa”nti? “Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā bhagavannettikā bhagavampaṭisaraṇā. Sādhu, bhante, bhagavantaññeva paṭibhātu etassa [T 4.0274] bhāsitassa attho. Bhagavato sutvā bhikkhū dhāressantī”ti. “Tena hi, ānanda, suṇohi, sādhukaṃ manasi karohi; bhāsissāmī”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā ānando bhagavato paccassosi. Bhagavā etadavoca – “tisso imā, ānanda, vedanā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā vuccanti, ānanda, vedanā…pe… phassasamudayā…pe… khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo paṭippassaddho hoti, doso paṭippassaddho hoti, moho paṭippassaddho hotī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

264. Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. To the Venerable Ānanda, who was seated to one side, the Blessed One said this: “What, Ānanda, is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the practice that is the way leading to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification of feeling? What is the danger? What is the escape?”

“Venerable sir, for us, the teachings have the Blessed One as their root, the Blessed One as their guide, and the Blessed One as their refuge. It would be good, venerable sir, if the meaning of this utterance were to be made clear by the Blessed One himself. Having heard it from the Blessed One, the monks will remember it.”

“In that case, Ānanda, listen and pay close attention; I will speak.”

“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.

The Blessed One said this: “Ānanda, there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, Ānanda, are called feelings. … From the arising of contact … For a monk whose taints are destroyed, lust has subsided, hatred has subsided, and delusion has subsided.”

7. Paṭhamasambahulasuttaṃ

7. The First Discourse to a Number of Bhikkhus

265. Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “katamā nu kho, bhante, vedanā, katamo vedanāsamudayo, katamo vedanānirodho, katamā vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Ko vedanāya assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇa”nti? “Tisso [P 4.0222] imā, bhikkhave, vedanā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā vuccanti, bhikkhave, vedanā. Phassasamudayā [M 2.0422] vedanāsamudayo; phassanirodhā vedanānirodho. Ayameva [V 2.0218] ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi. Yaṃ vedanaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ vedanāya assādo. Yā vedanā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā, ayaṃ vedanāya ādīnavo. Yo vedanāya [T 4.0275] chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ, idaṃ vedanāya nissaraṇaṃ.

265. Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One; having approached, they paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, those bhikkhus said to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, are feelings? What is the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the path leading to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification in feeling? What is the danger in feeling? What is the escape from feeling?” “There are, bhikkhus, these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, bhikkhus, are called feelings. From the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling; from the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling. This very Noble Eightfold Path is the path leading to the cessation of feeling, that is: right view… right concentration. Whatever pleasure and joy arise in dependence on feeling, this is the gratification in feeling. That feeling is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change: this is the danger in feeling. The removal and abandoning of desire and lust for feeling: this is the escape from feeling.

“Atha kho pana, bhikkhave, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṃ nirodho akkhāto. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vācā niruddhā hoti…pe… khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo niruddho hoti, doso niruddho hoti, moho niruddho hoti. Atha kho pana, bhikkhave, mayā anupubbasaṅkhārānaṃ vūpasamo akkhāto. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vācā vūpasantā hoti…pe… khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo vūpasanto hoti, doso vūpasanto hoti, moho vūpasanto hoti. Chayimā, bhikkhave, passaddhiyo. Paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vācā paṭippassaddhā hoti. Dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa vitakkavicārā paṭippassaddhā honti. Tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa pīti paṭippassaddhā hoti. Catutthaṃ jhānaṃ samāpannassa assāsapassāsā paṭippassaddhā honti. Saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samāpannassa saññā ca vedanā ca paṭippassaddhā honti. Khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgo paṭippassaddho hoti, doso paṭippassaddho hoti, moho paṭippassaddho hotī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

“Furthermore, bhikkhus, I have declared the cessation of formations in sequence. For one who has attained the first jhāna, speech has ceased… For a bhikkhu whose cankers are destroyed, lust has ceased, hatred has ceased, delusion has ceased. Furthermore, bhikkhus, I have declared the calming of formations in sequence. For one who has attained the first jhāna, speech is calmed… For a bhikkhu whose cankers are destroyed, lust is calmed, hatred is calmed, delusion is calmed. There are, bhikkhus, these six tranquillities. For one who has attained the first jhāna, speech is tranquillized. For one who has attained the second jhāna, applied and sustained thought are tranquillized. For one who has attained the third jhāna, rapture is tranquillized. For one who has attained the fourth jhāna, in-breaths and out-breaths are tranquillized. For one who has attained the cessation of perception and feeling, perception and feeling are tranquillized. For a bhikkhu whose cankers are destroyed, lust is tranquillized, hatred is tranquillized, delusion is tranquillized.”

8. Dutiyasambahulasuttaṃ

8. The Second Discourse with a Number of Bhikkhus

266. Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu…pe… ekamantaṃ [P 4.0223] nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavā etadavoca – “katamā nu kho, bhikkhave, vedanā, katamo vedanāsamudayo, katamo [T 4.0276] vedanānirodho, katamā vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Ko vedanāya assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇa”nti? “Bhagavaṃmūlakā no, bhante, dhammā…pe…” “tisso imā, bhikkhave, vedanā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā vuccanti, bhikkhave, vedanā…pe… phassasamudayā…pe…. (Yathā purimasuttante, tathā vitthāretabbo.) [V 2.0219] Aṭṭhamaṃ.

266. Then a number of bhikkhus approached the Blessed One… Seated to one side, the Blessed One said this to those bhikkhus: “What, bhikkhus, are feelings? What is the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the path leading to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification in feeling? What is the danger in feeling? What is the escape from feeling?” “For us, venerable sir, the teachings are rooted in the Blessed One…” “There are, bhikkhus, these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, bhikkhus, are called feelings… From the arising of contact… (This should be elaborated as in the previous discourse.)

9. Pañcakaṅgasuttaṃ

9. The Discourse with Pañcakaṅga

267. Atha [M 2.0423] kho pañcakaṅgo thapati yenāyasmā udāyī tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ etadavoca – “kati nu kho, bhante udāyi, vedanā vuttā bhagavatā”ti? “Tisso kho, thapati, vedanā vuttā bhagavatā. Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā kho, thapati, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā”ti. Evaṃ vutte, pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ etadavoca – “na kho, bhante udāyi, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā. Dve vedanā vuttā bhagavatā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā. Yāyaṃ, bhante, adukkhamasukhā vedanā, santasmiṃ esā paṇīte sukhe vuttā bhagavatā”ti. Dutiyampi kho āyasmā udāyī pañcakaṅgaṃ thapatiṃ etadavoca – “na kho, thapati, dve vedanā vuttā bhagavatā. Tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā. Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā tisso vedanā [T 4.0277] vuttā bhagavatā”ti. Dutiyampi kho pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ [P 4.0224] etadavoca – “na kho, bhante udāyi, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā. Dve vedanā vuttā bhagavatā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā. Yāyaṃ, bhante, adukkhamasukhā vedanā, santasmiṃ esā paṇīte sukhe vuttā bhagavatā”ti. Tatiyampi kho [V 2.0220] āyasmā udāyī pañcakaṅgaṃ thapatiṃ etadavoca – “na kho, thapati, dve vedanā vuttā bhagavatā. Tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā. Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā”ti. Tatiyampi kho pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ etadavoca – “na kho, bhante udāyi, tisso vedanā vuttā bhagavatā. Dve vedanā vuttā bhagavatā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā. Yāyaṃ, bhante, adukkhamasukhā vedanā, santasmiṃ esā paṇīte sukhe vuttā bhagavatā”ti. Neva sakkhi āyasmā udāyī pañcakaṅgaṃ thapatiṃ saññāpetuṃ, na panāsakkhi pañcakaṅgo thapati āyasmantaṃ udāyiṃ saññāpetuṃ. Assosi kho āyasmā ānando āyasmato udāyissa pañcakaṅgena thapatinā saddhiṃ imaṃ kathāsallāpaṃ.

267. Then the carpenter Pañcakaṅga approached the Venerable Udāyī, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga said to the Venerable Udāyī: "Venerable Udāyī, how many feelings have been spoken of by the Blessed One?" "Carpenter, the Blessed One has spoken of three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, carpenter, are the three feelings that have been spoken of by the Blessed One." When this was said, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga said to the Venerable Udāyī: "Venerable Udāyī, the Blessed One has not spoken of three feelings. The Blessed One has spoken of two feelings: pleasant feeling and painful feeling. Venerable sir, this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling has been spoken of by the Blessed One as sublime and peaceful pleasure." For a second time, the Venerable Udāyī said to the carpenter Pañcakaṅga: "Carpenter, the Blessed One has not spoken of two feelings. The Blessed One has spoken of three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These are the three feelings that have been spoken of by the Blessed One." For a second time, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga said to the Venerable Udāyī: "Venerable Udāyī, the Blessed One has not spoken of three feelings. The Blessed One has spoken of two feelings: pleasant feeling and painful feeling. Venerable sir, this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling has been spoken of by the Blessed One as sublime and peaceful pleasure." For a third time, the Venerable Udāyī said to the carpenter Pañcakaṅga: "Carpenter, the Blessed One has not spoken of two feelings. The Blessed One has spoken of three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These are the three feelings that have been spoken of by the Blessed One." For a third time, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga said to the Venerable Udāyī: "Venerable Udāyī, the Blessed One has not spoken of three feelings. The Blessed One has spoken of two feelings: pleasant feeling and painful feeling. Venerable sir, this neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling has been spoken of by the Blessed One as sublime and peaceful pleasure." The Venerable Udāyī was not able to convince the carpenter Pañcakaṅga, nor was the carpenter Pañcakaṅga able to convince the Venerable Udāyī. The Venerable Ānanda heard this conversation between the Venerable Udāyī and the carpenter Pañcakaṅga.

Atha kho āyasmā ānando yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā ānando yāvatako [M 2.0424] āyasmato udāyissa pañcakaṅgena thapatinā saddhiṃ ahosi kathāsallāpo taṃ sabbaṃ bhagavato ārocesi.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda reported to the Blessed One the entire conversation that had taken place between the Venerable Udāyī and the carpenter Pañcakaṅga.

“Santameva, ānanda, pariyāyaṃ pañcakaṅgo [T 4.0278] thapati udāyissa bhikkhuno nābbhanumodi; santañca panānanda, pariyāyaṃ udāyī bhikkhu pañcakaṅgassa thapatino nābbhanumodi. Dvepi mayā, ānanda, vedanā vuttā pariyāyena. Tissopi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena. Pañcapi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena. Chapi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena. Aṭṭhārasāpi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena. Chattiṃsāpi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena. Aṭṭhasatampi [P 4.0225] mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena. Evaṃ pariyāyadesito kho, ānanda, mayā dhammo. Evaṃ pariyāyadesite kho, ānanda, mayā dhamme ye aññamaññassa subhāsitaṃ sulapitaṃ, na samanumaññissanti, na samanujānissanti, na samanumodissanti, tesaṃ etaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – bhaṇḍanajātā kalahajātā vivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ mukhasattīhi vitudantā viharissantīti viharissanti (sī. pī. ka.). Evaṃ pariyāyadesito kho, ānanda, mayā dhammo. Evaṃ pariyāyadesite kho, ānanda, mayā dhamme ye aññamaññassa subhāsitaṃ sulapitaṃ samanumaññissanti samanujānissanti samanumodissanti, tesaṃ etaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – samaggā sammodamānā avivadamānā khīrodakībhūtā aññamaññaṃ piyacakkhūhi sampassantā viharissantī”ti.

“Ānanda, the carpenter Pañcakaṅga did not approve of the monk Udāyī's valid point, and the monk Udāyī did not approve of the carpenter Pañcakaṅga's valid point. Ānanda, by way of method, I have spoken of two feelings. By way of method, I have spoken of three feelings. By way of method, I have spoken of five feelings. By way of method, I have spoken of six feelings. By way of method, I have spoken of eighteen feelings. By way of method, I have spoken of thirty-six feelings. By way of method, I have spoken of one hundred and eight feelings. Thus, Ānanda, the Dhamma has been taught by me by way of method.
