When the Dhamma has been taught by me in such a way by method, for those who do not appreciate, approve, or rejoice in what is well-spoken and well-said by one another—it is to be expected that they will live quarreling, disputing, and in conflict, wounding each other with verbal spears. Thus, Ānanda, the Dhamma has been taught by me by way of method. When the Dhamma has been taught by me in such a way by method, for those who do appreciate, approve, and rejoice in what is well-spoken and well-said by one another—it is to be expected that they will live in harmony, rejoicing together, without conflict, like milk and water blended, regarding each other with affectionate eyes.”

“Pañcime, ānanda, kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā…pe… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Ime kho, ānanda, pañca kāmaguṇā[T 4.0279]. Yaṃ kho, ānanda[V 2.0221], ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ – idaṃ vuccati kāmasukhaṃ. Ye kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘etaṃparamaṃ santaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti – idaṃ nesāhaṃ nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

“Ānanda, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure. Which five? Forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, lovely, pleasing, of a dear nature, connected with sensual craving, and arousing passion… and so on… tangible objects cognizable by the body—desirable, lovely, pleasing, of a dear nature, connected with sensual craving, and arousing passion. These, Ānanda, are the five strands of sensual pleasure. The pleasure and joy, Ānanda, that arise dependent on these five strands of sensual pleasure—this is called sensual pleasure. If anyone were to say, ‘This is the ultimate, peaceful pleasure and joy that they experience,’ I would not approve of that. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure.”

“Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca. Ye [P 4.0226] kho, ānanda, evaṃ [M 2.0425] vadeyyuṃ – ‘etaṃparamaṃ santaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti – idaṃ nesāhaṃ nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial thought and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure. Indeed, Ānanda, should any say: ‘This is the supreme, peaceful pleasure and joy that they experience,’ I do not grant this to them. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure.

“Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu, vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca. Ye kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘etaṃparamaṃ santaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti – idaṃ [T 4.0280] nesāhaṃ nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure? Here, Ānanda, with the stilling of initial and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and abides in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without initial and sustained thought, and is filled with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure. Should any say: ‘This is the supreme, peaceful pleasure and joy that they experience,’ I do not grant this to them. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure.

“Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati sato ca sampajāno, sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca. Ye kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘etaṃparamaṃ santaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti – idaṃ nesāhaṃ nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure? Here, Ānanda, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu abides equanimous, mindful, and clearly comprehending, and experiences pleasure with the body. He enters and abides in the third jhāna, of which the noble ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, he abides in pleasure.’ This, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure. Should any say: ‘This is the supreme, peaceful pleasure and joy that they experience,’ I do not grant this to them. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure.

“Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda[V 2.0222], bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā dukkhassa ca pahānā pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca. Ye kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘etaṃparamaṃ santaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti – idaṃ nesāhaṃ nānujānāmi[P 4.0227]. Taṃ kissa hetu? Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure? Here, Ānanda, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and abides in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure. Should any say: ‘This is the supreme, peaceful pleasure and joy that they experience,’ I do not grant this to them. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure.

“Katamañcānanda[T 4.0281], etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā, paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā, nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā, ‘ananto ākāso’ti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca. Ye kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘etaṃparamaṃ santaṃ [M 2.0426] sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti – idaṃ nesāhaṃ nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure? Here, Ānanda, by completely transcending perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of resistance, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, a bhikkhu, aware that ‘space is infinite,’ enters and abides in the base of the infinity of space. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure. Should any say: ‘This is the supreme, peaceful pleasure and joy that they experience,’ I do not grant this to them. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure.

“Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma, ‘anantaṃ viññāṇa’nti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca. Ye kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘etaṃparamaṃ santaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti – idaṃ nesāhaṃ nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure? Here, Ānanda, by completely transcending the base of the infinity of space, a bhikkhu, aware that ‘consciousness is infinite,’ enters and abides in the base of the infinity of consciousness. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure. Should any say: ‘This is the supreme, peaceful pleasure and joy that they experience,’ I do not grant this to them. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure.

“Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma, ‘natthi kiñcī’ti ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca[T 4.0282]. Ye kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘etaṃparamaṃ santaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti – idaṃ nesāhaṃ nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

And what, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure? Here, Ānanda, by completely transcending the base of the infinity of consciousness, a bhikkhu, aware that ‘there is nothing,’ enters and abides in the base of nothingness. This, Ānanda, is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure. Should any say: ‘This is the supreme, peaceful pleasure and joy that they experience,’ I do not grant this to them. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, there is another pleasure more excellent and more sublime than that pleasure.

“Katamañcānanda[V 2.0223], etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda[P 4.0228], etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca. Ye kho, ānanda, evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘etaṃparamaṃ santaṃ sukhaṃ somanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedentī’ti – idaṃ nesāhaṃ nānujānāmi. Taṃ kissa hetu? Atthānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

And what, Ānanda, is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than that happiness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the dimension of nothingness, enters and dwells in the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. This, indeed, Ānanda, is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than that happiness. As for those, Ānanda, who would say, ‘This is the supreme, peaceful happiness and joy that they experience,’ I do not grant them that. For what reason? Because, Ānanda, there is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than that happiness.

“Katamañcānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca? Idhānanda, bhikkhu sabbaso nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ kho, ānanda, etamhā sukhā aññaṃ sukhaṃ abhikkantatarañca paṇītatarañca.

And what, Ānanda, is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than that happiness? Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, by completely transcending the dimension of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, enters and dwells in the cessation of perception and feeling. This, indeed, Ānanda, is another happiness more excellent and more sublime than that happiness.

“Ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, ānanda, vijjati yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ samaṇo gotamo āha, tañca sukhasmiṃ [M 2.0427] paññapeti. Tayidaṃ kiṃsu, tayidaṃ kathaṃsū’ti? Evaṃvādino, ānanda, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘na kho, āvuso[T 4.0283], bhagavā sukhaññeva vedanaṃ sandhāya sukhasmiṃ paññapeti. Yattha yattha, āvuso, sukhaṃ upalabbhati, yahiṃ yahiṃ yaṃ hiyaṃ hi sukhaṃ (sī. pī.), yahiṃ yahiṃ sukhaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) ma. ni. 2.91, taṃ taṃ tathāgato sukhasmiṃ paññapetī’”ti. Navamaṃ.

Indeed, Ānanda, it is possible that wanderers of other sects might say this: ‘The ascetic Gotama speaks of the cessation of perception and feeling, and he designates it as happiness. What, now, is this? How, now, is this?’ Wanderers of other sects who speak thus, Ānanda, should be answered in this way: ‘Friends, the Blessed One does not designate it as happiness with reference only to pleasant feeling. Rather, friends, wherever happiness is obtained, in whatever place it is found, the Tathāgata designates that as happiness.’”

10. Bhikkhusuttaṃ

10. The Discourse to the Bhikkhus

268. “Dvepi mayā, bhikkhave, vedanā vuttā pariyāyena, tissopi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena, pañcapi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena, chapi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena, aṭṭhārasāpi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena, chattiṃsāpi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena, aṭṭhasatampi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena. Evaṃ pariyāyadesito, bhikkhave, mayā dhammo. Evaṃ pariyāyadesite kho, bhikkhave, mayā dhamme ye aññamaññassa subhāsitaṃ sulapitaṃ na samanumaññissanti, na samanujānissanti, na samanumodissanti, tesaṃ etaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ [P 4.0229] – bhaṇḍanajātā kalahajātā vivādāpannā aññamaññaṃ mukhasattīhi vitudantā viharissantīti. Evaṃ pariyāyadesito, bhikkhave, mayā dhammo. Evaṃ pariyāyadesite kho, bhikkhave, mayā dhamme ye aññamaññassa subhāsitaṃ sulapitaṃ samanumaññissanti samanujānissanti samanumodissanti, tesaṃ [V 2.0224] etaṃ pāṭikaṅkhaṃ – samaggā sammodamānā avivadamānā khīrodakībhūtā aññamaññaṃ piyacakkhūhi sampassantā viharissantīti.

268. “Bhikkhus, I have spoken of feelings in two ways by means of exposition; I have spoken of feelings in three ways... in five ways... in six ways... in eighteen ways... in thirty-six ways... and in one hundred and eight ways by means of exposition. Thus, Bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been taught by me discursively. When the Dhamma has been so taught by me discursively, it can be expected of those who do not delight in, approve of, or rejoice at what is well-spoken and well-said by one another that they will live quarrelsome, contentious, and given to dispute, piercing one another with the spears of their mouths. Thus, Bhikkhus, the Dhamma has been taught by me discursively. When the Dhamma has been so taught by me discursively, it can be expected of those who delight in, approve of, and rejoice at what is well-spoken and well-said by one another that they will live in concord, rejoicing, without dispute, blended like milk and water, looking upon one another with loving eyes.”

“Pañcime, bhikkhave, kāmaguṇā…pe… ṭhānaṃ kho panetaṃ, bhikkhave, vijjati yaṃ aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evaṃ vadeyyuṃ – ‘saññāvedayitanirodhaṃ [T 4.0284] samaṇo gotamo āha, tañca sukhasmiṃ paññapeti. Tayidaṃ kiṃsu, tayidaṃ kathaṃsū’ti? Evaṃvādino, bhikkhave, aññatitthiyā paribbājakā evamassu vacanīyā – ‘na kho, āvuso, bhagavā sukhaññeva vedanaṃ sandhāya sukhasmiṃ paññapeti. Yattha yattha, āvuso, sukhaṃ upalabbhati yahiṃ yahiṃ yaṃ hi yaṃ hi (sī. pī.), taṃ taṃ tathāgato sukhasmiṃ paññapetī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

“Bhikkhus, there are these five strands of sensual pleasure... It is possible, Bhikkhus, that wanderers of other sects might say this: ‘The ascetic Gotama speaks of the cessation of perception and feeling, and he designates it as happiness. What, now, is this? How, now, is this?’ Wanderers of other sects who speak thus, Bhikkhus, should be answered in this way: ‘Friends, the Blessed One does not designate it as happiness with reference only to pleasant feeling. Rather, friends, wherever happiness is obtained, in whatever place it is found, the Tathāgata designates that as happiness.’” The tenth.

Rahogatavaggo dutiyo.

The Chapter on Seclusion, the Second.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary for this chapter:

Rahogataṃ [M 2.0428] dve ākāsaṃ, agāraṃ dve ca ānandā;

Sambahulā duve vuttā, pañcakaṅgo ca bhikkhunāti.

Seclusion, two on Space, the House, and two on Ānanda; two are spoken on Many Bhikkhus, and Pañcakaṅga and the Bhikkhu.

3. Aṭṭhasatapariyāyavaggo

3. The Chapter on the Hundred and Eight Methods

1. Sīvakasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse with Sīvaka

269. Ekaṃ [T 4.0285][P 4.0230] samayaṃ bhagavā rājagahe viharati veḷuvane kalandakanivāpe. Atha kho moḷiyasīvako paribbājako yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṃ sammodi. Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho moḷiyasīvako paribbājako bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “santi, bho gotama, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘yaṃ kiñcāyaṃ purisapuggalo paṭisaṃvedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā sabbaṃ taṃ pubbekatahetū’ti. Idha idha pana (syā. kaṃ. pī. ka.) bhavaṃ gotamo kimāhā”ti?

269. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels' Feeding Place. Then the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One. Having concluded this courteous and memorable talk, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable Gotama, there are some ascetics and brahmins who have such a saying and such a view: ‘Whatever this individual person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that has past action as its cause.’ Here, what does the Venerable Gotama say?”

“Pittasamuṭṭhānānipi [V 2.0225] kho, sīvaka, idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti. Sāmampi kho etaṃ, sīvaka, veditabbaṃ evaṃ veditabbaṃ (syā. kaṃ. ka.) yathā pittasamuṭṭhānānipi idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti; lokassapi kho etaṃ, sīvaka, saccasammataṃ yathā pittasamuṭṭhānānipi idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti. Tatra, sīvaka, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘yaṃ kiñcāyaṃ purisapuggalo paṭisaṃvedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā sabbaṃ taṃ pubbekatahetū’ti. Yañca sāmaṃ ñātaṃ tañca atidhāvanti, yañca loke saccasammataṃ tañca atidhāvanti. Tasmā tesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ micchāti vadāmi.

“Sīvaka, some feelings that arise here have bile as their origin. This, Sīvaka, should be known by oneself, how some feelings that arise here have bile as their origin; and this, Sīvaka, is also acknowledged as true in the world, how some feelings that arise here have bile as their origin. In this regard, Sīvaka, those ascetics and brahmins who have such a saying and such a view: ‘Whatever this individual person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that has past action as its cause,’ they go beyond what is known by oneself, and they go beyond what is acknowledged as true in the world. Therefore, I say that those ascetics and brahmins are wrong.

“Semhasamuṭṭhānānipi kho, sīvaka…pe… vātasamuṭṭhānānipi kho, sīvaka…pe… [T 4.0286] sannipātikānipi kho, sīvaka…pe… utupariṇāmajānipi kho, sīvaka…pe… visamaparihārajānipi kho, sīvaka…pe… opakkamikānipi kho, sīvaka…pe… kammavipākajānipi [P 4.0231] kho, sīvaka, idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti. Sāmampi kho etaṃ, sīvaka, veditabbaṃ. Yathā kammavipākajānipi idhekaccāni [M 2.0429] vedayitāni uppajjanti; lokassapi kho etaṃ, sīvaka, saccasammataṃ. Yathā kammavipākajānipi idhekaccāni vedayitāni uppajjanti; tatra, sīvaka, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘yaṃ kiñcāyaṃ purisapuggalo paṭisaṃvedeti sukhaṃ vā dukkhaṃ vā adukkhamasukhaṃ vā sabbaṃ taṃ pubbekatahetū’ti. Yañca sāmaṃ ñātaṃ tañca atidhāvanti yañca loke saccasammataṃ tañca atidhāvanti. Tasmā tesaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ micchāti vadāmīti. Evaṃ vutte, moḷiyasīvako paribbājako bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – ‘abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama, abhikkantaṃ, bho gotama …pe… upāsakaṃ maṃ bhavaṃ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata’”nti.

“Sīvaka, some feelings arise from derangements of phlegm... from derangements of wind... from a combination of the humors... from changes in the seasons... from improper deportment... from assault... And some feelings, Sīvaka, arise here as the result of kamma. This, Sīvaka, should be known by oneself, how some feelings that arise here are the result of kamma; and this, Sīvaka, is also acknowledged as true in the world, how some feelings that arise here are the result of kamma. In this regard, Sīvaka, those ascetics and brahmins who have such a saying and such a view: ‘Whatever this individual person experiences—whether pleasure, pain, or neither-pain-nor-pleasure—all that has past action as its cause,’ they go beyond what is known by oneself, and they go beyond what is acknowledged as true in the world. Therefore, I say that those ascetics and brahmins are wrong.” When this was said, the wanderer Moḷiyasīvaka said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, Venerable Gotama! Excellent, Venerable Gotama! From this day forth, may the Venerable Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”

“Pittaṃ semhañca vāto ca, sannipātā utūni ca;

Visamaṃ opakkamikaṃ, kammavipākena aṭṭhamī”ti. paṭhamaṃ;

“Bile, phlegm, and wind, their combination and the seasons, improper deportment, assault, and with the result of kamma as the eighth.”

2. Aṭṭhasatasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on the One Hundred and Eight

270. “Aṭṭhasatapariyāyaṃ vo, bhikkhave, dhammapariyāyaṃ desessāmi. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamo [V 2.0226] ca, bhikkhave, aṭṭhasatapariyāyo, dhammapariyāyo? Dvepi mayā, bhikkhave, vedanā vuttā pariyāyena; tissopi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena; pañcapi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena; chapi [T 4.0287] mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena; aṭṭhārasāpi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena; chattiṃsāpi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena; aṭṭhasatampi mayā vedanā vuttā pariyāyena. “Katamā ca, bhikkhave, dve vedanā? Kāyikā ca cetasikā ca – imā vuccanti, bhikkhave, dve vedanā. Katamā [P 4.0232] ca, bhikkhave, tisso vedanā? Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā vuccanti, bhikkhave, tisso vedanā. Katamā ca, bhikkhave, pañca vedanā? Sukhindriyaṃ, dukkhindriyaṃ, somanassindriyaṃ, domanassindriyaṃ, upekkhindriyaṃ – imā vuccanti, bhikkhave, pañca vedanā. Katamā ca, bhikkhave, cha vedanā? Cakkhusamphassajā vedanā…pe… manosamphassajā vedanā – imā vuccanti, bhikkhave, cha vedanā. Katamā ca, bhikkhave, aṭṭhārasa vedanā? Cha somanassūpavicārā, cha domanassūpavicārā, cha upekkhūpavicārā – imā vuccanti, bhikkhave, aṭṭhārasa vedanā. Katamā ca, bhikkhave, chattiṃsa vedanā? Cha gehasitāni gehassitāni (aṭṭha.) somanassāni, cha nekkhammasitāni nekkhammassitāni (aṭṭha.) somanassāni, cha gehasitāni domanassāni, cha nekkhammasitāni [M 2.0430] domanassāni, cha gehasitā upekkhā[T 4.0288], cha nekkhammasitā upekkhā – imā vuccanti, bhikkhave, chattiṃsa vedanā. Katamañca, bhikkhave, aṭṭhasataṃ vedanā? Atītā chattiṃsa vedanā, anāgatā chattiṃsa vedanā, paccuppannā chattiṃsa vedanā – imā vuccanti, bhikkhave, aṭṭhasataṃ vedanā. Ayaṃ, bhikkhave, aṭṭhasatapariyāyo dhammapariyāyo”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

270. “Monks, I will teach you the exposition of the Dhamma with one hundred and eight aspects. Listen to it. And what, monks, is the exposition of the Dhamma with one hundred and eight aspects? By a method, monks, I have taught two feelings; by a method, I have taught three feelings; by a method, I have taught five feelings; by a method, I have taught six feelings; by a method, I have taught eighteen feelings; by a method, I have taught thirty-six feelings; by a method, I have taught one hundred and eight feelings. And what, monks, are the two feelings? Physical and mental—these, monks, are called the two feelings. And what, monks, are the three feelings? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling—these, monks, are called the three feelings. And what, monks, are the five feelings? The faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of displeasure, and the faculty of equanimity—these, monks, are called the five feelings. And what, monks, are the six feelings? Feeling born of eye-contact… feeling born of mind-contact—these, monks, are called the six feelings. And what, monks, are the eighteen feelings? Six examinations of joy, six examinations of displeasure, and six examinations of equanimity—these, monks, are called the eighteen feelings. And what, monks, are the thirty-six feelings? Six joys based on the household life, six joys based on renunciation, six displeasures based on the household life, six displeasures based on renunciation, six equanimities based on the household life, and six equanimities based on renunciation—these, monks, are called the thirty-six feelings. And what, monks, are the one hundred and eight feelings? The thirty-six feelings of the past, the thirty-six feelings of the future, and the thirty-six feelings of the present—these, monks, are called the one hundred and eight feelings. This, monks, is the exposition of the Dhamma with one hundred and eight aspects.”

3. Aññatarabhikkhusuttaṃ

3. A Certain Monk

271. Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “katamā nu kho, bhante, vedanā, katamo vedanāsamudayo, katamā vedanāsamudayagāminī paṭipadā? Katamo vedanānirodho, katamā vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Ko vedanāya assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇa”nti?

271. Then a certain monk approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, that monk said to the Blessed One: “What, venerable sir, is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the path leading to the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the path leading to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification in feeling, what is the danger, and what is the escape?”

“Tisso [P 4.0233] imā, bhikkhu, vedanā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Imā vuccanti, bhikkhu, vedanā. Phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayo. Taṇhā vedanāsamudayagāminī [V 2.0227] paṭipadā. Phassanirodhā vedanānirodho. Ayameva ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā, seyyathidaṃ – sammādiṭṭhi…pe… sammāsamādhi. Yaṃ vedanaṃ paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, ayaṃ vedanāya assādo; yā vedanā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā, ayaṃ vedanāya ādīnavo; yo vedanāya chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ, idaṃ vedanāya nissaraṇa”nti. Tatiyaṃ.

“Monk, there are these three feelings—pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These are called feelings, monk. With the arising of contact comes the arising of feeling. Craving is the path leading to the arising of feeling. With the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling. This Noble Eightfold Path itself is the path leading to the cessation of feeling, that is—right view… right concentration. Whatever pleasure and joy arise dependent on feeling, this is the gratification in feeling. That feeling is impermanent, unsatisfactory, and subject to change—this is the danger in feeling. The subduing of desire and lust for feeling, the abandoning of desire and lust—this is the escape from feeling.”

4. Pubbasuttaṃ

4. Before

272. “Pubbeva [T 4.0289] me, bhikkhave, sambodhā anabhisambuddhassa bodhisattasseva sato etadahosi – ‘katamā nu kho vedanā, katamo vedanāsamudayo, katamā vedanāsamudayagāminī paṭipadā, katamo vedanānirodho, katamā vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Ko vedanāya assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇa’nti? Tassa mayhaṃ, bhikkhave, etadahosi – ‘tisso imā vedanā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Imā vuccanti vedanā. Phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayo. Taṇhā vedanāsamudayagāminī paṭipadā…pe… yo vedanāya chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ. Idaṃ vedanāya nissaraṇa’”nti. Catutthaṃ.

272. “Monks, before my awakening, while I was still an unawakened Bodhisatta, this thought occurred to me: ‘What is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the practice leading to the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the practice leading to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification in feeling, what is the danger, and what is the escape?’ Then, monks, this thought occurred to me: ‘There are these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These are called feelings. From the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling. Craving is the practice leading to the origin of feeling… Whatever is the removal of desire and lust, the abandoning of desire and lust for feeling, this is the escape from feeling.’” The Fourth.

5. Ñāṇasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Knowledge

273. “‘Imā [M 2.0431] vedanā’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādi. ‘Ayaṃ vedanāsamudayo’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi…pe… āloko udapādi. ‘Ayaṃ vedanāsamudayagāminī paṭipadā’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi…pe… ‘ayaṃ vedanānirodho’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi [V 2.0228] …pe… ‘ayaṃ [P 4.0234] vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi…pe… ‘ayaṃ vedanāya assādo’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu…pe… [T 4.0290] ‘ayaṃ vedanāya ādīnavo’ti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu…pe… ‘idaṃ kho nissaraṇa’nti me, bhikkhave, pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu cakkhuṃ udapādi, ñāṇaṃ udapādi, paññā udapādi, vijjā udapādi, āloko udapādī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

273. “Monks, concerning things unheard before, vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge, and light arose regarding the truth: ‘These are feelings.’ … ‘This is the origin of feeling.’ … ‘This is the practice leading to the origin of feeling.’ … ‘This is the cessation of feeling.’ … ‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of feeling.’ … ‘This is the gratification in feeling.’ … ‘This is the danger in feeling.’ … Regarding the truth: ‘This indeed is the escape,’ vision arose in me, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true knowledge, and light arose.” The Fifth.

6. Sambahulabhikkhusuttaṃ

6. The Discourse to a Number of Monks

274. Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṃsu; upasaṅkamitvā…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ etadavocuṃ – “katamā nu kho, bhante, vedanā, katamo vedanāsamudayo, katamā vedanāsamudayagāminī paṭipadā? Katamo vedanānirodho, katamā vedanānirodhagāminī paṭipadā? Ko vedanāya assādo, ko ādīnavo, kiṃ nissaraṇa”nti? “Tisso imā, bhikkhave, vedanā – sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Imā vuccanti, bhikkhave, vedanā. Phassasamudayā vedanāsamudayo. Taṇhā vedanāsamudayagāminī paṭipadā. Phassanirodhā…pe… yo vedanāya chandarāgavinayo chandarāgappahānaṃ. Idaṃ vedanāya nissaraṇa”nti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

274. Then a number of monks approached the Blessed One… Seated to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, what is feeling? What is the origin of feeling? What is the practice leading to the origin of feeling? What is the cessation of feeling? What is the practice leading to the cessation of feeling? What is the gratification in feeling, what is the danger, and what is the escape?” “Monks, there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, monks, are called feelings. From the arising of contact, there is the arising of feeling. Craving is the practice leading to the origin of feeling. From the cessation of contact… Whatever is the removal of desire and lust, the abandoning of desire and lust for feeling, this is the escape from feeling.” The Sixth.

7. Paṭhamasamaṇabrāhmaṇasuttaṃ

7. The First Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins

275. “Tisso imā, bhikkhave, vedanā. Katamā tisso? Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā [M 2.0432] vā brāhmaṇā vā imāsaṃ tissannaṃ vedanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti. Na me te, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samaṇesu vā samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu [V 2.0229] vā brāhmaṇasammatā, na ca pana te āyasmanto sāmaññatthaṃ vā brahmaññatthaṃ vā diṭṭheva [T 4.0291] dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharanti. Ye ca kho keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā imāsaṃ tissannaṃ vedanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavaṃ ca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ pajānanti. Te kho me, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā samaṇesu ceva samaṇasammatā brāhmaṇesu ca brāhmaṇasammatā. Te ca panāyasmanto sāmaññatthañca brahmaññatthañca, diṭṭheva dhamme sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

275. “Monks, there are these three feelings. Which three? A pleasant feeling, a painful feeling, and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as it really is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape concerning these three feelings—I do not consider them to be ascetics among ascetics or brahmins among brahmins, and those venerable ones do not, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life, enter upon and dwell in the goal of asceticism or the goal of the brahmin life. But, monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins do understand as it really is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape concerning these three feelings—I consider them to be ascetics among ascetics and brahmins among brahmins, and those venerable ones, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life, enter upon and dwell in the goal of asceticism and the goal of the brahmin life.” Seventh.

8. Dutiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasuttaṃ

8. The Second Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins

276. “Tisso [P 4.0235] imā, bhikkhave, vedanā. Katamā tisso? Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā. Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā imāsaṃ tissannaṃ vedanānaṃ samudayañca atthaṅgamañca assādañca ādīnavañca nissaraṇañca yathābhūtaṃ nappajānanti…pe… pajānanti…pe… sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

276. “Monks, there are these three feelings. Which three? A pleasant feeling, a painful feeling, and a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand as it really is the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape concerning these three feelings… (this should be elaborated as in the preceding discourse) …and those venerable ones, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life, enter upon and dwell in the goal of asceticism and the goal of the brahmin life.” Eighth.

9. Tatiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasuttaṃ

9. The Third Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins

277. “Ye hi keci, bhikkhave, samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā vedanaṃ nappajānanti, vedanāsamudayaṃ nappajānanti, vedanānirodhaṃ nappajānanti, vedanānirodhagāminiṃ paṭipadaṃ nappajānanti…pe… pajānanti…pe… sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā upasampajja viharantī”ti. Navamaṃ.

277. “Monks, whatever ascetics or brahmins do not understand feeling, do not understand the origin of feeling, do not understand the cessation of feeling, do not understand the practice leading to the cessation of feeling… (this should be elaborated as in the first discourse on ascetics and brahmins) …and those venerable ones, having realized it for themselves with direct knowledge in this very life, enter upon and dwell in the goal of asceticism and the goal of the brahmin life.” Ninth.

10. Suddhikasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on the Simple

278. “Tisso [V 2.0230] imā, bhikkhave, vedanā. Katamā tisso? Sukhā vedanā, dukkhā vedanā, adukkhamasukhā vedanā – imā kho, bhikkhave, tisso [T 4.0292] vedanā”ti. Dasamaṃ.

278. “Monks, there are these three feelings. What three? Pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. These, monks, are the three feelings.” The tenth.

11. Nirāmisasuttaṃ

11. The Discourse on the Spiritual

279. “Atthi[M 2.0433], bhikkhave, sāmisā pīti, atthi nirāmisā pīti, atthi nirāmisā nirāmisatarā pīti; atthi sāmisaṃ sukhaṃ, atthi nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ, atthi nirāmisā nirāmisataraṃ sukhaṃ; atthi sāmisā upekkhā, atthi nirāmisā upekkhā, atthi nirāmisā nirāmisatarā upekkhā; atthi sāmiso vimokkho, atthi nirāmiso vimokkho, atthi nirāmisā nirāmisataro vimokkho. Katamā ca, bhikkhave, sāmisā pīti? Pañcime, bhikkhave, kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā…pe… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Ime kho, bhikkhave, pañca kāmaguṇā. Yā kho, bhikkhave, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati pīti, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sāmisā pīti.

279. “Bhikkhus, there is worldly joy, there is unworldly joy, and there is a joy more unworldly still; there is worldly pleasure, there is unworldly pleasure, and there is a pleasure more unworldly still; there is worldly equanimity, there is unworldly equanimity, and there is an equanimity more unworldly still; there is worldly liberation, there is unworldly liberation, and there is a liberation more unworldly still. And what, bhikkhus, is worldly joy? There are these five cords of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing… and so on… tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing. These, bhikkhus, are the five cords of sensual pleasure. The joy that arises in dependence on these five cords of sensual pleasure—this, bhikkhus, is called worldly joy.

“Katamā [P 4.0236] ca, bhikkhave, nirāmisā pīti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, nirāmisā pīti.

“And what, bhikkhus, is unworldly joy? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial application and sustained application, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. With the stilling of initial application and sustained application, he enters and abides in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without initial application and sustained application, and has rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called unworldly joy.

“Katamā [T 4.0293] ca, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisatarā pīti? Yā kho, bhikkhave, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ paccavekkhato, dosā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ paccavekkhato, mohā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ paccavekkhato uppajjati pīti, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisatarā pīti.

“And what, bhikkhus, is the joy that is more unworldly still? Whatever joy arises for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed when he reviews his mind as liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, and liberated from delusion—this, bhikkhus, is called the joy that is more unworldly still.

“Katamañca[V 2.0231], bhikkhave, sāmisaṃ sukhaṃ? Pañcime, bhikkhave, kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā…pe… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Ime kho, bhikkhave, pañca kāmaguṇā. Yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sāmisaṃ sukhaṃ.

“And what, bhikkhus, is worldly pleasure? There are these five cords of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing… and so on… tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing. These, bhikkhus, are the five cords of sensual pleasure. Whatever pleasure and mental joy arise in dependence on these five cords of sensual pleasure—this, bhikkhus, is called worldly pleasure.

“Katamañca[M 2.0434], bhikkhave, nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Vitakkavicārānaṃ vūpasamā ajjhattaṃ sampasādanaṃ cetaso ekodibhāvaṃ avitakkaṃ avicāraṃ samādhijaṃ pītisukhaṃ dutiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Pītiyā ca virāgā upekkhako ca viharati sato ca sampajāno sukhañca kāyena paṭisaṃvedeti, yaṃ taṃ ariyā ācikkhanti – ‘upekkhako satimā sukhavihārī’ti tatiyaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, nirāmisaṃ sukhaṃ.

“And what, bhikkhus, is unworldly pleasure? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states… enters and abides in the first jhāna… he enters and abides in the second jhāna. With the fading away of rapture, he abides in equanimity, and mindful and clearly comprehending, he experiences pleasure with the body. He enters and abides in the third jhāna, of which the Noble Ones declare: ‘Equanimous and mindful, he abides in pleasure.’ This, bhikkhus, is called unworldly pleasure.

“Katamañca, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisataraṃ sukhaṃ? Yaṃ kho, bhikkhave, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ paccavekkhato, dosā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ paccavekkhato[P 4.0237], mohā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ paccavekkhato uppajjati [T 4.0294] sukhaṃ somanassaṃ, idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisataraṃ sukhaṃ.

“And what, bhikkhus, is the pleasure that is more unworldly still? Whatever pleasure and mental joy arise for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed when he reviews his mind as liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, and liberated from delusion—this, bhikkhus, is called the pleasure that is more unworldly still.

“Katamā ca, bhikkhave, sāmisā upekkhā? Pañcime, bhikkhave, kāmaguṇā. Katame pañca? Cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā…pe… kāyaviññeyyā phoṭṭhabbā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā. Ime kho, bhikkhave, pañca kāmaguṇā. Yā kho, bhikkhave, ime pañca kāmaguṇe paṭicca uppajjati upekkhā, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, sāmisā upekkhā.

“And what, bhikkhus, is worldly equanimity? There are these five cords of sensual pleasure. What five? Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing… and so on… tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and enticing. These, bhikkhus, are the five cords of sensual pleasure. The equanimity that arises in dependence on these five cords of sensual pleasure—this, bhikkhus, is called worldly equanimity.

“Katamā ca, bhikkhave, nirāmisā upekkhā? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu sukhassa ca pahānā, dukkhassa ca pahānā, pubbeva somanassadomanassānaṃ atthaṅgamā, adukkhamasukhaṃ upekkhāsatipārisuddhiṃ [V 2.0232] catutthaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, nirāmisā upekkhā.

“And what, bhikkhus, is unworldly equanimity? Here, bhikkhus, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous passing away of joy and sorrow, a bhikkhu enters and abides in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity. This, bhikkhus, is called unworldly equanimity.

“Katamā ca, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisatarā upekkhā? Yā kho, bhikkhave, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ paccavekkhato, dosā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ paccavekkhato, mohā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ paccavekkhato uppajjati upekkhā, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisatarā upekkhā.

“And what, bhikkhus, is the equanimity that is more unworldly still? Whatever equanimity arises for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed when he reviews his mind as liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, and liberated from delusion—this, bhikkhus, is called the equanimity that is more unworldly still.

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, sāmiso vimokkho? Rūpappaṭisaṃyutto vimokkho sāmiso vimokkho.

“And what, bhikkhus, is worldly liberation? Liberation connected with form is worldly liberation.

“Katamo [M 2.0435] ca, bhikkhave, nirāmiso vimokkho? Arūpappaṭisaṃyutto vimokkho nirāmiso vimokkho.

“And what, bhikkhus, is unworldly liberation? Liberation connected with the formless is unworldly liberation.

“Katamo [T 4.0295] ca, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisataro vimokkho? Yo kho, bhikkhave, khīṇāsavassa bhikkhuno rāgā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ paccavekkhato, dosā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ paccavekkhato, mohā cittaṃ vimuttaṃ paccavekkhato uppajjati vimokkho, ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, nirāmisā nirāmisataro vimokkho”ti. Ekādasamaṃ.

“And what, bhikkhus, is the liberation that is more unworldly still? Whatever liberation arises for a bhikkhu whose taints are destroyed when he reviews his mind as liberated from lust, liberated from hatred, and liberated from delusion—this, bhikkhus, is called the liberation that is more unworldly still.”

Aṭṭhasatapariyāyavaggo tatiyo.

The Chapter of the One Hundred and Eight Ways, the third.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Sīvakaaṭṭhasataṃ [P 4.0238] bhikkhu, pubbe ñāṇañca bhikkhunā;

Samaṇabrāhmaṇā tīṇi, suddhikañca nirāmisanti.

Sīvaka, Aṭṭhasata, Bhikkhu; three Pubbeñāṇa and Bhikkhunā; three Samaṇabrāhmaṇa; Suddhika and Nirāmisa.

Vedanāsaṃyuttaṃ samattaṃ.

The Connected Discourses on Feeling is completed.

3. Mātugāmasaṃyuttaṃ

3. The Connected Discourses on Womankind

1. Paṭhamapeyyālavaggo

1. The First Chapter of Repetitions

1. Mātugāmasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on Womankind

280. “Pañcahi[T 4.0296][V 2.0233][M 2.0436], bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgato mātugāmo ekantaamanāpo hoti purisassa. Katamehi pañcahi? Na ca rūpavā hoti, na ca bhogavā hoti, na ca sīlavā hoti, alaso ca hoti, pajañcassa na labhati – imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahi aṅgehi samannāgato mātugāmo ekantaamanāpo hoti purisassa. Pañcahi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgato mātugāmo ekantamanāpo hoti purisassa. Katamehi pañcahi? Rūpavā ca hoti, bhogavā ca hoti, sīlavā ca hoti, dakkho ca hoti analaso, pajañcassa labhati – imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahi aṅgehi samannāgato mātugāmo ekantamanāpo hoti purisassā”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

280. “Bhikkhus, a woman endowed with five qualities is entirely displeasing to a man. What five? She is not beautiful, she is not wealthy, she is not virtuous, she is lazy, and she does not bear him offspring. These, bhikkhus, are the five qualities with which a woman is endowed that make her entirely displeasing to a man. Bhikkhus, a woman endowed with five qualities is entirely pleasing to a man. What five? She is beautiful, she is wealthy, she is virtuous, she is skillful and not lazy, and she bears him offspring. These, bhikkhus, are the five qualities with which a woman is endowed that make her entirely pleasing to a man.”

2. Purisasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on a Man

281. “Pañcahi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgato puriso ekantaamanāpo hoti mātugāmassa. Katamehi pañcahi? Na ca rūpavā hoti, na ca bhogavā hoti, na ca sīlavā hoti, alaso ca hoti, pajañcassa na labhati – imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahi [P 4.0239] aṅgehi samannāgato puriso ekantaamanāpo hoti mātugāmassa. Pañcahi, bhikkhave, aṅgehi samannāgato puriso ekantamanāpo hoti mātugāmassa. Katamehi pañcahi? Rūpavā ca hoti, bhogavā ca hoti, sīlavā ca hoti, dakkho ca hoti analaso, pajañcassa labhati – imehi [V 2.0234] kho, bhikkhave, pañcahi aṅgehi samannāgato puriso [T 4.0297] ekantamanāpo hoti mātugāmassā”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

281. “Bhikkhus, a man endowed with five qualities is entirely displeasing to a woman. What five? He is not handsome, he is not wealthy, he is not virtuous, he is lazy, and he does not beget her offspring. These, bhikkhus, are the five qualities with which a man is endowed that make him entirely displeasing to a woman. Bhikkhus, a man endowed with five qualities is entirely pleasing to a woman. What five? He is handsome, he is wealthy, he is virtuous, he is skillful and not lazy, and he begets her offspring. These, bhikkhus, are the five qualities with which a man is endowed that make him entirely pleasing to a woman.”

3. Āveṇikadukkhasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on Sufferings Peculiar to Women

282. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, mātugāmassa āveṇikāni dukkhāni, yāni mātugāmo paccanubhoti, aññatreva purisehi. Katamāni pañca? Idha, bhikkhave[M 2.0437], mātugāmo daharova samāno patikulaṃ gacchati, ñātakehi vinā hoti. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, mātugāmassa paṭhamaṃ āveṇikaṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ mātugāmo paccanubhoti, aññatreva purisehi. Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, mātugāmo utunī hoti. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, mātugāmassa dutiyaṃ āveṇikaṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ mātugāmo paccanubhoti, aññatreva purisehi. Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, mātugāmo gabbhinī hoti. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, mātugāmassa tatiyaṃ āveṇikaṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ mātugāmo paccanubhoti, aññatreva purisehi. Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, mātugāmo vijāyati. Idaṃ, bhikkhave, mātugāmassa catutthaṃ āveṇikaṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ mātugāmo paccanubhoti, aññatreva purisehi. Puna caparaṃ, bhikkhave, mātugāmo purisassa pāricariyaṃ upeti. Idaṃ kho, bhikkhave, mātugāmassa pañcamaṃ āveṇikaṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ mātugāmo paccanubhoti, aññatreva purisehi. Imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañca mātugāmassa āveṇikāni dukkhāni, yāni mātugāmo paccanubhoti, aññatreva purisehī”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

282. “Bhikkhus, there are these five sufferings peculiar to a woman, which a woman experiences apart from men. What five? Here, bhikkhus, a woman, while still young, goes to her husband’s family and is separated from her relatives. This, bhikkhus, is the first suffering peculiar to a woman, which a woman experiences apart from men. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a woman menstruates. This, bhikkhus, is the second suffering peculiar to a woman, which a woman experiences apart from men. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a woman becomes pregnant. This, bhikkhus, is the third suffering peculiar to a woman, which a woman experiences apart from men. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a woman gives birth. This, bhikkhus, is the fourth suffering peculiar to a woman, which a woman experiences apart from men. Furthermore, bhikkhus, a woman attends upon a man. This, bhikkhus, is the fifth suffering peculiar to a woman, which a woman experiences apart from men. These, bhikkhus, are the five sufferings peculiar to a woman, which a woman experiences apart from men.”

4. Tīhidhammehisuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on Three Things

283. “Tīhi[T 4.0298][P 4.0240], bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo yebhuyyena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi tīhi? Idha, bhikkhave, mātugāmo pubbaṇhasamayaṃ maccheramalapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā agāraṃ ajjhāvasati. Majjhanhikasamayaṃ issāpariyuṭṭhitena cetasā agāraṃ ajjhāvasati. Sāyanhasamayaṃ kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhitena cetasā agāraṃ ajjhāvasati. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, tīhi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo yebhuyyena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

283. “Bhikkhus, endowed with three things, a woman, for the most part, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. With what three? Here, bhikkhus, a woman dwells at home in the morning with a mind overcome by the stain of stinginess. At midday, she dwells at home with a mind overcome by jealousy. In the evening, she dwells at home with a mind overcome by sensual lust. Bhikkhus, endowed with these three things, a woman, for the most part, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell.”

5. Kodhanasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on the Wrathful

284. Atha [V 2.0235] kho āyasmā anuruddho yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā anuruddho bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “idhāhaṃ, bhante, mātugāmaṃ passāmi dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjantaṃ. Katīhi nu kho, bhante, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo [M 2.0438] kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjatī”ti?

284. Then the Venerable Anuruddha approached the Blessed One; having approached, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Anuruddha said to the Blessed One: ‘Here, venerable sir, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing the human, I see a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, being reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. Endowed with how many qualities, venerable sir, does a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, get reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell?’”

“Pañcahi kho, anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho ca hoti, ahiriko ca hoti, anottappī ca hoti, kodhano ca hoti, duppañño ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato [P 4.0241] mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

“Endowed with five qualities, Anuruddha, a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. What five? She is faithless, shameless, reckless, wrathful, and unwise. Endowed with these five qualities, Anuruddha, a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell.”

6. Upanāhīsuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on the Resentful

285. “Pañcahi[T 4.0299], anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho ca hoti, ahiriko ca hoti, anottappī ca hoti, upanāhī ca hoti, duppañño ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

285. 'Anuruddha, a woman endowed with five qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. What five? She is faithless, shameless, without fear of wrongdoing, harbors resentment, and is unwise. Anuruddha, a woman endowed with these five qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell.' The sixth.

7. Issukīsuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on Envy

286. “Pañcahi, anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho ca hoti, ahiriko ca hoti, anottappī ca hoti, issukī ca hoti, duppañño ca hoti – imehi kho[V 2.0236], anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

286. 'Anuruddha, a woman endowed with five qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. What five? She is faithless, shameless, without fear of wrongdoing, is envious, and is unwise. Anuruddha, a woman endowed with these five qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell.' The seventh.

8. Maccharīsuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on Miserliness

287. “Pañcahi, anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho ca hoti, ahiriko ca hoti, anottappī ca hoti, maccharī ca hoti, duppañño ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi [M 2.0439] dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo…pe… apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

287. 'Anuruddha, a woman endowed with five qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. What five? She is faithless, shameless, without fear of wrongdoing, is miserly, and is unwise. Anuruddha, a woman endowed with these five qualities... and so on... is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell.' The eighth.

9. Aticārīsuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on Adultery

288. “Pañcahi[T 4.0300][P 4.0242], anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo…pe… apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho ca hoti, ahiriko ca hoti, anottappī ca hoti, aticārī ca hoti, duppañño ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo…pe… upapajjatī”ti. Navamaṃ.

288. 'Anuruddha, a woman endowed with five qualities... and so on... is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell. What five? She is faithless, shameless, without fear of wrongdoing, is adulterous, and is unwise. Anuruddha, a woman endowed with these five qualities... and so on... is reborn.' The ninth.

10. Dussīlasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on Immorality

289. “Pañcahi, anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo…pe… nirayaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho ca hoti, ahiriko ca hoti, anottappī ca hoti, dussīlo ca hoti, duppañño ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo…pe… nirayaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

289. 'Anuruddha, a woman endowed with five qualities... and so on... is reborn in hell. What five? She is faithless, shameless, without fear of wrongdoing, is immoral, and is unwise. Anuruddha, a woman endowed with these five qualities... and so on... is reborn in hell.' The tenth.

11. Appassutasuttaṃ

11. The Discourse on Being Unlearned

290. “Pañcahi, anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo…pe… nirayaṃ upapajjati[V 2.0237]. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho ca hoti, ahiriko ca hoti, anottappī ca hoti, appassuto ca hoti, duppañño ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo…pe… nirayaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Ekādasamaṃ.

290. 'Anuruddha, a woman endowed with five qualities... and so on... is reborn in hell. What five? She is faithless, shameless, without fear of wrongdoing, is unlearned, and is unwise. Anuruddha, a woman endowed with these five qualities... and so on... is reborn in hell.' The eleventh.

12. Kusītasuttaṃ

12. The Discourse on Laziness

291. “Pañcahi, anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo…pe… nirayaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho ca hoti, ahiriko ca hoti, anottappī ca hoti, kusīto ca hoti, duppañño ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo…pe… [T 4.0301] apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Dvādasamaṃ.

291. 'Anuruddha, a woman endowed with five qualities... and so on... is reborn in hell. What five? She is faithless, shameless, without fear of wrongdoing, is lazy, and is unwise. Anuruddha, a woman endowed with these five qualities... and so on... is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell.' The twelfth.

13. Muṭṭhassatisuttaṃ

13. The Discourse on Lapsed Mindfulness

292. “Pañcahi[M 2.0440], anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo…pe… nirayaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Assaddho [P 4.0243] ca hoti, ahiriko ca hoti, anottappī ca hoti, muṭṭhassati ca hoti, duppañño ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo…pe… nirayaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Terasamaṃ.

292. 'Anuruddha, a woman endowed with five qualities... and so on... is reborn in hell. What five? She is faithless, shameless, without fear of wrongdoing, is of lapsed mindfulness, and is unwise. Anuruddha, a woman endowed with these five qualities... and so on... is reborn in hell.' The thirteenth.

14. Pañcaverasuttaṃ

14. The Discourse on the Five Enmities

293. “Pañcahi, anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo…pe… nirayaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Pāṇātipātī ca hoti, adinnādāyī ca hoti, kāmesumicchācārī ca hoti, musāvādī ca hoti, surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhāyī ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Cuddasamaṃ.

293. 'Anuruddha, a woman endowed with five qualities... and so on... is reborn in hell. What five? She is one who takes life, one who takes what is not given, one who engages in sexual misconduct, one who speaks falsehoods, and one who partakes of intoxicating drinks and spirits which are the cause of heedlessness. Anuruddha, a woman endowed with these five qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a place of ruin, in hell.' The fourteenth.

Paṭhamapeyyālavaggo.

The First Chapter of Abbreviated Texts.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary:

Mātugāmo [V 2.0238] puriso ca, āveṇikā tidhammo ca dve manāpāmanāpāca, āveṇikā tīhi anuruddho (sabbattha);

Kodhano upanāhī ca, issukī maccharena ca;

Aticārī ca dussīlo, appassuto ca kusīto;

Muṭṭhassati pañcaveraṃ, kaṇhapakkhe pakāsito.

A woman and a man, exclusive qualities, and three qualities; Angry and bearing resentment, envious and avaricious; Unfaithful and immoral, unlearned and lazy; Of lapsed mindfulness, with the five enmities—these are declared in the dark section.

2. Dutiyapeyyālavaggo

2. The Second Chapter of Abbreviated Texts

1. Akkodhanasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on Non-Anger

294. Atha kho āyasmā anuruddho yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā…pe… ekamantaṃ nisinno kho āyasmā anuruddho bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “idhāhaṃ, bhante, mātugāmaṃ passāmi dibbena cakkhunā visuddhena atikkantamānusakena [M 2.0441] kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjantaṃ. Katīhi nu kho, bhante, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjatī”ti?

294. Then the Venerable Anuruddha approached the Blessed One; having approached... and so on... having sat down to one side, the Venerable Anuruddha said this to the Blessed One: ‘Venerable Sir, here I see with the divine eye, which is purified and surpasses that of humans, a woman being reborn, with the breakup of the body, after death, in a good destination, a heavenly world. Venerable Sir, endowed with how many qualities is a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world?’”

“Pañcahi [T 4.0302] kho, anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Saddho ca hoti, hirimā ca hoti, ottappī ca hoti, akkodhano ca hoti, paññavā ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo [P 4.0244] kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“Indeed, Anuruddha, a woman endowed with five qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. With which five? She has faith, has a sense of shame, has fear of wrongdoing, is not angry, and has wisdom. Indeed, Anuruddha, endowed with these five qualities, a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.” First.

2. Anupanāhīsuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on Non-Resentment

295. “Pañcahi, anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Saddho ca hoti, hirimā ca hoti, ottappī [V 2.0239] ca hoti, anupanāhī ca hoti, paññavā ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

295. “Anuruddha, a woman endowed with five qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. With which five? She has faith, she has a sense of shame, she has a sense of moral dread, she is not resentful, and she is wise. Indeed, Anuruddha, a woman endowed with these five qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.” The second.

3. Anissukīsuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on Non-Envy

296. “Pañcahi, anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Saddho ca hoti, hirimā ca hoti, ottappī ca hoti, anissukī ca hoti, paññavā ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

296. “Anuruddha, a woman endowed with five qualities, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. With which five? She has faith, she has a sense of shame, she has a sense of moral dread, she is not envious, and she is wise. Indeed, Anuruddha, endowed with these five qualities, a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.” The third.

4. Amaccharīsuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on Non-Avarice

297. Amaccharī ca hoti, paññavā ca hoti…pe…. Catutthaṃ.

297. She is not avaricious and is wise… and so on…. The fourth.

5. Anaticārīsuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Non-Transgression

298. Anaticārī ca hoti, paññavā ca hoti…pe…. Pañcamaṃ.

298. She does not transgress against her husband and is wise… and so on…. The fifth.

6. Susīlasuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Good Moral Conduct

299. Sīlavā ca hoti, paññavā ca hoti…pe…. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

299. She is virtuous and wise… and so on…. The sixth.

7. Bahussutasuttaṃ

7. The Discourse on Being Learned

300. Bahussuto [M 2.0442] ca hoti, paññavā ca hoti…pe…. Sattamaṃ.

300. She is learned and wise… and so on…. The seventh.

8. Āraddhavīriyasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on Aroused Energy

301. Āraddhavīriyo [V 2.0240] ca hoti, paññavā ca hoti…pe…. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

301. She has aroused energy and wise… and so on…. The eighth.

9. Upaṭṭhitassatisuttaṃ

9. The Discourse on Established Mindfulness

302. “Upaṭṭhitassati [P 4.0245] ca [T 4.0303] hoti, paññavā ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Navamaṃ.

302. ‘She has established mindfulness and is wise—endowed with these five qualities, Anuruddha, a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.’ The ninth.

Ime aṭṭha suttantasaṅkhepā.

These eight are summaries of the discourses.

10. Pañcasīlasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on the Five Precepts

303. “Pañcahi, anuruddha, dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Katamehi pañcahi? Pāṇātipātā paṭivirato ca hoti, adinnādānā paṭivirato ca hoti, kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato ca hoti, musāvādā paṭivirato ca hoti, surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhānā paṭivirato ca hoti – imehi kho, anuruddha, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjatī”ti. Dasamaṃ.

303. ‘Anuruddha, endowed with five qualities, a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. With which five? She abstains from the destruction of life; she abstains from taking what is not given; she abstains from misconduct in sensual pleasures; she abstains from false speech; and she abstains from liquor, wine, and intoxicants, which are the basis for negligence. Endowed with these five qualities, Anuruddha, a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world.’ The tenth.

Dutiyapeyyālavaggo.

The Second Chapter of Repetitions.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse for that is:

Dutiye ca anuruddho (sabbattha) akkodhano, anupanāhī anissukī;

Amaccharī anaticārī, sīlavā ca bahussuto;

Vīriyaṃ sati sīlañca, sukkapakkhe pakāsito.

In the second [chapter]: non-anger, non-resentment, non-envy; non-avarice, non-transgression, being virtuous, and being learned; energy, mindfulness, and the precepts were declared in the bright fortnight.

3. Balavaggo

3. The Chapter on Powers

1. Visāradasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on Confidence

304. “Pañcimāni[T 4.0304][V 2.0241][M 2.0443][P 4.0246], bhikkhave, mātugāmassa balāni. Katamāni pañca? Rūpabalaṃ, bhogabalaṃ, ñātibalaṃ, puttabalaṃ, sīlabalaṃ – imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañca mātugāmassa balāni. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahi balehi samannāgato mātugāmo visārado agāraṃ ajjhāvasatī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

304. ‘Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of a woman. What five? The power of beauty, the power of wealth, the power of relatives, the power of children, and the power of virtue—these, indeed, bhikkhus, are the five powers of a woman. Endowed with these five powers, bhikkhus, a woman dwells at home self-assured.’ First.

2. Pasayhasuttaṃ

2. The Discourse on Coercion

305. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, mātugāmassa balāni. Katamāni pañca? Rūpabalaṃ, bhogabalaṃ, ñātibalaṃ, puttabalaṃ, sīlabalaṃ – imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañca mātugāmassa balāni. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahi balehi samannāgato mātugāmo sāmikaṃ pasayha agāraṃ ajjhāvasatī”ti. Dutiyaṃ.

305. ‘Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of a woman. What five? The power of beauty, the power of wealth, the power of relatives, the power of children, and the power of virtue—these, indeed, bhikkhus, are the five powers of a woman. Endowed with these five powers, bhikkhus, a woman dwells at home having coerced her husband.’ The second.

3. Abhibhuyyasuttaṃ

3. The Discourse on Overwhelming

306. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, mātugāmassa balāni. Katamāni pañca? Rūpabalaṃ, bhogabalaṃ, ñātibalaṃ, puttabalaṃ, sīlabalaṃ – imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañca mātugāmassa balāni. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahi balehi samannāgato mātugāmo sāmikaṃ abhibhuyya vattatī”ti. Tatiyaṃ.

306. ‘Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of a woman. What five? The power of beauty, the power of wealth, the power of relatives, the power of children, and the power of virtue—these, indeed, bhikkhus, are the five powers of a woman. Endowed with these five powers, bhikkhus, a woman lives having overwhelmed her husband.’ The third.

4. Ekasuttaṃ

4. The Discourse on One

307. “Ekena ca kho, bhikkhave, balena samannāgato puriso mātugāmaṃ abhibhuyya vattati. Katamena ekena balena? Issariyabalena abhibhūtaṃ mātugāmaṃ neva rūpabalaṃ tāyati, na [V 2.0242] bhogabalaṃ tāyati, na ñātibalaṃ tāyati, na puttabalaṃ tāyati, na sīlabalaṃ tāyatī”ti. Catutthaṃ.

307. ‘Indeed, bhikkhus, a man endowed with one power lives having overwhelmed a woman. With what one power? With the power of authority. For a woman overwhelmed by the power of authority, the power of beauty does not protect her, the power of wealth does not protect her, the power of relatives does not protect her, the power of children does not protect her, and the power of virtue does not protect her.’ The fourth.

5. Aṅgasuttaṃ

5. The Discourse on Factors

308. “Pañcimāni[T 4.0305][P 4.0247], bhikkhave, mātugāmassa balāni. Katamāni pañca? Rūpabalaṃ, bhogabalaṃ, ñātibalaṃ, puttabalaṃ, sīlabalaṃ. Rūpabalena ca, bhikkhave, mātugāmo samannāgato hoti, na ca bhogabalena – evaṃ so tenaṅgena aparipūro hoti. Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, mātugāmo rūpabalena ca samannāgato hoti, bhogabalena ca – evaṃ so tenaṅgena paripūro hoti. Rūpabalena [M 2.0444] ca, bhikkhave, mātugāmo samannāgato hoti, bhogabalena ca, na ca ñātibalena – evaṃ so tenaṅgena aparipūro hoti. Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, mātugāmo rūpabalena ca samannāgato hoti, bhogabalena ca, ñātibalena ca – evaṃ so tenaṅgena paripūro hoti. Rūpabalena ca, bhikkhave, mātugāmo samannāgato hoti, bhogabalena ca, ñātibalena ca, na ca puttabalena – evaṃ so tenaṅgena aparipūro hoti. Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, mātugāmo rūpabalena ca samannāgato hoti, bhogabalena ca, ñātibalena ca, puttabalena ca – evaṃ so tenaṅgena paripūro hoti. Rūpabalena ca, bhikkhave, mātugāmo samannāgato hoti, bhogabalena ca, ñātibalena ca, puttabalena ca, na ca sīlabalena – evaṃ so tenaṅgena aparipūro hoti. Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, mātugāmo rūpabalena ca samannāgato hoti, bhogabalena ca, ñātibalena ca, puttabalena ca, sīlabalena ca – evaṃ so tenaṅgena paripūro hoti. Imāni kho[T 4.0306], bhikkhave, pañca mātugāmassa balānī”ti. Pañcamaṃ.

308. ‘Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of a woman. What five? The power of beauty, the power of wealth, the power of relatives, the power of children, and the power of virtue. Bhikkhus, a woman might be endowed with the power of beauty but not with the power of wealth; thus she is incomplete in that factor. But when, bhikkhus, a woman is endowed with both the power of beauty and the power of wealth, then she is complete in that factor. Bhikkhus, a woman might be endowed with the power of beauty and the power of wealth, but not with the power of relatives; thus she is incomplete in that factor. But when, bhikkhus, a woman is endowed with the power of beauty, the power of wealth, and the power of relatives, then she is complete in that factor. Bhikkhus, a woman might be endowed with the power of beauty, the power of wealth, and the power of relatives, but not with the power of children; thus she is incomplete in that factor. But when, bhikkhus, a woman is endowed with the power of beauty, the power of wealth, the power of relatives, and the power of children, then she is complete in that factor. Bhikkhus, a woman might be endowed with the power of beauty, the power of wealth, the power of relatives, and the power of children, but not with the power of virtue; thus she is incomplete in that factor. But when, bhikkhus, a woman is endowed with the power of beauty, the power of wealth, the power of relatives, the power of children, and the power of virtue, then she is complete in that factor. These, indeed, bhikkhus, are the five powers of a woman.’ The fifth.

6. Nāsentisuttaṃ

6. The Discourse on Expulsion

309. “Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, mātugāmassa balāni. Katamāni pañca? Rūpabalaṃ, bhogabalaṃ, ñātibalaṃ, puttabalaṃ, sīlabalaṃ. Rūpabalena [P 4.0248] ca, bhikkhave, mātugāmo samannāgato hoti, na ca sīlabalena, nāsenteva naṃ, kule na vāsenti. Rūpabalena ca, bhikkhave, mātugāmo samannāgato hoti, bhogabalena ca, na ca sīlabalena, nāsenteva naṃ, kule na vāsenti. Rūpabalena ca, bhikkhave, mātugāmo samannāgato hoti, bhogabalena ca, ñātibalena ca, na ca sīlabalena, nāsenteva naṃ, kule na vāsenti. Rūpabalena ca, bhikkhave, mātugāmo samannāgato hoti, bhogabalena ca, ñātibalena ca[V 2.0243], puttabalena ca, na ca sīlabalena, nāsenteva naṃ, kule na vāsenti. Sīlabalena ca, bhikkhave, mātugāmo samannāgato hoti, na ca rūpabalena, vāsenteva naṃ, kule na nāsenti. Sīlabalena ca, bhikkhave, mātugāmo samannāgato hoti, na ca bhogabalena, vāsenteva naṃ, kule na nāsenti. Sīlabalena ca, bhikkhave, mātugāmo samannāgato hoti, na ca ñātibalena, vāsenteva naṃ, kule na nāsenti. Sīlabalena ca, bhikkhave, mātugāmo samannāgato hoti, na ca puttabalena, vāsenteva naṃ, kule na nāsenti. Imāni [T 4.0307] kho, bhikkhave, pañca mātugāmassa balānī”ti. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

309. “Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of a woman. What five? The power of beauty, the power of wealth, the power of relatives, the power of children, and the power of virtue. Bhikkhus, when a woman is endowed with the power of beauty but not with the power of virtue, they expel her; they do not let her stay in the family. Bhikkhus, when a woman is endowed with the power of beauty and the power of wealth but not with the power of virtue, they expel her; they do not let her stay in the family. Bhikkhus, when a woman is endowed with the power of beauty, the power of wealth, and the power of relatives but not with the power of virtue, they expel her; they do not let her stay in the family. Bhikkhus, when a woman is endowed with the power of beauty, the power of wealth, the power of relatives, and the power of children but not with the power of virtue, they expel her; they do not let her stay in the family. Bhikkhus, when a woman is endowed with the power of virtue but not with the power of beauty, they let her stay; they do not expel her from the family. Bhikkhus, when a woman is endowed with the power of virtue but not with the power of wealth, they let her stay; they do not expel her from the family. Bhikkhus, when a woman is endowed with the power of virtue but not with the power of relatives, they let her stay; they do not expel her from the family. Bhikkhus, when a woman is endowed with the power of virtue but not with the power of children, they let her stay; they do not expel her from the family. These, indeed, bhikkhus, are the five powers of a woman.”

7. Hetusuttaṃ

7. The Cause Discourse

310. “Pañcimāni[M 2.0445], bhikkhave, mātugāmassa balāni. Katamāni pañca? Rūpabalaṃ, bhogabalaṃ, ñātibalaṃ, puttabalaṃ, sīlabalaṃ. Na, bhikkhave, mātugāmo rūpabalahetu vā bhogabalahetu vā ñātibalahetu vā puttabalahetu vā kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Sīlabalahetu kho, bhikkhave, mātugāmo kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjati. Imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañca mātugāmassa balānī”ti. Sattamaṃ.

310. “Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of a woman. What five? The power of beauty, the power of wealth, the power of relatives, the power of children, and the power of virtue. It is not because of the power of beauty, or because of the power of wealth, or because of the power of relatives, or because of the power of children, bhikkhus, that a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. It is because of the power of virtue, bhikkhus, that a woman, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. These, indeed, bhikkhus, are the five powers of a woman.”

8. Ṭhānasuttaṃ

8. The Discourse on Possibilities

311. “Pañcimāni[P 4.0249], bhikkhave, ṭhānāni dullabhāni akatapuññena mātugāmena. Katamāni pañca? Patirūpe kule jāyeyyanti – idaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamaṃ ṭhānaṃ dullabhaṃ akatapuññena mātugāmena. Patirūpe kule jāyitvā patirūpaṃ kulaṃ gaccheyyanti – idaṃ, bhikkhave, dutiyaṃ ṭhānaṃ dullabhaṃ akatapuññena mātugāmena. Patirūpe kule jāyitvā, patirūpaṃ kulaṃ gantvā, asapatti agāraṃ ajjhāvaseyyanti – idaṃ, bhikkhave, tatiyaṃ ṭhānaṃ dullabhaṃ akatapuññena mātugāmena. Patirūpe kule jāyitvā, patirūpaṃ kulaṃ gantvā, asapatti agāraṃ ajjhāvasantī puttavatī assanti – idaṃ, bhikkhave, catutthaṃ ṭhānaṃ dullabhaṃ akatapuññena mātugāmena. Patirūpe kule jāyitvā, patirūpaṃ kulaṃ gantvā, asapatti agāraṃ ajjhāvasantī puttavatī samānā sāmikaṃ abhibhuyya vatteyyanti – idaṃ, bhikkhave, pañcamaṃ ṭhānaṃ dullabhaṃ akatapuññena [V 2.0244] mātugāmena[T 4.0308]. Imāni kho, bhikkhave, pañca ṭhānāni dullabhāni akatapuññena mātugāmenāti.

311. “Bhikkhus, these five possibilities are difficult to obtain for a woman who has not made merit. What five? ‘May I be born in a suitable family’—this, bhikkhus, is the first possibility that is difficult for a woman who has not made merit to obtain. ‘Having been born in a suitable family, may I go to a suitable family’—this, bhikkhus, is the second possibility that is difficult for a woman who has not made merit to obtain. ‘Having been born in a suitable family and gone to a suitable family, may I dwell at home without a co-wife’—this, bhikkhus, is the third possibility that is difficult for a woman who has not made merit to obtain. ‘Having been born in a suitable family, gone to a suitable family, and dwelling at home without a co-wife, may I have children’—this, bhikkhus, is the fourth possibility that is difficult for a woman who has not made merit to obtain. ‘Having been born in a suitable family, gone to a suitable family, dwelling at home without a co-wife, and having children, may I live having prevailed over my husband’—this, bhikkhus, is the fifth possibility that is difficult for a woman who has not made merit to obtain. These, bhikkhus, are the five possibilities that are difficult for a woman who has not made merit to obtain.”

“Pañcimāni, bhikkhave, ṭhānāni sulabhāni katapuññena mātugāmena. Katamāni pañca? Patirūpe kule jāyeyyanti – idaṃ, bhikkhave, paṭhamaṃ ṭhānaṃ sulabhaṃ katapuññena mātugāmena.
