Do you know whether those Lambacūḷaka retainers of the Koliyans are virtuous or immoral?' 'I know, venerable sir, that the Lambacūḷaka retainers of the Koliyans are immoral, of evil character. Among those in the world who are immoral and of evil character, the Lambacūḷaka retainers of the Koliyans are some of them.' 'If someone were to say, ‘Pāṭaliya the headman knows the Lambacūḷaka retainers of the Koliyans as immoral and of evil character, therefore Pāṭaliya the headman is also immoral and of evil character,’ would they be speaking rightly?' 'Certainly not, venerable sir! The Lambacūḷaka retainers of the Koliyans are one thing, and I am another. The nature of the Lambacūḷaka retainers of the Koliyans is one thing, and my nature is another.' 'You, headman, are allowed this argument: ‘Pāṭaliya the headman knows the Lambacūḷaka retainers of the Koliyans as immoral and of evil character, but Pāṭaliya the headman is not immoral or of evil character.’ Why then should the Tathāgata not be allowed this: ‘The Tathāgata knows deceit, but the Tathāgata is not deceitful’? I fully understand deceit, headman, and the result of deceit. And I fully understand how one who practices deceit, on the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a realm of ruin, in hell.'

“Pāṇātipātaṃ cāhaṃ, gāmaṇi, pajānāmi, pāṇātipātassa ca vipākaṃ, yathāpaṭipanno ca pāṇātipātī kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Adinnādānaṃ cāhaṃ, gāmaṇi, pajānāmi, adinnādānassa ca vipākaṃ, yathāpaṭipanno ca adinnādāyī kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Kāmesumicchācāraṃ cāhaṃ, gāmaṇi, pajānāmi, kāmesumicchācārassa [T 4.0421] ca vipākaṃ, yathāpaṭipanno ca kāmesumicchācārī kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Musāvādaṃ cāhaṃ, gāmaṇi, pajānāmi, musāvādassa ca vipākaṃ, yathāpaṭipanno ca musāvādī kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Pisuṇavācaṃ cāhaṃ, gāmaṇi, pajānāmi, pisuṇavācāya ca vipākaṃ, yathāpaṭipanno ca pisuṇavāco kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Pharusavācaṃ cāhaṃ, gāmaṇi, pajānāmi, pharusavācāya ca vipākaṃ, yathāpaṭipanno ca pharusavāco kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Samphappalāpaṃ [P 4.0343] cāhaṃ, gāmaṇi, pajānāmi, samphappalāpassa ca vipākaṃ, yathāpaṭipanno ca samphappalāpī kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Abhijjhaṃ cāhaṃ, gāmaṇi, pajānāmi, abhijjhāya ca vipākaṃ, yathāpaṭipanno ca abhijjhālu kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Byāpādapadosaṃ cāhaṃ, gāmaṇi, pajānāmi, byāpādapadosassa ca vipākaṃ, yathāpaṭipanno ca byāpannacitto kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi. Micchādiṭṭhiṃ cāhaṃ, gāmaṇi, pajānāmi, micchādiṭṭhiyā ca vipākaṃ, yathāpaṭipanno [T 4.0422] ca micchādiṭṭhiko kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā apāyaṃ duggatiṃ vinipātaṃ nirayaṃ upapajjati tañca pajānāmi.

Gāmaṇi, I understand the destruction of life, and I understand the result of the destruction of life. And I understand how one who destroys life, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell; that too I understand. Gāmaṇi, I understand taking what is not given, and I understand the result of taking what is not given. And I understand how one who takes what is not given, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell; that too I understand. Gāmaṇi, I understand sexual misconduct, and I understand the result of sexual misconduct. And I understand how one who engages in sexual misconduct, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell; that too I understand. Gāmaṇi, I understand false speech, and I understand the result of false speech. And I understand how one who speaks falsely, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell; that too I understand. Gāmaṇi, I understand slanderous speech, and I understand the result of slanderous speech. And I understand how one who speaks slanderously, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell; that too I understand. Gāmaṇi, I understand harsh speech, and I understand the result of harsh speech. And I understand how one who speaks harshly, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell; that too I understand. Gāmaṇi, I understand frivolous speech, and I understand the result of frivolous speech. And I understand how one who speaks frivolously, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell; that too I understand. Gāmaṇi, I understand covetousness, and I understand the result of covetousness. And I understand how one who is covetous, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell; that too I understand. Gāmaṇi, I understand ill will and malevolence, and I understand the result of ill will and malevolence. And I understand how one with a mind of ill will, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell; that too I understand. Gāmaṇi, I understand wrong view, and I understand the result of wrong view. And I understand how one who holds wrong view, with the breakup of the body, after death, is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a state of ruin, in hell; that too I understand.

“Santi [V 2.0323] hi, gāmaṇi, eke samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘yo koci pāṇamatipāteti, sabbo so diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedayati. Yo koci adinnaṃ ādiyati, sabbo so diṭṭheva dhamme [M 2.0523] dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedayati. Yo koci kāmesu micchā carati, sabbo so diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedayati. Yo koci musā bhaṇati, sabbo so diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedayatī’”ti.

Indeed, Gāmaṇi, there are some ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold this view: ‘Whoever destroys a living being, all of them experience pain and sorrow in this very life. Whoever takes what is not given, all of them experience pain and sorrow in this very life. Whoever engages in sexual misconduct, all of them experience pain and sorrow in this very life. Whoever speaks falsely, all of them experience pain and sorrow in this very life.’

“Dissati kho pana, gāmaṇi, idhekacco mālī kuṇḍalī sunhāto sunahāto (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) suvilitto kappitakesamassu itthikāmehi rājā maññe paricārento. Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso kiṃ akāsi mālī kuṇḍalī sunhāto suvilitto kappitakesamassu itthikāmehi rājā maññe paricāretī’ti? Tamenaṃ [P 4.0344] evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso rañño paccatthikaṃ pasayha jīvitā voropesi. Tassa rājā attamano abhihāramadāsi. Tenāyaṃ puriso mālī kuṇḍalī sunhāto suvilitto kappitakesamassu, itthikāmehi rājā maññe paricāretī’”ti.

But it is seen here, Gāmaṇi, that a certain person—wearing a garland and earrings, well-bathed and well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed—enjoys sensual pleasures with women as if he were a king. People say of him: ‘Sirs, what has this man done that he wears a garland and earrings, is well-bathed and well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, and enjoys sensual pleasures with women as if he were a king?’ And they are told in reply: ‘Sirs, this man forcibly deprived the king’s enemy of life. The king, being pleased, gave him a reward. That is why this man wears a garland and earrings, is well-bathed and well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, and enjoys sensual pleasures with women as if he were a king.’

“Dissati kho, gāmaṇi, idhekacco daḷhāya rajjuyā pacchābāhaṃ gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhitvā khuramuṇḍaṃ karitvā kharassarena paṇavena rathiyāya rathiyaṃ rathikāya rathikaṃ (sī.) siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṃ parinetvā, dakkhiṇena dvārena nikkhāmetvā, dakkhiṇato [T 4.0423] nagarassa sīsaṃ chijjamāno. Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso kiṃ akāsi, daḷhāya rajjuyā pacchābāhaṃ gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhitvā khuramuṇḍaṃ karitvā kharassarena paṇavena rathiyāya rathiyaṃ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṃ parinetvā dakkhiṇena dvārena nikkhāmetvā dakkhiṇato nagarassa sīsaṃ chindatī’ti chijjatīti (katthaci)? Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso rājaverī itthiṃ vā purisaṃ vā jīvitā voropesi, tena naṃ rājāno gahetvā evarūpaṃ kammakāraṇaṃ kārentī’”ti.

It is seen here, Gāmaṇi, that a certain person—having been bound with his arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope, his head shaved with a razor, paraded from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads to the sound of a harsh drum, and led out through the southern gate—is being beheaded south of the city. People say of him: ‘Sirs, what has this man done that they bind his arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope, shave his head with a razor, parade him from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads to the sound of a harsh drum, lead him out through the southern gate, and cut off his head south of the city?’ And they are told in reply: ‘Sirs, this man was an enemy of the king; he deprived a woman or a man of life. Therefore, the kings, having seized him, inflict this kind of punishment.’

“Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gāmaṇi, api nu te evarūpaṃ diṭṭhaṃ vā sutaṃ vā”ti? “Diṭṭhañca no, bhante, sutañca suyyissati cā”ti. “Tatra, gāmaṇi, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘yo koci pāṇamatipāteti, sabbo so diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedayatī’ti, saccaṃ vā te āhaṃsu musā vā”ti? “Musā, bhante”. “Ye pana te tucchaṃ musā vilapanti, sīlavanto vā te dussīlā vā”ti? “Dussīlā[P 4.0345], bhante”. “Ye pana te dussīlā [M 2.0524] pāpadhammā micchāpaṭipannā vā te sammāpaṭipannā vā”ti? “Micchāpaṭipannā, bhante”[V 2.0324]. “Ye pana te micchāpaṭipannā micchādiṭṭhikā vā te sammādiṭṭhikā vā”ti? “Micchādiṭṭhikā, bhante”. “Ye pana te micchādiṭṭhikā kallaṃ nu tesu pasīditu”nti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“What do you think, village headman? Have you seen or heard of such a thing?” “We have seen it, venerable sir, and heard it, and we will hear of it.” “In that case, village headman, those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘Whoever destroys life, all of them experience suffering and displeasure in this very life’—do they speak truth or falsehood?” “Falsehood, venerable sir.” “But those who utter empty falsehoods—are they virtuous or unvirtuous?” “Unvirtuous, venerable sir.” “And those who are unvirtuous, of evil nature—are they practicing rightly or practicing wrongly?” “Practicing wrongly, venerable sir.” “And those who are practicing wrongly—are they of right view or wrong view?” “Of wrong view, venerable sir.” “And those who are of wrong view—is it proper to have confidence in them?” “It is not, venerable sir.”

“Dissati kho pana, gāmaṇi, idhekacco mālī kuṇḍalī…pe… itthikāmehi [T 4.0424] rājā maññe paricārento. Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso kiṃ akāsi mālī kuṇḍalī…pe… itthikāmehi rājā maññe paricāretī’ti? Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso rañño paccatthikassa pasayha ratanaṃ ahāsi pasayha adinnaṃ ratanaṃ ādiyi (ka.). Tassa rājā attamano abhihāramadāsi. Tenāyaṃ puriso mālī kuṇḍalī…pe… itthikāmehi rājā maññe paricāretī’”ti.

“But here, village headman, a certain person is seen adorned with garlands and earrings… being served with sensual pleasures related to women, as if he were a king. They say of him: ‘Sirs, what has this man done that he is adorned with garlands and earrings… and is served with sensual pleasures related to women, as if he were a king?’ And they say of him: ‘Sirs, this man forcibly took a treasure from the king's enemy. Pleased with that, the king gave him a reward. That is why this man is adorned with garlands and earrings… and is served with sensual pleasures related to women, as if he were a king.’”

“Dissati kho, gāmaṇi, idhekacco daḷhāya rajjuyā…pe… dakkhiṇato nagarassa sīsaṃ chijjamāno tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso kiṃ akāsi daḷhāya rajjuyā…pe… dakkhiṇato nagarassa sīsaṃ chindatī’ti? Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso gāmā vā araññā vā adinnaṃ theyyasaṅkhātaṃ ādiyi. Tena naṃ rājāno gahetvā evarūpaṃ kammakāraṇaṃ kārentī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gāmaṇi, api nu te evarūpaṃ diṭṭhaṃ vā sutaṃ vā”ti? “Diṭṭhañca no, bhante, sutañca suyyissati cā”ti. “Tatra[P 4.0346], gāmaṇi, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘yo koci adinnaṃ ādiyati, sabbo so diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedayatī’ti, saccaṃ vā te āhaṃsu musā vāti…pe… kallaṃ nu tesu pasīditu”nti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Here, village headman, a certain person is seen with a strong rope… having his head cut off south of the city. They say of him: ‘Sirs, what has this man done that with a strong rope… they cut off his head south of the city?’ And they say of him: ‘Sirs, this man took what was not given, amounting to theft, from a village or a forest. Therefore, the kings have seized him and are inflicting such punishment.’ What do you think, village headman? Have you seen or heard of such a thing?” “We have seen it, venerable sir, and heard it, and we will hear of it.” “In that case, village headman, those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘Whoever takes what is not given, all of them experience suffering and displeasure in this very life’—do they speak truth or falsehood?... Is it proper to have confidence in them?” “It is not, venerable sir.”

“Dissati kho pana, gāmaṇi, idhekacco mālī kuṇḍalī…pe… itthikāmehi rājā maññe paricārento. Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu [T 4.0425] – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso kiṃ akāsi mālī kuṇḍalī…pe… itthikāmehi rājā maññe paricāretī’ti? Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso rañño paccatthikassa dāresu cārittaṃ āpajji. Tassa rājā attamano abhihāramadāsi. Tenāyaṃ puriso mālī kuṇḍalī…pe… itthikāmehi rājā maññe paricāretī’”ti.

“But here, village headman, a certain person is seen adorned with garlands and earrings… being served with sensual pleasures related to women, as if he were a king. They say of him: ‘Sirs, what has this man done that he is adorned with garlands and earrings… and is served with sensual pleasures related to women, as if he were a king?’ And they say of him: ‘Sirs, this man engaged in misconduct with the wives of the king’s adversary. Pleased with that, the king gave him a reward. That is why this man is adorned with garlands and earrings… and is served with sensual pleasures related to women, as if he were a king.’”

“Dissati [V 2.0325][M 2.0525] kho, gāmaṇi, idhekacco daḷhāya rajjuyā…pe… dakkhiṇato nagarassa sīsaṃ chijjamāno. Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso kiṃ akāsi daḷhāya rajjuyā…pe… dakkhiṇato nagarassa sīsaṃ chindatī’ti? Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso kulitthīsu kulakumārīsu cārittaṃ āpajji, tena naṃ rājāno gahetvā evarūpaṃ kammakāraṇaṃ kārentī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gāmaṇi, api nu te evarūpaṃ diṭṭhaṃ vā sutaṃ vā”ti? “Diṭṭhañca no, bhante, sutañca suyyissati cā”ti. “Tatra, gāmaṇi, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘yo koci kāmesu micchā carati, sabbo so diṭṭheva dhamme dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedayatī’ti, saccaṃ vā te āhaṃsu musā vāti…pe… kallaṃ nu tesu pasīditu”nti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Here, village headman, a certain person is seen with a strong rope… having his head cut off south of the city. They say of him: ‘Sirs, what has this man done that with a strong rope… they cut off his head south of the city?’ And they say of him: ‘Sirs, this man engaged in misconduct with women of good family and maidens of good family. Therefore, the kings have seized him and are inflicting such punishment.’ What do you think, village headman? Have you seen or heard of such a thing?” “We have seen it, venerable sir, and heard it, and we will hear of it.” “In that case, village headman, those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘Whoever engages in sexual misconduct, all of them experience suffering and displeasure in this very life’—do they speak truth or falsehood?... Is it proper to have confidence in them?” “It is not, venerable sir.”

“Dissati [P 4.0347] kho pana, gāmaṇi, idhekacco mālī kuṇḍalī sunhāto suvilitto kappitakesamassu itthikāmehi rājā maññe paricārento. Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso kiṃ akāsi [T 4.0426] mālī kuṇḍalī sunhāto suvilitto kappitakesamassu itthikāmehi rājā maññe paricāretī’ti? Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso rājānaṃ musāvādena hāsesi. Tassa rājā attamano abhihāramadāsi. Tenāyaṃ puriso mālī kuṇḍalī sunhāto suvilitto kappitakesamassu itthikāmehi rājā maññe paricāretī’”ti.

“But here, village headman, a certain person is seen adorned with garlands and earrings, well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, being served with sensual pleasures related to women, as if he were a king. They say of him: ‘Sirs, what has this man done that he is adorned with garlands and earrings, well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, and is served with sensual pleasures related to women, as if he were a king?’ And they say of him: ‘Sirs, this man amused the king with false speech. Pleased with that, the king gave him a reward. That is why this man is adorned with garlands and earrings, well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, and is served with sensual pleasures related to women, as if he were a king.’”

“Dissati kho, gāmaṇi, idhekacco daḷhāya rajjuyā pacchābāhaṃ gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhitvā khuramuṇḍaṃ karitvā kharassarena paṇavena rathiyāya rathiyaṃ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṃ parinetvā dakkhiṇena dvārena nikkhāmetvā dakkhiṇato nagarassa sīsaṃ chijjamāno. Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso kiṃ akāsi daḷhāya rajjuyā pacchābāhaṃ gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhitvā khuramuṇḍaṃ karitvā kharassarena paṇavena rathiyāya rathiyaṃ siṅghāṭakena siṅghāṭakaṃ parinetvā, dakkhiṇena dvārena nikkhāmetvā, dakkhiṇato nagarassa sīsaṃ chindatī’ti? Tamenaṃ evamāhaṃsu – ‘ambho! Ayaṃ puriso gahapatissa vā gahapatiputtassa vā musāvādena atthaṃ bhañji, tena naṃ rājāno gahetvā evarūpaṃ kammakāraṇaṃ kārentī’ti. Taṃ kiṃ maññasi, gāmaṇi, api nu te evarūpaṃ diṭṭhaṃ vā sutaṃ vā”ti? “Diṭṭhañca no[M 2.0526], bhante, sutañca suyyissati cā”ti. “Tatra, gāmaṇi, ye te samaṇabrāhmaṇā evaṃvādino evaṃdiṭṭhino – ‘yo koci musā bhaṇati, sabbo so diṭṭheva dhamme [P 4.0348] dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ paṭisaṃvedayatī’ti, saccaṃ vā te āhaṃsu musā [T 4.0427] vā”ti[V 2.0326]? “Musā, bhante”. “Ye pana te tucchaṃ musā vilapanti sīlavanto vā te dussīlā vā”ti? “Dussīlā, bhante”. “Ye pana te dussīlā pāpadhammā micchāpaṭipannā vā te sammāpaṭipannā vā”ti? “Micchāpaṭipannā, bhante”. “Ye pana te micchāpaṭipannā micchādiṭṭhikā vā te sammādiṭṭhikā vā”ti? “Micchādiṭṭhikā, bhante”. “Ye pana te micchādiṭṭhikā kallaṃ nu tesu pasīditu”nti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”.

“Here, village headman, a certain person is seen with his arms tightly bound behind his back with a strong rope, his head shaven with a razor, being paraded from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads to the sound of a harsh drum; having been led out through the southern gate, his head is being cut off south of the city. Regarding him, people would say: ‘Sirs! What has this man done that they bind his arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope, shave his head with a razor, parade him from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads to the sound of a harsh drum, lead him out through the southern gate, and cut off his head south of the city?’ In reply, they would say: ‘Sirs! This man ruined the welfare of a householder or a householder’s son by lying. Therefore, the kings have seized him and are inflicting such punishment.’ What do you think, village headman? Have you seen or heard of such a thing?” “We have seen it, venerable sir, and heard of it, and will hear of it.” “In that case, village headman, those ascetics and brahmins who speak thus and hold such a view: ‘Whoever speaks falsely, all of them experience suffering and displeasure in this very life’—do they speak truth or falsehood?” “Falsehood, venerable sir.” “But those who utter empty falsehoods—are they virtuous or unvirtuous?” “Unvirtuous, venerable sir.” “And those who are unvirtuous and of evil qualities—are they practicing rightly or practicing wrongly?” “Practicing wrongly, venerable sir.” “And those who are practicing wrongly—are they of right view or of wrong view?” “Of wrong view, venerable sir.” “And for those who are of wrong view—is it proper to place confidence in them?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.”

“Acchariyaṃ, bhante, abbhutaṃ, bhante! Atthi me, bhante, āvasathāgāraṃ. Tattha atthi mañcakāni, atthi āsanāni, atthi udakamaṇiko, atthi telappadīpo. Tattha yo samaṇo vā brāhmaṇo vā vāsaṃ upeti, tenāhaṃ yathāsatti yathābalaṃ saṃvibhajāmi. Bhūtapubbaṃ, bhante, cattāro satthāro nānādiṭṭhikā nānākhantikā nānārucikā, tasmiṃ āvasathāgāre vāsaṃ upagacchuṃ”.

“It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is amazing, venerable sir! I have, venerable sir, a guest house. There are couches there, seats, a water pot, and an oil lamp. Whatever ascetic or brahmin comes to stay there, I share with them according to my ability and strength. Formerly, venerable sir, four teachers with differing views, differing inclinations, and differing preferences came to stay in that guest house.”

“Eko satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – ‘natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ, natthi hutaṃ, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko. Natthi ayaṃ loko, natthi paro loko, natthi mātā, natthi pitā, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī’”ti.

“One teacher was of such a doctrine, of such a view: ‘There is no fruit in what is given, no fruit in what is sacrificed, no fruit in what is offered. There is no fruit or result of good and bad actions. There is no this world, no other world. There is no mother, no father. There are no spontaneously arisen beings. There are in the world no ascetics or brahmins who are well-gone and well-practiced, who proclaim this world and the other world after having realized them for themselves by direct knowledge.’”

“Eko satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – ‘atthi dinnaṃ, atthi yiṭṭhaṃ[P 4.0349], atthi hutaṃ, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, atthi [T 4.0428] ayaṃ loko, atthi paro loko, atthi mātā, atthi pitā, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā, ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī’”ti.

“One teacher was of such a doctrine, of such a view: ‘There is fruit in what is given, there is fruit in what is sacrificed, there is fruit in what is offered. There is fruit and result of good and bad actions. There is this world, there is the other world. There is mother, there is father. There are spontaneously arisen beings. There are in the world ascetics and brahmins who are well-gone and well-practiced, who proclaim this world and the other world after having realized them for themselves by direct knowledge.’”

“Eko satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – ‘karoto kārayato, chindato chedāpayato, pacato pācāpayato, socayato socāpayato, kilamato kilamāpayato, phandato phandāpayato, pāṇamatipātayato, adinnaṃ ādiyato, sandhiṃ chindato, nillopaṃ harato, ekāgārikaṃ [M 2.0527] karoto, paripanthe tiṭṭhato, paradāraṃ gacchato, musā bhaṇato, karoto na karīyati pāpaṃ. Khurapariyantena cepi cakkena yo imissā pathaviyā pāṇe ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ ekaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ kareyya, natthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo. Dakkhiṇaṃ cepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya hananto ghātento [V 2.0327] chindanto chedāpento pacanto pācāpento, natthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo. Uttaraṃ cepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya dadanto dāpento yajanto yajāpento, natthi tatonidānaṃ puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo. Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena natthi puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo’”ti.

“One teacher was of such a doctrine, of such a view: ‘For one who acts or causes another to act, for one who cuts or causes another to cut, for one who torments or causes another to torment, for one who grieves or causes another to grieve, for one who is weary or causes another to be weary, for one who trembles or causes another to tremble, for one who destroys life, for one who takes what is not given, for one who breaks into a house, for one who plunders, for one who commits dacoity, for one who ambushes on the highway, for one who goes to another’s wife, for one who speaks falsehood—for one who so acts, no evil is done. Even if with a razor-edged wheel one were to make all the living beings on this earth into a single heap of flesh, a single pile of flesh, there would be no evil from that cause, no coming of evil. Even if one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges killing and causing to kill, cutting and causing to cut, tormenting and causing to torment, there would be no evil from that cause, no coming of evil. Even if one were to go along the northern bank of the Ganges giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, there would be no merit from that cause, no coming of merit. Through generosity, self-control, restraint, and truthful speech, there is no merit, no coming of merit.’”

“Eko satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – ‘karoto kārayato, chindato chedāpayato, pacato pācāpayato, socayato socāpayato, kilamato kilamāpayato, phandato phandāpayato, pāṇamatipātayato, adinnaṃ ādiyato, sandhiṃ [T 4.0429] chindato, nillopaṃ harato, ekāgārikaṃ karoto, paripanthe tiṭṭhato, paradāraṃ gacchato[P 4.0350], musā bhaṇato, karoto karīyati pāpaṃ. Khurapariyantena cepi cakkena yo imissā pathaviyā pāṇe ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ ekaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ kareyya, atthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, atthi pāpassa āgamo. Dakkhiṇaṃ cepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya hananto ghātento chindanto chedāpento pacanto pācāpento, atthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, atthi pāpassa āgamo. Uttaraṃ cepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya dadanto dāpento, yajanto yajāpento, atthi tatonidānaṃ puññaṃ, atthi puññassa āgamo. Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena atthi puññaṃ, atthi puññassa āgamo’”ti.

There is one teacher who holds such a view and speaks thus: ‘For one who acts, or causes another to act; for one who cuts, or causes another to cut; for one who torments, or causes another to torment; for one who grieves, or causes another to grieve; for one who wearies, or causes another to weary; for one who trembles, or causes another to tremble; for one who destroys life, takes what is not given, breaks into a house, plunders, commits a robbery in one house, lies in ambush, goes to another’s wife, or speaks falsehood—for one who acts thus, evil is done. Even if with a razor-edged wheel one were to make the living beings on this earth into a single mass of flesh, a single heap of flesh, there is evil from that cause, there is an arising of evil. Even if one were to go to the southern bank of the Ganges killing, causing to kill, cutting, causing to cut, tormenting, causing to torment, there is evil from that cause, there is an arising of evil. Even if one were to go to the northern bank of the Ganges giving, causing to give, sacrificing, causing to sacrifice, there is merit from that cause, there is an arising of merit. Through giving, through discipline, through restraint, and through truthful speech, there is merit, there is an arising of merit.’

“Tassa mayhaṃ, bhante, ahudeva kaṅkhā, ahu vicikicchā – ‘kosu nāma imesaṃ bhavataṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ saccaṃ āha, ko musā’”ti?

Then, venerable sir, doubt arose in me, uncertainty arose: ‘Which of these venerable ascetics and brahmins speaks the truth, and which speaks falsely?’

“Alañhi te, gāmaṇi, kaṅkhituṃ, alaṃ vicikicchituṃ. Kaṅkhanīye ca pana te ṭhāne vicikicchā uppannā”ti. “Evaṃ pasannohaṃ, bhante, bhagavati. Pahoti me bhagavā tathā dhammaṃ desetuṃ yathāhaṃ imaṃ kaṅkhādhammaṃ pajaheyya”nti.

“It is indeed fitting for you to doubt, headman, fitting for you to be uncertain. For uncertainty has arisen in you about a matter that is doubtful.” “I am thus confident, venerable sir, in the Blessed One. The Blessed One is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might abandon this state of doubt.”

“Atthi, gāmaṇi, dhammasamādhi. Tatra ce tvaṃ cittasamādhiṃ paṭilabheyyāsi. Evaṃ tvaṃ imaṃ kaṅkhādhammaṃ pajaheyyāsi. Katamo ca, gāmaṇi, dhammasamādhi? Idha, gāmaṇi, ariyasāvako pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya pāṇātipātā paṭivirato [M 2.0528] hoti, adinnādānaṃ pahāya adinnādānā paṭivirato [T 4.0430] hoti, kāmesumicchācāraṃ pahāya kāmesumicchācārā paṭivirato hoti, musāvādaṃ pahāya musāvādā paṭivirato [P 4.0351] hoti, pisuṇaṃ vācaṃ pahāya pisuṇāya vācāya paṭivirato hoti[V 2.0328], pharusaṃ vācaṃ pahāya pharusāya vācāya paṭivirato hoti, samphappalāpaṃ pahāya samphappalāpā paṭivirato hoti, abhijjhaṃ pahāya anabhijjhālu hoti, byāpādapadosaṃ pahāya abyāpannacitto hoti, micchādiṭṭhiṃ pahāya sammādiṭṭhiko hoti.

“Headman, there is a concentration established in the Dhamma. If you were to attain concentration of mind therein, you could thus abandon this state of doubt. And what, headman, is the concentration established in the Dhamma? Here, headman, a noble disciple, having abandoned the destruction of life, abstains from the destruction of life; having abandoned taking what is not given, he abstains from taking what is not given; having abandoned sexual misconduct, he abstains from sexual misconduct; having abandoned false speech, he abstains from false speech; having abandoned divisive speech, he abstains from divisive speech; having abandoned harsh speech, he abstains from harsh speech; having abandoned idle chatter, he abstains from idle chatter; having abandoned covetousness, he is uncovetous; having abandoned the corruption of ill will, he is of a mind without ill will; having abandoned wrong view, he is of right view.

“Sa kho so, gāmaṇi, ariyasāvako evaṃ vigatābhijjho vigatabyāpādo asammūḷho sampajāno paṭissato mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ, iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyāpajjena pharitvā viharati. So iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yvāyaṃ satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ, natthi hutaṃ, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, natthi ayaṃ loko, natthi paro loko, natthi mātā, natthi pitā, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā, sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentī’ti. ‘Sace tassa bhoto satthuno saccaṃ vacanaṃ, apaṇṇakatāya mayhaṃ, yvāhaṃ yohaṃ (sī. syā. kaṃ. pī.) na kiñci [T 4.0431] kañci (?) byābādhemi tasaṃ vā thāvaraṃ vā? Ubhayamettha ubhayattha me (?) ma. ni. 2.95 pāḷiyā saṃsandetabbaṃ kaṭaggāho, yaṃ camhi kāyena saṃvuto vācāya saṃvuto manasā saṃvuto, yañca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissāmī’ti paraṃ maraṇā na upapajjissāmīti (?). Tassa pāmojjaṃ jāyati. Pamuditassa pīti jāyati. Pītimanassa kāyo passambhati. Passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedayati. Sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Ayaṃ kho, gāmaṇi, dhammasamādhi[P 4.0352]. Tatra ce tvaṃ cittasamādhiṃ paṭilabheyyāsi, evaṃ tvaṃ imaṃ kaṅkhādhammaṃ pajaheyyāsi.

“Then, headman, that noble disciple—thus free from covetousness, free from ill will, undeluded, clearly comprehending, and mindful—dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. So above, below, across, and everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without affliction. He reflects thus: ‘Regarding that teacher who holds such a view and speaks thus: “There is no giving, no offering, no sacrifice; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously arisen beings; there are in the world no ascetics or brahmins who are well-gone and well-practiced, who proclaim this world and the other world after realizing them for themselves by direct knowledge”—if that venerable teacher’s word is true, this practice of mine is faultless, in that I harm no being, whether trembling or firm. This is a winning hand in both respects: that I am restrained in body, speech, and mind, and that with the breakup of the body, after death, I will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Joy arises in him. When he is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This, headman, is the concentration established in the Dhamma. If you were to attain concentration of mind therein, you could thus abandon this state of doubt.”

“Sa kho so, gāmaṇi, ariyasāvako evaṃ vigatābhijjho vigatabyāpādo asammūḷho sampajāno paṭissato mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā [M 2.0529] catutthaṃ, iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyāpajjena pharitvā viharati. So iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yvāyaṃ satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – atthi dinnaṃ, atthi yiṭṭhaṃ, atthi hutaṃ, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, atthi ayaṃ loko, atthi paro loko, atthi mātā, atthi pitā, atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā, sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā [V 2.0329] pavedentī’ti. ‘Sace tassa [T 4.0432] bhoto satthuno saccaṃ vacanaṃ, apaṇṇakatāya mayhaṃ, yvāhaṃ na kiñci byābādhemi tasaṃ vā thāvaraṃ vā? Ubhayamettha kaṭaggāho, yaṃ camhi kāyena saṃvuto vācāya saṃvuto manasā saṃvuto, yañca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissāmī’ti. Tassa pāmojjaṃ jāyati. Pamuditassa pīti jāyati. Pītimanassa kāyo passambhati. Passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedayati. Sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Ayaṃ kho, gāmaṇi, dhammasamādhi. Tatra ce tvaṃ cittasamādhiṃ paṭilabheyyāsi, evaṃ tvaṃ imaṃ kaṅkhādhammaṃ pajaheyyāsi.

Then, Gāmaṇi, that noble disciple—thus devoid of covetousness, devoid of ill will, unbewildered, clearly comprehending, and mindful—dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, identifying with all, he dwells pervading the entire world of beings with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without affliction. He reflects thus: ‘As to that teacher who holds such a doctrine and such a view that: “There is what is given, there is what is offered, there is what is sacrificed; there is the fruit and result of good and bad actions; there is this world and the next world; there is mother and father; there are spontaneously arisen beings; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who are well-gone, well-practicing, who, having realized this world and the next for themselves by direct knowledge, make it known”—if the words of that venerable teacher are true, then for me, who harms no being, whether trembling or steadfast, this is an unfailing position. In both respects, this is a victorious grasp: that I am restrained in body, speech, and mind, and that with the breakup of the body, after death, I shall be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Joy arises in him. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This, Gāmaṇi, is concentration in the Dhamma. If, in this, you were to attain concentration of mind, you could thus abandon this state of doubt.

“Sa kho so, gāmaṇi, ariyasāvako evaṃ vigatābhijjho vigatabyāpādo asammūḷho sampajāno paṭissato mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ, iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyāpajjena [P 4.0353] pharitvā viharati. So iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yvāyaṃ satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – karoto kārayato, chindato chedāpayato, pacato pācāpayato, socayato socāpayato, kilamato kilamāpayato, phandato phandāpayato, pāṇamatipātayato, adinnaṃ ādiyato, sandhiṃ chindato, nillopaṃ harato, ekāgārikaṃ karoto, paripanthe tiṭṭhato, paradāraṃ gacchato, musā bhaṇato, karoto na karīyati pāpaṃ. Khurapariyantena cepi cakkena yo imissā pathaviyā pāṇe ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ [T 4.0433] ekaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ kareyya, natthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo. Dakkhiṇañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya hananto ghātento chindanto chedāpento pacanto pācāpento, natthi tatonidānaṃ [M 2.0530] pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo. Uttarañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya dadanto dāpento, yajanto yajāpento, natthi tatonidānaṃ puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo. Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena natthi puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo’ti. ‘Sace tassa bhoto satthuno saccaṃ vacanaṃ, apaṇṇakatāya mayhaṃ, yvāhaṃ na kiñci byābādhemi tasaṃ vā thāvaraṃ vā? Ubhayamettha kaṭaggāho, yaṃ camhi kāyena saṃvuto vācāya saṃvuto manasā saṃvuto, yañca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissāmī’ti paraṃ maraṇā na upapajjissāmīti (?). Tassa pāmojjaṃ jāyati. Pamuditassa pīti jāyati. Pītimanassa kāyo passambhati. Passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedayati. Sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Ayaṃ kho, gāmaṇi, dhammasamādhi tatra ce tvaṃ cittasamādhiṃ paṭilabheyyāsi, evaṃ tvaṃ imaṃ kaṅkhādhammaṃ pajaheyyāsi.

Then, Gāmaṇi, that noble disciple—thus devoid of covetousness, devoid of ill will, unbewildered, clearly comprehending, and mindful—dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, identifying with all, he dwells pervading the entire world of beings with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without affliction. He reflects thus: ‘As to that teacher who holds such a doctrine and such a view that: “For one who acts or causes another to act, who cuts or causes another to cut, who torments or causes another to torment, who grieves or causes another to grieve, who is weary or causes another to be weary, who trembles or causes another to tremble, who takes life, who takes what is not given, who breaks into a house, who plunders, who commits burglary, who lies in ambush, who commits adultery, who speaks falsehood—for one who does these things, no evil is done. Even if one were to make the living beings on this earth into a single mass of flesh, a single heap of flesh, with a razor-edged wheel, there is no evil from that cause, no arising of evil. If one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges killing and causing to kill, cutting and causing to cut, tormenting and causing to torment, there is no evil from that cause, no arising of evil. If one were to go along the northern bank of the Ganges giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, there is no merit from that cause, no arising of merit. Through giving, taming, restraint, and truthful speech, there is no merit, no arising of merit”—if the words of that venerable teacher are true, then for me, who harms no being, whether trembling or steadfast, this is an unfailing position. In both respects, this is a victorious grasp: that I am restrained in body, speech, and mind, and that with the breakup of the body, after death, I shall be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Joy arises in him. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This, Gāmaṇi, is concentration in the Dhamma. If, in this, you were to attain concentration of mind, you could thus abandon this state of doubt.

“Sa [V 2.0330] kho so, gāmaṇi, ariyasāvako evaṃ vigatābhijjho vigatabyāpādo asammūḷho sampajāno paṭissato mettāsahagate cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ, iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya [P 4.0354] sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ mettāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena [T 4.0434] averena abyāpajjena pharitvā viharati. So iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yvāyaṃ satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – karoto kārayato, chindato chedāpayato, pacato pācāpayato, socayato socāpayato, kilamato kilamāpayato, phandato phandāpayato, pāṇamatipātayato, adinnaṃ ādiyato, sandhiṃ chindato, nillopaṃ harato, ekāgārikaṃ karoto, paripanthe tiṭṭhato, paradāraṃ gacchato, musā bhaṇato, karoto karīyati pāpaṃ. Khurapariyantena cepi cakkena yo imissā pathaviyā pāṇe ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ ekaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ kareyya, atthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, atthi pāpassa āgamo. Dakkhiṇañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya hananto ghātento chindanto chedāpento pacanto pācāpento, atthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, atthi pāpassa āgamo. Uttarañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya dadanto dāpento, yajanto yajāpento, atthi tatonidānaṃ [M 2.0531] puññaṃ, atthi puññassa āgamo. Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena atthi puññaṃ atthi puññassa āgamoti. Sace tassa bhoto satthuno saccaṃ vacanaṃ, apaṇṇakatāya mayhaṃ, yvāhaṃ na kiñci byābādhemi tasaṃ vā thāvaraṃ vā? Ubhayamettha kaṭaggāho, yaṃ camhi kāyena saṃvuto vācāya saṃvuto manasā saṃvuto, yañca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissāmī’ti. Tassa pāmojjaṃ jāyati. Pamuditassa pīti jāyati. Pītimanassa kāyo passambhati. Passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedayati. Sukhino cittaṃ [T 4.0435] samādhiyati. Ayaṃ kho, gāmaṇi, dhammasamādhi. Tatra ce tvaṃ cittasamādhiṃ paṭilabheyyāsi, evaṃ tvaṃ imaṃ kaṅkhādhammaṃ pajaheyyāsi.

Then, Gāmaṇi, that noble disciple—thus devoid of covetousness, devoid of ill will, unbewildered, clearly comprehending, and mindful—dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, treating all beings as oneself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, and without ill will. He reflects thus: ‘That teacher who has such a doctrine and such a view—that for one who acts or causes another to act, for one who cuts or causes another to cut, for one who torments or causes another to torment, for one who grieves or causes another to grieve, for one who becomes weary or causes another to become weary, for one who trembles or causes another to tremble, for one who takes life, for one who takes what is not given, for one who breaks into a house, for one who plunders, for one who commits burglary, for one who lies in ambush, for one who goes to another’s wife, for one who speaks falsehood—for one who does these things, evil is done. If one were to make the living beings on this earth into a single mass of flesh, a single heap of flesh, with a razor-edged discus, there is evil from that cause, there is an arising of evil. And if one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges, killing and causing to kill, cutting and causing to cut, tormenting and causing to torment, there is evil from that cause, there is an arising of evil. And if one were to go along the northern bank of the Ganges, giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, there is merit from that cause, there is an arising of merit. Through giving, self-control, restraint, and truthful speech, there is merit, there is an arising of merit.’ If the words of that venerable teacher are true, it is an unerring practice for me, as I do not harm any being, whether trembling or stable. In both ways, victory is grasped by me: that I am restrained in body, speech, and mind, and that with the breakup of the body, after death, I shall be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Joy arises in him. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This, Gāmaṇi, is concentration in the Dhamma. If you were to attain concentration of mind therein, you would thus abandon this state of doubt.

“Sa kho so, gāmaṇi, ariyasāvako evaṃ vigatābhijjho vigatabyāpādo asammūḷho sampajāno paṭissato karuṇāsahagate [P 4.0355] cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati…pe… muditāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati…pe….

Then, Gāmaṇi, that noble disciple, being thus devoid of covetousness, devoid of ill will, unbewildered, clearly comprehending, and mindful, dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by compassion... and so on... with a mind accompanied by altruistic joy, he dwells pervading one direction... and so on...

“Sa kho so, gāmaṇi, ariyasāvako evaṃ vigatābhijjho vigatabyāpādo asammūḷho sampajāno paṭissato upekkhāsahagate cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ, iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena [V 2.0331] cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyāpajjena pharitvā viharati. So iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yvāyaṃ satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – natthi dinnaṃ, natthi yiṭṭhaṃ, natthi hutaṃ natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, natthi ayaṃ loko natthi paro loko, natthi mātā natthi pitā natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentīti. Sace tassa bhoto satthuno saccaṃ vacanaṃ, apaṇṇakatāya mayhaṃ, yvāhaṃ na kiñci byābādhemi tasaṃ vā thāvaraṃ vā? Ubhayamettha kaṭaggāho, yaṃ camhi kāyena saṃvuto vācāya saṃvuto manasā saṃvuto[T 4.0436], yañca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissāmī’ti. Tassa pāmojjaṃ jāyati. Pamuditassa pīti jāyati. Pītimanassa kāyo passambhati. Passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedayati. Sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Ayaṃ [M 2.0532] kho, gāmaṇi, dhammasamādhi. Tatra ce tvaṃ cittasamādhiṃ paṭilabheyyāsi, evaṃ tvaṃ imaṃ kaṅkhādhammaṃ pajaheyyāsi.

Then, Gāmaṇi, that noble disciple—thus devoid of covetousness, devoid of ill will, unbewildered, clearly comprehending, and mindful—dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere, treating all beings as oneself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind accompanied by equanimity—vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, and without ill will. He reflects thus: ‘That teacher who has such a doctrine and such a view—that there is no result from what is given, no result from what is offered, no result from what is sacrificed; there is no fruit or result of good and bad actions; there is no this world, no other world; there is no mother, no father; there are no spontaneously arisen beings; there are in the world no ascetics and brahmins who are well-gone, well-practiced, and who, having realized this world and the other world for themselves through direct knowledge, make it known.’ If the words of that venerable teacher are true, it is an unerring practice for me, as I do not harm any being, whether trembling or stable. In both ways, victory is grasped by me: that I am restrained in body, speech, and mind, and that with the breakup of the body, after death, I shall be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Joy arises in him. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This, Gāmaṇi, is concentration in the Dhamma. If you were to attain concentration of mind therein, you would thus abandon this state of doubt.

“Sa kho so, gāmaṇi, ariyasāvako evaṃ vigatābhijjho vigatabyāpādo asammūḷho sampajāno paṭissato upekkhāsahagate cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ, iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena [P 4.0356] averena abyāpajjena pharitvā viharati. So iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yvāyaṃ satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – atthi dinnaṃ, atthi yiṭṭhaṃ, atthi hutaṃ, atthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko, atthi ayaṃ loko atthi paro loko, atthi mātā atthi pitā atthi sattā opapātikā, atthi loke samaṇabrāhmaṇā sammaggatā sammāpaṭipannā ye imañca lokaṃ parañca lokaṃ sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedentīti. Sace tassa bhoto satthuno saccaṃ vacanaṃ, apaṇṇakatāya mayhaṃ, yvāhaṃ na kiñci byābādhemi tasaṃ vā thāvaraṃ vā? Ubhayamettha kaṭaggāho, yaṃ camhi kāyena saṃvuto vācāya saṃvuto manasā saṃvuto, yañca kāyassa [T 4.0437] bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissāmī’ti. Tassa pāmojjaṃ jāyati. Pamuditassa pīti jāyati. Pītimanassa kāyo passambhati. Passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedayati. Sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Ayaṃ kho, gāmaṇi, dhammasamādhi. Tatra ce tvaṃ cittasamādhiṃ paṭilabheyyāsi, evaṃ tvaṃ imaṃ kaṅkhādhammaṃ pajaheyyāsi.

“Then, village headman, that noble disciple—free from covetousness, free from ill will, undeluded, clearly comprehending, and mindful—dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, in all places, identifying with all, he dwells pervading the entire world of beings with a mind accompanied by equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without affliction. He reflects thus: ‘That teacher holds such a view and such a doctrine: “There is a result to what is given, sacrificed, and offered; there is fruit and result of good and bad deeds; there is this world and the other world; there are mother and father; there are spontaneously arisen beings; there are in the world ascetics and brahmins who have gone the right way and are practicing rightly, who, having realized for themselves through direct knowledge, declare this world and the other world.” If that venerable teacher’s word is true, then for me this is an unfailing position, since I harm no being, whether trembling or steadfast. In this, a sure bet is won on two counts: that I am restrained in body, speech, and mind, and that with the breakup of the body, after death, I will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Joy arises in him. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil feels happiness. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This, village headman, is the concentration of the Dhamma. If you were to attain this concentration of mind, you would abandon this state of doubt.”

“Sa [V 2.0332] kho so, gāmaṇi, ariyasāvako evaṃ vigatābhijjho vigatabyāpādo asammūḷho sampajāno paṭissato upekkhāsahagate cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ, iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyāpajjena pharitvā viharati. So iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yvāyaṃ satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – karoto kārayato, chedato chedāpayato, pacato pācāpayato, socayato socāpayato, kilamato kilamāpayato, phandato phandāpayato, pāṇamatipātayato, adinnaṃ ādiyato, sandhiṃ chindato, nillopaṃ harato, ekāgārikaṃ [M 2.0533] karoto, paripanthe tiṭṭhato, paradāraṃ gacchato, musā bhaṇato, karoto na karīyati pāpaṃ[P 4.0357]. Khurapariyantena cepi cakkena yo imissā pathaviyā pāṇe ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ ekaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ kareyya, natthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo. Dakkhiṇañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya hananto ghātento chindanto chedāpento pacanto pācāpento, natthi tatonidānaṃ [T 4.0438] pāpaṃ, natthi pāpassa āgamo. Uttarañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya dadanto dāpento, yajanto yajāpento, natthi tatonidānaṃ puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo. Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena natthi puññaṃ, natthi puññassa āgamo’ti. ‘Sace tassa bhoto satthuno saccaṃ vacanaṃ, apaṇṇakatāya mayhaṃ, yvāhaṃ na kiñci byābādhemi tasaṃ vā thāvaraṃ vā? Ubhayamettha kaṭaggāho, yaṃ camhi kāyena saṃvuto vācāya saṃvuto manasā saṃvuto, yañca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissāmī’ti. Tassa pāmojjaṃ jāyati. Pamuditassa pīti jāyati. Pītimanassa kāyo passambhati. Passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedayati. Sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Ayaṃ kho, gāmaṇi, dhammasamādhi. Tatra ce tvaṃ cittasamādhiṃ paṭilabheyyāsi, evaṃ tvaṃ imaṃ kaṅkhādhammaṃ pajaheyyāsi.

“Then, village headman, that noble disciple—free from covetousness, free from ill will, undeluded, clearly comprehending, and mindful—dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by equanimity, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, in all places, identifying with all, he dwells pervading the entire world of beings with a mind accompanied by equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, without enmity, and without affliction. He reflects thus: ‘That teacher holds such a view and such a doctrine: “For one who acts or causes another to act, who cuts or causes another to cut, who strikes or causes another to strike, who grieves or causes another to grieve, who becomes weary or causes another to become weary, who trembles or causes another to tremble; for one who destroys life, takes what is not given, breaks into a house, plunders, robs a single house, stands as a waylayer, commits adultery, or speaks falsely—for one who does these things, no evil is done. Even if one were to make the living beings on this earth into a single mass of flesh, a single pile of flesh, with a razor-edged wheel, there is no evil from that source, no arising of evil. If one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges killing and causing to kill, cutting and causing to cut, striking and causing to strike, there is no evil from that source, no arising of evil. If one were to go along the northern bank of the Ganges giving and causing to give, sacrificing and causing to sacrifice, there is no merit from that source, no arising of merit. Through giving, restraint, self-control, and truthful speech, there is no merit, no arising of merit.” If that venerable teacher’s word is true, then for me this is an unfailing position, since I harm no being, whether trembling or steadfast. In this, a sure bet is won on two counts: that I am restrained in body, speech, and mind, and that with the breakup of the body, after death, I will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Joy arises in him. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil feels happiness. For one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated. This, village headman, is the concentration of the Dhamma. If you were to attain this concentration of mind, you would abandon this state of doubt.”

“Sa kho so, gāmaṇi, ariyasāvako evaṃ vigatābhijjho vigatabyāpādo asammūḷho sampajāno paṭissato upekkhāsahagate cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharati, tathā dutiyaṃ, tathā tatiyaṃ, tathā catutthaṃ, iti uddhamadho tiriyaṃ sabbadhi sabbattatāya sabbāvantaṃ lokaṃ upekkhāsahagatena cetasā vipulena mahaggatena appamāṇena averena abyāpajjena pharitvā viharati. So iti paṭisañcikkhati – ‘yvāyaṃ satthā evaṃvādī evaṃdiṭṭhi – karoto kārayato, chindato [T 4.0439] chedāpayato, pacato pācāpayato, socayato socāpayato, kilamato kilamāpayato, phandato phandāpayato, pāṇamatipātayato, adinnaṃ ādiyato, sandhiṃ chindato, nillopaṃ [V 2.0333][P 4.0358] harato, ekāgārikaṃ karoto, paripanthe tiṭṭhato, paradāraṃ gacchato, musā bhaṇato, karoto karīyati pāpaṃ. Khurapariyantena cepi cakkena yo imissā pathaviyā pāṇe ekaṃ maṃsakhalaṃ ekaṃ maṃsapuñjaṃ kareyya, atthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, atthi pāpassa āgamo. Dakkhiṇañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya hananto [M 2.0534] ghātento chindanto chedāpento pacanto pācāpento, atthi tatonidānaṃ pāpaṃ, atthi pāpassa āgamo. Uttarañcepi gaṅgāya tīraṃ gaccheyya dadanto dāpento, yajanto yajāpento, atthi tatonidānaṃ puññaṃ, atthi puññassa āgamo. Dānena damena saṃyamena saccavajjena atthi puññaṃ, atthi puññassa āgamo’ti. ‘Sace tassa bhoto satthuno saccaṃ vacanaṃ, apaṇṇakatāya mayhaṃ, yvāhaṃ na kiñci byābādhemi tasaṃ vā thāvaraṃ vā? Ubhayamettha kaṭaggāho, yaṃ camhi kāyena saṃvuto vācāya saṃvuto manasā saṃvuto, yañca kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ upapajjissāmī’ti. Tassa pāmojjaṃ jāyati. Pamuditassa pīti jāyati. Pītimanassa kāyo passambhati. Passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vedayati. Sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyati. Ayaṃ kho, gāmaṇi, dhammasamādhi. Tatra ce tvaṃ cittasamādhiṃ paṭilabheyyāsi, evaṃ tvaṃ imaṃ kaṅkhādhammaṃ pajaheyyāsī”ti.

Then, village chief, that noble disciple, being thus devoid of covetousness, devoid of ill will, unbewildered, clearly comprehending, and mindful, dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with equanimity; likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, and across, everywhere and in every way, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, measureless, without hostility, and without ill will. He reflects thus: ‘There is a teacher with this doctrine, with this view: “For one who acts or makes others act, who cuts or makes others cut, who torments or makes others torment, who causes sorrow or makes others sorrow, who wearies or makes others weary, who makes tremble or makes others tremble, who takes life, takes what is not given, breaks into houses, plunders, commits burglary, lies in ambush on highways, goes to another’s wife, speaks falsehood—for one who acts, evil is done. Even if with a razor-edged wheel one were to make the living beings on this earth into a single heap of flesh, a single mass of flesh, from that cause there is evil, there is an influx of evil. If one were to go along the southern bank of the Ganges killing, slaughtering, cutting, making others cut, tormenting, making others torment, from that cause there is evil, there is an influx of evil. If one were to go along the northern bank of the Ganges giving gifts, making others give, sacrificing, making others sacrifice, from that cause there is merit, there is an influx of merit. Through giving, taming, restraint, and truthful speech, there is merit, there is an influx of merit.”’ ‘If the word of that venerable teacher is true, then for me, who harms no being, whether trembling or firm, this practice is incontrovertible. Herein, it is a winning grasp in both ways: that I am restrained in body, speech, and mind, and that with the breakup of the body, after death, I will be reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world.’ Joy arises in him. For one who is joyful, rapture arises. For one with a rapturous mind, the body becomes tranquil. One with a tranquil body experiences happiness. The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated. This, village chief, is concentration in the Dhamma. If you were to attain concentration of mind therein, you would thus abandon this state of doubt.”

Evaṃ [T 4.0440] vutte, pāṭaliyo gāmaṇi bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “abhikkantaṃ, bhante, abhikkantaṃ, bhante…pe… ajjatagge pāṇupetaṃ saraṇaṃ gata”nti. Terasamaṃ.

When this was said, Pāṭaliya the village chief said to the Blessed One: “Excellent, venerable sir! Excellent, venerable sir! … May the Blessed One remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forward for as long as life lasts.” The thirteenth.

Gāmaṇisaṃyuttaṃ samattaṃ.

The Gāmaṇi Saṃyutta is complete.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse:

Caṇḍo [P 4.0359] puṭo yodhājīvo, hatthasso asibandhako;

Desanā saṅkhakulaṃ maṇicūḷaṃ, bhadrarāsiyapāṭalīti.

Caṇḍa, Puṭa, Yodhājīva, Hatthi and Assa, Asibandhaka; Desanā, Saṅkhakula, Maṇicūḷa, Bhadra, Rasiya, and Pāṭali.

9. Asaṅkhatasaṃyuttaṃ

9. The Connected Discourses on the Unconditioned

1. Paṭhamavaggo

1. The First Chapter

1. Kāyagatāsatisuttaṃ

1. Mindfulness Directed to the Body

366. Sāvatthinidānaṃ[V 2.0334][M 2.0535]. “Asaṅkhatañca [T 4.0441] vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi asaṅkhatagāmiñca maggaṃ. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamañca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhataṃ? Yo, bhikkhave, rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo – idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhataṃ. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Kāyagatāsati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo”.

366. At Sāvatthī. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the unconditioned and the path leading to the unconditioned. Listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, is the unconditioned? The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion—this, bhikkhus, is called the unconditioned. And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Mindfulness directed to the body. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned.”

“Iti kho, bhikkhave, desitaṃ vo mayā asaṅkhataṃ, desito asaṅkhatagāmimaggo. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, satthārā karaṇīyaṃ sāvakānaṃ hitesinā anukampakena anukampaṃ upādāya, kataṃ vo taṃ mayā. Etāni, bhikkhave, rukkhamūlāni, etāni suññāgārāni. Jhāyatha nijjhāyatha (ka.), bhikkhave, mā pamādattha; mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvattha. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī”ti. Paṭhamaṃ.

“Thus, bhikkhus, the unconditioned has been taught to you by me, and the path leading to the unconditioned has been taught. Whatever is to be done by a teacher for his disciples, out of compassion—a teacher who is a well-wisher and compassionate—that I have done for you. These, bhikkhus, are the roots of trees; these are empty dwellings. Meditate, bhikkhus, do not be heedless; do not have regrets later. This is our instruction to you.”

2. Samathavipassanāsuttaṃ

2. Serenity and Insight

367. “Asaṅkhatañca [P 4.0360] vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi asaṅkhatagāmiñca maggaṃ. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamañca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhataṃ? Yo, bhikkhave, rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo – idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhataṃ. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Samatho ca vipassanā ca. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe…. Dutiyaṃ.

367. “Bhikkhus, I will teach you the unconditioned and the path leading to the unconditioned. Listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, is the unconditioned? The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion. This, bhikkhus, is called the unconditioned. And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Serenity and insight. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned….”

3. Savitakkasavicārasuttaṃ

3. With Applied and Sustained Thought

368. “Katamo [T 4.0442][V 2.0335] ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Savitakkasavicāro samādhi, avitakkavicāramatto samādhi, avitakkaavicāro samādhi – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe…. Tatiyaṃ.

368. “And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Concentration with applied and sustained thought; concentration without applied thought but with sustained thought; concentration without applied and sustained thought. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned….”

4. Suññatasamādhisuttaṃ

4. The Concentration of Emptiness

369. “Katamo [M 2.0536] ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Suññato samādhi, animitto samādhi, appaṇihito samādhi – ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe…. Catutthaṃ.

369. “And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? The concentration of emptiness, the signless concentration, the undirected concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned….”

5. Satipaṭṭhānasuttaṃ

5. The Foundations of Mindfulness

370. “Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe…. Pañcamaṃ.

370. “And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? The four foundations of mindfulness. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned….”

6. Sammappadhānasuttaṃ

6. The Right Exertions

371. “Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Cattāro sammappadhānā. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe…. Chaṭṭhaṃ.

371. “And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? The four right exertions. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned….”

7. Iddhipādasuttaṃ

7. The Bases of Spiritual Power

372. “Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Cattāro iddhipādā. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe…. Sattamaṃ.

372. “And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? The four bases of spiritual power. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned….”

8. Indriyasuttaṃ

8. The Faculties

373. “Katamo [V 2.0336][P 4.0361] ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Pañcindriyāni. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe…. Aṭṭhamaṃ.

373. “And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? The five faculties. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned….”

9. Balasuttaṃ

9. The Powers

374. “Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Pañca balāni. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe…. Navamaṃ.

374. And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? The five powers. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned... and so on... Ninth.

10. Bojjhaṅgasuttaṃ

10. The Discourse on the Factors of Enlightenment

375. “Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Satta bojjhaṅgā. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe…. Dasamaṃ.

375. And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? The seven factors of enlightenment. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned... and so on... Tenth.

11. Maggaṅgasuttaṃ

11. The Discourse on the Path Factors

376. “Katamo [M 2.0537] ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo. Iti kho, bhikkhave[T 4.0443], desitaṃ vo mayā asaṅkhataṃ, desito asaṅkhatagāmimaggo. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, satthārā karaṇīyaṃ sāvakānaṃ hitesinā anukampakena anukampaṃ upādāya kataṃ vo taṃ mayā. Etāni, bhikkhave, rukkhamūlāni, etāni suññāgārāni. Jhāyatha, bhikkhave, mā pamādattha; mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvattha. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanī”ti. Ekādasamaṃ.

376. And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? The Noble Eightfold Path. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned. Thus, bhikkhus, the unconditioned has been taught to you by me, and the path leading to the unconditioned has been taught. Whatever a teacher should do for his disciples, seeking their welfare, out of compassion, that has been done by me for you. These, bhikkhus, are the roots of trees; these are empty dwellings. Meditate, bhikkhus, do not be negligent, lest you regret it afterwards. This is our instruction to you.

Paṭhamo vaggo.

The First Chapter.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Kāyo [V 2.0337] samatho savitakko, suññato satipaṭṭhānā;

Sammappadhānā iddhipādā, indriyabalabojjhaṅgā;

Maggena ekādasamaṃ, tassuddānaṃ pavuccati.

Body, serenity, applied thought, emptiness, the foundations of mindfulness; the right exertions, the bases of spiritual power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment; with the path as the eleventh, its summary is declared.

2. Dutiyavaggo

2. The Second Chapter

1. Asaṅkhatasuttaṃ

1. The Discourse on the Unconditioned

377. “Asaṅkhatañca [T 4.0444][P 4.0362] vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi asaṅkhatagāmiñca maggaṃ. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamañca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhataṃ? Yo, bhikkhave, rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo – idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhataṃ. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Samatho. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo. Iti kho, bhikkhave, desitaṃ vo mayā asaṅkhataṃ, desito asaṅkhatagāmimaggo. Yaṃ, bhikkhave, satthārā karaṇīyaṃ sāvakānaṃ hitesinā anukampakena anukampaṃ upādāya, kataṃ vo taṃ mayā. Etāni, bhikkhave, rukkhamūlāni, etāni suññāgārāni. Jhāyatha, bhikkhave, mā pamādattha; mā pacchā vippaṭisārino ahuvattha. Ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanīti.

377. Bhikkhus, I will teach you the unconditioned and the path leading to the unconditioned. Listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, is the unconditioned? The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion—this, bhikkhus, is called the unconditioned. And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Serenity. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned. Thus, bhikkhus, the unconditioned has been taught to you by me, and the path leading to the unconditioned has been taught. Whatever a teacher should do for his disciples, seeking their welfare, out of compassion, that has been done by me for you. These, bhikkhus, are the roots of trees; these are empty dwellings. Meditate, bhikkhus, do not be negligent, lest you regret it afterwards. This is our instruction to you.

“Asaṅkhatañca [M 2.0538] vo, bhikkhave, desessāmi asaṅkhatagāmiñca maggaṃ. Taṃ suṇātha. Katamañca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhataṃ? Yo, bhikkhave, rāgakkhayo dosakkhayo mohakkhayo – idaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhataṃ. Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Vipassanā. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo. Iti kho, bhikkhave, desitaṃ vo mayā asaṅkhataṃ…pe… ayaṃ vo amhākaṃ anusāsanīti.

Bhikkhus, I will teach you the unconditioned and the path leading to the unconditioned. Listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, is the unconditioned? The destruction of lust, the destruction of hatred, the destruction of delusion—this, bhikkhus, is called the unconditioned. And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Insight. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned. Thus, bhikkhus, the unconditioned has been taught to you by me... and so on... This is our instruction to you.

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Savitakko [P 4.0363] savicāro samādhi. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo [T 4.0445] ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Avitakko [V 2.0338] vicāramatto samādhi. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Avitakko avicāro samādhi. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe….

And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Concentration with initial application and sustained application. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned... and so on... And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Concentration without initial application but with sustained application only. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned... and so on... And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Concentration without initial application and without sustained application. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned... and so on...

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Suññato samādhi. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Animitto samādhi. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Appaṇihito samādhi. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe….

And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Concentration on emptiness. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned... and so on... And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Concentration on the signless. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned... and so on... And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Concentration on the aimless. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned... and so on...

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vedanāsu vedanānupassī viharati…pe… ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo [P 4.0364] ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu citte cittānupassī…pe… ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo [T 4.0446] ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati…pe… ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe….

And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in the world. This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned... and so on... And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... and so on... This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned... and so on... And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the mind in the mind... and so on... This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned... and so on... And what, bhikkhus, is the path leading to the unconditioned? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating dhammas in dhammas... and so on... This, bhikkhus, is called the path leading to the unconditioned... and so on...

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ anuppādā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu uppannānaṃ [M 2.0539] pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pahānā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati [V 2.0339] cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu uppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ ṭhitiyā [P 4.0365] asammosāya bhiyyobhāvāya vepullāya bhāvanāya pāripūriyā chandaṃ janeti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati cittaṃ paggaṇhāti padahati. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe….

And what, monks, is the path leading to the Unconditioned? Here, monks, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states. This, monks, is called the path leading to the Unconditioned… And what, monks, is the path leading to the Unconditioned? Here, monks, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil, unwholesome states. This, monks, is called the path leading to the Unconditioned… And what, monks, is the path leading to the Unconditioned? Here, monks, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. This, monks, is called the path leading to the Unconditioned… And what, monks, is the path leading to the Unconditioned? Here, monks, a monk generates desire, makes an effort, arouses energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the maintenance, for the non-confusion, for the increase, for the abundance, for the development, and for the fulfillment of arisen wholesome states. This, monks, is called the path leading to the Unconditioned…

“Katamo [T 4.0447] ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo …pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vīriyasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cittasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vīmaṃsasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārasamannāgataṃ iddhipādaṃ bhāveti. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe….

And what, monks, is the path leading to the Unconditioned? Here, monks, a monk develops the base of psychic power endowed with concentration based on desire and with formations of striving. This, monks, is called the path leading to the Unconditioned… And what, monks, is the path leading to the Unconditioned? Here, monks, a monk develops the base of psychic power endowed with concentration based on energy and with formations of striving. This, monks, is called the path leading to the Unconditioned… And what, monks, is the path leading to the Unconditioned? Here, monks, a monk develops the base of psychic power endowed with concentration based on mind and with formations of striving. This, monks, is called the path leading to the Unconditioned… And what, monks, is the path leading to the Unconditioned? Here, monks, a monk develops the base of psychic power endowed with concentration based on investigation and with formations of striving. This, monks, is called the path leading to the Unconditioned…

“Katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu saddhindriyaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo [P 4.0366] ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vīriyindriyaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ…pe… ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu satindriyaṃ bhāveti…pe… ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo [T 4.0448] ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu samādhindriyaṃ bhāveti…pe… ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paññindriyaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ virāganissitaṃ [M 2.0540] nirodhanissitaṃ vossaggapariṇāmiṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe….

And what, monks, is the path leading to the Unconditioned? Here, monks, a monk develops the faculty of faith, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment. This, monks, is called the path leading to the Unconditioned… And what, monks, is the path leading to the Unconditioned? Here, monks, a monk develops the faculty of energy, which is based on seclusion… This, monks, is called the path leading to the Unconditioned… And what, monks, is the path leading to the Unconditioned? Here, monks, a monk develops the faculty of mindfulness… This, monks, is called the path leading to the Unconditioned… And what, monks, is the path leading to the Unconditioned? Here, monks, a monk develops the faculty of concentration… This, monks, is called the path leading to the Unconditioned… And what, monks, is the path leading to the Unconditioned? Here, monks, a monk develops the faculty of wisdom, which is based on seclusion, based on dispassion, based on cessation, and resulting in relinquishment. This, monks, is called the path leading to the Unconditioned…

“Katamo [V 2.0340] ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu saddhābalaṃ bhāveti vivekanissitaṃ…pe… ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vīriyabalaṃ bhāveti…pe… ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu satibalaṃ bhāveti…pe… ayaṃ vuccati, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo…pe… katamo [P 4.0367] ca, bhikkhave, asaṅkhatagāmimaggo?
